title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Sihang Li,Xiaofeng Guo,Jinkun Cao,Charlie Cheng,Ruihan Yang,Chen Feng,Guanya Shi,Haozhi Qi
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: Many everyday tasks require controlling contact force as well as motion. On a humanoid, this force must often be coordinated across both hands and the whole body, and cannot be specified by kinematic trajectories alone. Therefore, we present FLoRe, a framework for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation. We collect robot-free demonstrations using two force-sensing UMI-style handheld grippers for hand motion and contact wrenches, and wearable trackers for body motion. A force-reactive diffusion policy takes vision, proprioception, and measured wrenches as input, then predicts actions and per-hand force commands. A hybrid compliance whole-body controller with force tracking executes these commands while maintaining balance: an integral of the force error measured by real force/torque (F/T) sensors lets each hand track force accurately along the commanded direction and remain compliant along the others. In simulation, the controller tracks per-hand force commands of varied magnitude and direction, with little loss in whole-body motion accuracy. Across three contact-rich tasks on the robot, the force-reactive policy succeeds in 80% of rollouts, compared with 26.7% for a position-only policy trained on the same demonstrations and executed by the same controller. For more details, please visit our website: https://louis-leee.github.io/FLoRe/.
introduction:
Humanoid robots offer a general-purpose embodiment for working in environments built for people. Many tasks in these environments, such as pushing a cart, moving a heavy box, and wiping a surface, require the robot to control contact force as well as motion. However, learned humanoid loco-manipulation is commonly formulated as generating and tracking motion references [1, 2, 3]. Tracking a demonstrated hand trajectory alone does not reproduce the demonstrated force, which also depends on contact geometry, stiffness, and object motion. Unlike a fixed-base arm, a humanoid must stay balanced under these contact loads, coordinating its hands, torso, and legs while regulating force.

Two difficulties stand in the way. The first is data: imitation learning requires scalable demonstrations that record contact force alongside motion. Existing robot-free interfaces for whole-body demonstration collection record motion but not force [4, 5].
The second is execution: the robot must accurately apply the desired force. Current learned humanoid whole-body controllers track motion alone, or treat force as a disturbance to reject or a stiffness to lower [6, 7]. Tracking a commanded contact force has been shown only on quadrupedal manipulators, using estimated rather than measured force [8, 9], which is not accurate enough. A humanoid instead needs to track force at both hands together with whole-body motion while maintaining balance.

We present FLoRe, a framework for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation. Its robot-free force-annotated data collection system records contact force with each demonstration; the policy learns to predict this force, and the controller tracks it. The system pairs two UMI-style handheld grippers [10] with a chest tracker and two ankle trackers [4, 11]. Each gripper carries a wrist camera, a pose tracker, and a six-axis F/T sensor [12, 13]. The applied wrench is thus recorded alongside hand, torso, and foot motion. The robot uses the same gripper–sensor assembly.

For the high-level planner, we propose a force-reactive diffusion policy [14]. It observes wrist images, robot state, and the measured wrench at each hand, then predicts a chunk [15] of action, gripper widths, and per-hand desired force. Force enters as both an input and an output. The input lets the policy react to interactions that images do not reveal. The output is commanded to the controller [13], rather than used only as an auxiliary target [16]. This connects the force measured during demonstration to the deployed force.

To track the commanded forces, we develop a whole-body controller with hybrid compliance. It outputs only joint positions, so each hand’s force command becomes a shift of its position target. In contact, an integral of the force error measured at the wrist adjusts this shift until the hand exerts the commanded force, whatever the contact stiffness. Along uncommanded axes, the same integral lets the hand yield to external pushes. Each hand thus tracks force along the commanded direction and complies along the others, without switching modes. We train the controller in simulation [17] and deploy it on the robot using wrist F/T measurements.

We deploy FLoRe on a Unitree G1 and evaluate three whole-body contact-rich tasks: pushing a gantry hanging another robot, bimanual box rotation, and board wiping. In simulation, the controller realises in-contact force error of about 1 N per hand while tracking whole-body motion. On the real robot, FLoRe succeeds in 80% of rollouts, compared with 26.7% for a position-only policy trained on the same demonstrations and executed by the same controller with force commands disabled. Withholding only the force command reduces success to 36.7%, while removing only the force observation reduces it to 66.7%. Both contribute to the final performance.
Our key contributions are:

A robot-free pipeline for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation from demonstrations that record both motion and contact wrench.

A learned whole-body controller that tracks per-hand force together with keypoint motion while remaining compliant to external forces and maintaining balance.

Evaluation in simulation and on three contact-rich tasks on a Unitree G1, where force commands and force observations both improve task success over position-only control.

1. A robot-free pipeline for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation from demonstrations that record both motion and contact wrench.

2. A learned whole-body controller that tracks per-hand force together with keypoint motion while remaining compliant to external forces and maintaining balance.

3. Evaluation in simulation and on three contact-rich tasks on a Unitree G1, where force commands and force observations both improve task success over position-only control.

title: Differentiable Contact Dynamics for Legged Locomotion: Policy Learning and Contact-Implicit Trajectory Optimization
authors: Gijeong Kim,Seungbin Oh,Dongyun Kang,Hae-Won Park
comment: Submitted to Transactions on Robotics
abstract:
This paper proposes a smooth analytic gradient for frictional contact and applies it to
policy learning and contact-implicit trajectory optimization for legged
locomotion. The exact contact sensitivity is available in closed form but describes changes within the current contact mode, providing no first-order information toward neighboring contact modes.
The proposed gradient replaces
this sensitivity only in the backward pass, leaving the hard-contact forward
solve unchanged and the realized rollout feasible. A central-path relaxation of the
de Saxcé-corrected second-order-cone complementarity problem for Coulomb
friction smooths the conditions defining the separating, clamping, and sliding
modes. The relaxed sensitivity is evaluated at a point on the central path
obtained by a Newton iteration initialized from the hard-contact solution. The
sensitivity remains continuous through contact-mode transitions and converges
to the exact sensitivity as the relaxation vanishes. Using 100,000 samples and
less than 2 min of training on a desktop PC, policy learning with the proposed
gradient produces a policy that transfers to hardware without
fine-tuning. On hardware, the robot under a trotting policy withstands pushes and traverses debris and
slippery ground. In trajectory optimization, the proposed gradient reaches contact-rich solutions missed by exact and Signorini-relaxed gradients. Project page: https://diffcontact.github.io
introduction:
The first-order gradient through contact in a differentiable
physics simulator provides a common computational primitive for two classes of
methods in contact-rich robot control. The first is policy learning, in which model-free
reinforcement learning is widely used and policy-gradient estimates are
computed from rollouts across thousands of parallel
environments [1, 2, 3]. First-order policy
learning [4, 5] preserves the same objective
but replaces the score-function (REINFORCE)
estimate [6, 7] with a typically lower-variance
first-order estimate [8]. This estimate can be obtained by differentiating through the simulator, with comparable policies learned from fewer samples [9].
The second is trajectory optimization. Contact-implicit trajectory
optimization (CITO) methods determine when and where contacts are made and
broken without a prescribed contact-mode
sequence [10, 11, 12]. Shooting-based DDP/iLQR
methods [13, 14] use the same transition
Jacobians as the policy-learning estimator and have been applied online in
receding-horizon control for contact-rich locomotion [15].

For legged robots, both tools are limited by the contact sensitivity provided
by differentiable simulation. A simulator may be differentiable without
providing a useful first-order direction toward a neighboring contact
mode [16, 17]. The exact contact sensitivity is available in
closed form [18, 19], but it is evaluated with the active
set, or contact-mode assignment, held fixed and therefore describes only the
response within the current mode. A clamped contact is linearized as remaining
clamped, providing no first-order information toward liftoff or slip, and the
sensitivity changes discontinuously when the active set changes. In
contact-implicit optimization, this mode-restricted sensitivity keeps the local
search near the contact sequence of the nominal
trajectory [15, 18, 20]. In first-order policy learning, the same
Jacobians enter backpropagation through time (BPTT), where they can produce
fragile or ineffective optimization in contact-rich
systems [16, 17, 21, 22].

Prior work addresses contact sensitivity in policy learning and CITO in different ways. In policy learning, methods shorten the differentiation horizon [9, 22], use a reduced-order model for the backward pass [23], or smooth contact in the forward rollout [24]. Shorter horizons can help with long-horizon gradient instability, but do not change the contact sensitivity within each window. In CITO, transcription methods optimize contact impulses alongside the trajectory [11, 12, 25], whereas shooting methods rely on transition Jacobians from the contact dynamics [13, 14, 15]. Other approaches smooth the forward contact model [26, 20], differentiate relaxed contact solutions [27, 28], or estimate gradients across perturbed solves [29, 30]. For shooting-based CITO with a hard-contact forward solve, however, the exact contact sensitivity remains tied to the current contact mode and offers limited first-order guidance toward a different mode [18]. Relaxing only the Signorini condition during differentiation [15] partly addresses this limitation by providing directions for contact make/break transitions, but leaves sliding and normal–tangential coupling unaddressed.

We therefore propose a contact sensitivity obtained by relaxing the full frictional contact condition only in the backward pass, providing search directions toward neighboring contact modes while retaining the hard-contact forward solve. The de Saxcé correction expresses frictional contact as a single second-order-cone complementarity condition [31, 32]. Relaxing this condition along a central path [33] couples normal and tangential contact sensitivities across separation, clamping, and sliding. These coupled sensitivities are available in every contact mode, allowing the optimizer to change modes through gradient-based updates. We further investigate their role in guiding transitions to sliding, where a normal-only relaxation lacks the required tangential information.

We test the effect of this sensitivity in two optimal-control settings using a quadruped robot: first-order policy learning and contact-implicit trajectory optimization. In each setting, we compare the exact [19], Signorini-relaxed [15], and proposed sensitivities while keeping the forward contact model, objective, and initialization fixed. The policy-learning experiments ask whether single-environment BPTT can produce locomotion policies that transfer directly to hardware. The trajectory-optimization experiments ask whether the proposed sensitivity improves contact-rich motion generation and recovery from unmodeled external pulls by enabling contact-mode changes and foot repositioning.

The main contributions are:

An analytic backward contact sensitivity that relaxes the complete de Saxcé-corrected frictional contact law along its central path while retaining the hard-contact forward solve. It provides first-order directions toward separation, sliding, and clamping in every contact mode and recovers the exact sensitivity as the relaxation vanishes.

The proposed gradient in BPTT-based first-order policy learning and contact-implicit trajectory optimization guides contact-mode changes and yields improved policies and lower-cost contact-rich trajectories.

Hardware demonstration of quadruped policy learning with the proposed
gradient for trotting, pacing, and gait-free locomotion. Trotting policies obtained
using 100,000 samples in under 2 min are tested on hardware
without fine-tuning under pushes, debris, and low-friction surfaces.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows.
Section II reviews related work and Section III the
optimal control and contact dynamics background. Section IV
states the required contact sensitivity, Section 2 derives the
proposed gradient, and Section VI the implementation details.
Sections VII and VIII present the policy-learning and
trajectory-optimization demonstrations, and Section IX
concludes.

1. An analytic backward contact sensitivity that relaxes the complete de Saxcé-corrected frictional contact law along its central path while retaining the hard-contact forward solve. It provides first-order directions toward separation, sliding, and clamping in every contact mode and recovers the exact sensitivity as the relaxation vanishes.

2. The proposed gradient in BPTT-based first-order policy learning and contact-implicit trajectory optimization guides contact-mode changes and yields improved policies and lower-cost contact-rich trajectories.

3. Hardware demonstration of quadruped policy learning with the proposed
gradient for trotting, pacing, and gait-free locomotion. Trotting policies obtained
using 100,000 samples in under 2 min are tested on hardware
without fine-tuning under pushes, debris, and low-friction surfaces.

title: Profiling a Frontier Agent with EBench: From Direct Control to Harness with Policy
authors: Yifei Yao,Yude Zou,Guanbo Jiao,Xing Gao,Ning Gao,Yukai Wang,Jiantong Chen,Zihou Zhu,Xinyu Li,Ningyu Yan,Shuai Wang,Jianming Ma,Haoyu Guo,Weinan Zhang,Chunhua Shen
comment: Project page:this https URL
abstract: Frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can control robots without robot-specific training, but how their capabilities compare and interact with post-trained vision-language-action (VLA) and world action model (WAM) policies across manipulation demands remains to be thoroughly evaluated. In this report, we evaluate GPT-6-Astra on EBench as the core of an agent that controls a robot through an agent harness under the same visual and proprioceptive observation protocol as post-trained policies. We study two agent configurations: direct control, in which the agent generates waypoint commands directly, and harness with policy, in which it can also invoke a post-trained VLA or WAM policy for action execution. Under direct control, the agent achieves competitive overall performance relative to post-trained policies. It leads on short-horizon tasks and exhibits the least performance variation across generalization dimensions, whereas it underperforms post-trained policies on long-horizon tasks, tabletop manipulation, and high-precision contact-rich tasks. In the harness with policy, invoking a post-trained VLA or WAM combines the complementary strengths of both components, raising overall task success to the level of the strongest compared post-trained policies while substantially reducing token cost. However, performance remains below the per-task upper bound of the standalone components due to suboptimal policy invocation, fixed-instruction execution without subgoals, and grasp disruption when the agent resumes control. Overall, our study characterizes the capability boundary of a frontier MLLM agent and suggests directions for improving future agent harness design. Project page: https://internrobotics.github.io/EBench-Astra-Tech-Report/.
introduction:
Transferring knowledge from large pretrained models to robotics has become a primary approach to general-purpose robot control (Firoozi et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2026b; Shen et al., 2026). Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt vision-language backbones for end-to-end visuomotor control (Kim et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025b; Black et al., 2025a; Ma et al., 2026a; GigaBrain Team et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026a), whereas world action models (WAMs) jointly model future visual dynamics and actions to utilize the physical and temporal priors of video generative models (Ye et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Yuan et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026b; Cai et al., 2026a). Both approaches rely on post-training with robot manipulation trajectories: although effective within their training distributions, their generalization is bounded by the scale and diversity of collected robot data. By contrast, frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) acquire stronger emergent capabilities from massive-scale pretraining data, and this training scale remains costly to replicate with embodied data alone.

Without robot-specific post-training, frontier MLLMs provide an alternative approach through their spatial understanding and embodied reasoning capabilities (Zhang et al., 2026a; Rao, 2026). GPT-6-Astra (OpenAI, 2026), for example, can generate end-effector (EEF) commands directly from camera observations and language instructions (Zhang et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026; Jia et al., 2026; Lou et al., 2026). Combined with an agent harness that supplies its prompt, observation interface, and tools, the model serves as the core of an agent that controls the robot in closed loop, as formalized in Section 3. Beyond direct control, recent studies explore a harness with policy in which the agent invokes a post-trained policy for action execution (Zhang et al., 2026b; Xu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a). Such a harness combines the agent’s task planning, progress monitoring, and error recovery with the closed-loop visuomotor control that the policy learns from robot demonstrations.

Although prior studies have evaluated both direct control and a harness with policy, they have not comprehensively profiled these agent configurations against post-trained VLA and WAM policies across diverse manipulation demands. Specifically, two central questions remain to be addressed. First, under direct control, on which tasks does the agent outperform post-trained VLAs and WAMs, where does it fall short, and what limits its performance? Second, in a harness-with-policy setting, how does invoking a post-trained policy complement the agent’s direct control, which limitations of direct control can it alleviate, and what new failure modes arise when the agent invokes a policy for execution and subsequently resumes decision-making?

To further explore these questions, we evaluate GPT-6-Astra as the core of an agent on EBench (Gao et al., 2026). This diagnostic manipulation benchmark categorizes tasks by mobility, manipulation precision, and task horizon and evaluates robustness along the generalization dimensions of unseen objects, unseen backgrounds, paraphrased instructions, and their mixture. For a fair comparison, the agent operates under the same observation protocol as post-trained policies, receiving only RGB camera images and proprioceptive robot states without depth, camera calibration, or simulator ground truth. For each task, the agent receives a task description annotated by GPT-6-Astra from a single training episode as single-shot in-context learning (ICL). Across all 510 test episodes, we evaluate both direct control and a harness with policy invoking either the VLA π0.5\pi_{0.5} or the WAM InternW0-Δ\Delta, compare each configuration against the post-trained policies on the EBench leaderboard, and analyze execution trajectories across paired episodes.

Under direct control, the GPT-6-Astra-based agent achieves a 46.7% overall success rate and a 0.654 stage-completion score, outperforming post-trained policies such as Qwen-RobotManip and π0.5\pi_{0.5} trained on 6,600 in-domain demonstrations. Among the compared post-trained policies, the agent ranks first on short-horizon tasks with a 73.2% success rate, shows the smallest success-rate variation across the four generalization dimensions, and completes a novel composite instruction zero-shot on which both compared post-trained policies fail. Conversely, its success rate drops to 27.3% on long-horizon tasks, 20.0% on tabletop manipulation, and 11.3% on high-precision contact-rich tasks. Trajectory analysis shows that while the agent performs well at visual grounding and in-episode error recovery, its physical execution is limited by long action chunks between observations and by contact geometry that it must infer explicitly from RGB views.

Invoking a post-trained policy through the agent harness increases the overall success rate to 53.0% with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 56.0% with InternW0-Δ\Delta and reduces the agent’s token cost per success by more than half. With InternW0-Δ\Delta, the harness surpasses all post-trained policies compared in Table 1. The harness with policy retains the agent’s high success rate on short-horizon tasks and improves performance on long-horizon and bimanual tasks where the post-trained policy is competent. At the same time, case analysis identifies two limitations of the current harness with policy. First, neither component resolves high-precision contact-rich manipulation. Second, agent and policy coordinate loosely in three respects: the agent invokes the policy for most execution steps even on tasks where that policy alone rarely succeeds, the policy follows the fixed task instruction instead of the agent’s subgoal, and the agent often leaves a held grasp unmaintained when it resumes control after a policy invocation, which makes object drops more frequent.

The main contributions of this report are as follows:

Paired evaluation across agent configurations and post-trained policies. Under the same observation protocol as post-trained policies, we evaluate an GPT-6-Astra-based agent under direct control and in a harness with policy across all 510 EBench test episodes. We compare both agent configurations against standalone post-trained VLA and WAM policies across all task groups and generalization dimensions.

Characterization of agent capabilities under direct control. We locate where the GPT-6-Astra-based agent leads or trails eight post-trained policies while using only a single annotated task demonstration and no parameter updates, trace its unsuccessful episodes to their failure mechanisms, and examine its in-episode adaptation, the safety of its execution, and its zero-shot composition of skills on a novel instruction. Together, these analyses show where the agent and the policies complement each other.

Analysis of harness with policy and implications for agent harness design. We evaluate the harness with either policy against each of its components on every task, trace the episodes that newly fail under the harness and those that fail with both policies to their decisive incidents, and analyze the agent’s policy invocation and the resulting token cost. These analyses locate the remaining gap to the better component in policy invocation, subgoal passing, and grasp maintenance when the agent resumes control, which informs the design of future agent harnesses.

1. Paired evaluation across agent configurations and post-trained policies. Under the same observation protocol as post-trained policies, we evaluate an GPT-6-Astra-based agent under direct control and in a harness with policy across all 510 EBench test episodes. We compare both agent configurations against standalone post-trained VLA and WAM policies across all task groups and generalization dimensions.

2. Characterization of agent capabilities under direct control. We locate where the GPT-6-Astra-based agent leads or trails eight post-trained policies while using only a single annotated task demonstration and no parameter updates, trace its unsuccessful episodes to their failure mechanisms, and examine its in-episode adaptation, the safety of its execution, and its zero-shot composition of skills on a novel instruction. Together, these analyses show where the agent and the policies complement each other.

3. Analysis of harness with policy and implications for agent harness design. We evaluate the harness with either policy against each of its components on every task, trace the episodes that newly fail under the harness and those that fail with both policies to their decisive incidents, and analyze the agent’s policy invocation and the resulting token cost. These analyses locate the remaining gap to the better component in policy invocation, subgoal passing, and grasp maintenance when the agent resumes control, which informs the design of future agent harnesses.

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
authors: Benjamin Pikus,Daniel Saunders,Mircea Mironenco,Salman Mohammadi,Mathew Mathew,Sirou Zhu,Divya Makkar,Xuhua Huang,Qinbo Li,Supreeth Narasimhaswamy,Siyuan Cen,Thomas Neff,Dejia Xu,Shyamal Buch
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract:
A robot policy needs to understand what a task is asking for in a scene, and how to move the robot to accomplish that task.
To achieve these two skills, we introduce Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP), a recipe that teaches a small off-the-shelf vision-language model to control a robot via a simple tool harness.
We use a pretrained 27B parameter model to bootstrap world understanding and reasoning, followed by supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on simple simulated tasks to teach it how to move the robot.
Without any real-world robot data during training, ZAP reaches 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra in our harness and outperforming the MolmoAct2 VLA (33.3%), while running 3×\times faster and 17×\times cheaper than GPT-6 Astra.
We demonstrate that ZAP also generalizes to completely new objects, goals, strategies, and language by seating a test tube in a rack (and choosing a different hole in the rack when prompted), handing a test tube between arms mid-air, drawing an X on a tic-tac-toe board, and playing chess.
These goals and types of manipulation don’t appear in our training data.
Furthermore, ZAP also transfers to an unseen embodiment.
On a single-arm Franka, ZAP reaches 55.9% on RoboLab-120, 4.9 percentage points ahead of the leading VLA/WAM baseline.
introduction:
A robot policy has to do two difficult things at once: it needs semantic reasoning to understand instructions in a potentially unfamiliar scene, and motion control to translate that understanding into precise physical actions.

We introduce Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP), which adds motion to a small pretrained vision-language model through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), entirely in simulation.
We evaluate how these skills carry over to new tasks, real hardware, and a new embodiment.
Existing methods tend to trade off performance in one of these areas for the others, and broadly fall into three groups (Table 1).

Models that directly output robot actions. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs) learn semantic reasoning & motion control from robot action data [1, 2, 3, 4]. Because diverse action data is scarce, both skills end up tied to the training distribution: the policy often generalizes poorly to new prompts, objects, scenes and goals, and a new task usually means training again.

Code that directly drives the robot. In Code as Policies [5, 6], a language model writes a program that composes perception and control APIs.
This is quick and reliable when the situations it will face can be anticipated when the program is written, but struggles outside that script, for example with an unexpected failure, an unfamiliar object or an ambiguous instruction. Adapting to a new task or scene means rewriting the program.

Large frontier models controlling the robot through tools. Frontier language models interacting with the robot via an agentic harness bring world understanding, reasoning and generalization  [7, 8, 9]. But they are not explicitly trained to move a robot, and a trillion-parameter model is slow and costs dollars for a task that smaller policy models, when they can do them, do in seconds and cost pennies.

ZAP combines semantic reasoning from vision-language pretraining with motion control learned entirely in simulation. We start with Qwen 3.6 27B [10], which contributes world understanding and reasoning. We then teach the model motion control in simulation - first SFT on its own mined successful traces, followed by RL across 40 pick-and-place, stacking, and reorientation tasks. Neither stage uses real-world robot demonstrations. At test time, the policy combines pretrained semantic reasoning with learned motion control to perform real-world tasks it was never trained to execute, generalizing to new objects, goals, and robot embodiments.

Our contributions are as follows:

Teacher-free training of an agent policy in simulation. We teach a pretrained vision-language model to control a robot with no frontier teacher and no real robot data. The model commands end-effector poses and gripper openings through a harness that is identical in simulation and on hardware. We seed it with successful traces mined from its own rollouts, then refine it with RL using a dense reward ladder that credits partial progress (§3).

Transfer to hardware and new embodiment. With no real-world robot training data, ZAP matches GPT-6 Astra on 10 real tasks at 3×\times the speed and 1/17 the cost. The same checkpoint transfers without retraining to a completely new embodiment (single-arm Franka) exceeding the performance of leading VLA/WAM baselines on RoboLab-120 (§4).

Generalization to new goals, language, and reasoning. ZAP combines pretrained semantic reasoning with learned motion control to execute real-world tasks unseen during robot training. The policy handles new objects and goals, follows instructions for manipulation strategies it never practiced, and applies complex reasoning to tasks such as chess and drawing (§5).

title: SPECOLA: A Tool for Specification Driven Robot Evaluation
authors: Immanuel Ampomah Mensah,Hadas Kress-Gazit
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Formal Languages and Automata Theory (cs.FL)
abstract: Simulation benchmarks are a useful way to measure progress in robotics; typically they provide success rate as the dominant measure of performance. However, success rate reports only whether a rollout completed the task, hiding by what margin it succeeded, how sensitive the success is to goal parameter changes, requirements it may have violated, and whether success persisted. Signal Temporal Logic (STL) provides a formal language for capturing specifications; it can be used to define requirements, and measure how close a robot behavior is to satisfying or violating them. Using STL monitors in a simulator, however, requires exposing simulator state and mapping it to specification-relevant signals. We present Specola, a tool for evaluating robot behaviors in simulation with respect to STL specifications. Specola provides an interface for writing specifications over simulator signals, and creates and manages the relevant monitors while a policy executes. We provide a Python API and command-line interface for integrating monitoring into existing policy execution loops. We provide an adapter interface for connecting new simulators, and provide adapters for nine simulation environments and benchmarks, including LIBERO, RoboCasa, Isaac Lab, and RoboDojo. We provide case studies that illustrate the nuanced evaluation that Specola enables. Code and adapters are available at github.com/specola-eval/specola.
introduction:
The recent rapid advances in generative AI, foundation models, and agentic AI, result in a fast iteration cycle for robot policies that leverage these technologies to create robots capable of complex tasks. An enabler for rapid progress in robot learning, and robotics more generally, is the use of simulations and simulation benchmarks [1, 2, 3].

The most common metric used in the community to assess progress and relative performance of robot policies is through the use of success rate–the percentage of robot executions or rollouts that result in task success, as determined by the benchmark. While
success rate is useful for comparing outcomes, it reduces our understanding of how a policy performs. Two unsuccessful rollouts may differ in how close they come to satisfying the task or in which parts of it they complete, and a successful rollout might be on the cusp of failing. Furthermore, even the division between success and failure depends on thresholds defined by a benchmark, for example how close an object is to a target pose; policies successfully executing a task in different ways may exhibit different success rates, since success depends on the chosen threshold, thus providing a misleading signal to the community regarding progress in the field.

Signal Temporal Logic (STL)[4], is a formal specification language that provides a rigorous foundation for expressing requirements over continuous signals–here robot and environment state. In addition to Boolean semantics (True/False), it admits a qualitative semantics; it can be used to calculate, for a given rollout, a signed robustness score that indicates not only if the specification holds, but how close the rollout is to satisfying or violating the specification.

Tracking a rollout’s robustness score with respect to a specification is done through STL monitors. These monitors use continuous signals and an STL formula to produce the score. To run an STL monitor in simulation requires exposing the simulator state (robot and environment state) and mapping it to the formula-relevant signals.

Contributions: We present Specola, a tool for evaluating robot behavior in simulation using STL specifications and monitors it automatically creates and deploys to track the robustness score. Specola (i) automatically detects all the signals that can be monitored, (ii) includes a specification writing interface that facilitates writing specifications, (iii) provides a Python API and command-line interface that integrate monitoring into existing policy execution loops and report robustness scores during a rollout, and (iv) in order to make Specola interface with any simulator, we have designed an adapter interface. We provide adapters for RoboCasa [3], LIBERO [2], Meta-World [1], dm_control [5], MA-MuJoCo [6], PyBullet [7], Isaac Lab [8], RoboDojo [9], and CARLA [10]. We also provide instructions on how to write an adapter for other simulators. In the following we show case studies for the insight Specola can provide regarding policy performance.

title: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains
authors: Elias Hofele,Thomas Trapp,David Timmermann,Tristan Schnell,Georg Heppner,Arne Roennau
comment: To be published in the proceedings of the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Biomimetics (ROBIO)
abstract:
Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown impressive capabilities in high-level reasoning and task planning for robots.
However, specialized domains remain a challenge for VLMs’ image interpretation and grounding abilities.
We introduce TrySee, a modular closed-loop robot task planning pipeline integrating general-purpose VLM reasoning with domain-specific perception and established robotics components.
The system consists of an inherently reactive cyclic planning pipeline, augmented with domain-specific modular vision preprocessing, to provide online grounding.
Finally, a dynamic preprocessing selection mechanism contributes to the scalability of the pipeline.
The system requires neither VLM fine-tuning nor end-to-end demonstrations and adapts through replaceable perception modules and motion planning.
The approach is evaluated on planning tasks across 5 widely different domains, including a real-world robot disassembly task.
The field tests in a brownfield environment demonstrate the approach’s practicality in integrating VLM planning into specialized robotic systems with limited domain-specific training data.
introduction:
The idea of controlling robots with natural language has long been a staple of science fiction.
However, accomplishing even simple tasks, such as “Clean up the table.”, requires a complex understanding of the world and the robot’s capabilities, as well as drawing on many of the core challenges in robotics, such as perception, manipulation, and planning.

With the recent advances in Vision Language Models (VLMs) [1] [2], significant progress has been made in enabling robot reasoning and planning by leveraging vast amounts of real-world knowledge [3] [4].
While VLM-based systems have produced impressive results for tasks in everyday environments (such as offices or homes), they still struggle in more specialized domains, including industrial and scientific applications [5] [6].
This is attributable to these domains being underrepresented in the VLMs’ training data.
The resulting performance gap is a barrier to the more widespread adoption of VLMs in these fields, in which data collection and annotation is often particularly expensive and time-consuming.

A fundamental requirement for VLMs to generate effective robot task plans is the ability to ground their language understanding in the robot’s perception and action capabilities.
In other words, the objects and features comprising the robot’s environment must be linked to the semantics used in the given task, and these, in turn, must be linked to the concrete movements and poses necessary to interact with them.
General-purpose VLMs often fail at the first step for recondite objects, and their image-level outputs alone do not provide sufficiently reliable geometric targets for robot execution.
A practical planning system therefore requires explicit interfaces connecting domain-specific perception, VLM-level semantics, and the robot’s action capabilities.

In this work, we tackle the challenge of VLM grounding in specialized domains by presenting a modular pipeline for VLM-based robot task planning.
Rather than fine-tuning the model or replacing the entire existing robot software stack, TrySee compensates the general-purpose VLM’s limitations in object recognition and robot pose generation by connecting its reasoning abilities with replaceable domain-specific perception modules and established motion-planning components.
This allows the pipeline to be adaptable to different domains and tasks, through targeted perception models without requiring end-to-end robot demonstrations.

In TrySee, the VLM incrementally generates and verifies short-horizon action sequences, while the perception modules provide semantic object labels, visual masks, and executable target poses.
This provides online grounding that is continuously updated as the environment changes.
For object-dense environments, the VLM can request preprocessing only for the information relevant to the current verification step.

Our approach enables the VLM to generate task plans for a variety of domains.
We evaluate the pipeline using tasks across 5 vastly different domains (see Fig. 1), including e-waste recycling, a workshop environment, and an agricultural setting.
The focus is on complex, multi-step tasks.
In order to underline the real-world applicability of our approach, we also implement the pipeline on a real robot and evaluate it in an industrial recycling environment.

title: FISRF: Flexible Instructional Scaffolding Reflection Framework for Robotics Task Planning with Large Language Model
authors: Qingmiao Liang,Jiatao Zhang,Runxin Zou,Yufan Song,Wei Song,Yuhua Zheng
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely adopted for reflective error correction in task planning; however, existing approaches primarily rely on autonomous exploration, rendering them prone to accumulating erroneous experiences during early interactions with new environments. To address this limitation, we propose the Flexible Instructional Scaffolding Reflection Framework (FISRF), an agent–mentor architecture that estimates the robot’s Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) in task planning and adaptively selects reflection strategies and mentor guidance, thereby facilitating the accumulation of effective error-correction experience. Experiments in ALFWorld and on real-world robotic platforms demonstrate that FISRF reduces the average number of error-correction rounds by 37% and redundant reasoning by 25.1%, while improving the overall task success rate by 8%. Project webpage : https://fisrfplanning.github.io/
introduction:
Recent advances in robot task planning increasingly leverage large language models (LLMs) to generate coherent multi-step plans [1, 2]. Despite strong performance on complex tasks, LLM-based planners remain susceptible to hallucinations and logical inconsistencies [3]. To alleviate these limitations, reflection
. RETROFORMER [4] and Reflexion [5] extend the ReAct [6] framework by incorporating reflective feedback through textual gradients. Another research line [7, 8, 9] integrates tree-search strategies with reflection loops to support more deliberate exploration. More recent systems, such as Expel [10] and AutoManual [11], construct environment-specific rule libraries that enable structured retrospective error analysis. Furthermore, FCRF [12] and Thinkless [13] quantify task complexity to adaptively adjust reflection intensity (see Figure 1), thereby transforming reflection from a fixed procedure into a flexible mechanism.

Most existing reflection methods rely on robots operating autonomously under predefined reflection procedures, enabling effective experience accumulation in familiar or structured tasks. However, when robots enter new environments, they often lack effective experience to handle unfamiliar problems and may be unable to correct seemingly simple errors. These early-stage errors can accumulate, leading to numerous ineffective attempts and resulting in reduced efficiency and degraded performance.(Figure 1) We therefore ask: How can robots rapidly accumulate effective experience in new environments while maintaining a certain degree of autonomy?

To address these limitations, we build on the theory of Instructional Scaffolding from educational psychology [14]. This theory suggests that a learner’s problem-solving ability improves most effectively when guidance is provided within their Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD)—the gap between what can be accomplished independently and what can be achieved with appropriate guidance. When persistent obstacles arise during independent exploration, targeted instruction that addresses core difficulties facilitates knowledge internalization and transfer, enabling more robust mastery of complex skills.

This raises a key challenge:
the lack of a quantitative and operational formulation of the robot’s Zone of Proximal Development in task planning. Addressing this problem requires formalizing and automating the dynamic guidance mechanisms traditionally provided by human teachers. Specifically, the robot’s task performance must be quantitatively and adaptively modeled to establish a capability baseline and delineate its developmental boundaries. Based on this baseline, appropriate guidance strategies should be automatically generated. Moreover, the framework must progressively withdraw external support and consolidate assisted experience into autonomous, generalizable competence, thereby forming a closed loop from guided learning to independent execution.

Motivated by the aforementioned challenge, we propose the Flexible Scaffolding Reflection Framework (FISRF), an online approach that provides adaptive guidance to large language models based on task performance. FISRF is grounded in instructional scaffolding theory and adopts an agent–mentor architecture. The Agent module consists of three components: 1) an Actor LLM that generates action sequences; 2) an Evaluator LLM that determines ZPD entry by dynamically modeling two ZPD factors: difficulty of correction (D​CDC) and magnitude of improvement (M​IMI); and 3) Self-Reflection LLMs that perform experience summarization and lesson extraction.
The Mentor module is implemented as a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) component with a structured knowledge base. It retrieves task-relevant context and generates state-conditioned guidance grounded in the agent’s reflective feedback. After task execution, the agent evaluates its performance to determine ZPD entry. If the condition is satisfied, it requests mentor guidance and integrates the retrieved guidance with self-reflection for subsequent planning, thereby reducing redundant trials and enabling efficient, adaptive experience accumulation.

To assess the effectiveness of the proposed framework, we conduct experiments on the ALFWorld [15] household planning benchmark. The tasks in the dataset are systematically organized into six categories based on their operational characteristics. Empirical results indicate that our approach attains superior performance across all task types.
In summary, our contributions are fourfold:

We propose FISRF, an adaptive agent–mentor reflection framework that balances autonomous exploration and external guidance.

We operationalize the ZPD for robotic task planning using difficulty of correction and magnitude of improvement, enabling dynamic selection of reflection strategies.

We validate FISRF in ALFWorld and real-world robotic tasks, demonstrating improved task success, correction efficiency, and reflection flexibility.

title: Continuous-Time Safe Planning and Control for Agile Quadrupeds
authors: Gage MacLin,Mason Peterson,Camilla Tabasso,Venanzio Cichella,Joshua Migdal,Tye Brady,Taskin Padir
abstract: Agile quadruped navigation in dynamic environments demands trajectories that are both dynamically feasible and provably collision-free. Most real-time planners achieve tractability through a convex reduction that requires simplified kinematic models, discarding motion that the robot can readily execute, and certify safety only at discretization points, leaving open possible inter-sample collisions with moving obstacles. We present a real-time motion planning framework that retains the fully-actuated S​E​(2)SE(2) model of a quadruped, with its anisotropic, heading-coupled velocity bounds, and accepts the resulting nonconvexity. By parameterizing trajectories as composite Bernstein polynomials, we exploit the convex hull property to certify collision avoidance and the input bounds over the entirety of each planning horizon. Solved at online replanning rates, the optimization runs in closed loop, commanding body velocities to the locomotion controller. We validate the approach in simulation against ablations and external baselines, and in hardware experiments on a quadruped navigating among unknown moving obstacles, recovering both lateral and heading-coupled motion that simplified models exclude.
introduction:
Quadrupedal robots are transitioning from demonstration platforms to working tools on construction sites, in warehouses, and in other spaces shared with people, vehicles, and machines. Advances in model predictive control (MPC) and whole-body control have enabled dynamic gaits, omnidirectional locomotion, and traversal of unstructured terrain [1, 2]. In particular, quadrupeds admit a rich set of motion primitives, including lateral translation and heading-dependent velocity limits, i.e., distinct bounds on longitudinal and lateral body velocities. Yet, to remain computationally tractable, the high-level planners that provide references for these controllers typically plan over simplified kinematic models, discarding much of this motion capability [3, 4, 5].

This conservatism has computational origins, inherited from aerial robotics, where real-time trajectory optimization first matured. Quadrotor motion can be accurately approximated via differentially flat kinematic models, where the full state and input are recovered algebraically from a low-dimensional flat output and its derivatives. Dynamic feasibility can then be enforced by construction on a polynomial trajectory, often allowing planning to reduce to a convex program rather than a traditionally burdensome nonlinear program (NLP) [6, 7]. Preserving the convex program requires convexifying the collision constraints as well, commonly by confining the trajectory to safe corridors of convex polytopes [8]. Other planners forgo convexity in the obstacle terms altogether, introducing separating-hyperplane decision variables [9] or soft gradient penalties on obstacle proximity [10]. Combined with polynomial bases such as Bézier and B-spline, whose control points bound the trajectory and its derivatives [11], flatness is used to enable replanning at high rates even in cluttered and dynamic environments [9].

For a quadruped, however, this pipeline breaks at the velocity limits. A quadruped’s velocity commands are bounded in the body frame, with distinct longitudinal and lateral limits that rotate with the heading, and these bounds are nonconvex in the flat outputs, so the flat structure yields no computational advantage. A planner that insists on the convex reduction must then downgrade the model, often to an integrator that ignores the heading coupling or to a unicycle that forbids lateral motion, and in either case it discards motion that the locomotion controller can readily execute.

Our formulation abandons the convex reduction in two ways. The kinematics enter as nonlinear equality constraints, and collision avoidance enters as hard keep-out constraints that are nonconvex in the decision variables. This cost is no longer prohibitive, as nonlinear planners can run at rates compatible with online replanning for ground robots [12], quadruped navigation [13], and non-differentially flat systems [14], aided by structure-exploiting transcriptions, mature sparse NLP solvers, and warm-started replanning.

A conventional direct transcription, which discretizes the trajectory and enforces the constraints at the resulting nodes, leaves the trajectory uncertified between them. We instead parameterize the pose and input trajectories as composite Bernstein polynomials [15, 16], sequences of low-degree Bernstein polynomials joined at knots. A polynomial in this basis lies within the convex hull of its coefficients, so bounding the coefficients bounds the continuous curve, a property that flat planners already exploit for feasibility [9, 17], and one that is least conservative when the degree is low. The velocity bounds and the obstacle clearance are polynomial functions of the trajectory, so the convex hull property can be used to certify these constraints for all tt.

We show that the computational cost of this nonconvexity is modest, and that the recovered lateral and heading-coupled motion allows a quadruped to reach goals faster and with fewer collisions than one planned with a simplified model. Our contributions are as follows:

We formulate quadruped trajectory generation as a receding-horizon NLP, replanning as the robot moves, over composite Bernstein polynomials using the fully-actuated S​E​(2)SE(2) kinematics, with anisotropic velocity and collision constraints certified for all tt.

We show that the resulting NLP solves in 16 ms median on an onboard NVIDIA Jetson, replanning at ∼36\sim 36 Hz, twice the refresh rate of the onboard perception.

We demonstrate in closed-loop simulations over 50 scenarios that our planner reaches the goal 1.6–2.7×\times faster than every tested kinematic ablation and external baseline, with the fewest collisions among moving obstacles.

We deploy the full stack (Fig. 2) onboard a real quadruped across 22 consecutive traversals totaling 392 m among unknown moving robots, with perception, planning, and control running in real time.

title: Environment Edits as a Corrective Signal for Reward Learning
authors: Isaac Ngui,Courtney McBeth,Nancy M. Amato
comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026 Workshop on Learning from Corrections
abstract: Robot corrections allow people to adjust a robot’s behavior, but a single correction changes many features. Also, preferences about object attributes and relationships between objects cannot be expressed by moving the robot. We propose environment edits as a complementary form of feedback. The robot’s motion is held constant as the human edits the scene, so the only explanation for the edit is the moved object. We introduce Feature Learning from Environmental and Robot-Relational Edit Traces (FERRET), which learns preferences from both robot and environment corrections. We show that environment edits are able to disambiguate features and learn preferences that robot corrections alone cannot.
introduction:
Robots that work beside people should support the ability for the people in their surroundings to correct their behavior.
When a robot does something wrong, a human can take the robot arm and move it, indicating how they would like the robot to behave and updating its objective [2, 1, 7].
Corrections like this are quick and they identify preferences about the robot’s motion, such as speed or posture, well.
Feature-learning methods such as Feature Expansive Reward Learning (FERL) [4] extend this idea to features that the robot does not already know through asking the human to move the robot along a feature trace from where the feature is strongly expressed to where it is not.

A correction is less clear about the world around the robot.
When a person drags a robot arm away from a laptop on a table, the drag also moves the arm from the table edge, lengthens the path, and changes the arm’s posture.
Each of these is a candidate explanation for what the human way trying to convey, and the learner can fit the correction while learning the wrong one.
With several objects on the table, the ambiguity compounds as the correction does not say which object mattered, whether it mattered because of the type of object or state state of the objet, such as a cup being full of water or not.
Some preferences are not able to be expressed by moving the robot in the first place.
“Keep the cup away from the laptop” does not change when the robot moves, so no robot correction carries it.

We ask what happens if the person corrects the environment instead.
The robot’s motion is fixed and replayed while the person edits the scene until the current motion is acceptable.
Interventions can happen on either the robot trajectory or the scene, where a scene intervention leaves every motion feature unchanged, so the edit can only be explained by the object that moved.
These two components are not competitors, but compliments with scene edits capturing preferences about objects, their attributes, and their relations to one another while robot corrections capture preferences about the motion of the robot itself.
Additionally, a robot correction or a scene edit placed at the boundary of acceptability can reveal how much a preference is worth against the cost of moving.

We propose FERRET (Feature Learning from Environmental and Robot-Relational Edit Traces), which learns preference features from either kind of trace. We explore two different model architectures, one with hand-built relations that capture relationships in the scene, and a graph model that learns important relations within its network.
Our contributions include:
1) an exploration of environment edits as a means of human feedback for preference learning,
2) a proposal of two distinct model architectures for learning human preferences from both robot or environment feature traces,
3) an experimental comparison of these model architectures showing their strengths and weaknesses relative to each other and existing work.

title: VPR-Space: A Benchmark for Visual Place Recognition in Space Analog Domains
authors: Richard Fechner,Peer Neubert
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Visual Place Recognition (VPR) is an important means for loop closure detection in visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM).
While state-of-the-art VPR and SLAM approaches show impressive results in urban and feature-rich natural environments, the vast, repetitive, and feature-poor environments of extraterrestrial surfaces like on the Moon or Mars, together with their challenging illumination conditions, pose severe challenges for existing approaches. This paper presents a novel benchmark, VPR-Space, to evaluate VPR capabilities on extraterrestrial surfaces.
There are three main contributions:
(1) We collected and curated sixteen VPR database-query datasets based on existing data from Space Analog Domains (SAD), terrestrial environments that resemble properties of the Moon or Mars. The collection includes a wide range of challenges regarding environment, viewpoint change, and illumination conditions. All datasets were manually corrected for ground-truth camera pose errors and unwanted camera artfacts.
(2) To address the ill-posed nature of VPR, we propose a novel approach to generate the ground-truth information in VPR benchmarks.
Instead of defining that a query and datbase image show the same place if and only if their camera poses are within fixed position and viewing direction thresholds, we propose to make the decision dependent on whether the match would be valuable in the downstream SLAM task.
To avoid the overhead and restrictions of evaluating VPR in-the-loop within SLAM systems, we provide VPR ground-truth (GT) matrices based on the performance of an ensemble of state-of-the-art Relative Pose Estimators (RPE).
Under this GT we require a VPR method to identify exactly those image pairs for which a subsequently applied RPE is expected to provide a valuable pose estimate in a SLAM context.
(3) We evaluated nine state-of-the-art VPR approaches. The results show considerable room for improvement and indicate directions for future research.
Detailed results, data, and code will be made available upon publication of the paper. We provide a pre-release version of the dataset on github: https://github.com/rfechner/VPR-Space
introduction:
Reliable camera-based navigation is an important capability of autonomous mobile systems in GNSS-denied environments such as the surfaces of the Moon and Mars. The potential of, and challenges associated with, such navigation systems have recently been highlighted by the initial success and subsequent crash of the Mars helicopter Ingenuity. A likely cause being the inability of the visual navigation system to find features on the homogeneous surface of Mars [17].
In the context of camera-based navigation, Visual Place Recognition (VPR) addresses the problem of identifying matching image pairs between a query set and a database set of images depicting the same places. It is an important component of loop-closure detection in Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) where it enables the correction of accumulated errors of odometry-based trajectory estimates.
Existing SLAM and VPR approaches achieve impressive performance in urban and feature-rich natural environments like forests. However, the visual characteristics of extraterrestrial planetary surfaces, such as those of the Moon or Mars, differ fundamentally from these environments. They more closely resemble Earth’s stone and sand deserts or volcanic sites, exhibiting regolith and topographic structures such as craters and wrinkle ridges. The vast, often homogeneous and feature-poor landscapes, together with harsh illumination conditions can pose severe challenges for image descriptors.
This is illustrated in Fig. 1, which shows the distributions of descriptor similarities for image pairs depicting either the same place (orange) or different places (blue). The two distributions are even more difficult to separate in the challenging Moon-like environment (right) than in the challenging urban environment (left). Combined with the low error tolerance of space missions, this motivates the need for careful analysis and evaluation of visual navigation algorithms under planetary-like conditions.

In this paper, we present VPR-Space, a benchmark for VPR approaches that provides (1) challenging combinations of curated database and query image sets with planetary-like conditions, and (2) carefully created ground-truth information about which image pairs depict the same place. Both parts are non trivial.
Collecting large amounts of extraterrestrial on-site data is impractical. An established alternative for preparation of space missions is using Space Analog Domains (SADs), areas on the Earth that resemble properties of the Moon or Mars [27]. Table I lists available SAD-based datasets for the evaluation of SLAM systems.
Sec. III will describe how we selected, manually curated, and preprocessed the available data in order to create representative database and query sets for the VPR-Space benchmark.

For the second part, creating the ground-truth (GT) information for evaluation of VPR approaches, a major challenge is the ill-posed nature of the VPR problem: There is no unique correct answer whether two images show the same place or not [30].
As will be discussed in Sec. II-C, the usual approach to create GT in existing VPR datasets is based on the ground truth pose difference between the two images (Pose thresholding) or overlap in field of view with a limited maximum distance (Frustum overlap).
In this paper, we propose a different approach to VPR-GT generation: According to [10], the quality of a VPR result is driven by its value for the downstream task. To avoid the overhead and restrictions of evaluating VPR in-the-loop within a SLAM system, we propose to use the performance of an ensemble of Relative Pose Estimators (RPE) as an oracle that identifies valuable matches (i.e., the RPE quality is used to generate the GT matrices). This can address two problems of VPR-GT generation in large and open environments, and in environments with very harsh illumination conditions, both common properties of SADs:

Problem 1: Fig. 2 illustrates how two images that can be considered to show the same place but which are taken far apart from one another, do not match when deciding correspondence based on pose distance or frustum overlap. The proposed RPE-GT includes this match if and only if we expect RPE approaches to find a valuable pose transformation.

The proposed RPE-GT includes this match if and only if we expect RPE approaches to find a valuable pose transformation.

Problem 2: Fig. 3 illustrates an example image pair that is taken from the exact same camera pose but due to extreme lighting conditions, a low error relative pose estimate cannot be made. A GT based on pose distance or frustum overlap would include this match, although it would potentially introduce additional errors in a SLAM system.

Sec. III-C will provide details on this RPE-based ground truth creation.
Sec. IV will then evaluate state-of-the-art (SotA) VPR approaches on the proposed benchmark.
In summary, the main contributions of this paper are:

VPR-Space, a challenging VPR benchmark for space analog domains, with 16 database-query sequence pairs derived from existing space analog SLAM datasets.

We propose and discuss a novel method to construct an application-driven ground truth for VPR. It leverages a set of SotA relative pose estimators to decide whether two images should match.

We evaluate nine SotA VPR methods on VPR-Space.

The benchmark with detailed results, evaluation code, as well as the code to reconstruct the benchmark from the raw SLAM datasets will be made available on the benchmark website upon paper publication.

title: Revisiting Direct Control: A Field Evaluation of Sensor Fusion Efficacy in Teleoperating Full-Scale Autonomous Vehicles via Bird's Eye View
authors: Stanisław Kuczma,Sławomir K. Tadeja,Michał R. Nowicki
comment: Accepted at 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
abstract: In autonomous driving, robot teleoperation serves as a critical safety fallback mechanism, requiring operators to assume direct control in the event of system failure. While recent research has pivoted toward high-level supervisory control or simulation-based studies, these approaches often fail to capture the physical dynamics and sensory demands of driving a full-scale vehicle. To address this gap, we evaluated the impact of spatial data representation on operator performance using a real car-sized vehicle in a field experiment with N=18N=18 participants. We compared three visualization interfaces: (i) a standard camera feed baseline, with two bird’s-eye views (BEV) from (ii) a raw LiDAR point cloud, and (iii) a sensor fusion of LiDAR and camera data streams. Conversely to prior passive-observation studies suggesting that sensor-fusion BEV may hinder awareness, our active-control results demonstrate that such representation significantly outperforms the standard LiDAR BEV in perceived usability (p≤0.0001p\leq 0.0001) and cognitive task load (p=0.01p=0.01, NASA-TLX score: 34.58/10034.58/100) while also being significantly better than the Camera-only view (p=0.043p=0.043). The fused interface also led to statistically significant reductions in task completion time (p=0.0461p=0.0461) and superior usability (SUS: 77.9/10077.9/100) compared to those of the Camera-only and LiDAR-only views. By synthesizing objective performance data with comprehensive subjective assessments, we demonstrate that BEV fusion maximizes safety margins while minimizing the operator’s mental demand. These findings challenge existing teleoperation conventions and provide an empirically validated approach for designing robust remote piloting systems.
introduction:
Self-driving vehicles are rapidly redefining mobility, with industry leaders such as Waymo and Tesla deploying autonomous technologies in public spaces. While such automated driving systems have reached series-level implementation, their operational design domains [1] remain restricted to specific environments and low speeds. Consequently, teleoperation has emerged as a critical bridge technology and a vital safety fallback, allowing remote human operators to assume control when the autonomous system encounters a scenario beyond its existing capabilities [2].

At the same time, consumer preferences underscore the necessity of human-in-the-loop systems. A recent survey [3] found that 58% of respondents prefer remote human control over full autonomy for navigating unexpected or ethically complex situations [4]. However, the transition to remote control introduces a significant physical disconnection between the operator and the vehicle. Teleoperators must contend with transmission latency and restricted field of view (FoV), lacking the ability to sense vehicle forces [5] or hear [6] their immediate surroundings. Effective data visualization is therefore paramount for bridging this sensory gap and enhancing operator situational awareness [7]. Conversely, poorly designed interfaces risk overloading operators with irrelevant or unclear information, eroding trust in autonomy, and increasing the likelihood of errors [8].

A critical disparity exists in current literature, i.e. while user interface designs are becoming more sophisticated, many evaluations rely on static clickable prototypes (mock-ups)  [9, 10], miniature, non-real-life-size robotic platforms [11, 12, 13], and simulations [14, 15]. These low-fidelity environments often fail to replicate the complex motion inertia and sensory dynamics inherent in full-scale vehicle control [16]. Furthermore, while the bird’s-eye view (BEV) has become the state-of-the-art representation for machine learning-based perception tasks [17], it can be characterized as an inferior or overwhelming visualization for human operators compared to standard camera feeds [18].

This paper addresses these gaps by presenting a comprehensive comparative analysis of sensor data representations—ranging from standard perspective RGB video streams to Camera-LiDAR BEV fusion (see Fig. 1.1-3)—conducted on a full-scale Pixloop vehicle platform (see Fig. 1.4). Through a field experiment with human operators (N=18N=18) driving a real vehicle, we determined which modality best optimized operator performance under real vehicle dynamics.

In summary, we contribute the following:

The design of a modular teleoperation interface that leverages unified Camera-LiDAR BEV visualizations to mitigate the sensory limitations of remote control and enhance operator performance in the context of full-scale vehicle dynamics.

An empirical, field-based evaluation showing that findings from low-fidelity setups do not fully scale to real-world dynamics, specifically proving that BEV fusion significantly reduces workload and decreases risk in full-scale operations.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas,Alejandro Romero,Richard J. Duro
abstract:
This work explores a multimodal approach to the alignment of the behavior of open-ended learning autonomous robots with human purposes through the use of large language models (LLMs) as cultural enablers. While autonomous robots can generate their own skills and goals through interaction with the environment, they often lack mechanisms to ensure that these remain relevant and aligned to those of human users. The proposed approach makes use of the general and cultural knowledge contained in LLMs and VLMs to establish a multimodal interactive alignment process in which human purposes, expressed in natural language, are transformed into motivational components of a robot architecture in the form of robot missions and drives that guide the behavior of the robot.
The system is structured into three layers for semantic alignment, mission generation, and drive modeling. This design enables a bidirectional interaction loop: human inputs define high-level purposes, robots expand them into executable missions making use of multimodal information relayed by LLMs and VLMs, and feedback maintains alignment with human intent.
Experiments in simulation and with a physical robot demonstrate that the process produces valid missions and behaviors, supporting effective human–agent alignment in interactive scenarios with autonomous robots.
introduction:
A central objective of cognitive and developmental robotics is to construct artificial agents that acquire increasingly sophisticated competencies through prolonged interaction with their environment. Inspired by human cognitive development, developmental robotics emphasizes intrinsically motivated exploration, incremental skill acquisition, and the progressive organization of behavior [1, 2]. In parallel, the paradigm of Open-Ended Learning (OEL) formalizes the capacity of autonomous systems to continuously generate new goals and expand their behavioral repertoire beyond predefined tasks or datasets [3]. Together, these perspectives frame autonomy not as the execution of fixed policies, but as an ongoing developmental process.

Within cognitive architectures, such developmental open-endedness is commonly achieved through motivation-based control systems [4, 5, 6]. In these systems, behavior is regulated by internal motivational variables that define why the agent acts, allowing goals and skills to emerge as means to regulate internal states. We refer to these domain-independent motivations as robot purposes.

Robot purposes include designer-embedded needs, such as homeostatic requirements and intrinsic motivations that drive exploration and competence acquisition [7, romero2024autonomous], as well as externally derived purposes, or missions, which reflect what human users expect the robot to accomplish during runtime. Both needs and missions are operationalized through drives – quantitative variables encoding the urgency of satisfying a given purpose [8]. By acting to regulate its drives, the robot autonomously discovers goals and learns skills that are grounded in the robot’s sensorimotor system. Alignment is achieved when the resulting behavior fulfills human expectations [9].

However, integrating human purposes into a developmental, open-ended system presents a significant challenge. Human intentions are expressed through natural language – ambiguous, context-dependent, and culturally grounded [10] – whereas motivational architectures require structured, formally defined representations [11]. This discrepancy creates a semantic gap that may lead to misaligned internal purposes, undermining trust and safety [9]. Explainability [12] and grounding strategies [13] address aspects of this issue, but they do not fully solve the problem of embedding human purposes into the motivational dynamics that drive developmental learning.

Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) provide powerful tools for interpreting linguistic instructions and relating them to perceptual context. Nevertheless, employing such models as end-to-end robot controllers raises concerns regarding explainability, controllability, safety, and the absence of explicit motivational structure [14]. From a developmental perspective, delegating control to monolithic policies risks bypassing the very mechanisms – intrinsic motivation, goal discovery, and incremental learning – that underpin autonomous cognitive growth.

We therefore adopt a complementary view: LLMs and VLMs are integrated not as end-to-end control policies, but as high-level semantic and cultural knowledge resources that provide structured priors to a motivation-based cognitive architecture. These multimodal models support the interpretation and clarification of human purposes, constraining the space of plausible missions. The discovery of specific goals and skills, however, remains grounded in the robot’s developmental learning processes and regulated by explicit drives. In this way, large models inform but do not replace the motivational dynamics that sustain autonomous development.

To operationalize this perspective, we propose a multimodal alignment framework composed of three layers: (1) semantic alignment, which interprets and refines human purposes through interactive dialogue; (2) mission generation, which translates aligned purposes into structured, domain-consistent missions; and (3) drive modeling, which transforms missions into quantitative drive functions embedded in the motivational system. An explicit alignment need, implemented as an alignment drive, motivates the robot to seek clarification until a coherent internal representation of the intended purpose is achieved.

The contributions of this work are threefold: (i) a cognitively and developmentally grounded framework for embedding human purposes into a motivational architecture supporting open-ended learning; (ii) the integration of specialized LLM- and VLM-based modules as semantic priors within this architecture; and (iii) experimental validation in simulation and on a physical robotic platform, demonstrating effective human–robot alignment while preserving autonomous developmental processes.

By combining multimodal semantic mediation with explicit motivational regulation, this work contributes to the design of developmental autonomous systems that can sustain long-term growth while remaining aligned with human intentions.
