title: Robot-Aligned 3D Gaussian Splatting for Precise Reaching with Wrist-Camera VLA Policies
authors: Zuoxu Wang,Xiao Liang
abstract:
Efficient robotic data collection remains a major bottleneck for vision-language-action (VLA) policy learning, especially for tasks requiring accurate end-effector positioning and camera-action alignment. This challenge is particularly severe in electronic-waste disassembly, where robots operate in cluttered assemblies of densely packed, visually similar components. Full digital-twin simulation is difficult because many parts are thin, reflective, or mechanically complex, making accurate object-level meshes and contact models difficult to obtain.
In this work, we focus on pre-contact reaching and propose a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based data generation pipeline for wrist-camera VLA adaptation. Our method reconstructs the real workspace with 3DGS and renders diverse wrist-camera observations from robot-aligned poses. These observations are paired with smooth, structured reaching trajectories to provide robot-aligned visual-action supervision for VLA fine-tuning. We further augment the VLA policy with an instruction-conditioned reach verifier that estimates target proximity and provides reliable termination before physical interaction.
Experiments in motherboard disassembly demonstrate precise VLA-based reaching using wrist-camera observations alone, without an external side-view camera. With π\pi0.5, 1,500 generated trajectories achieve 80.0% precise-reaching success across three targets, compared with 58.7% using 150 teleoperated demonstrations, while requiring less than 10 minutes of active human capture.
Project website: https://001-wang.github.io/PrecisionReach-GS/
introduction:
Precise reaching is a fundamental requirement for real-world robotic manipulation. Before a robot can grasp, pull, insert, place, cut, or otherwise interact with an object, it must first move its end-effector to the correct target region [1, 2, 3, 4]. This requirement becomes especially challenging in robotic disassembly, where targets include small components such as screws and memory modules as well as larger but fragile components such as GPUs [5, 6]. These components are often densely arranged and surrounded by neighboring parts, leaving little tolerance for reaching errors [7, 8]. Once the robot reaches the correct interaction region, subsequent actions can often be handled by task-specific controllers or skill modules, making target-oriented reaching a critical bottleneck between visual perception and successful manipulation [9].

Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a promising framework for learning such reaching behavior directly from visual observations and task instructions [10, 11, 12, 13]. By mapping camera observations and language commands to robot actions, VLA policies can learn visually grounded motion generation without requiring each target or task to be manually encoded. With sufficiently large, diverse, and well-aligned demonstrations, VLA models have the potential to generate accurate and adaptive reaching actions across different target objects, viewpoints, and instructions. This makes VLA particularly attractive for manipulation tasks where the robot must understand both the semantic meaning of the target and its spatial location in the scene. Importantly, in many manipulation tasks, the pre-contact reaching stage occupies a large portion of the VLA-controlled action sequence, as the robot must progressively move from an initial pose to the target interaction region before executing the final physical skill. Therefore, improving the data efficiency and reliability of reaching behavior can substantially benefit the overall VLA manipulation pipeline.

However, the effectiveness of VLA models is strongly tied to data scale and data quality [14, 15, 16, 17]. To learn precise reaching behavior, the policy requires many demonstrations in which the visual observation, language instruction, robot state, and action are consistently aligned. In practice, collecting such data on real robots remains difficult. Most demonstrations are collected through human teleoperation, which is slow, expensive, and difficult to scale [18, 19]. This problem becomes more severe when robot access is limited, because data collection occupies the physical robot for long periods and reduces the time available for training, testing, and other experiments. Moreover, human-collected demonstrations often introduce noise that can directly affect VLA learning. Teleoperated trajectories may be jerky, inaccurate, or contain unnecessary corrective motions [20, 21]. For example, an operator may move the robot toward an approximate region, realize that the target has been missed, and then perform several small adjustments before reaching the desired position. While this behavior is natural during manual operation, it creates ambiguous supervision for the policy: the model may learn both the intended reaching motion and the accidental correction behavior. In addition, delays between camera capture, robot state recording, and action execution can cause visual observations to be paired with slightly mismatched actions. Such camera-action misalignment is especially harmful for precise reaching, where small spatial errors can determine whether the robot reaches the correct component or misses it.

A natural alternative is to generate demonstrations in simulation, but building a full digital-twin simulator for electronic-waste disassembly is also challenging. Motherboards contain many densely packed components with different sizes, materials, and appearances, including small screws and connectors as well as larger but fragile parts such as GPUs, heat sinks, and memory modules. Many of these components are thin, reflective, or mechanically complex, making accurate object-level mesh reconstruction, material modeling, and contact simulation difficult. As a result, full simulation requires substantial manual modeling effort and can still introduce a large sim-to-real gap if the geometry, camera viewpoint, or physical interaction does not match the real workspace.

In addition to data collection and simulation, camera configuration also affects the scalability of VLA training and deployment. Many robot-learning systems use fixed external cameras or multi-view observations, which provide useful global context but require stable placement and calibration [22, 23]. In contrast, we consider a harder wrist-camera-only setting, where the viewpoint moves with the end-effector and the policy must infer both target location and motion correction from a narrow, continuously changing view. This reduces dependence on fixed side-view cameras, but also makes precise reaching more data-demanding, since the policy needs diverse and well-aligned wrist-camera observations to learn reliable corrections.

In this work, we propose PrecisionReach-GS, a lightweight real-to-sim-to-real pipeline for data-efficient VLA fine-tuning in a wrist-camera-only setting. As shown in Fig. 1, the pipeline first reconstructs the real task environment with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), preserving the cluttered background, object layout, and visual complexity of the physical workspace. Unlike full digital-twin simulators that require object-level meshes, collision models, and contact dynamics, PrecisionReach-GS focuses on the pre-contact reaching stage, where realistic wrist-camera observations and robot-aligned action labels are the main requirements. The system samples feasible starting poses, renders diverse wrist-camera observations, generates smooth reaching trajectories toward target components, and organizes the resulting observation–action pairs for VLA fine-tuning. During deployment, the fine-tuned VLA policy predicts reaching actions from wrist-camera observations, while a lightweight verifier determines whether the robot has reached the target interaction region. As a result, the user only specifies the target task and desired data scale, and the pipeline produces structured wrist-camera training data without large-scale teleoperation or a complete physical digital twin.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We propose PrecisionReach-GS, a lightweight real-to-sim-to-real framework that uses 3DGS as a photorealistic workspace representation for VLA adaptation, avoiding object-level meshes, contact models, and full physics-based digital twins.

We develop a robot-aligned visual-action generation method that maps the reconstructed scene into the robot frame, samples kinematically feasible starting poses, and generates synchronized wrist-camera observations, robot states, and smooth reaching actions with minimal human intervention.

We introduce an instruction-conditioned reach verifier that complements the VLA policy with instruction-conditioned reach assessment, enabling more reliable stopping under the distinct geometric precision requirements of different manipulation targets.

We experimentally validate the proposed pipeline in a robotic motherboard disassembly scenario, demonstrating that wrist-camera-only VLA fine-tuning, together with reach verification, can achieve precise target reaching and support successful downstream manipulation skills.

1. We propose PrecisionReach-GS, a lightweight real-to-sim-to-real framework that uses 3DGS as a photorealistic workspace representation for VLA adaptation, avoiding object-level meshes, contact models, and full physics-based digital twins.

2. We develop a robot-aligned visual-action generation method that maps the reconstructed scene into the robot frame, samples kinematically feasible starting poses, and generates synchronized wrist-camera observations, robot states, and smooth reaching actions with minimal human intervention.

3. We introduce an instruction-conditioned reach verifier that complements the VLA policy with instruction-conditioned reach assessment, enabling more reliable stopping under the distinct geometric precision requirements of different manipulation targets.

4. We experimentally validate the proposed pipeline in a robotic motherboard disassembly scenario, demonstrating that wrist-camera-only VLA fine-tuning, together with reach verification, can achieve precise target reaching and support successful downstream manipulation skills.

title: Context-Aware Generation and Modulation of Expressive Motion Behavior using Multimodal Foundation Models
authors: Till Hielscher,Fabio Scaparro,Kai O. Arras
abstract: Expressive robot motion positively impacts human-robot interaction by improving user engagement, likability, or task performance. We present a novel approach to automatically generate and modulate complex, expressive full-body gesture sequences from a multimodal (text, audio, video) context description. Based on a unified mathematical implementation of the Principles of Animation using Dynamic Movement Primitives, we use multimodal foundation models to generate such sequences along with parametric motion variations that are highly context-aware. This method extends the state of the art in terms of flexibility and generality by being interpretable, composable, and working across different robot morphologies. Moreover, we integrate the system into a continuous control framework and leverage knowledge distillation to learn a much smaller model, significantly improving token efficiency and system latency. Results from a user study with a human-like platform indicate that participants judged our system’s motions to be better aligned with the interaction context than motions produced under a non-modulated or API-level condition. We also demonstrate how the system generates expressive motion for robots with different kinematics, showcasing its versatility. Paper webpage: https://gen-mod-expressive-motion-behavior.github.io/.
introduction:
Non-verbal communication via gaze, gestures, or facial expressions is a crucial component of socially intelligent behavior for humans and robots.
Robot-performed gestures are often seen as a defining property of social robots (De Wit et al., 2023), and by using their physical embodiment and presence, they are perceived more positively and persuasive than, for example, interactive virtual agents (Li, 2015). Therefore, the design and use of expressive robotic body motion are critical for achieving natural and effective communication with socially interactive robots.
Key questions include how movements are shaped, selected, and timed, the extent of their expression, and their integration with speech, context, and the course of interaction.
This paper tackles several of the above questions, namely how body motion can be represented to facilitate learning, execution, and modulation – i.e., context-sensitive variations of the same motion –, and how basic gestures can be automatically selected, timed, and varied such that interlocutors perceive the robot’s behavior as aligned with the interaction context.

The variety of expressive human body motion appears to be open-ended. One way to tackle this complexity practically is categorizing gestures into communicative functions such as deictic, iconic, or symbolic, and reusing standardized sets of pre-recorded gestures (Tan et al., 2021). By providing a small set of exemplars for each function, a robot can cover many real-world situations without the need to generate joint-level trajectories on the fly.
We build on such motion datasets and adopt recent work (Hielscher et al., 2025) that employs Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) to represent, modulate, and compose basic gestures into expressive body language. Originally developed for motor skill learning from imitation or demonstration, e.g., for robot manipulation, DMPs offer properties highly relevant for this task. As shown in (Hielscher et al., 2025), they provide a unified implementation of the Principles of Animation and enable modulation of key principles through a low-dimensional, interpretable parameter set. This allows animators – and large language models – to stylize full-body motion along the well-established dimensions of the Principles of Animation across different kinematic configurations. They are also online adaptive in the sense that gestures are parametrized by a static or dynamic goal in space towards which gestures are executed.

However, unlike (Hielscher et al., 2025), which was limited to the “how” in generating expressive body language, we focus on the “what” and “when” and automate the generation process given the multimodal description of a context. To this end, we integrate multimodal foundation models into a continuous control framework, leveraging their extensive world knowledge to explore novel possibilities for social robot motion design. This also extends prior work that used only large language models and simpler motion representations (Mahadevan et al., 2024). Specifically, our contributions are:

A system for automated context-aware modulation and composition of basic gestures, represented as Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs), into expressive body language. The method is robot-agnostic with respect to kinematics and integrates multimodal context inputs, including text, image, and audio.

A method that applies knowledge distillation, a technique to transfer the knowledge of a large, computationally expensive foundation model to a smaller, more efficient model. The results are reduced inference cost and significantly smaller system latencies.

A user study with a human-like robot that confirms the validity of the approach over a non-modulated and API-level motion condition, as well as qualitative experiments that demonstrate the system’s ability to generate expressive body language across robot morphologies using a manipulator and a four-legged robot.

1. A system for automated context-aware modulation and composition of basic gestures, represented as Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs), into expressive body language. The method is robot-agnostic with respect to kinematics and integrates multimodal context inputs, including text, image, and audio.

2. A method that applies knowledge distillation, a technique to transfer the knowledge of a large, computationally expensive foundation model to a smaller, more efficient model. The results are reduced inference cost and significantly smaller system latencies.

3. A user study with a human-like robot that confirms the validity of the approach over a non-modulated and API-level motion condition, as well as qualitative experiments that demonstrate the system’s ability to generate expressive body language across robot morphologies using a manipulator and a four-legged robot.

title: RoboDoctor: Training-Free Recursive Self-Improvement for Robot Policies
authors: Heyang Yu,Haomin Li,Sihang Li,Jixin Yan,Shiyun Peng,Wanqi Zhong,Tianyu Xin,Yuan Yao,Xiaoyu Tian,Yiming Li
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Project Page:this https URL
abstract: Generalist robot policies and language-model agents provide complementary capabilities, but completing a task also requires adapting their use to the consequences of physical interaction. We study execution as a locus of adaptation: feedback guides the current action and supplies evidence for revising subsequent decisions under fixed model weights. We introduce RoboDoctor, a training-free framework that connects diagnosis, grounded action, and persistent experience across three revision targets. The harness allocates control between policy and agent; intervention determines when to assist while preserving useful policy behavior; and operation refines physical methods through observed effects. Linked experience records retain the reason for a decision, the attempted method, its outcome, and conditions for reuse. On a curated archive of 54 RoboDojo-Sim task entries, RoboDoctor achieves a five-dimension mean score of 57.10, with a native success rate of 49.44%. Recorded interactions illustrate strategy changes, selective correction, and grasp revision. These findings characterize execution-time adaptation in the evaluated system; controlled trials remain necessary to isolate the contribution of cross-episode experience.
introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models and world action models (WAM) have expanded the range of manipulation behaviors available from a single model (Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025a; Ye et al., 2026). Language-model agents add complementary capabilities in task interpretation, planning, and tool use (Ahn et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2022). Translating these capabilities into complete task execution also requires managing their consequences: each interaction changes the conditions under which later actions must succeed. A grasp can be locally successful yet leave an object poorly positioned for the next step. Robot capability therefore depends on how available behaviors are coordinated, evaluated, and revised through physical interaction. This raises a system-level question: how can a robot use execution feedback to adapt the way it deploys existing model capabilities?

Robot agents already incorporate environmental feedback into planning, detect execution failures, and use reflection to refine action selection (Huang et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025). Building on this progress, we study the decisions that arise when an agent and a continuous robot policy share responsibility for execution. A deviation may require a local correction, a different contact method, or a change in the strategy that organizes the task. These responses operate at different levels and can interfere with one another: correcting alignment may preserve a useful grasp, whereas repeatedly restoring that grasp may perpetuate an ineffective strategy. The challenge is to identify what needs revision while retaining behavior that remains useful.

Recent embodied recursive self-improvement (RSI) systems use physical feedback to revise execution harnesses and accumulate reusable skills (MMLab & PhysicalRSI contributors, 2026; Song et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). Within this direction, our perspective is that execution is itself a locus of adaptation. Physical interaction serves two roles: it advances the task and provides evidence about how the available capabilities should be used. That evidence can regulate the next action and become external experience for subsequent attempts. With both policy and agent weights fixed, the adaptive state lies in control organization, intervention decisions, and the accumulated methods that inform future behavior. Preserving successful behavior is central to this process: a failure should prompt revision at the level implicated by the feedback, without discarding competence that the same interaction has demonstrated.

Making this perspective operational requires connecting diagnosis to physical evidence. Recognizing a slipped grasp does not specify a stable contact, and reaching a commanded pose does not establish that the object moved as intended. Likewise, a successful correction supports a reusable lesson only under conditions justified by the observation. An alignment principle may apply in another scene even when its original displacement does not. We therefore link the reason for a decision to the attempted physical method, its observed effect, and its conditions of applicability. Reuse calls for checking those conditions and grounding the method again in the current scene.

We introduce RoboDoctor, a framework that implements this perspective through three coupled revision targets (Figure 1). Harness RSI allocates control responsibility between policy and agent. Intervention RSI determines when assistance is warranted and which policy behavior to preserve. Operation RSI refines how an intended physical change is achieved. A Hybrid controller lets the policy propose primary motion while the Doctor reviews and selectively corrects it; a Direct controller assigns planning and action to the Doctor through the same grounded tools (Su et al., 2026). Observed outcomes guide selection between these controllers, and linked experience records support revision within and across episodes. Recursive self-improvement here refers to updating and reusing this external state under frozen model weights; the evaluated harness selects between predefined controllers.

We evaluate RoboDoctor through a curated archive of 54 RoboDojo-Sim task entries (Chen et al., 2026). The selected Refinement outcomes achieve an Overall score of 57.10, compared with 49.74 during Warmup. The capability profile in Figure 1 shows that the largest gains occur in Generalization and Open instruction following, while Long-Horizon performance decreases. The accompanying examples illustrate alignment correction and grasp revision; Section 5 examines these interactions alongside a change in task strategy. The archive supports analysis of these mechanisms and their associated performance; its retrospective selection and unequal coverage do not isolate the causal benefit of cross-episode experience (Section 4.1).

Our contributions are: (i) a training-free execution framework that connects control allocation, selective intervention, and physical operation as coupled targets of adaptation; (ii) an experience mechanism that links diagnosis, method, outcome, and applicability to guide subsequent use of fixed model capabilities; and (iii) a 54-task empirical analysis combining aggregate outcomes with recorded evidence of how execution decisions change.

title: Distributed Predictive Flocking for a Swarm of Miniature Vibration-Driven Robots in a Confined Arena
authors: Prajol Shrestha,Siddhant Mohapatra,Filip Novkoski,Julian Oelhaf,Nicolas Vandewalle,Ana-Sunčana Smith,Andreas Maier
comment: Submitted to Robotics and Autonomous Systems
abstract: Coordinating many miniature robots in a confined arena, with no leader, central planner, or global map, is a core challenge for swarm robotics. As the swarm grows denser, collision avoidance becomes the limiting factor, and the number of safely coexisting robots depends on the formulation of the inter-robot safety constraint. We present a distributed predictive flocking controller in which each robot solves its own nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) problem, optimizing swarm cohesion and alignment costs, inter-robot and obstacle safety, and a task objective, while exchanging only predicted trajectories with local neighbors. Within this generalized controller architecture, solved in real time, we compare six barrier and control-barrier-function (CBF) safety formulations on a digital twin of an open-source vibration-driven bristlebot in a 0.64​m20.64\,\mathrm{m^{2}} arena. A look-ahead discrete-time CBF performs best overall, with the fewest collisions and the widest inter-robot margins across nearly every swarm size tested. We deploy it on phototaxis, phototactic orbiting, and cohesion without a stimulus tasks, using swarm sizes starting from ten robots and up to the geometric packing limit. The swarm holds well: collisions stay low in small swarms, rising steeply as the packing limit approaches, while coordination and cohesion degrade gently rather than collapsing. The swarm is found not to trade safety for order, keeping both across the confined arena, with local alignment high at every swarm size.
introduction:
Autonomous multi-robot systems are a promising approach for tasks in cluttered,
inaccessible, or hazardous spaces, from confined-structure inspection to search in
collapsed buildings and medical micro-robotics [1]. In these settings,
many miniature robots must coordinate in proximity within a tight, bounded arena. As
in natural swarms, such as flocking of starlings, schooling of fish, the crowded colonies
of ants and honey bees, and even the collective migration of cells, robust group behavior
emerges from purely local interactions among simple
agents [2, 3, 4], with no central
control [1].
Miniaturization, however, tightly bounds onboard compute, memory, and
power [5], demanding control that is theoretically principled yet
computationally light. Moreover, when the arena is fixed, a growing number of robots
increases the density of the swarm and hinders smooth motion. When it is also cluttered
with obstacles, coordination is even harder. In this scenario, collision avoidance becomes
the central challenge.

The standard way to coordinate such a swarm from purely local interactions is Reynolds’
boid model [6, 7], which reduces collective
motion to three local rules (cohesion, alignment, and separation) that produce coherent
group motion without global information [8]. Early control laws
formalized these as artificial potential fields over a communication
graph [9, 10], and reactive
velocity-matching rules scale to tens of drones [11]. Such
reactive methods, however, offer no predictive horizon, no formal safety guarantee under
nonlinear dynamics, and no systematic handling of kinodynamic limits. These shortcomings
are especially severe in confined, high-density settings, where many underactuated robots
have little room to recover from unsafe motions.

Model predictive control (MPC) [12] addresses these limitations. For
the nonlinear dynamics of mobile robots, this takes the form of nonlinear MPC (NMPC). It
solves a
finite-horizon optimal control problem (OCP) online, which provides closed-loop feedback,
constraint satisfaction, and explicit multi-objective trade-offs. Distributed MPC (DMPC)
extends this to a swarm by splitting the
global problem into per-agent OCPs coupled through shared
constraints [13, 14, 15, 16].
Solvers such as the Sequential Quadratic Programming real-time iteration
(SQP-RTI) [17] solve each per-agent OCP in real time. Similarly,
optimization-based
swarm planners achieve strong real-world navigation [18, 19, 20, 21]. These methods are mainly developed for
point-to-point navigation [14, 22], with collision avoidance
typically encoded as geometric constraints such as separating hyperplanes or safe
corridors.

The closest works embed Reynolds behaviors in NMPC. They have been demonstrated on up to 16
quadrotors [23, 24], leader-follower
teams [25, 26, 27], and fixed-wing unmanned
aerial vehicles (UAVs) [28]. Most share one regime. They assume sparse flight in large 3D
airspace, with the swarm migrating toward a shared goal. Even when several obstacles are
present, they remain sparse relative to the available space, keeping the environment
effectively low-density. Few address the opposite regime that we target, where many
underactuated robots coordinate at high density in a fixed, confined, and cluttered
arena under a task objective such as following a light gradient. Here, the
inter-robot safety formulation, not free-space planning, governs how many robots can
coexist. Each of these works, however, fixes a single safety formulation in advance,
usually a distance constraint or a penalty. It remains open which formulation fits the
most robots into a fixed arena with minimal collisions.

Safety formulations differ in how collision avoidance is encoded as a constraint in the
OCP. Such a constraint is classically formulated using a barrier function h⁡(x)h(x) whose safe set 𝒮={x∣h⁡(x)≥0}\mathcal{S}=\{x\mid h(x)\geq 0\} is kept forward invariant to certify safety [29], typically imposed as a
hard [30] or soft [31] distance constraint. A Control
Barrier Function (CBF) [29] relaxes this strict boundary condition by allowing h⁡(x)h(x) to decrease at a rate bounded by a class-𝒦\mathcal{K} function, and its discrete-time form
(Dt-CBF) [32] imposes this at each MPC stage.
Zeng et al. [33] enforces it as a hard constraint, which is often infeasible.
Feasibility is restored by softening the decay with slack
variables [34, 35, 36], adding
terminal barrier terms [37, 38], or anchoring a
soft CBF with one hard step [39]. Beyond feasibility, when the constraint
has relative degree greater than one, as for a distance constraint under unicycle
dynamics, a higher-order CBF (HOCBF) [40, 41] chains
the barrier conditions. Lu et al. [39] compare a distance-constraint MPC, a
hard discrete-time CBF, a slacked CBF, and their combination on a common footing, but for
a single robot. In the multi-robot setting, safety is enforced by reactive
schemes [42, 43], by post-hoc CBF-QP (quadratic
program) filters [44], or by a CBF inside a decentralized MPC with
neighbors as predicted
trajectories [45, 46, 47, 48].
A formulation’s collision performance, however, likely changes with the swarm density. A
comparison across densities is required to find the best one.

In this work, we investigate the maximum number of miniature robots a distributed
predictive controller can flock in a fixed arena, and design a controller to push that
limit. Each robot solves its own NMPC combining Reynolds cohesion, alignment, and
separation (gated by neighbor presence) with inter-robot/obstacle safety and the task
objective. It selects the KK nearest neighbors within the communication radius and
exchanges predicted trajectories synchronously as OCP parameters, giving a fully
distributed, leader-free architecture with no central planner or global map. We evaluate
it on a physics-informed digital twin [49] of the
GRASPion [50], an open-source vibration-driven bristlebot studied as
an active-matter model system. We characterize how densely the swarm packs a
0.64​m20.64\,\mathrm{m^{2}} arena while sustaining two behaviors. These are phototaxis (ascending toward a
moving Gaussian light gradient) and a phototactic orbital mode (orbiting the source
along the intensity level-set). We compare six inter-robot safety formulations on a common
footing (Section 3.3). A slacked barrier paired with a discrete-time CBF
at a forward handle [51] sustains the highest density with the
fewest collisions.
The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

A distributed predictive control system for dense swarms of miniature vibration-driven robots. Each robot solves its own NMPC fusing flocking, safety, and the task objective, coupled to neighbors only through exchanged predicted trajectories.

Demonstration that a single controller generalizes across qualitatively different collective behaviors. The same architecture produces gradient-ascending phototaxis, stable phototactic orbital formation, and generic flocking with no modification to the safety or coordination layers, showing that task objectives and coordination structure are separable and that new tasks can be added without re-deriving safety guarantees.

A careful comparison of six inter-robot safety formulations within one identical controller, isolating the safety constraint as the only varying factor. The Look-ahead Slack Dt-CBF gives the best overall trade-off for the phototaxis deployment target.

Characterization of the operating swarm density that the controller sustains in a fixed arena. The swarm stays cohesive with few collisions in small swarms; collisions rise steeply towards the geometric packing limit, as saturation sets in, while coordination and feasibility degrade gently rather than collapse.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 presents the robot model, light field, control architecture overview, behavior generation, flocking rules, and the DMPC OCP. Section 3 reports the simulation results, including the safety-formulation study (Section 3.3), the analysis of collective behavior (Section 3.4), and the quantification of collision avoidance under different tasks (Section 3.5). Section 4 summarizes the work and provides an outlook for future studies.

title: Preemptive Instruction Following with Resumption
authors: Zerun Liu,Lechao Cheng,Yimin Liu,Shengeng Tang,Yaxiong Wang,Zhun Zhong
abstract: Long-horizon embodied navigation may be interrupted by a higher-priority instruction before the current task sequence is complete. The agent must finish its current atomic task, execute the inserted task, and resume the remaining sequence from the updated environment state, where its viewpoint and available navigation candidates may have changed. To evaluate this capability, we introduce PIFR benchmark, a novel task for runtime task preemption and resumption in embodied navigation. PIFR includes single, repeated, and nested interruption settings, with stage-specific metrics for inserted-task completion, resumption of the original task, and completion of the full sequence. Evaluations show that recovery performance varies across interruption conditions, while aggregate success can obscure differences in interruption handling and resumption. We further propose a lightweight candidate-ranking baseline to improve target re-grounding after interruption. Together, PIFR and the baseline provide a systematic framework for studying interruption handling and task recovery in long-horizon embodied navigation.
introduction:
Embodied navigation research has advanced the ability of agents to understand their surroundings, follow instructions, and complete navigation tasks through work on vision-language navigation (Anderson et al., 2018), embodied simulation (Savva et al., 2019), interactive navigation (Thomason et al., 2020), and spatial memory in partially observed environments (Chaplot et al., 2020a; Wani et al., 2020). Subsequent studies have expanded the range of tasks and goal specifications. For example, TEACh (Padmakumar et al., 2022) investigates multi-step household tasks guided by human instructions; NaviLLM (Zheng et al., 2024) models diverse navigation tasks through a unified language interface; and GOAT-Bench (Khanna et al., 2024) evaluates long-horizon navigation with sequential category, language, and image goals. Other work studies context-dependent sequential grounding (Zhang et al., 2024b), combines visual grounding with active exploration (Zhu et al., 2025), maintains spatial representations over extended execution (Yang et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2025), or investigates asynchronous interaction, task prioritization, and runtime preemption (Wang et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). These studies advance different capabilities relevant to long-horizon navigation, interaction, and task scheduling. However, to the best of our knowledge, existing embodied navigation benchmarks do not systematically evaluate the complete process in which an agent receives a higher-priority instruction while executing a base task sequence, completes its current atomic task before switching to the inserted task, and resumes the base sequence from the updated environmental state after completing the inserted task. Aggregate navigation success alone also cannot distinguish performance in handling the inserted task, resuming the original task, and completing the full sequence. A dedicated benchmark is therefore needed to evaluate runtime task preemption and resumption in a controlled, stage-specific manner.

We study runtime task preemption and resumption. Let the base task sequence be A=(EA1,EA2,…,EAn)A=(E_{A_{1}},E_{A_{2}},\ldots,E_{A_{n}}). If the agent receives a higher-priority instruction while executing an atomic task, it first completes that task, then suspends the remaining tasks in AA and executes the inserted task. Once the inserted task is complete, the agent resumes AA at the next unexecuted atomic task. Here, resumption refers to restoring the logical progress of the base sequence and re-grounding its next objective from the current environmental state; it does not require returning to the pre-interruption position or reusing the original route.

Figure 1 illustrates this process. The agent is initially assigned the base sequence A=(EA1,EA2,EA3)A=(E_{A_{1}},E_{A_{2}},E_{A_{3}}): retrieve food from a refrigerator, retrieve a book, and complete a subsequent task. While executing EA1E_{A_{1}}, the agent receives a higher-priority inserted task EBE_{B}, which requires organizing the cabinets. To ensure that the current atomic task is completed, the agent finishes EA1E_{A_{1}} before suspending the unexecuted tasks EA2E_{A_{2}} and EA3E_{A_{3}} and switching to EBE_{B}. After completing EBE_{B}, the agent resumes AA at EA2E_{A_{2}} and then proceeds to EA3E_{A_{3}}. Because the inserted task may change the agent’s location, viewpoint, and available navigation candidates, resuming EA2E_{A_{2}} requires the agent to re-ground its target and plan from the current state, rather than return to its pre-interruption position or follow the original route.

To address this gap, we introduce PIFR, a benchmark for evaluating runtime task preemption and resumption in embodied navigation. PIFR examines whether an agent can handle an inserted task and subsequently resume its suspended task sequence under diverse goal specifications and interruption structures, including single, repeated, and nested interruptions. This design enables evaluation beyond conventional task completion by distinguishing performance during task interruption and subsequent resumption.

Evaluations on PIFR show that recovery performance varies with interruption conditions and goal specifications. They also reveal that aggregate navigation success can mask differences in an agent’s ability to handle inserted tasks and resume suspended ones. To study this challenge, we further propose PIFR-Rank, a lightweight candidate-ranking baseline aimed at improving target re-grounding after an interruption. Together, PIFR and PIFR-Rank provide an evaluation benchmark and a reference method for investigating task recovery in long-horizon embodied navigation.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce PIFR, a benchmark for runtime task preemption and resumption in embodied navigation. The curated datasets cover diverse goal specifications and single, repeated, and nested interruption structures.

We develop a continuous-execution protocol and stage-specific evaluation measures to assess inserted-task completion, resumption of the base task, and completion of the full task sequence, enabling systematic analysis of navigation performance under different interruption conditions.

We propose PIFR-Rank, a lightweight candidate-ranking baseline that improves target re-grounding after interruption through candidate-level supervision while preserving the original navigation pipeline.

1. We introduce PIFR, a benchmark for runtime task preemption and resumption in embodied navigation. The curated datasets cover diverse goal specifications and single, repeated, and nested interruption structures.

2. We develop a continuous-execution protocol and stage-specific evaluation measures to assess inserted-task completion, resumption of the base task, and completion of the full task sequence, enabling systematic analysis of navigation performance under different interruption conditions.

3. We propose PIFR-Rank, a lightweight candidate-ranking baseline that improves target re-grounding after interruption through candidate-level supervision while preserving the original navigation pipeline.

title: Enhancing Deep Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Motion Planning via Task Decomposition
authors: Yuanzhi He,Victor Romero-Cano,Jiayu Xu,Juan David Hernández,Gualtiero Colombo
comment: Accepted to IEEE MSN 2026.
abstract: Training robotic manipulation policies in simulation is widely adopted due to safety and cost efficiency; however, tasks involving obstacles remain under-performing and often converge slowly under Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). To address this challenge, we propose a task decomposition framework for DRL that integrates Transfer Learning (TL) with Reward Redesign (RR) to improve learning efficiency and robustness in obstacle environments. The TL strategy selectively transfers only the first-layer critic parameters across structurally related tasks, since that layer captures general state–action representations while deeper layers encode reward- and obstacle-specific value geometry; RR decomposes tasks into staged sub-objectives to provide denser optimization signals. Experiments on the PyBullet Panda platform show consistent gains in obstacle settings. On Push with obstacle, our method achieves 0.83±0.050.83\pm 0.05, outperforming the strongest baseline (Truncated Quantile Critics (TQC), 0.77±0.060.77\pm 0.06) by approximately 7.8%7.8\%. On Slide with obstacle, performance reaches 0.95±0.020.95\pm 0.02, exceeding Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) (0.84±0.060.84\pm 0.06) by about 11%11\% success rates. In addition to higher final performance, forward transfer reduces convergence time by up to 70%70\% in obstacle tasks, and RR shortens sparse-reward Pick-and-Place training from roughly 0.750.75M to 0.200.20M steps (≈73%\approx 73\% reduction). The best policy is deployed on a real Franka Emika FR3 robot as a qualitative feasibility demonstration.
introduction:
Robotics research has increasingly shifted toward simulation environments rather than training directly on real robots [1]. This trend is mainly driven by the high cost of trial-and-error in real-world settings, safety risks to physical hardware, and the time-consuming and labor-intensive nature of collecting large-scale interaction data. In contrast, simulation platforms enable low-cost, risk-free experimentation with highly controllable scenarios, making them well suited for large-scale and repetitive training processes [2, 3].
In this study, we adopt the PyBullet Panda environments, whose robot arm model closely matches the kinematic structure and joint constraints of real manipulators such as the Franka arm [4], building on the goal-conditioned robotics benchmarks established in prior work [5, 6].

Despite the success of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) in robotic manipulation tasks such as grasping, pushing, and object transportation, increasing task complexity often leads to a rapid growth in training cost and model instability. In particular, the solution of tasks that require the robot to jointly solve manipulation and collision-free path planning problems enlarges the observation and action spaces. Under such conditions, training policies from scratch typically demands a large number of interaction samples, substantial computational resources, and often suffers from slow or unstable convergence [7, 8, 9]. We address this as obstacle-aware, goal-conditioned manipulation policy learning, in which the policy must reach a goal, interact with the object, and avoid the collision region introduced by an obstacle, all learned implicitly from interaction rather than from an explicit geometric planner.

To address these challenges, we propose a task decomposition framework that integrates Transfer Learning (TL) with Reward Redesign (RR) to improve learning efficiency and performance in a set of obstacle tasks. The policy is first trained on a relatively simpler source task to acquire fundamental knowledge. The learned knowledge is then transferred to a more complex target task by reusing selected network parameters. In pick-and-place environments, we further redesign multi-step task rewards by decomposing them into multiple staged feedback signals corresponding to intermediate sub-tasks, where rewards are assigned to the approaching, grasping, and transporting stages.

We evaluate the proposed framework on three manipulation tasks: Push, Pick-and-Place, and Slide, each with obstacle-free and obstacle settings, where a cubic obstacle was introduced in the obstacle environments. Snapshots of obstacle environments are illustrated in Fig. 1. Through systematic comparisons, we show that few-shot TL together with RR improves success rates and reduces training time across most task settings, with one exception, Pick-and-Place with obstacle, which we discuss in detail.

Although first-layer transfer, reward shaping, and task decomposition build on established ideas, our emphasis is on a minimal and controlled combination of them and on understanding when such transfer helps and when it does not. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

We propose a unified task decomposition framework for DRL that combines few-shot TL and RR to enhance learning efficiency and performance for obstacle-aware robotic manipulation tasks.

We introduce a controlled transfer strategy that reuses only the first-layer critic parameters across tasks, and analyze why this layer is the appropriate transfer target through a transfer-depth comparison (first-layer vs. all-layer vs. from scratch).

We design a staged reward formulation that decomposes multi-step task objectives into interpretable sub-task rewards, accelerating convergence without compromising final task performance.

We conduct extensive evaluations on multiple manipulation tasks in both obstacle-free and obstacle environments, including a systematic study of forward, double, reverse, and neutral transfer, and demonstrate real-world feasibility through a deployment on a Franka Emika FR3 robot.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 details the proposed approach. Section 4 presents and discusses the experimental results in both simulation and real-world environments. Section 5 concludes the paper and discusses potential future work.

1. We propose a unified task decomposition framework for DRL that combines few-shot TL and RR to enhance learning efficiency and performance for obstacle-aware robotic manipulation tasks.

2. We introduce a controlled transfer strategy that reuses only the first-layer critic parameters across tasks, and analyze why this layer is the appropriate transfer target through a transfer-depth comparison (first-layer vs. all-layer vs. from scratch).

3. We design a staged reward formulation that decomposes multi-step task objectives into interpretable sub-task rewards, accelerating convergence without compromising final task performance.

4. We conduct extensive evaluations on multiple manipulation tasks in both obstacle-free and obstacle environments, including a systematic study of forward, double, reverse, and neutral transfer, and demonstrate real-world feasibility through a deployment on a Franka Emika FR3 robot.

title: DEX-PHD: A Dexterous Portable Handheld Device for Multimodal Data Collection
authors: Jooyoung Hong,Noboru Myers,Obin Kwon,Yixian Yang,Joohyung Kim
abstract: Existing manipulation data collection methods typically offer either accurate robot-state acquisition through kinematic-chain-based teleoperation or convenient, portable operation through vision-based approaches. We present DEX-PHD, a portable handheld device that combines these advantages for dexterous manipulation by integrating a dexterous robot hand, continuous per-finger control, and multimodal logging. The system records proprioceptive information, fingertip contact data, and wrist-camera video, while the operator directly controls the robot hand through joint-level mapping. Its untethered design enables data collection across diverse environments. We demonstrate DEX-PHD on contact-rich tasks requiring coordinated multi-finger manipulation and deploy the collected demonstrations through open-loop replay on a physical humanoid robot. The results show that open-loop replay preserves the main temporal patterns of finger motion and task-relevant contact. Therefore, DEX-PHD provides a practical platform for portable, multimodal dexterous manipulation data collection.
introduction:
Robots have been increasingly deployed in industrial and household environments, where many tasks are repetitive, tedious, or physically demanding. As these applications expand, robust data collection becomes critical for advancing robotic manipulation capabilities. In particular, dexterous manipulation requires datasets that capture not only motion but also contact, force, and proprioceptive information [1, 2, 3]. However, collecting such data at scale remains challenging because many existing systems rely on controlled environments, specialized hardware, or complex calibration procedures.

Existing methods for demonstration data collection present a trade-off between data quality and user convenience. Kinematic-chain-based teleoperation systems, including leader-follower devices and exoskeletons, can provide accurate robot-action trajectories and high-quality joint-level data. However, these systems often require expensive hardware and bulky or fixed setups, limiting portability and scalable data collection. In contrast, vision-based methods, including approaches based on egocentric video, provide convenient and accessible data collection. Nevertheless, they depend on visual pose estimation and retargeting, may require substantial computation, and make it difficult to incorporate contact and proprioceptive information.

Handheld devices offer a promising intermediate approach by combining simple setup with portable, in-the-wild data collection [4, 5]. However, most existing handheld systems employ parallel grippers or tool-based interfaces, limiting their ability to capture continuous, coordinated multi-finger motion. They also provide limited access to synchronized hand-state and fingertip-contact information. For dexterous manipulation, there is therefore a need for a portable collection interface that retains the convenience of vision-based systems while providing direct, high-quality robot-hand data.

To bridge the gap between direct robot-hand data collection and portable operation, we present DEX-PHD, a portable handheld device that physically integrates a dexterous robot hand with continuous per-finger control and synchronized multimodal logging, as shown in Fig. 1. Continuous trigger and knob inputs are mapped directly to the corresponding robot-hand joints, enabling the operator to control the dexterous hand through a joint-level mapping. The device records hand joint states, fingertip force signals, and wrist-camera video using onboard storage. Its battery-powered, untethered configuration enables data collection across diverse environments without an external computer or fixed robot platform.

The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

A portable handheld device that physically integrates a dexterous robot hand and enables continuous, per-finger joint-level command generation directly in the robot-hand command space.

A synchronized multimodal logging framework that records wrist-view video, robot-hand commands, measured finger states, and fingertip force signals during contact-rich manipulation.

A replayability evaluation showing that demonstrations collected with DEX-PHD can be reproduced on a physical humanoid robot, with quantitative analysis of joint trajectory tracking and task-relevant contact-pattern similarity.

title: RoKON: Efficient and Adaptive Data-Enabled Predictive Control for Robotic Manipulation
authors: Akshun Sharma,Zhongqi Wei,Buqing Ou,Frederike Dümbgen
abstract:
Data-enabled predictive control has recently emerged as a promising control paradigm, enabling a transparent optimal-control formulation without the need to learn an explicit dynamics model.
This paper presents a number of extensions paving the path towards its use in real-time robotics tasks.
Following recent work, we utilize a nonlinear predictor based on Gaussian kernels to represent the relationship between input and output data. We propose a damped Gauss–Newton method that enables real-time control by efficiently exploiting the least-squares structure of the control problem. In addition, we introduce a hybrid buffer management strategy that incorporates informative online data while retaining relevant offline data, allowing the predictor to account for changes in the dynamics. We demonstrate the tracking performance and computational suitability of the
proposed method in MuJoCo using a Franka Research 3 arm pushing a block across surface, without prior knowledge of its changing friction values.
introduction:
Robotic systems increasingly operate in settings where an accurate model of the environment is difficult to obtain. Contact, friction, and actuator dynamics can introduce behaviors that are expensive to model and identify, particularly when a robot interacts with previously unseen objects or surfaces [1]. Data-driven control is a control paradigm that either identifies a system model from measured data and subsequently uses it to determine control actions (indirect data-driven control) [2, 3], or directly constructs control actions from measured input–output data without identifying an explicit model (direct data-driven control) [10].

Large-scale robot-learning efforts have demonstrated the benefits of
aggregating diverse datasets [4]. Collecting such datasets on
physical robots, however, requires substantial time, supervision, and hardware access, while exploratory actions may result in task failures or hardware damage [5, 6]. In such cases, the controller must extract useful dynamical information from a comparatively small number of input–output measurements. Prior work has demonstrated that data-driven control can achieve accurate closed-loop performance using only a small number of training samples [7, 8, 9].

A prominent framework for direct data-driven control is Data-enabled Predictive Control (DeePC) [10]. DeePC builds on Willems’ fundamental lemma, which states that, for a controllable linear time-invariant (LTI) system driven by a sufficiently persistently exciting input, the columns of a Hankel matrix constructed from one measured trajectory span all finite-length trajectories of the system [11]. DeePC embeds this data-based trajectory
representation into a constrained finite-horizon optimization problem and solves it in a receding-horizon manner without explicitly identifying a state-space model.

Despite extensive developments in the control community, DeePC has only recently begun to receive attention for robotic systems. Existing studies have demonstrated that DeePC can achieve effective closed-loop
control in several robotic settings, including trajectory tracking in aerial
robotics [12], soft-robot
control [13], and simulated robotic-arm tasks [14]. Although these studies demonstrate its practical potential beyond strictly linear systems, the trajectory parameterization underlying standard DeePC is exact only for controllable linear time-invariant systems. Its application to nonlinear robotic systems therefore commonly relies on locally linear representations constructed around the current operating condition [15], or on lifting the measured variables into a feature space in which the nonlinear dynamics admit an approximately linear representation [16].

A more recent extension, Robust and Kernelized DeePC
(RoKDeePC) [18], addresses nonlinear behavior
differently by representing the multistep input–output mapping in a
reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) [17]. Kernel
evaluations measure similarity between recorded trajectories and provide an
implicit representation of the nonlinear multistep predictor without
constructing an explicit nonlinear state-space model or selecting a
finite-dimensional set of lifting functions. RoKDeePC embeds this kernelized predictor directly into a constrained receding-horizon control problem. However, the resulting optimization is nonconvex and requires more computational effort compared to DeePC. Furthermore, the original formulations of DeePC and RoKDeePC use a fixed offline dataset, and its computational cost increases as that dataset (buffer) grows. To address these limitations, we introduce RoKON, an adaptive kernelized
DeePC framework designed for real-time control under changing dynamics.
RoKON retains the nonlinear dependence of the Gaussian kernel on the future inputs and updates a fixed-capacity hybrid data buffer using informative online measurements. We evaluate RoKON on a robotic pushing task across surfaces with varying friction. The contributions of this work are threefold:

We propose a damped Gauss–Newton method to solve the nonconvex RoKDeePC problem efficiently. Compared with the original projected-gradient method used in RoKDeePC, our method exploits the least-squares structure of the control problem, making it significantly faster.

We introduce a hybrid data buffer strategy in which a small offline recorded dataset initializes a fixed-capacity buffer and online trajectories progressively replace a subset of prior data. The buffer admits informative samples only, allowing the predictor to adapt to changing friction surfaces while maintaining bounded memory and computation.

We validate RoKON in MuJoCo simulation on a robotic pushing task under varying friction conditions, and show favorable performance compared with MPC and state-of-the-art data-enabled predictive control baselines.

1. We propose a damped Gauss–Newton method to solve the nonconvex RoKDeePC problem efficiently. Compared with the original projected-gradient method used in RoKDeePC, our method exploits the least-squares structure of the control problem, making it significantly faster.

2. We introduce a hybrid data buffer strategy in which a small offline recorded dataset initializes a fixed-capacity buffer and online trajectories progressively replace a subset of prior data. The buffer admits informative samples only, allowing the predictor to adapt to changing friction surfaces while maintaining bounded memory and computation.

3. We validate RoKON in MuJoCo simulation on a robotic pushing task under varying friction conditions, and show favorable performance compared with MPC and state-of-the-art data-enabled predictive control baselines.

title: Model-Aware Generation of Safety-Critical Scenes for Robust End-to-End Driving via Distilled Planner Surrogates
authors: Khaled M. Seyam(1),Julian Wiederer(2),Samar Fathalah(1),Markus Braun(2),Bin Yang(1) ((1) University of Stuttgart, Germany, (2) Mercedes-Benz AG, Germany)
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
End-to-end driving models perform well on standard benchmarks but collide frequently in safety-critical scenarios. We present a failure-mode analysis on NeuroNCAP which shows that 95.9% of DiffusionDrive’s collisions are planning failures despite reliable detection, pinpointing the bottleneck in planning rather than perception. We attribute this to a fundamental data imbalance, as safety-critical interactions are rare in real driving logs, so planners are hardly ever trained on them. We close this gap with a novel model-aware framework that generates safety-critical training scenes against a specific planner. Each planner is attacked at the bird’s-eye-view (BEV) level through a differentiable surrogate distilled from its own planning head. This keeps the expensive video renderer out of the attack loop.
We extract 50 scenes per planner, each pairing an attack with a safe escape trajectory that serves as the fine-tuning label.
A fully automated quality-diversity search generates both the attacks and the escapes, so that their variety is not specified by hand.
Only these scenes are rendered to fine-tune the planner, which reduces the computational cost significantly.
Fine-tuning on these scenes roughly halves the closed-loop collision rate of two planners on NeuroNCAP (SparseDrive 28.0%→\to12.2%, DiffusionDrive 37.5%→\to19.2%) while largely preserving normal driving. A cross-planner transfer experiment shows that the gain comes from targeting the specific planner. Each planner improves most on the scenes generated against itself, and DiffusionDrive fine-tuned on SparseDrive’s scenes retains only 6.7 of its 18.3-point collision-rate reduction.
introduction:
End-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving has shown strong performance on standard benchmarks, yet the models are limited by the data they are trained on.
Real-world driving datasets are heavily skewed toward normal, uneventful driving, with safety-critical interactions accounting for less than 0.03% of real-world driving time [1]. Such situations are inherently rare in naturalistic driving and cannot be deliberately staged at scale for safety, cost, and legal reasons.
As soon as these models encounter scenarios outside their training distribution, performance degrades sharply.
On Challenger, which generates physically plausible videos for adversarial scenarios such as cut-ins, sudden lane changes, and blind-spot intrusions, the collision rate of state-of-the-art E2E models increases by up to 26×\times compared to standard nuScenes evaluation [2].
While Challenger stress-tests models through video-based adversarial replay, NeuroNCAP evaluates in closed-loop, where the ego executes its own plan and failures hidden in open loop appear, on harder scenarios including oncoming vehicles, stationary vehicles, and side collisions [3].
There SparseDrive results in a collision rate of 28.0% and DiffusionDrive in 37.5%.

Since collecting safety-critical driving data at scale remains impractical, several directions have been explored to synthetically close this gap.
Video generation models such as MagicDriveV2 [4] can synthesize photorealistic multi-view driving videos.
Yet they are evaluated almost exclusively on perceptual quality metrics like FID and FVD, and their videos have so far served perception tasks such as 3D detection and tracking [5, 6] rather than planning.
Methods that do generate training data for the planner either derive it from validation failures without closed-loop evaluation [7] or simulate hundreds of thousands of scenes reconstructed from logged drives [8].
In both cases the scenarios come from existing data rather than being designed as interactions.
Adversarial scenario generation designs such interactions deliberately, but either at the state level without photorealistic rendering [9, 10, 11] or, as in Challenger [2], against the logged ego trajectory rather than against a planner.
No existing method generates photorealistic adversarial scenes optimized against a specific vision-based planner.

To locate the bottleneck behind these E2E failures, we decompose every closed-loop collision on NeuroNCAP into a perception or a planning failure by checking whether the planner detected and tracked the adversary.
In 95.9% of DiffusionDrive’s collisions, the threat is detected, so the model sees the danger but fails to react.
Targeting this weakness with generated scenes requires the gradient of a collision objective with respect to the adversary’s behavior.
For a vision-based planner, whose input is rendered video, this gradient would have to pass through the video renderer, which is computationally infeasible.
We therefore attack a surrogate instead.
We distill the target planner π\pi into a differentiable surrogate planner π^\hat{\pi}, which consists of the planner’s own planning head, copied and frozen, behind a small trained adapter that takes ground-truth bird’s-eye-view (BEV) state instead of images.
The failure analysis justifies this construction, since perception is reliable.
Gradients through π^\hat{\pi} are cheap and point at the planner’s specific failure modes rather than at a generic driving prior.
Every generated scene is therefore optimized against the planner to be fine-tuned.

Those gradients drive the attack search, steering an adversarial vehicle in BEV to maximize collision risk for the planner.
A quality-diversity search spreads the attacks over different behaviors, so the types of attack are found by the search rather than specified by hand.
A geometric solver then computes a safe escape trajectory for every scene as its fine-tuning label and rejects scenes for which no escape exists.
The search costs around 30 GPU-hours per planner, and only the 50 surviving scenes are later rendered photorealistically.
We evaluate closed-loop on NeuroNCAP, open-loop on Challenger’s adversarial replay, and on clean nuScenes to confirm that fine-tuning does not degrade normal driving.
These 50 scenes roughly halve each planner’s closed-loop collision rate on NeuroNCAP (SparseDrive 28.0% to 12.2%, DiffusionDrive 37.5% to 19.2%; Fig. 1) while normal driving is largely preserved.

In short, our contributions are:

A failure-mode analysis on NeuroNCAP showing that 95.9% of DiffusionDrive’s closed-loop collisions are planning failures despite reliable detection, which motivates fine-tuning the planning head only.

A novel differentiable surrogate of a vision-based E2E planner, built from the planner’s own frozen planning head behind a small adapter over ground-truth BEV state and validated against the real planner.

To our knowledge, the first model-aware pipeline for generating photorealistic safety-critical scenes for vision-based E2E planners. It optimizes attacks through the surrogate with a quality-diversity search, labels each scene with a geometrically solved escape, and rejects scenes for which no escape exists. With 50 scenes per planner, it roughly halves the closed-loop collision rate of two planners.

A cross-planner transfer experiment showing that each planner improves most on the scenes generated against itself, and that this benefit is larger for DiffusionDrive than for SparseDrive. The gain therefore comes from targeting the specific planner rather than from adversarial data in general.

1. A failure-mode analysis on NeuroNCAP showing that 95.9% of DiffusionDrive’s closed-loop collisions are planning failures despite reliable detection, which motivates fine-tuning the planning head only.

2. A novel differentiable surrogate of a vision-based E2E planner, built from the planner’s own frozen planning head behind a small adapter over ground-truth BEV state and validated against the real planner.

3. To our knowledge, the first model-aware pipeline for generating photorealistic safety-critical scenes for vision-based E2E planners. It optimizes attacks through the surrogate with a quality-diversity search, labels each scene with a geometrically solved escape, and rejects scenes for which no escape exists. With 50 scenes per planner, it roughly halves the closed-loop collision rate of two planners.

4. A cross-planner transfer experiment showing that each planner improves most on the scenes generated against itself, and that this benefit is larger for DiffusionDrive than for SparseDrive. The gain therefore comes from targeting the specific planner rather than from adversarial data in general.

title: MATE-BT: A Behavior-Tree-Based Framework for Hierarchically Decentralized Mission Autonomy in Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Teams
authors: Sunbeen Lee,Hoseon Gi,Jik Hur,Inmo Jang
abstract:
Multi-robot teams executing predefined missions must adapt to runtime changes and sustain mission management despite robot failures.
This paper proposes MATE-BT (Mission, Allocation, and Task Execution with Behavior Trees), a hierarchically decentralized framework that separates mission execution, allocation, and task execution.
An active onboard leader manages mission progression and team-level task assignment, with authority transferable to another leader-capable robot after failure.
Interchangeable decentralized methods resolve target assignments, while each robot adapts its local behavior through planning and acting with behavior trees.
Webots simulations and real-robot experiments demonstrate mission continuity despite new targets and robot failures, including active-leader failure.
In the physical experiments, all MATE-BT computation runs onboard.
Hardware-in-the-loop resource measurements further support onboard execution on Jetson Orin Nano and Raspberry Pi 5.
By updating only the affected layers without full-plan regeneration, MATE-BT maintained a response time of approximately 130 ms with 30 robots and 120 targets.
Comparisons of four target-assignment plugins reveal scenario-dependent trade-offs between mission completion time and total travel distance.
introduction:
Heterogeneous teams combine platforms with different capabilities and responsibilities for mission management and task execution [1].
In crewed–uncrewed operations, for example, onboard automation can support mission management on a crewed platform while uncrewed robots autonomously execute delegated tasks [2].
Such teams must sustain predefined missions despite environmental changes, platform failures, and disrupted communication with external mission management.
This calls for decentralized mission autonomy based on onboard computation and inter-robot communication [3].

Runtime disturbances can require responses at different functional levels [4, 5].
At the task-execution level, a capable UGV may suppress a newly blocking fire before continuing toward its assigned victim, changing its local action sequence while retaining the assignment.
At the allocation level, a growing fire may require additional robots, or a robot failure may require unfinished work to be reassigned.
At the mission-execution level, the team must retain the ability to manage mission progression despite robot failures.
These cases motivate separating mission execution, allocation, and task execution so that disturbances can be addressed at the affected levels.

Prior work has addressed different aspects of these functional requirements.
For example, planning and acting with behavior trees (BTs), denoted PA-BT in this paper, supports reactive robot-local behavior adaptation [6], while decentralized multi-robot task allocation (MRTA) methods coordinate assignments through local computation and communication [7, 8, 9].
Hierarchical multi-robot BTs provide a basis for organizing mission progression, allocation, and local execution [10].

We propose MATE-BT (Mission, Allocation, and Task Execution with Behavior Trees), which connects these mechanisms in a layered onboard execution framework.
MATE-BT adopts a hierarchical form of decentralization: an active onboard leader manages mission progression and team-level task assignment, while target assignment and task execution are decentralized across robots; if the active leader fails, another leader-capable robot assumes mission-management authority.

This section reviews mission execution architectures for multi-robot autonomy, focusing on how mission management, task allocation, and robot-level execution are organized.
The architectures discussed below use BTs for execution, benefiting from reactive behavior through condition reevaluation and fallbacks, as well as modular composition and subtree reuse [11, 12].
The discussion here is organized by the responsibilities assigned to robots: (1) executing dispatched actions only; (2) managing local task execution under centralized coordination; and (3) participating in decentralized coordination decisions.

In monolithic architectures, mission management, task allocation, and task execution are encoded in a centrally generated symbolic plan, leaving each robot to execute only the actions dispatched to it.
PlanSys2 [13], a ROS 2 successor inspired by ROSPlan [14], compiles a Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) plan into a BT and dispatches its actions to robots.
When a change invalidates the plan, execution requires a plan-level update and regeneration.
The work in [15] extends this structure by partitioning execution among team-specific BT executors and selecting local replanning, robot reallocation, or full replanning according to failure impact.
Despite their different recovery scopes, both approaches rely on centrally generated symbolic plans that prescribe robot actions.

These architectures assign complete tasks, rather than individual actions, and delegate their execution to robot-local BTs.
The HTN-based methods in [16, 17] derive agent-specific task plans through centralized planning or plan decomposition.
The framework in [18] centrally optimizes assignments and schedules, and that in [19] has a central unit select assignments from bids the robots estimate locally.
Despite these differences, authority over mission progression and allocation remains central, and each robot adapts only within the task it has been assigned.

In single robotic systems, [20, 21] manage mission phases or operating modes using finite-state machines (FSMs) above local BT execution, but do not address decentralized coordination among independent robots.

These architectures move at least part of the coordination authority to the robots, allowing them to participate in task allocation or delegation through local decision-making and inter-robot communication.
An early BT architecture in [10] replicates global-task, task-assignment, and local-execution trees across robots, allowing each robot to compute mission progression and team-wide assignments.
However, it does not specify how conflicting decisions are reconciled when local information differs, a broader challenge in decentralization [22], and evaluates fault tolerance analytically without simulated or physical robot experiments.

[23] retains a central mission controller but allows robots to auction prerequisite actions and extend their local BTs online.
The work in [24] distributes designated subtree execution through utility-based delegation, while [25] extends this idea with decentralized auctions for capability implementations and executing robots.
These approaches distribute task allocation or delegation, but either retain centralized mission management or do not specify how mission management continues after the loss of its executing component.

The studies reviewed in this subsection evaluate their proposed coordination mechanisms through analysis or simulation without reporting physical multi-robot experiments.
To our knowledge, no existing physical demonstration integrates onboard mission management, decentralized allocation, and robot-local execution while evaluating mission continuity after the failure of either a task-executing robot or the active mission manager.

1) Layered execution with hierarchical decentralization:
MATE-BT separates mission execution, task allocation, and task execution so that a disturbance can be handled at the layer whose decision it affects.
The mission-management and team-level task-assignment functions are replicated across onboard leader-capable robots, allowing authority to transfer after active-leader failure while retaining the mission policy.
Target assignments are resolved through decentralized MRTA using local computation and inter-robot communication, while each robot adapts its behavior locally through PA-BT.

2) Interchangeable decentralized target assignment:
A common plugin interface allows several established decentralized MRTA methods [7, 8, 9] to be interchanged without changing either the mission-management or task-execution structure.
Controlled comparisons within each scenario show that plugin choice affects mission performance, with no method consistently preferred across the tested scenarios.

3) System-level evaluation of responsiveness and mission continuity:
A comparison with a monolithic baseline shows that, by updating only the affected assignments instead of regenerating the full mission plan, MATE-BT handles newly added targets and limits response-time growth as mission scale increases.
Webots simulations and four-robot physical experiments demonstrate mission continuity after either a task-executing robot or the active leader fails.
In the physical experiments, all MATE-BT computation runs onboard, while central infrastructure supplies only the communication layer and detected-target information.
Resource measurements on Jetson Orin Nano and Raspberry Pi 5, spanning real-robot and hardware-in-the-loop tests, quantify the CPU and memory overhead of onboard BT execution.
