title: EmbodiedLab: Benchmarking Embodied Agents That Act to Know
authors: Hongcheng Gao,Zelin Zheng,Alex Zhou,Jay Zhu,Shijia Ge,Yazhe Wang,Xiping Li,Jianshu Zeng,Di Wu,Xuan Shangguan,Yexing Wan,Lingyu He,Yongli Wang,Xiaohan Yu,Zhiqi Jia,Yue Liu,Bryan Hooi,Yinpeng Dong,Wentao Zhang,Sihang Wu,Xiao He
comment: Technical report. . Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Embodied agents are expected to accomplish real-world goals by deciding for themselves how and when to interact with their surroundings.
For many such goals, changing the physical state of the world is the means rather than the end: the agent changes the state of a system through interaction, observes the feedback, and explores until it either achieves the goal itself (e.g., discovering physical laws) or learns what the goal requires; it acts to know.
Manipulation benchmarks stop at acting to change, with the target state given; scientific discovery benchmarks evaluate knowing but replace physical experimentation with symbolic actions or numerical queries.
We introduce EmbodiedLab, a benchmark in which a robot must act to know.
Quantitative science experiments make this setting controllable: the parameters of the system are resampled for every instance, so the result cannot be known in advance, yet it can be scored exactly.
Across 30 experiments in five disciplines on 14 apparatus platforms, the agent receives an objective and the apparatus, chooses its own procedure, and operates a physics-based simulated laboratory, reading the instruments through its cameras.
Evaluation checks what the agent came to know, grounded in readings recorded during the episode, as well as the physical state the task requires; every experiment is verified to be solvable.
We evaluate six frontier models in their developers’ coding agents with native observation and control, with added perception and motion planning, and with manipulation skills distilled from the strongest agents.
With native control, even the strongest agent succeeds less than half the time; for every agent, most failures arise in interacting with the apparatus, and manipulation skills help weaker agents more than perception and planning.
The benchmark and its evaluation code are available at https://github.com/HexaFuture/EmbodiedLab.
introduction:
What distinguishes embodied intelligence from traditional robotics is who decides how to interact with the world [1, 2].
A traditional robot carries out a procedure engineered in advance for its task; an embodied agent is given a goal and must decide for itself what to interact with, how and when, in the environment it finds [3, 4].
Many real-world goals, such as finding out whether a wire is live, why a pump fails to start, or how to set a power supply so that it holds its voltage under load, cannot be reached by acting toward a known target.
The agent must first change the physical state of the system through interaction, observe the feedback, and explore until it either reaches the goal itself or learns what the goal requires; what it comes to know decides how it proceeds.
We call this acting to know: action whose purpose is to uncover information, with changing the physical state as its means [5, 6].
Embodied agents that couple frontier foundation models with tools and skills have begun to address tasks of this form [7, 8, 9], solving long-horizon dexterous tasks without task-specific training [10] and adapting robots to the protocols of real biology laboratories [11].

Existing benchmarks evaluate the two ends of this process apart.
Manipulation benchmarks specify the state the scene should reach and score whether the robot reaches it [12, 13, 14, 15].
Embodied agents built on frontier models are still evaluated on these benchmarks [10, 16, 17, 18], and the few benchmarks built for such agents keep the same form [8, 19, 20]; laboratory robotics benchmarks extend it to instruments and protocol steps [21, 22, 23, 24, 25].
They stop at acting to change: the target is given, so nothing has to be found out.
Benchmarks for scientific discovery do ask the agent to find something out, a hidden law or parameter, and let it design its experiments [26, 27, 28, 29, 30]; but an experiment is a text command or a choice of inputs, and its result returns as text or as an exact value, so no physical action stands between the agent and the information.
In a real task the two are coupled: how the agent acts decides what it can observe, and what it observes decides how it acts next.

Quantitative science experiments are a controlled entry point to this setting.
An experiment poses an objective about a physical system rather than a procedure: determine one of its properties, predict its response, or configure an apparatus to meet a specification.
To meet it, the agent must set up and operate the apparatus, take readings under conditions of its own choosing and analyze them, and, for a prediction or a configuration, act again on what it has learned (Fig. 2).
The physical laws involved are familiar, yet the parameters of the system are resampled for every instance, so the result must be established on the system at hand; because it is a physical quantity or state, it can be hidden from the agent and scored exactly.
The difficulty arises from the physics and the experimental method, as in a teaching laboratory.

To this end, we introduce EmbodiedLab, a simulated laboratory of 30 quantitative experiments in mechanics, electricity, optics, thermal physics and chemistry on 14 apparatus platforms, operated by a robot arm with a two-finger gripper and observed through three cameras (EmbodiedLab: Benchmarking Embodied
Agents That Act to Know).
Its task, environment and metric each follow from acting to know (Table 1).
The task states the objective, the apparatus and the rules, and prescribes no method.
The environment is open as a real laboratory is: the bench offers more instruments, tools and materials than any one method needs, every operation is physical, readings appear on scales, pointers and displays that the agent reads through its cameras or in the records of data-logging instruments, and the agent acts through a code interface on which it builds its own tools for perception, control and analysis.
The metric checks what the agent came to know: a run succeeds only if its result lies within a tolerance set by the instruments, rests on readings recorded in the same episode, and leaves the bench in the state the task requires.
The last condition belongs to acting to know: the agent must undo every change it made except those the objective requires, and so keep track of them over the whole episode.

EmbodiedLab exposes its interface at three nested levels that take over more and more of the acting while leaving the experiment to the agent, so the change in success across levels shows how much of an agent’s failure lies in acting: T0 gives camera images, robot state and joint control, T1 adds privileged perception and motion planning, and T2 adds manipulation skills distilled from the strongest agents’ successful runs (Section 3.2).
We evaluate six frontier models from five developers, each in the coding agent released by its developer at its middle reasoning setting, at T0 and T1, and the three whose runs contributed no skills also at T2 (Section 4).
Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra reach success rates of 43.3% and 40.0% at T0, the other agents at most 28.3%; for the strongest agents the stages with the lowest pass rates are knowing the result and restoring the bench, while the other agents lose most of their runs before their readings suffice.
Perception and motion planning change the success rate by at most 10 points, and manipulation skills raise it by 10 to 27 points, yet no agent that receives them reaches the strongest agent at T1.

Our contributions are summarized as follows.

A task formulation for acting to know. We formulate embodied tasks in which the agent must change the physical state of a system to find out what its goal requires, instantiate them as quantitative experiments whose objective is a property, a prediction or a configuration, and describe how such tasks are constructed and validated.

A validated benchmark. EmbodiedLab comprises 30 experiments in five disciplines on 14 apparatus platforms in an open laboratory environment, scored on the result, the evidence recorded in the episode and the required bench state. Every experiment is verified to be solvable and has its tolerance set by its instruments. We release the benchmark with its evaluation code.

Evaluation across levels of support. We evaluate six frontier models in their developers’ coding agents at three nested levels, and measure where their runs stop and what each level changes. The strongest agent reaches a success rate of 43.3% at T0; added perception and planning help little, and manipulation skills help the weaker agents most.

We formulate embodied tasks in which the agent must change the physical state of a system to find out what its goal requires, instantiate them as quantitative experiments whose objective is a property, a prediction or a configuration, and describe how such tasks are constructed and validated.

3. Evaluation across levels of support. We evaluate six frontier models in their developers’ coding agents at three nested levels, and measure where their runs stop and what each level changes. title: Resilient Decentralized Radar-LiDAR-Inertial Odometry in Challenging Subterranean Environments
authors: Moumita Mukherjee,Avijit Banerjee,Anton Koval,George Nikolakopoulos
abstract: Accurate localization in GPS-denied and visually degraded environments affected by smoke, dust, or fog remains a critical challenge for autonomous systems. While LiDAR provides high-resolution spatial perception, its performance deteriorates under particulate occlusion. In contrast, frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar offers robustness under such conditions but suffers from sparse measurements and outliers. This article presents a resilient decentralized LiDAR Radar Inertial Odometry (LRIO) framework that fuses the complementary strengths of LiDAR, radar, and inertial sensing to achieve robust pose estimation in challenging subterranean environments. At the core of the framework is an Adaptive Residual Thresholding (ART) mechanism that autonomously detects temporal sensor degradation and selectively adjusts the fusion process to minimize unreliable measurements. Building on this, a Robust Error-Tolerant Optimal Information Filter (RETOIF) is employed within a decentralized fusion architecture to integrate LiDAR-inertial and multiple radar-inertial odometry estimates in a fault-aware manner, enhancing resilience to environmental disturbances and intermittent sensor failures. The proposed framework is evaluated using real-world sensor data collected in GPS-denied subterranean tunnels under smoke-free and smoke-degraded conditions. In the smoke-free experiment, the proposed RETOIF framework achieves a root mean square localization error (RMSE) of 2.1733, compared with 2.9929 for the conventional centralized LRIO approach, corresponding to a 27.4% reduction in RMSE. Experimental results further demonstrate the framework’s ability to maintain pose estimation under smoke-induced sensor degradation, highlighting its potential for resilient autonomous navigation and mapping in challenging subterranean environments.
introduction:
Following the DARPA Subterranean Challenge [1, 2], autonomous navigation in subterranean (Sub-T) environments has become a key research focus, driving advances in perception, localization, and mapping under extreme conditions. Sub-T settings, such as lava tubes, mines, and tunnels, lack GPS and often impair visual sensors due to low light. While LiDAR and vision based methods have enabled accurate localization in many cases [3], their performance degrades severely in dense smoke, dust, fog, and precipitation [4, 5]. These environmental factors limit the reliability of LiDAR in real-world Sub-T deployments [6, 7]. FMCW radars offer a promising complementary modality, providing robust and consistent performance in poor visibility. Motivated by the complementary strengths of LiDAR and radar, this work presents a decentralized LiDAR Radar Inertial Odometry (LRIO) framework designed for resilient localization in GPS-denied and visually degraded environments. The proposed framework minimizes the limitations of individual sensors, enhances robustness against environmental degradation, and enables reliable odometry and mapping for autonomous robotic operation in challenging Sub-T environments.

Compared to the dense, structured, and low-noise observations obtained from LiDAR, radar sensors yield measurements that are sparse, noisy, locally clustered, and prone to flickering frequently. An example of this distinction is illustrated in Fig. 1. These radars provide range and Doppler velocity measurements only when relative speed exists between the autonomous vehicle and its surroundings. Moreover, radar point clouds are susceptible to multipath reflections and dynamic objects such as pedestrians [8], which introduce outliers into the measurements. Consequently, ego-velocity estimation and relative pose derived from radar data can exhibit substantial drift [9, 10, 11] influenced by factors such as sensor placement, highly dynamic environments [8], and reflections from surfaces like walls and floors. Despite these challenges, recent progress in radar perception has led to notable improvements in ego velocity and pose estimation, dynamic target tracking, and environmental mapping.

In the related community, various types of radar sensors have already been utilized for localization, each producing unique characteristics of the point cloud. These include Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radars [12],[13], Doppler radars [14], advanced 4D automotive radars [10], [11], [15] and 4D imaging radars [16]. Among these, 4D imaging radars [10], [16] often produce rich point cloud structures, facilitating pose estimation through scan matching algorithms like ICP. The estimated relative pose, obtained from scan matching algorithms, combined with velocity estimates and IMU measurements, is integrated into an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) to derive odometry information. The study in [9] suggests that a single EKF can effectively estimate pose from raw point clouds from radar sensors. Moreover, they implicitly assume smooth, reflective environments, which limits their robustness in challenging environments like Sub-T. Thus, in our previous work for RIO [17] the field deployment and datasets obtained from continuous IWR6843AoP millimetre-wave radars faced difficulties in achieving reliable pose estimation using a single EKF. Since, these radars produce point clouds with a lack of discernible structure, depicted in Fig. 1 and consist of only a few scattered points moving around the robot. That sparsity renders scan-matching algorithms ineffective, leading to complete dead-reckoning with substantial drift in such scenarios. The proposed MRIO algorithm [17]presents a novel two-stage Extended Kalman Filtering (EKF) framework, designed as a loosely coupled architecture.

The performance of Radar Inertial Odometry (RIO) is strongly affected by radar mounting geometry, field of view, and environmental conditions such as pedestrian movements, dynamic scenes, glass doors and windows, and reflective floors, all of which can degrade odometry accuracy. To overcome this drift during unknown tunnel exploration, multi-sensor fusion becomes imperative. LiDAR remains a standard modality for 3D perception owing to its accurate range measurements [18], yet its reliability declines significantly in smoke, fog, and similar adverse conditions, as demonstrated in Fig. 2. In contrast, FMCW radars maintain stable performance in dust, fog, rain, and snow due to their longer wavelengths, making them a robust complement to LiDAR. Consequently, combining LiDAR and radar enables more resilient localization and mapping by exploiting the complementary strengths of both modalities.

The LRIO framework in [13] uses a sliding-window factor graph to fuse LiDAR, radar, and IMU data, improving robustness through tightly coupled multimodal fusion. However, its batch optimization can introduce latency, limiting responsiveness in dynamic or degraded environments. The continuous-time LiDAR radar inertial odometry in [19] tightly integrates LiDAR point to plane constraints, raw IMU data, and radar Doppler measurements for improved outlier resilience, but this tightly coupled formulation increases computational cost, and its coarse to fine initialization may struggle under poor initial estimates or sensor degradation. Super Odometry [20] provides an IMU centric pipeline with a dynamic octree for efficient point organization and strong performance in challenging conditions, yet it remains sensitive to IMU drift and incurs additional computational overhead. The centralized EKF-based LiDAR radar fusion in [21] is simpler but prone to drift under adverse weather or LiDAR degradation due to its lack of adaptive degradation handling. To address these limitations, the proposed LRIO based on the RETOIF framework performs classical detection through residual generation, and adaptive thresholding for detection of outliers and eliminates these outliers through the FROIF framework [22]. This enables reliable selection of the most probable measurements for downstream fusion, resulting in accurate and robust pose estimation.

Robust state estimation in multi-sensor fusion requires effective handling of sensor anomalies. While centralized fusion mitigates persistent anomalies via covariance tuning, it cannot adapt to temporal sensor failures. This is evident in LiDAR–Inertial Odometry (LIO), where dense smoke causes localized and temporary degradation in mapping and localization. Due to its limited ability to rapidly adjust covariance during such short-term disruptions, centralized fusion is less effective. In contrast, decentralized fusion dynamically adapts covariance based on sensor reliability, enabling robust handling of transient failures. Prior works [23, 24, 22, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29] consistently demonstrate its superior resilience and performance.

In decentralized fusion [22, 30, 31], failure detection and isolation rely on thresholding to identify sensor-induced inaccuracies. Adaptive thresholding enables real-time performance monitoring, distinguishing nominal from degraded behaviour and autonomously rejecting inaccurate measurements. Multi-layer fusion architectures [30] further enhance reliability, with early layers performing complementary detection [26, 27] and subsequent layers isolating faults [22]. Thresholding thus remains central to robust anomaly detection and decision-making. A major limitation of fixed, preconfigured threshold based schemes is their assumption that optimal operational thresholds are known in advance. In practice, such predefined values are often suboptimal, as no single constant threshold can reliably accommodate all scenarios across a dataset. Even with well-chosen initial thresholds, continuous adaptation is required to reflect changing conditions of system dynamics. Most decentralized fusion methods rely on covariance based metrics derived from the innovation vector of the Kalman filtering [32, 33]. Although these metrics capture changes caused by sensor degradation, they cannot determine the temporal duration of failure, a limitation noted in prior work [26, 27, 34]. Another Residue analysis algorithms typically use statistical tests such as the t-test or Chi-square tests. However, these statistical methods depend on batch processing. Rather than relying on fixed thresholds derived from historical data, the proposed decentralized LiDAR radar fusion approach employs adaptive thresholding to assess sensor degradation through statistical evaluation of residuals. The Adaptive Residual Thresholding (ART) framework determines thresholds in real time using instantaneous residual information, without dependence on accumulated data. Consequently, the proposed Robust Error-Tolerant Optimal Information Filter (RETOIF) is well-suited for online implementation, eliminating reliance on batch processing and reducing latency associated with conventional statistical methods.

In contrast to existing state of the art methods, this article presents a novel Resilient Complementary fusion LRIO based localization, enabling robust pose estimation in GPS-denied, visually degraded subterranean environments. By tightly fusing complementary sensing modalities. The proposed framework maintains accurate localization, particularly under severe smoke conditions where LiDAR reliability degrades. The key contributions of this work are as follows:

This article proposes a decentralized multi-sensor fusion architecture that integrates LiDAR inertial odometry from a 3D Velodyne LiDAR and four heterogeneous FMCW TI IWR6843AOP radars using the RETOIF framework. By fusing these five complementary sources of measurement with different modalities in a decentralized manner, the proposed RETOIF algorithm improves pose accuracy and robustness through cross-modal sensing synergy.

A novel adaptive thresholding scheme is introduced to autonomously detect temporal sensor degradation using the residual of maximum likelihood state estimates.

In addition to providing reliable pose estimates for autonomous navigation, the proposed LRIO framework also enables the construction of a global map by transforming radar body-frame point clouds into a global reference frame.

For performance analysis of the proposed method, a series of representative experiments in real Subterranean terrain were conducted using a Pioneer 3-AT ground robotic platform equipped with LiDAR, radar, and IMU sensors. The platform was tested in three distinct scenarios within a GPS-denied subterranean environment: (a) No smoke scenario (b) mild smoke scenario, and (c) dense smoke scenario. All experiments were carried out along identical trajectories within the same environment to ensure consistent conditions for assessing the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. Experimental results and comparison with centralized fusion have demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed decentralized approach.

title: VisGeo-PipeTrack: A Visual Geometric Servo Control Framework with MPC-RCAPID Control for UAV-Based Dynamic Pipes Tracking
authors: Zhenyang Gao,Jianlin Chen,Yang Yu,Honghao Shan,Jiale Gao,Ziyan Jia
comment: Submit to IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems IEEE TITS
abstract: While unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly deployed for pipeline inspection, prevailing research predominantly assumes static pipes. In real-world industrial environments, pipes often exhibit dynamic movements, such as vibrations. This imposes more stringent requirements on UAVs’ adaptive control and computational efficiency than in static scenarios. Therefore, this paper proposes a servo control framework named VisGeo-PipeTrack, which utilizes geometric constraints to enable UAV tracking of dynamic pipes. To achieve efficient UAV positioning, YOLOv5 is employed to detect labels on the pipe. The positions are derived from visual geometric constraints based on these detected labels to enable precise localization. To address tracking control challenges, a model predictive control based real-time corrected adaptive PID (MPC-RCAPID) controller is proposed. This controller employs the Recursive Least Squares method for real-time model estimation and integrates rolling horizon optimization to dynamically adjust PID parameters. Experiments conducted on both the AirSim simulator and the Tello UAV platform validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Simulation comparisons with standard PID, fractional-order PID, adaptive PID, and fuzzy PID demonstrate that MPC-RCAPID achieves the shortest settling time (3.26 s) and the lowest average tracking error (3.52%). In physical experiments on the Tello platform, compared with standard PID control, MPC-RCAPID reduces the average tracking error by 55.52%, 26.72%, and 26.52% across the three test dimensions. These results demonstrate that VisGeo-PipeTrack facilitates efficient autonomous tracking in dynamic pipe environments.
introduction:
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), owing to their high maneuverability and compact size, have emerged as a core technology for autonomous inspection within confined spaces, including industrial pipes and ventilation ducts [1] [2]. They are primarily useful in overcoming the accessibility constraints faced by human personnel and ground-based robotic systems, thereby providing critical support for industrial inspection tasks.

Inspections within confined spaces present challenges intrinsic to such environments, including limited volume, poor lighting, and aerodynamic disturbances [3] [4]. These characteristics impose stringent demands on UAV systems, particularly regarding positioning accuracy, attitude control robustness, and interference resistance [5]. Beyond these requirements, confined operational spaces often present dynamic changes, such as vibration in industrial piping systems. It imposes additional demands on system stability and adaptive control. Such dynamic changes induce variations in the pipeline’s position, thereby increasing the risk of in-flight collisions for the UAV[6]. However, extant research lacks effective solutions for UAV flight within dynamic pipes. Targeted technological innovation is therefore imperative to achieve breakthroughs for UAV operations in these environments.

Extensive research has developed effective solutions for UAV navigation within static pipeline environments. Current systems are typically designed with the assumption of fixed positions and lack mechanisms to respond to dynamic positional changes. Wang et al. proposed an autonomous flight system integrating virtual omnidirectional perception with airflow disturbance planning [7]. Their system enables navigation in static tunnels as narrow as 0.5m in diameter, including those with complex cross-sections. However, it assumes fixed tunnel geometry and position, neglecting inherent tunnel motion. Zhao et al. developed an H-shaped tilt-rotor quadcopter with a disturbance observer and fixed-time sliding mode control for stable [8]. The quadcopter performs high-angle flights in static narrow passages. It is effective for fixed environments like rubble but lacks adaptation to passage displacement. Martin et al. used a robotic platform to characterize duct aerodynamics and achieved stable hovering in a static 35cm duct via neural network localization [9], yet their work does not account for dynamic effects like duct vibration or translation. Xie et al. employed deep reinforcement learning to traverse static gaps at tilt angles up to 60∘60^{\circ}, but the gap properties were predefined and unchanging[10]. Chen et al. implemented a reinforcement learning strategy for real-time attitude adjustment in response to static gaps, with the dynamic response limited to the UAV’s own pose [11]. Wang et al. introduced a velocity planning method optimizing perception and aerodynamic stability in static tunnels, but the method does not incorporate mechanisms for tunnel dynamics[12]. In summary, existing control strategies universally presuppose static environments. When dynamic motion occurs in pipes, current methods lack the capability to update positional references and control targets in real time. It results in accumulating state estimation errors and lagging control responses, which consequently elevate collision risk. This gap restricts the practical deployment of UAVs in dynamic confined spaces and thus underscores the necessity for an efficient control framework.

To address the above challenges, this paper proposes a servo control framework, named VisGeo-PipeTrack, for UAV-based dynamic pipes tracking based on visual geometry. The structure of the control framework is shown in Fig. 1, which is characterized by two technical contributions:

A lightweight visual positioning system is realized through YOLOv5 label detection and geometric constraint resolution [13]. It employs YOLOv5 to detect labels attached to the pipe. The geometric intersections derived from these detected labels serve as target points for UAV tracking. This strategy ensures positioning accuracy while reducing computational overhead, thereby improving the UAV’s dynamic response [14].

A lightweight visual positioning system is realized through YOLOv5 label detection and geometric constraint resolution [13]. It employs YOLOv5 to detect labels attached to the pipe. The geometric intersections derived from these detected labels serve as target points for UAV tracking. This strategy ensures positioning accuracy while reducing computational overhead, thereby improving the UAV’s dynamic response [14].

A model predictive control-based real-time corrected adaptive PID (MPC-RCAPID) control strategy. It consists of three integrated components: (1) Tracking error prediction through model predictive control (MPC); (2) Real-time model parameter estimation via the recursive least squares (RLS) algorithm [15]; (3) Online PID parameter optimization in rolling time domain. This integration resolves limitations of standard PID controllers with fixed parameters and insufficient adaptability.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section II introduces the basic technologies (YOLOv5 target detection algorithm, PID controller and dynamic pipes movement). Section III elaborates the pipe localization method based on visual geometric constraints. Section IV presents the design principle of the MPC-RCAPID control strategy. In Section V, the performance of the proposed framework is verified by simulation and physical experiments. Section VI concludes the paper and looks forward to future research directions.

title: Reward-Guided RRT* for Budgeted Task and Motion Planning
authors: Vinícius Araújo de Oliveira,Gabriel Ferreira Mendes Lourenço,Paulo L. J. Drews-Jr,Armando Alves Neto,Douglas G. Macharet
abstract: Robotic missions involving spatially distributed tasks often require jointly selecting rewarding locations and planning feasible motions under limited travel budgets. This paper proposes Reward-Guided RRT*, a new sampling-based framework that constructs a budget-feasible mission through a sequence of locally joint task-selection-and-motion-planning stages, evaluated directly in the continuous state space, without requiring a precomputed task-transition graph. The method incrementally builds a mission using reward-guided RRT* searches, while a return-feasibility procedure ensures that each selected task can be visited without violating the mission budget. Experiments with increasing obstacle complexity and number of tasks show solutions comparable to VNS-PRM* while requiring substantially fewer sampled states. We also extend the framework to Dubins steering and evaluate it in CoppeliaSim with a scaled car-like robotic platform, demonstrating its ability to incorporate vehicle kinematic constraints.
introduction:
Many robotic applications require an autonomous vehicle to perform a collection of spatially distributed tasks while operating under limited resources. Examples include inspection, environmental monitoring, search and rescue, and data collection. In these scenarios, the vehicle must simultaneously determine where to perform tasks and how to move between them. Visiting additional task locations may increase the mission reward, but it also consumes the travel budget and can make it impossible to reach the final destination. This coupling between discrete task selection and continuous motion planning becomes particularly challenging in environments with obstacles, nonholonomic constraints, or other motion constraints.

In this context, the Orienteering Problem (OP) [1] provides a natural abstraction for this class of missions. Given a set of reward-bearing locations and a limited travel budget, the objective is to select and visit a subset of locations that maximizes the collected reward (Fig. 1). Classical OP methods, however, assume that the underlying graph and its travel costs are available beforehand [2]. In Robotics, building such a graph may require a large number of pairwise motion-planning queries and may provide only a discrete approximation of the continuous state space. Moreover, task selection and motion planning are typically treated as separate stages, despite their strong interdependence.

This paper investigates an alternative sampling-based scheme in which promising task locations and feasible motions are discovered jointly. Rather than first constructing a complete roadmap and subsequently solving a discrete OP, we incrementally grow a search tree from the initial state while directing exploration toward reward-bearing locations. Each branch represents a feasible partial mission, including both a continuous path and the set of tasks visited along it. The resulting tree therefore serves as an implicit representation of the relevant task-transition graph.

This formulation offers a natural advantage over roadmap-based approaches, such as the Probabilistic Roadmap Method (PRM), for single-mission budgeted planning [3]. PRM is well suited to multi-query motion planning, but its roadmap construction generally separates the exploration of the state space from the subsequent task-selection process. In contrast, RRT-based approaches grow directly from the current mission state and can incorporate motion feasibility and constraints during expansion. Collision avoidance, vehicle kinematics, nonholonomic motion, and other local feasibility conditions can be directly enforced when generating each tree edge [4]. Furthermore, the tree can maintain the accumulated travel cost and explicitly account for the cost required to reach a prescribed terminal state or return to the initial state. This enables task selection and motion feasibility to be evaluated within a unified incremental planning process.

Here we propose the Reward-Guided RRT*, a sampling-based approach for budgeted task and motion planning with predefined rewards. Rewards are associated with specific task locations and are collected only when those locations are visited. Tree expansion is biased toward promising unvisited tasks, while the accumulated travel cost and terminal feasibility are explicitly considered. RRT* [5] rewiring is used to improve the motion cost of promising branches, allowing the planner to discover increasingly efficient paths and potentially visit additional reward-bearing locations within the available budget. The approach can support both fixed-goal missions and closed-circuit missions in which the vehicle must return to its initial state.

title: Labference: Benchmarking the Reasoning-Action Connection in Robotic Laboratories
authors: Shitong Liu,Jingwei Zhang,Sheng Lian,Xinyu Zhuang,Kaiwen Guo,Quan Liu,Chunhai Zhao,Jiaxin He,Fan Yang,Manli Tao,Tingyu Yuan,Jinqiao Wang,Hongwei Shi,Chaomin Guo,Xiao-jing Liu,Xiangyu Zhu,Zhuang Xiong,Feichan Yang,Chaoyang Zhao,Zhiyong Liu
abstract: Realizing Embodied AI for Science requires robots to translate experimental goals into reliable physical procedures, reducing hazardous and repetitive human work while generating evidence for scientific discovery. Although language-based planning and learned manipulation provide complementary capabilities, their integration requires robots to adapt subsequent operations to actual execution outcomes. For example, an unsuccessful placement changes what must be done next, even when the experimental goal remains unchanged. Existing benchmarks assess planning, manipulation, and laboratory workflows through task completion and reasoning or execution metrics; however, aggregate performance leaves the connection between outcome-dependent choices and physical execution unresolved. To address this evaluation gap, we introduce Labference, a benchmark for evaluating how observed physical outcomes guide subsequent choices and how those choices translate into robotic laboratory actions. Its evaluation protocol is designed to test outcome-dependent behavioral adaptation through controlled evidence variations, while independently measuring operation selection, physical execution, and task completion. Matched Oracle-assisted continuations from shared checkpoints then assess which forms of support improve subsequent choices and task completion. Initial weighing evaluations reveal target-selection errors in the tested VLA policies despite successful object transfers, whereas GPT-driven control achieves correct selection but encounters execution failures and substantial computation costs. Together, these findings highlight the need to connect task-appropriate reasoning with reliable, timely action. By making this connection measurable and diagnosable, Labference supports targeted improvements toward autonomous experimentation for Embodied AI for Science.
introduction:
Autonomous laboratories promise to reduce hazardous, repetitive human work and accelerate scientific exploration by connecting experimental design, physical execution, and the interpretation of results. Realizing this promise requires reliable handling of samples, reagents, and instruments, often around chemicals, heated vessels, and moving equipment where sustained precision and attention are essential. Laboratory automation can reduce hands-on exposure and repetitive workload while increasing throughput [1, 2]; the longer-term goal is a laboratory that selects experiments, carries them out, and uses the resulting evidence to guide its next investigation [3, 4]. For that cycle to produce meaningful scientific evidence, the robot must preserve experimental requirements throughout the physical procedure and adapt when an operation produces an unexpected result.

Progress in experimental planning and robot control provides complementary foundations for this goal. For example, Coscientist has demonstrated synthesis planning, instrument programming, and experiment optimization with tool support [5], while vision-language-action policies such as RT-2 map visual observations and instructions to robot actions across varied manipulation settings [6]. Systems also connect these capabilities directly: SayCan grounds language-based skill selection in robotic affordances, and RoboChemist combines multimodal planning, visual targets, and execution monitoring for chemical procedures [7, 2]. Although these advances establish routes from high-level requirements to physical action, an attempted operation can leave the scene in a state different from the one the plan assumed. As objects move and measurements change, the robot must therefore use the observed outcome to determine what remains to be done and guide its next action accordingly.

The ability to execute a skill thus differs from the ability to apply it appropriately: the same grasp-and-insert motion can satisfy or violate a procedure depending on the selected tube, destination, and timing. Geometric grounding methods such as VoxPoser and ReKep translate language and visual evidence into spatial objectives or manipulation constraints [8, 9]; when an outcome changes the required operation, the system must also revise the objective guiding those constraints. Laboratory autonomy therefore involves two coupled feedback loops: measurements guide the next experiment, while manipulation outcomes guide the next operation within it [10, 11]. Both depend on selecting appropriate operations and executing them while maintaining sample identity, meeting geometric tolerances, and respecting instrument timing and procedural dependencies [12, 13].

For instance, when loading two equal-mass tubes into opposite centrifuge slots, the destination of the second tube depends on where the first tube actually settles. If the first tube enters a different slot from the intended one, the second destination changes; if insertion fails, the robot must complete that placement before advancing. The same dependence appears in feedback weighing: for a 200 g target, a stable reading of 150 g calls for adding 50 g, whereas a reading of 180 g calls for 20 g. Because a weight that misses the pan leaves the load unchanged, the next adjustment must follow the measured result rather than the attempted placement. In both cases, the robot must apply a procedural rule to an observed outcome and direct its manipulation skill to the resulting target.

Where loading and weighing use current occupancy or readouts, sample retrieval additionally depends on an earlier observed result. For example, if a colleague or another robot moves a rack after a tube has been placed, an instruction to retrieve that tube still refers to the same sample even though its world position has changed. Among visually identical tubes, successful retrieval therefore requires remembering the sample’s actual local slot and locating that slot in the rack’s current pose. Since grasping a neighboring tube can succeed physically while violating the procedure, retrieval evaluation must distinguish the remembered target association, its current localization, and the execution of the grasp.

Across these examples, the reasoning–action connection has a concrete meaning: commands must preserve the selected object, destination, quantity, and timing, while subsequent choices must reflect the observed result. A changed pose calls for updated motion, a failed placement calls for recovery, and confirmed progress enables the next operation. Evaluating this connection addresses a central requirement of Embodied AI for Science: turning experimental plans into physical procedures that satisfy their requirements and produce interpretable outcomes.

These operational demands create a corresponding measurement problem. Chemistry3D, AutoBio, LabUtopia, Labimus, and LabDex establish foundations in scientific simulation, instrument interaction, dexterity, quantitative precision, and extended workflows [14, 12, 15, 16, 17], while LABSHIELD examines hazard perception and safety-critical planning [18]. Reasoning benchmarks further study plan adaptation, history-dependent manipulation, and decision-making interfaces [19, 20, 21]. Although these evaluations characterize important aspects of laboratory competence, deployment also requires understanding how outcome interpretation, operation selection, and execution work together: does a changed physical outcome lead to the required change in choice, and does that choice guide successful manipulation? Aggregate completion scores combine wrong-target selection with failed execution, whereas isolated interface scores leave their downstream effects unresolved. Addressing this gap requires controlled changes to physical evidence and targeted support within the same procedure, so that both the adaptation of choices and their consequences can be measured.

Addressing this gap calls for three connected measurements. To test evidence use, the same goal and rule must require different choices after different outcomes; controlled variations distinguish this adaptation from repetition of a predictable sequence [22]. Once a choice is identified, choice and execution must be recorded separately so that selecting the wrong slot and failing to insert into the correct slot remain distinct outcomes. To make the diagnosis actionable, matched support conditions must then test what changes when state recognition, operation selection, localization, or execution receives assistance. Common physical checkpoints connect these measurements: they fix the starting condition, identify the tested interface, and expose the consequence of support during continued manipulation.

Within this evaluation, we use state-dependent reasoning to denote applying a task’s rules to current evidence and relevant interaction history to select an operation, object, destination, or appropriate waiting and stopping condition. The observable relationship between evidence and choice therefore supplies the evaluation target, while physical confirmation establishes whether the resulting action fulfilled the requirement.

We introduce Labference, a benchmark for studying this relationship during robotic laboratory manipulation (Figure 1). Each task specifies the relevant evidence, the set of legal next operations, and the physical events that confirm progress. For example, a placement advances the task once the object is released, supported, and stable, while a weighing decision uses a stable measured load. By tying progress to these events, the formulation accommodates multiple valid operation orders and grounds subsequent decisions in actual outcomes. Controlled instance pairs then preserve the goal and task rule while varying the evidence that should change the choice; online evaluation separately records the first identifiable choice, its execution, and overall completion, together with subsequent correction and recovery. This structure accommodates spatial occupancy, measured quantities, equipment states, and sample-location history across laboratory procedures.

Once a behavioral failure has been identified, the next question is which support helps the system make progress. Labference addresses this question through online checkpoints that measure state recognition, operation selection, target localization, or execution from common physical starting conditions. Matched Oracle continuations then alter one registered input or interface output, allowing the subsequent choice and physical result to be compared with the base branch. For instance, observed occupancy can provide state support, a legal symbolic operation can provide decision support, and candidate coordinate frames can provide geometry support; a reference executor can also attempt the operation selected by the system. Comparing these outcomes alongside checkpoint errors helps identify targeted improvements for further testing.

The framework accommodates both native vision-language-action policies and agents that combine these policies with other tools, applying compatible support at declared observation or execution interfaces. Across these system designs, evaluation asks whether behavior responds to relevant evidence, whether the selected operation is carried out successfully, and which support improves subsequent performance. The resulting measurements can guide targeted improvements to be tested on held-out instances, connecting the diagnosis of operational failures to the broader goal of sustained autonomous experimentation.

Initial feedback-weighing evaluations illustrate the value of measuring selection and execution together: the tested VLA policies sometimes transfer an incorrect standard weight, whereas the revised GPT-driven system selects the required weight in all ten tested trials but completes eight. Even after correct selection, drops affect completion and prolonged deliberation limits practical deployment. These observations motivate further evaluation of how action generation and recovery preserve the chosen object, destination, or remembered target association, and how efficiently the system can respond to new evidence.

Our contributions are twofold:

An online benchmark for state-dependent laboratory operations. We connect physically confirmed outcomes to legal next choices, use controlled evidence variations to test behavioral adaptation, and measure selection, execution, and task completion separately.

A diagnostic protocol connecting choices to their consequences. Shared checkpoints and matched Oracle continuations measure accessible capabilities and the downstream benefit of targeted support, supporting systematic investigation of bottlenecks in laboratory autonomy.

1. An online benchmark for state-dependent laboratory operations. We connect physically confirmed outcomes to legal next choices, use controlled evidence variations to test behavioral adaptation, and measure selection, execution, and task completion separately.

2. A diagnostic protocol connecting choices to their consequences. Shared checkpoints and matched Oracle continuations measure accessible capabilities and the downstream benefit of targeted support, supporting systematic investigation of bottlenecks in laboratory autonomy.

title: Thermal-Headroom Routing for Efficient Robot Perception in Extreme Heat
authors: Sparsh Roy,Kevin Zhou,Arhaan Shah,Shreyan Garg,Vihaan Joshi-Apte,Maxim Kudryashov,Nanda Cheruvanthala
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Performance (cs.PF)

abstract:
A robot working in a Phoenix summer runs its detector on a small
embedded processor that heats itself. Once the chip reaches its thermal
limit, the governor throttles it and every detector configuration slows
down together. Adaptive inference routers pick a model size and input
resolution per frame and react to latency, which in hot weather arrives
after the router’s own earlier choices have already heated the chip. We
model this with an RC thermal plant wired in closed loop to a
deadline-constrained router over four YOLO11 configurations, and
propose Thermal-Headroom Routing (THR), which forecasts the chip
temperature in closed form and skips configurations that would cross
the throttle threshold. Heating measured on an Apple M5 under nonstop
YOLO11 inference fits the one-node model within 1 °C, with a time
constant and thermal resistance close to the values we assumed. We test
THR on seven real traces with camera
degradation, eight ambient temperatures and 20 seeds, with Holm
correction across traces, against a latency-belief router, a
fixed-threshold thermostat, duty caps tuned offline, and a control
given THR’s own heavy-model budget. With the deadline at the large
model’s median latency and the air between 45 and 55 °C, THR never
throttles and beats the belief router by 3.9 to 7.5 percentage points
of deadline misses and 12 to 15% of energy per on-time frame on every
trace. All temperature-aware policies, THR included, lie on one
accuracy-timeliness curve set by the share of heavy-model frames, so at
one ambient on a known chip a well-tuned thermostat matches THR. The
forecast pays off when conditions move away from the ones a rule was
tuned for. A duty cap tuned at 45 °C throttles 16% of the time at
50 °C and 31% at 55 °C, and on a chip 20% hotter than assumed an
88 °C thermostat throttles up to 29% of the time, while THR,
given that chip’s measured heating parameters, stays at zero. These
results hold, with larger effects, when every decision is given one
deadline period of wall-clock time. With 25% deadline slack,
throttling costs little and the belief router wins on on-time utility. Code and
outputs are public.11

introduction:
Consider a Jetson-class module in a sealed enclosure on a robot in the
Sonoran Desert, with the air at 45 °C. If the perception stack runs
its largest detector on every frame, the chip reaches its throttle
limit in about a minute. The governor then down-clocks it, and the
small models slow down along with the large one until the chip cools
[1, 2]. In our simulations a
policy that always runs the large model goes 12.5 s without an on-time
detection at 45 °C and 91 s at 55 °C. Fig. 1 shows one
two-minute mission at 45 °C: a router that reacts to latency drives
the chip into repeated throttle cycles, and THR keeps it just under the
line.

Adaptive inference is the usual answer to a tight latency budget.
Early-exit networks and routers choose cheaper computation per input or
per frame [3, 4, 5],
and contention-aware detectors such as ApproxDet [6]
also watch the load from co-located applications. These systems react
to latency once it has risen. On a hot chip that signal arrives late,
because the slowdown was caused by earlier choices and lasts tens of
seconds. Thermal-aware DVFS [7] and thermal-aware
multi-DNN scheduling on phones [8] address heat by
controlling frequency or placement. We ask a narrower question that
matters for robots with a fixed set of detector configurations: how
should the router itself use temperature, and how much does a
temperature forecast add over simpler rules? Belief-space perception
routing [9], which this work extends, left
thermal effects out of its contention model.

Our contributions:
(i) a closed-loop model of thermal contention for adaptive inference,
in which the router’s configuration choice sets the power input to an
RC thermal node with a hysteretic throttle (§III);
(ii) THR, a closed-form rule that keeps the forecast temperature under
the throttle limit at about 7 μ\mus per frame (§IV);
(iii) an evaluation against baselines chosen to beat it: a thermostat,
duty caps tuned offline, a matched-budget control in the spirit of the
matched-input controls of [10], a deadline
sweep, and five variations of the true chip, with 20 seeds and Holm
correction (§VI); and
(iv) an account of where THR helps and where it does not. Its gain
over latency-only routing comes from rationing the heavy model. The
forecast itself pays off when the chip heats differently from what a
fixed rule assumed, and with deadline slack, throttling costs less than
rationing does.

title: RetroNav: Scene-Grounded Retrospection and Retry for Self-Evolving Lifelong Navigation
authors: Diantao Tu,Yangdong Liu,Niannian Dai,Mengqi Rong,Shuhan Shen
abstract:
Existing robot navigation methods primarily focus on isolated tasks, overlooking the need to accumulate knowledge and experience across repeated navigation episodes.
Although recent lifelong navigation methods have explored cross-task knowledge accumulation, they mainly focus on scene knowledge while neglecting historical navigation experience and its connection to scene evidence, limiting the ability to reflect on past mistakes and improve future decisions.
To address this limitation, this paper presents RetroNav, a training-free self-evolving navigation framework that integrates navigation, memory accumulation, and failure reflection. Specifically, we develop a unified memory system that connects geometric and semantic scene knowledge with historical navigation experience, distinguishing objective observations from task-dependent interpretations.
After each navigation attempt, an independent evaluator determines whether a retry is necessary. If so, a Retrospection Agent revisits historical decisions using accumulated scene knowledge and navigation records, generating an evidence-grounded retry brief to guide the next attempt.
RetroNav achieves state-of-the-art performance across five navigation benchmarks.
Our method will be open-sourced at https://github.com/3dv-casia/RetroNav.
introduction:
Most existing robot navigation research focuses on isolated navigation tasks. In practical applications, however, robots often operate in the same environment over long periods, repeatedly performing navigation tasks and encountering familiar places and objects.
Each navigation episode, whether successful or not, may provide valuable environmental information for future tasks. Therefore, navigation systems should not only complete individual tasks but also accumulate knowledge and experience to reduce repeated exploration and improve subsequent decisions.

Recent studies have begun to investigate lifelong Navigation, exploring how robots can leverage historical information across tasks [18, 16, 39, 11, 46].
Existing methods primarily focus on accumulating scene knowledge, such as geometric structures, semantic information, and visual observations, while largely overlooking navigation experience, including how tasks were interpreted and decisions were made.
However, navigation failures may arise not only from insufficient environmental knowledge but also from incorrect interpretations or decisions.
For example, a robot may have already observed the correct target location but choose a wrong direction due to misinterpreting the instruction. Simply retaining scene knowledge cannot reveal such decision errors, while reusing previous decisions may repeat them. Therefore, effective lifelong navigation requires associating historical decisions with their underlying scene evidence, enabling navigation experience to be revisited and reused.

We argue that effective lifelong navigation requires integrating scene knowledge with historical navigation experience.
Scene knowledge captures the geometric and semantic structure of the environment, providing reusable information for future navigation. Navigation experience records how previous tasks were interpreted and executed, enabling robots to revisit historical decisions and reflect on potential errors.
By associating navigation experience with scene evidence, robots can continuously improve their navigation behavior through knowledge accumulation and failure reflection.

To this end, we propose RetroNav, a training-free self-evolving navigation framework that integrates navigation execution, memory accumulation, and failure reflection into a unified system, as illustrated in Fig. 1.
At each navigation step, the View Selection Agent interprets navigation instructions and selects a direction, while the Waypoint Selection Agent determines a suitable waypoint from geometrically feasible candidates.
Meanwhile, a Memory Builder accumulates scene knowledge from visual and geometric observations, while preserving navigation experience that captures historical decisions, their reasoning, and supporting scene evidence.
By linking scene knowledge with navigation experience, the unified memory supports both future navigation and retrospective reasoning. After each navigation attempt, an independent Evaluator assesses the navigation outcome and determines whether a retry is necessary. If so, a Retrospection Agent re-examines previous decisions using accumulated scene knowledge and navigation experience, generating an evidence-grounded Retry Brief to guide the next attempt.

Our contributions are threefold:

We propose RetroNav, a training-free self-evolving navigation framework that integrates navigation, memory accumulation, and failure reflection for lifelong navigation.

We develop a unified memory system that associates scene knowledge with historical navigation experience, enabling knowledge reuse and evidence-grounded reflection.

We introduce an evaluation-driven retry mechanism that reflects on historical decisions using accumulated scene knowledge and navigation experience to guide subsequent attempts.

1. We propose RetroNav, a training-free self-evolving navigation framework that integrates navigation, memory accumulation, and failure reflection for lifelong navigation.

2. We develop a unified memory system that associates scene knowledge with historical navigation experience, enabling knowledge reuse and evidence-grounded reflection.

3. We introduce an evaluation-driven retry mechanism that reflects on historical decisions using accumulated scene knowledge and navigation experience to guide subsequent attempts.

title: How Tuning, Reference Preview, Actuator Modeling, and Fallback Policies Change Quadrotor Controller Comparisons: A Reproducible Simulation Study
authors: Xuan-Quy Dao,Le-Minh Nguyen,Ngoc-Bich Le
comment: . Reproducible simulation study of quadrotor controller benchmarking
abstract: Quadrotor controller comparisons commonly report a single tracking error, although the resulting ranking also depends on tuning effort, reference information, actuator prediction, optimizer fallback, and command timing. We quantify these effects for cascade PID, hover LQR, boundary-layer sliding-mode control (BL-SMC), linear MPC with LQR fallback (LMPC-F), a preview-enabled LMPC-F, and a geometric S​O​(3)SO(3) controller on a common nonlinear plant with rotor gyroscopic coupling, motor lag, and saturation. A primary study (556 episodes at 50 Hz) combines matched twelve-candidate tuning, 400 paired evaluation episodes, and a 48-cell MPC factorial; a confirmation study (1462 episodes) repeats the evaluation on 50 fresh realizations with tuning budgets of 12, 24, and 48 candidates. A matched twelve-candidate tuning protocol changed the mean-RMSE ordering obtained with the fixed baseline settings, moving BL-SMC from last to first; the new ordering recurred on the fresh realizations, and a 48-candidate budget left it unchanged. Reference preview substantially reduced MPC tracking error and, on the figure-eight task, removed fallback activity. On an abrupt step, the outcome depended on the interplay between fallback policy, predictor, and actuator authority. Command timing also changed the outcome: replaying measured command-call delays terminated three of four nominal MPC configurations on a desktop computer and all four on a Raspberry Pi 5, whereas capping the solver at 100 iterations removed every deadline miss in the tested nominal timing profiles. Controller rankings therefore depend not only on tracking accuracy but also on the tuning protocol, reference information, fallback behavior, and implementation timing. We propose a reporting checklist covering tracking accuracy, tuning effort, completion and failure rates, fallback activity, applied-input variation, and command timing.
introduction:
Bouabdallah et al. compared PID and LQ control on an indoor micro quadrotor, where the observed differences depended on the model used for controller design [3]; they later compared backstepping and sliding-mode control [4] and extended backstepping to full position control [5]. Geometric tracking on S​E​(3)SE(3) [14] and differential-flatness-based control [15, 16] provide high-performance baselines beyond hover linearization. Kamel et al. [6] compared linear and nonlinear MPC for trajectory tracking, and Sun et al. [7] found that the relative merit of nonlinear MPC and flatness-based control depends on reference feasibility and on how the inner loop and rotor drag are handled. Time-optimal contouring MPC [17, 18] and data-driven or learned aerodynamic models [19] extend the operating envelope further. These studies motivate the present focus on implementation choices rather than on the feedback law alone.

Martini et al. [20] evaluated seven controller architectures over six missions on a nonlinear quadrotor model with motor lag and saturation. Safe-Control-Gym [21] provides symbolic dynamics, constraints, and repeatable disturbances for cart-pole and reduced-dimensional quadrotor tasks, and gym-pybullet-drones [22] offers a physics-based multi-agent environment for learning-based control. Zhang et al. [23] introduced a RotorPy-based suite for adaptive control under disturbances, uncertainty, and delayed actuation. Table 1 summarizes their documented features. Because plant models, interfaces, and objectives differ, the numerical results are not directly comparable with those reported here.

Stability and feasibility of constrained MPC are classically analyzed under exact, timely solutions [24, 25]. In practice, real-time MPC relies on fast QP solvers such as OSQP [26], qpOASES [27], or acados [28], with bounded iterations and early termination [13] or reduced-order prediction models [29]. Soft state constraints preserve feasibility, and with an exact penalty the original hard constraint is still satisfied whenever it is feasible [30, 31]; and computation delay degrades closed-loop behavior unless it is explicitly accounted for [12]. How fallback policies, solver acceptance rules, and measured delays jointly shape quadrotor tracking is rarely reported; this study makes these elements explicit and measurable. Related work in machine learning has highlighted the sensitivity of reported results to implementation and evaluation choices [32], while random and stratified sampling provide strong baselines for finite-budget hyperparameter optimization [33, 34]. The present protocol applies related concerns to classical and optimization-based flight-control benchmarking.

title: The Language of Deformation: Semantic Failure Analysis as a Prerequisite for Dexterous Manipulation of Deformable Objects
authors: Ignacio Cuiral-Zueco,David Hardman,Michele Pierallini,Erfan Shahriari
comment: . Accepted at the European Robotics Forum (ERF) 2026
abstract: Dexterous manipulation of rigid objects has reached a level of maturity where grasp stability, control, and planning strategies are successfully applied in industry and logistics. In contrast, manipulating deformable objects (cables, plastic pieces, cloth) remains far more challenging, as rigid-object methods do not account for their additional complexity. This paper identifies semantic failure analysis as a key step toward mature deformable-object manipulation and supports this claim with proof-of-concept experiments. Unlike rigid-object manipulation, where goals are well-defined in terms of criteria such as force balance and slippage, deformable-object manipulation involves a broader variety of failure modes arising from differences in materials, geometry, and behaviour. Typical failures include buckling, plastic deformation, pressure variations, and tearing. These diverse and often hard-to-detect events require distinct corrective strategies, making semantic failure analysis necessary. We define its key components and challenges and present experimental results supporting its potential as a research direction.
introduction:
A driver would not react to a brake failure in the same way as to a skid on ice. The difference lies in the semantic understanding of each event: brake failure (a sinking pedal) demands pumping the brakes, while traction loss (locked wheels) requires the opposite action of easing off them. The same principle applies to deformable-object manipulation, where failure modes differ widely in their characteristics and behaviour, each requiring a different — and sometimes non-intuitive — response.

For example, the corrective action needed to maintain a grasp on an object undergoing plastic compression differs sharply from that required when an object is about to buckle. In the first case, maintaining a tight grasp is essential, since even a slight reduction in compression may cause the permanently deformed object to slip. In the buckling case, however, the system should reduce compressive forces to prevent a sudden snap that releases the accumulated elastic energy. A capable manipulator must therefore distinguish these failure modes and respond accordingly.

By contrast, in rigid-object manipulation, explicit semantic reasoning has been less critical. Rigid-object behaviour defines a bounded problem space in which tasks, constraints, and corrective actions are described by well-established frameworks, and many strategies generalize across objects. As a result, the system itself rarely needs to classify diverse failure types.

In this paper, we argue that, given the greater variety and complexity of failure modes in deformable-object manipulation, semantic failure analysis is a necessary step toward robust and practical manipulation. After reviewing related work in Sec. 2, we define Semantic Failure Analysis for Deformable Object Manipulation (SFA-DOM) in Sec. 3 and identify the research challenges it entails. Sec. 4 describes proof-of-concept experiments that motivate SFA-DOM and support the identified challenges, and Sec. 5 summarizes our findings and future directions.

title: Zero-HLM: Generalizable Humanoid Loco-Manipulation without Real Robot Data
authors: Dianyi Yang,Mengya Liu,Zhumei Wang,Yu Liu,Xiaochen Zhang,Yixuan Li,Le Ma,Yuhang Yang,Weiqi Huang,Wei Liang,Baoxiong Jia,Siyuan Huang
abstract: Learning generalizable humanoid loco-manipulation remains bottlenecked by costly real-world demonstrations. Simulation offers a scalable alternative, but extending it to humanoids requires solving two coupled challenges: constructing scene-scale environments that are both visually faithful and physics-ready, and generating successful demonstrations under unified whole-body control. We present Zero-HLM, a real-to-sim-to-real framework that transforms smartphone captures and simulated source demonstrations into scalable training data for humanoid loco-manipulation. We couple Gaussian visual reconstruction with agentic physical scene construction to build interaction-ready digital twins with aligned visual and physical geometry. Within the environment, our motion–environment co-adaptation strategy synthesizes unified whole-body references and uses rollout feedback to restore interaction geometry when tracking deviations disrupt execution. From 45 source demonstrations teleoperated in simulation, Zero-HLM generates 4,800 physically validated demonstrations, averaging a 1.8×\bm{\times} speedup over real-world data collection. Policies trained solely on these data transfer zero-shot to a Unitree G1 across three long-horizon tasks. With GR00T N1.7, simulation-only training achieves 66.7% mean full-task success with a 20-percentage-point gain over real-data training under matched configurations. Across five generalization settings, pooled real-world success increases from 23% to 69% without additional real demonstrations. To support systematic evaluation, we establish a benchmark with nine skill stages and shared protocols for comparing models and studying data scaling.
introduction:
Humanoid robots combine mobility and dexterity with a morphology naturally suited to human environments. Recent advances in whole-body control and visuomotor policies have enabled diverse loco-manipulation behaviors [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8].
However, learning generalizable behaviors requires diverse interaction data that remain costly and difficult to collect on a physical humanoid [9, 10, 11, 12].

Simulation-based data generation offers a scalable alternative to costly physical collection, but its practical value depends on constructing simulation environments that support reliable sim-to-real transfer [13]. For humanoids, locomotion expands the workspace beyond a local manipulation area, while a moving egocentric camera observes the environment from changing positions and heights. This calls for scene-level reconstruction that preserves both visual fidelity and the physical geometry and dynamics required for interaction. Existing Gaussian-based real-to-sim-to-real methods have shown promising transfer in tabletop settings [14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20]. However, extending this paradigm to scene-scale humanoid interaction is considerably more demanding, as meshes extracted from Gaussian reconstructions can contain contact artifacts, and articulated mechanisms require additional modeling effort [15, 21].

Beyond reconstructing such environments, generating humanoid interaction data at scale remains challenging. Recent methods [10, 22, 23] simplify data generation by specifying locomotion and upper-body commands
separately. This separation can limit motion naturalness and support for
leg-critical interactions, motivating unified whole-body reference motion tracking [1, 2].
However, scaling data generation under unified tracking
presents two challenges: (i) Whole-body reference motion synthesis. Adapting source demonstrations to varied spatial configurations requires coordinated changes throughout the body while preserving task-relative interaction [24]. (ii) Execution mismatch. Whole-body controllers must reconcile reference tracking with balance and contact constraints, so precise state-by-state replay cannot be assumed [25]. Even kinematically valid reference motions may produce tracking deviations in the robot base and hands, disrupting intended object interactions.

To address these challenges, we propose Zero-HLM, a real-to-sim-to-real framework that combines visually faithful, physics-ready real-to-sim reconstruction with scalable demonstration generation under unified whole-body control.
First, inspired by recent MLLM-based agentic frameworks that produce faithful digital cousin reconstructions [26, 27], we propose Gaussian-Guided Agentic Real-to-Sim, which builds a scene-level digital twin by coupling a high-fidelity Gaussian reconstruction with an agentic pipeline that iteratively aligns the digital cousins to the real scene, using the Gaussian reconstruction as the alignment reference. We further composite the Gaussian rendering with the simulator’s rendering of the aligned scene, yielding a hybrid rendering that narrows the visual sim-to-real gap.
To tackle the mismatch between synthesized reference motions and their tracked execution, we introduce a motion–environment co-adaptation strategy for scalable data generation under unified whole-body control. Demonstration-Anchored Whole-Body Motion Synthesis combines locomotion planning with object-relative adaptation of source demonstrations, producing continuous whole-body reference motions for varied spatial configurations. Execution-Conditioned Correction then uses rollout feedback to adjust scene configurations and reference motions, restoring interactions disrupted by tracking deviations. We pair the resulting physically validated trajectories with photorealistic egocentric observations for policy training. Policies trained solely on our simulated data transfer directly to the real world and generalize across diverse scene configurations. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

We propose Zero-HLM, a real-to-sim-to-real framework
for unified humanoid loco-manipulation. It combines
Gaussian-guided agentic reconstruction with whole-body
data generation in visually faithful, physics-ready scenes.

We introduce motion–environment co-adaptation, which couples demonstration-anchored motion synthesis with execution-conditioned correction to compensate for tracking deviations, yielding 4,800 successful trajectories across three tasks at a 1.8×\times speedup over real-world collection.

We demonstrate direct sim-to-real transfer
and real-world generalization through simulation-only training.
With GR00T N1.7, simulation-only training yields a 20-percentage-point gain over real-data training under matched configurations. Across five extended generalization settings, pooled real-world success increases from 23% to 69% without additional real demonstrations.

We establish a humanoid loco-manipulation benchmark
comprising three long-horizon tasks and nine skill stages,
enabling systematic comparisons across diverse policy families under unified training and execution protocols.

1. We propose Zero-HLM, a real-to-sim-to-real framework
for unified humanoid loco-manipulation. It combines

data generation in visually faithful, physics-ready scenes.

2. We introduce motion–environment co-adaptation, which couples demonstration-anchored motion synthesis with execution-conditioned correction to compensate for tracking deviations, yielding 4,800 successful trajectories across three tasks at a 1.8×\times speedup over real-world collection.

3. We demonstrate direct sim-to-real transfer
and real-world generalization through simulation-only training.
With GR00T N1.7, simulation-only training yields a 20-percentage-point gain over real-data training under matched configurations. Across five extended generalization settings, pooled real-world success increases from 23% to 69% without additional real demonstrations.

comprising three long-horizon tasks and nine skill stages,
