title: PushAround: Collaborative Path Clearing via Physics-Informed Hybrid Search
authors: Zili Tang,Zongyuan Li,Zishao Qiao,Meng Guo
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). . Supplementary video and evaluation records are included as ancillary files. Video:this https URL
abstract:
Large vehicles in cluttered environments are often blocked by movable
obstacles, motivating mobile robot teams to clear traversable corridors.
Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) approaches often abstract obstacle
displacements while neglecting robot dimensions, obstacle mass, contact
geometry and forces, yielding physically infeasible plans.
PushAround is a physics-informed hybrid search that couples geometric
connectivity reasoning with short-horizon simulation to construct executable
clearing plans. Repeated W–clearance connectivity graph (WCCG) queries expose
frontier gaps requiring widening and rank them by estimated downstream costs.
The search generates direct or recursive pushing candidates, selecting
obstacles, directions, contacts and forces, and admits physics-evaluated
candidates.
Numerical experiments validate WCCG against standard connectivity checks and
demonstrate scaling to denser clutter and teams of up to four robots, with
robustness to simulated execution-side physical-parameter mismatch.
introduction:
In warehouses, disaster sites and urban spaces, movable
obstacles such as pallets, boxes and equipment can block large vehicles,
motivating mobile robot teams to clear traversable corridors.
Conventional path planners assume static obstacles and fail once routes are
blocked [1]. Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) creates
routes by pushing, pulling or rotating obstacles [2],
yet many methods abstract away robot dimensions, obstacle size and mass,
contact geometry, forces and dynamics, producing geometrically valid
but physically unrealizable plans. As shown in Fig. 1,
a large robot may be unable to reach obstacle boundaries while a small
robot lacks pushing force. Cooperative pushing by several small robots
offers an alternative, but simultaneous pushes can trigger chained motions
of several obstacles, introducing physical coupling that complicates planning.

NAMO extends motion planning to cluttered environments by planning obstacle
displacements through pushing, pulling, or
rotating [2, 3]. Later work considers heuristic search, learning-based local planning, physics-based rollouts, and collaborative pushing [3, 4, 5, 6, 7].
However, many NAMO formulations simplify robot geometry, actuation limits,
object mass, and contact dynamics, which can yield unrealizable plans.

Studies cover pushing mechanics and limit surfaces [8, 9], cooperative transport with robot swarms [10], multi-robot box pushing with reinforcement learning [11], collaborative pushing of polytopic objects in cluttered scenes [7], and learning-based loco-manipulation [12]. These studies focus on a prescribed object rather than multi-object corridor clearing.

Dynamics models, contact reasoning, and simulation feedback inform motion
generation: learned dynamics for humanoid
contact planning [13], multi-contact force control [14], demonstration-guided optimal control over contact modes [15], physics simulation interleaved with multi-agent pathfinding [16, 17], and learned physical priors [18, 19]. These methods typically address a prescribed target or a small set of objects. Corridor clearing instead requires choosing which of many movable obstacles to rearrange so that a larger vehicle can pass.

As shown in Fig. 2, this work introduces PushAround,
a physics-informed framework for collaborative multi-robot pushing that
constructs traversable corridors for large vehicles in cluttered environments.
Its central novelty is a hybrid search that jointly determines which obstacles
to displace and how to push them, coupling the high-level clearing sequence
with low-level pushing modes specifying contact points, directions and forces.
The framework integrates a W–clearance connectivity graph (WCCG) that certifies
vehicle passage under width constraints, frontier-gap ranking by estimated
effort, and pushing-mode generation under geometric and actuation constraints.
Guided by the selected gap, the search proposes direct pushes or recursively
clears blocking obstacles, and expands the plan through physics-evaluated
transitions that account for robot dimensions, object mass, contact geometry
and coupled pushing dynamics. Execution feedback updates connectivity and
triggers replanning when needed.

The contributions are twofold: (I) it introduces a unified framework that
couples collaborative pushing with physics-informed verification,
producing executable plans for path clearing in cluttered environments;
and (II) it demonstrates empirical gains in feasibility, efficiency and scalability over evaluated NAMO and
collaborative-clearing baselines, with robustness to execution-side physics
mismatch.

title: 3D-Force Estimation for Dual-arm Manipulation of Deformable Linear Objects via Factor Graphs
authors: Annika Delucchi,Vincenzo Di Paola,Bruno Marco Quadrelli,Matteo Zoppi
abstract:
Estimating forces acting on Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs) is challenging due to their underactuated nature. However, reliable contact estimation is crucial to precisely control them and enable safe manipulation tasks.
Differently from the various approaches presented in the literature, this work adopts a probabilistic formulation where the DLO state and sensors data are related through conditional distributions. In particular, factor graphs are used to determine magnitude, direction and location of a 3D force acting on a DLO, while simultaneously reconstructing its shape.
Since DLOs are not actuated and typically thin – like cables and wires – strain gauges and actuation readings are usually unpractical. Therefore, to overcome this issue, this work is tested using one type of sensing information only thus developing a generic technique suited for a wider variety of tasks.
Realistic tests are made by introducing noise on the measurements while the DLO follows a prescrived path in presence of external forces accurately estimated.
introduction:
Dual-arm manipulation of Deformable Linear Objects refers to the class of tasks where a slender flexible object — like ropes and cables — is guided into a desired shape by imposing a sequence of poses at its end tips. Indeed, threading, knotting and routing [1, 2, 3, 4] are just a few of the recurring movements necessary for their application in healthcare domain [5, 6, 7, 8], search and rescue [9], space applications [10] and so on. Beyond their impressive motion range, a primary motivation in studying DLOs lies in their intrinsic compliance making them well-suited for contact-rich tasks. In this context, although the physics of contact has been extensively studied in the past under both modelling and computational perpectives [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16], only recently researchers considered the contact in the field of DLOs’ manipulation [17, 18]. The explanation for this delay must be searched in the underactuated nature of DLOs which makes the contact estimation and thus their control highly complex. Therefore, we employ factor graphs [19] to foresee the contact along the DLO thus addressing one of the limitations that prevent their application in the aforementioned tasks.

Though actuated and then different11
1
            
            
          The DLO model does not include any actuation term., this approach has been applied in the proximal field of continuum robots which will provide the main reference for this work. In this context, early research focused on estimating loads applied at the robot’s tip [20, 21].
As the field further evolved, several approaches were proposed to estimate external forces acting also along robot’s backbone [22, 23, 24], combining vision-based information with other sensors, like actuation readings [25], strain gauges [26, 27], Fiber Bragg Grating [28] and laser scans [29].
Among them, it is possible to distinguish two main directions. The first formulates force estimation as an inverse problem, exploiting the kinematic or mechanical model of the robot and using sensors to infer the unknown external forces. Instead, the second adopts a probabilistic formulation, where the robot’s state and sensor measurements are related through conditional probability distributions, allowing force estimation even in weakly observable scenarios.

For the mentioned reasons, this article leverages the Graph-based method for the estimation of 3D forces acting on DLOs. Hence, without any assumption, location, direction and magnitude of the contact force are estimated simultaneously from discrete spatial information only. During the estimation, only discrete positions along the rod are assumed to be available through camera tracking, emulating a motion capture system based on reflective markers. This minimal sensing setup is dictated by the will of a practical solution, while existing approaches typically combine multiple sensing modalities [2, 30]. The use of a single type of information further emphasizes the challenge of estimating contact forces from limited measurements while simultaneously reconstructing the rod configuration.

The article is structured as follows. Section II reviews the Kirchhoff inextensible model, focusing on the proposed application. Section III introduces factor graphs and details the components for setting up the estimation problem. Section IV reports simulation results and Section V summarises and concludes the work.

title: VISTA: Active Exploration for Self-Improvement in Embodied Agents
authors: Zhang Zhang,Shengjun Zhang,Simin Huang,Min Chen,Chong Xia,Xin Fei,Yueqi Duan
comment: code:this https URL, project page:this https URL
abstract:
Agentic embodied intelligence plays a foundational role in open-ended, dynamic physical environments.
Rather than treating policy learning as an end-to-end mapping from instructions to actions, recent studies reveal that embodied systems depend not only on pre-trained foundation models, but also on harness.
Prior approaches largely treat rollouts as static logs for post-hoc reflection, producing
harness updates without autonomously testing and refining them through subsequent embodied interaction.
To address this challenge, we propose VISTA, a meta-agent framework that transforms post-hoc rollout reflection into active self-exploration for embodied harness improvement.
Specifically, VISTA maintains a harness graph that records the lineage of proposed harnesses, which enables the meta-agent to retrieve prior hypotheses, build on effective mechanisms, and avoid repeatedly exploring failed directions.
Each iteration begins from a retained harness version and its execution evidence. Rather than directly committing an update from these historical trajectories, the meta-agent actively explores in the environment.
It autonomously generates new rollouts, probes execution failures and recovery behaviors, and iteratively modifies the harness based on the resulting evidence. The refined harness is then evaluated afresh and added to the harness graph.
We evaluate VISTA on the LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin benchmarks.
Experimental results demonstrate that VISTA progressively improves task success and is more rollout-efficient than static reflection, achieving higher success rates with fewer simulator rollouts.
introduction:
Embodied artificial intelligence has emerged as a cornerstone for enabling autonomous systems to perceive, reason, and interact seamlessly within dynamic physical environments, offering transformative potential across household assistance, healthcare logistics, and industrial automation [4, 40]. Catalyzed by multimodal foundation models and large-scale embodiment datasets, learning-based paradigms have demonstrated increasingly competitive capabilities in executing atomic manipulation tasks [60, 39, 25, 3, 44, 51, 37, 55, 28].
But scaling end-to-end policies to long-horizon, multi-stage tasks remains notoriously difficult. End-to-end models suffer severely from compounding execution errors over extended trajectories, out-of-distribution generalization under perturbations, and prohibitive sample complexity when attempting to fit multi-modal, long-tail action distributions across heterogeneous task phases [1, 23].

To overcome these fundamental limitations, the convergence of frontier large language model (LLM) agents and robotics has established embodied agentic systems as a pivotal research frontier [32, 49, 22, 50, 56]. By coupling high-level symbolic reasoning and stateful tool orchestration with low-level control policies, agentic embodied architectures offer decisive advantages in managing long-horizon complexity: they facilitate modular hierarchical task decomposition, support active perception to resolve visual ambiguities, and enable closed-loop error diagnosis and autonomous recovery.
The performance, reliability, and long-horizon coherence of such systems depend not only on their pre-trained foundation model weights, but also fundamentally on their harness [54, 48].
Existing systems construct and improve these harnesses through code generation, reusable skills, and memory-guided execution [32, 49, 50, 56]. VISTA focuses on a complementary question: how can a coding agent improve an executable robot harness by acquiring additional evidence through direct interaction with the environment? Existing records do not always contain the observations or interventions needed to test a proposed explanation of a failure.

To address this issue, we propose VISTA, a meta-agent framework that unifies active environmental exploration with closed-loop harness adaptation to achieve embodied self-improvement. The meta-agent controls the development process: it selects what to inspect, which public sensing and control capabilities to invoke, and which autonomous tests to request. Evidence from these interactions guides executable harness revisions.
After development, the submitted harness is frozen and evaluated through fresh autonomous execution. Its code and evidence are retained in a harness DAG, allowing the meta-agent to retrieve prior hypotheses, reuse effective mechanisms, and explore from earlier candidates.

We evaluate VISTA on LIBERO-Pro [59], RoboCasa365 [38], and RoboTwin [9].
VISTA improves task success by accumulating executable mechanisms across development rounds. These results support harness development as a practical way to convert embodied experience into persistent changes in agent behavior.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose VISTA, a framework that departs from conventional handcrafted heuristics and static memory augmentation by framing the robot’s operational harness as an evolvable, executable control plane, realizing autonomous embodied self-improvement.

We introduce an active exploration mechanism where the meta-agent empowers the embodied system to actively gather diagnostic physical evidence, linking exploratory evidence to executable harness revisions. Furthermore, we develop a Harness Graph to track the evolutionary lineage of candidate harnesses, facilitating hypothesis retrieval, component reuse, and principled branch exploration.

We conduct comprehensive evaluations on the challenging LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that VISTA progressively improves manipulation success rates through accumulated experience, improving over the corresponding initial harnesses.

We introduce an active exploration mechanism where the meta-agent empowers the embodied system to actively gather diagnostic physical evidence, linking exploratory evidence to executable harness revisions. Furthermore, we develop a Harness Graph to track the evolutionary lineage of candidate harnesses, facilitating hypothesis retrieval, component reuse, and principled branch exploration.

3. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on the challenging LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that VISTA progressively improves manipulation success rates through accumulated experience, improving over the corresponding initial harnesses.

title: Context-dependent Runtime Construction of Safe Regions of Attraction from Design-Time Identification for Multi-Candidate Simplex Architectures
authors: Georg Jäger,Nils-Jonathan Friedrich,Norman Seyffer,José Cecílio,António Casimiro
abstract:
Deploying safety-critical cyber-physical systems requires control strategies that reconcile high performance and adaptability with rigorous safety guarantees.
Classical control strategies offer stability proofs but are conservative, while advanced optimization- and learning-based controllers achieve high performance but lack formal verification.
 rta (rta) architectures bridge this gap by introducing their own (dis-)advantages.
Safety filters use online optimization and introduce chattering, while Simplex permissiveness is bounded by the tightness of the certified  roa (roa) of its  ha (ha) controller.
Targeting this conservatism, we present a two-stage roa certification procedure leveraging contraction-based stability to establish a target set for Taylor-model-based reachability analysis.
We then treat the closed-loop system under ha control as a switched system, enabling: (a) runtime construction of context-dependent safe roa and (b) safe switching between ha candidates to optimize recovery and maximize the operating envelope of the uncertified  hp (hp) controller.
We validate this framework on a robotic path-tracking task using a three-stage evaluation:  ode (ode) simulation for theoretical verification, high-fidelity Gazebo simulation under unmodeled dynamics, and experiments on physical hardware.
Results show that the Simplex architecture maintains safety under fault injection and successfully shields a behavioral-cloning-trained hp controller.
Crucially, the decision module introduces negligible overhead (0.028 ms0.028\text{\,}\mathrm{ms} average, 4.13 ms4.13\text{\,}\mathrm{ms} worst-case), consuming under 10 %10\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of the control period.
introduction:
The deployment of autonomous  cps (cps) in safety-critical but complex and dynamic environments motivates a fundamental shift in control design.
It requires reconciling high performance and adaptability with strict safety guarantees.
Commonly, safety-critical systems rely on formal proofs to guarantee safety, which are conservative and limit capability [1, 2].
Conversely, advanced optimization- or learning-based controllers excel in dynamic environments but lack safety certificates due to their complex, black-box nature.

rta addresses this conflict by decoupling performance from safety.
These architectures monitor the system state and the actions proposed by the uncertified hp controller.
If deemed unsafe, inputs are overwritten, e.g., through safety filters or blending architectures, or control is switched to a verified ha controller to maintain a safe operating envelope as done in the Simplex architecture [3].
It permits hp control as long as the ha controller is guaranteed to recover the system.
A  dm (dm) monitors this condition, switching to the ha controller whenever continued hp execution would risk leaving the roa.

However, the practical value of this architecture depends on the conservatism of the ha’s approximated safe roa.
While over-approximation is unsafe, under-approximation forces the dm to switch prematurely, degrading overall system performance.
Existing methods address this partially.
Lyapunov and contraction analyses [4] guarantee formal safety but yield conservative inner approximations.
Reachability analysis [5] extends coverage but suffers from the wrapping effect.
Furthermore, using a single ha controller neglects the complementary coverage advantages a set of candidates can provide.

We leverage these observations for our contributions.
First, we present a two-stage procedure for certifying the roa of a controller.
A contraction-based stability analysis establishes a core roa that is used by Taylor-model reachability [6] as a target set and incrementally extended.
In both stages, we use partitioning of the parameter and state spaces to limit wrapping effects and further reduce conservatism, thereby generating a certified set of safe roa for a controller.
Along with other design-time artifacts, e.g., the maximal dwell time, we refer to this as the controller’s recovery profile ℛ\mathcal{R}.
This is used at runtime to construct the context-dependent roa, which we leverage in our second contribution.
There, we treat the closed-loop system under the ha controller as a switched system over a set of ha candidates.
This lets the dm not only switch between hp and ha modes, but also between ha candidates to optimize, e.g., recovery time.

To motivate the use of the Simplex architecture, Section II reviews the state of the art on rta architectures, where we further analyze safety filters and control blending as alternatives before considering approaches for identifying roa.
Section III then derives and discusses our main contributions.
Although use case agnostic, we use path tracking of a differential-drive mobile robot in outdoor scenarios (e.g., urban parcel delivery), with  rpp (rpp) [7] in the ha role as a running example to support explanations.
The resulting Simplex controller is evaluated in Section IV in three stages: ode-based simulation to validate the switching logic under the modeled dynamics, Gazebo simulation to analyze the prediction horizon needed under realistic dynamics, and real-world experiments on the platform shielding an  ml (ml) controller based on behavioral cloning.
Finally, Section V concludes and outlines directions for future work.

title: JevVLA: Jev-Inspired Energy-Based Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Policies
authors: Wei Wang,Wenqiao Zhang,Zheqi Lv,Zheng Dong,Yingjie Niu,Jiaqi Zhu,Jun Xiao,Chao Li,Yueting Zhuang
abstract:
Vision–language–action (VLA) policies can select among discrete candidates
for pick-and-place manipulation or generate continuous action chunks for
motion control. Improving both forms of decision making through a common
mechanism while retaining the capabilities of a pretrained policy is an
important adaptation problem. Inspired by Jev’s structured, probabilistic
decision interface, we propose JevVLA, a lightweight energy-based
adaptation framework for VLA policies. JevVLA instantiates this inspiration
by modeling the relative quality of action proposals: with the base policy
frozen, it learns a differentiable scalar energy conditioned on observations,
task context, and actions, using execution feedback, expert corrections, or
demonstration-derived preferences. JevVLA uses this single learned action
preference function in two ways: its values compare discrete candidates,
while its action gradients correct continuous actions or guide their
generation. Candidate selection and continuous control thus share one
trainable decision core.
Each benchmark uses independently trained weights and fixed input/output
encodings, while retaining the same core network with approximately 80,000
trainable parameters. On the held-out test sets, JevVLA improves task success over the respective
matched base-policy controls by 1.28, 2.31, 1.60, 1.52, and 1.28 percentage points on MetaWorld
MT50, VIMA, LanguageTable, LIBERO Plus, and CLIPort, respectively. These
results support the feasibility of a lightweight, Jev-inspired energy model
for adapting both discrete action selection and continuous action guidance.
The JevVLA implementation will be open-sourced at
https://github.com/ZJU4EmbodiedAI/JevVLA.
introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models connect visual observations and task
instructions to robot actions. By combining vision–language pretraining
with robot demonstrations, these models learn control policies that serve
multiple manipulation tasks, making the reuse and adaptation of existing
models an important direction in robot learning Kim et al. (2025a); Black et al. (2025).
However, producing a semantically plausible action does not ensure that an
operation will succeed in a particular scene: small geometric errors can
change the execution outcome Xu et al. (2026).
Further fine-tuning a pretrained policy, particularly through
full-parameter updates, often entails substantial computational costs and
additional task-specific data Kim et al. (2025a); Yang et al. (2026).
This motivates a practical question: how can lightweight adaptation improve
action decisions while retaining the action-generation capabilities of the
base policy?

This goal must accommodate differences in the action interfaces of robot
policies. Policies that predict pick-and-place actions can be adapted by
constructing a finite set of candidates and comparing their quality.
Policies that control robots through continuous action sequences can also
be adapted through corrections applied after action prediction or during
iterative generation Jiang et al. (2023); Shridhar et al. (2022); Chi et al. (2023); Black et al. (2024).
Both approaches require an assessment of relative action quality, but they
place different demands on the evaluator: candidate selection requires
comparable scores across actions, whereas continuous guidance requires
useful local correction directions in action space. We investigate how a
single lightweight evaluation architecture can support both requirements
across base policies with different native action representations.

Prior work has shown that scalar energies can represent implicit action
policies and support robot control through action optimization Florence et al. (2022).
For policy adaptation, learned value or performance estimates can select
among sampled action chunks or guide continuous action generation through
gradients Xu et al. (2026); Yang et al. (2026); Wang et al. (2026).
These advances establish the utility of action evaluation for improving
base policies. We study how to reuse the
function values and action gradients of a common scalar core to organize
candidate comparison and continuous correction within one adaptation
framework, while keeping the base policies frozen.

Jev provides an inspiration for this design through its structured,
probabilistic decision interface. Its public interface combines a state
with predefined options or scoring questions, returning structured results
and probability distributions that software can use for selection, ranking,
and branching Almeida (2026); TypeSafe AI (2026a).
This perspective motivates modeling action proposal and action evaluation
as separate components: the base policy proposes actions, and an adapter
represents preferences among them given the current observation and task
context. JevVLA draws on Jev’s public decision-interface concepts; its robotic
action energy, training objectives, and gradient-guidance mechanism are
developed independently. We extend explicit comparison among candidates to
continuous action space, using a differentiable scalar function both to
support selection and to provide local correction directions.

We propose JevVLA, a lightweight, Jev-inspired energy-based adaptation
framework (Figure 1). JevVLA takes observations, task context, and actions as inputs and
uses a conditional quadratic term together with a scalar residual network
to model action energy. Depending on the supervision available for each
benchmark, it converts executed-branch outcomes, expert corrections, or
demonstration-derived action preferences into ranking or gradient-learning
signals. At inference time, JevVLA compares energies over a finite candidate
set and incorporates the base-policy prior when available. For continuous
actions, it differentiates the same energy with respect to the action and
applies bounded corrections or guides action generation. The architectural
contribution is one trainable preference function for these two decision
interfaces: its value supports choice, and its derivative supplies the
continuous update. Each benchmark has fixed input/output encodings and
independently trained weights, while the energy core remains identical,
with 79,817 trainable parameters per adapter.

We evaluate this design on five robot manipulation benchmarks: MetaWorld
MT50, VIMA, LanguageTable, LIBERO Plus, and
CLIPort Yu et al. (2020); Jiang et al. (2023); Lynch et al. (2022); Fei et al. (2026); Shridhar et al. (2022).
These evaluations cover both candidate selection and continuous control.
After validation-set selection, JevVLA improves held-out test success over
the respective matched base-policy controls by
1.28, 2.31, 1.60, 1.52, and 1.28 percentage points.
These results provide empirical support for applying the same lightweight
energy architecture across different robot-policy interfaces.

Our contributions are threefold:

One action preference core for two VLA interfaces.
Values of a conditional scalar energy rank discrete proposals, while
gradients of that energy correct continuous actions and guide their
generation. The same trainable architecture supports both uses across
benchmarks, with independently learned weights.

Jev-inspired structured action decisions.
We make alternatives and their relative preferences explicit for
frozen robot policies, connecting action proposals to a probabilistic
comparison and executable selection rule.

Evaluation across five robot manipulation benchmarks.
Independently trained adapters with approximately 80,000 parameters
improve task success over matched base-policy controls in the specified
held-out test settings, providing cross-interface evidence for
the common architecture.

title: Learning Direct Control from Optimization for Dynamic Target Tracking
authors: Bing Sun,Yue Lin,Canhui Wen,Xin Chen,Yang Liu,Dong Wang,Huchuan Lu
abstract: Dynamic target tracking requires a mobile robot to maintain target visibility while navigating obstacles with smooth, feasible controls. Online trajectory optimization explicitly encodes these objectives but requires repeated numerical solving, whereas waypoint-based neural policies separate geometric prediction from control execution. We introduce LECO, a framework that transfers tracking optimization into offline learning of a direct-control policy. LECO predicts control sequences and maps them to trajectories through a differentiable kinematic model, allowing trajectory-level objectives to directly guide control learning. A decaying expert-guidance curriculum initializes effective tracking behavior and progressively shifts learning toward these task objectives. At deployment, a predictive safety lock checks short-horizon obstacle clearance and invokes a classical planning and control fallback when the predicted motion is unsafe or the target prediction is invalid. Across three simulated obstacle densities, LECO reduces root-mean-square linear jerk by 14.1–31.2% relative to the best competing method for this metric and achieves the highest tracking success rate, with per-cycle computation times of 4.25–5.63 ms. Experiments on two robot platforms further demonstrate tracking through indoor narrow passages and outdoor forest environments. These results demonstrate that learning direct control from optimization enables smooth and robust dynamic target tracking.
introduction:
Dynamic target tracking requires a mobile robot to keep a moving target in view while navigating the surrounding environment [1, 2]. In cluttered scenes, these requirements are tightly coupled: a collision-free maneuver may place an obstacle between the robot and the target, while maintaining visibility may require turning through narrow passages. The robot must therefore coordinate target distance, line of sight (LoS), obstacle clearance, and control smoothness under its own kinematic constraints. The central challenge is to translate these spatial tracking objectives into feasible control actions as both the target and the local environment change.

Trajectory optimization provides an explicit way to express these objectives. Optimization-based trackers account for target motion, visibility, and obstacle avoidance when generating robot trajectories [3, 4, 5], while model predictive control (MPC) incorporates motion constraints into control computation [6]. This approach requires numerical solving as observations change. Learning-based planners offer a complementary route by transferring trajectory costs into network training [7, 8]. For example, YOPOv2-Tracker learns motion-primitive offsets from trajectory costs and converts the resulting predictions into quadrotor commands [7]. Kinematics-aware learning also incorporates motion models into planning [9, 10]. These developments motivate learning tracking behavior directly in the control space of a mobile robot, so that visibility, clearance, and smoothness objectives shape the commands through the motion they produce.

Our key idea is to retain the explicit objectives of tracking optimization while moving their optimization into offline learning of a direct-control policy. A differentiable kinematic model provides the connection: it maps a predicted control sequence to a robot trajectory and propagates trajectory-level costs back to the policy. Target visibility and obstacle clearance can then guide control learning together with control smoothness, using the platform’s motion model throughout. This formulation connects what the robot should achieve in the environment with the controls it will execute.

We instantiate this idea in LECO, a framework for learning direct control from optimization for dynamic target tracking (Fig. 2). Given local geometry, robot motion, and target-relative observations, LECO predicts a future control sequence and rolls it out through a platform-specific differentiable kinematic model. Tracking objectives evaluated along this rollout jointly encourage the desired target distance, clear lines of sight, obstacle clearance, and smooth motion. A decaying expert-guidance curriculum establishes effective tracking behavior early in training, then progressively shifts learning toward these task objectives. The expert thus provides an initialization for control learning, while the final policy is refined by the quality of the motion it predicts.

At deployment, LECO executes the first predicted control in a receding-horizon manner, avoiding iterative task optimization in the neural branch. A predictive safety lock checks obstacle clearance along the short-horizon rollout before execution. When the predicted motion is unsafe or the target prediction is invalid, it invokes a classical hybrid A* [11] and MPC [6] branch for obstacle avoidance or target reacquisition. Neural execution resumes once the target prediction and clearance checks permit it and the lock duration has elapsed. This deployment strategy combines learned direct control with explicit motion checks and a fallback that continues to serve the tracking task.

Experiments validate this formulation for smooth and robust tracking. Across three simulated obstacle densities, LECO achieves the lowest root-mean-square linear jerk and the highest tracking success rate among the evaluated methods, with per-cycle computation times of 4.25–5.63 ms. In the 150-obstacle setting, it achieves an 86% success rate and a 6.32% occlusion rate. Further evaluations in dense layouts and temporary obstacle disturbances show that the neural policy supplies 88.57–95.81% of control decisions. Real-world experiments with platform-specific policies on the differential-drive Unitree G1D and Ackermann-steered AgileX HUNTER 2.0 demonstrate tracking through indoor narrow passages and outdoor forest environments (Fig. 1).

Our main contributions are as follows:

We introduce LECO, a direct-control learning framework for dynamic target tracking that propagates trajectory-level tracking objectives through a differentiable kinematic rollout to the control policy.

We develop a decaying expert-guidance curriculum for visibility-aware control learning and a predictive safety lock that combines neural execution with classical fallback for obstacle avoidance and target reacquisition.

We demonstrate improved control smoothness and tracking success across three simulated obstacle densities, and validate the framework on two robot platforms in indoor and outdoor environments.

The source code and implementation details will be made publicly available.

1. We introduce LECO, a direct-control learning framework for dynamic target tracking that propagates trajectory-level tracking objectives through a differentiable kinematic rollout to the control policy.

2. We develop a decaying expert-guidance curriculum for visibility-aware control learning and a predictive safety lock that combines neural execution with classical fallback for obstacle avoidance and target reacquisition.

3. We demonstrate improved control smoothness and tracking success across three simulated obstacle densities, and validate the framework on two robot platforms in indoor and outdoor environments.

title: Quantile-Based Command-Reserve MPC for Current-Command Gimbal Pointing
authors: Yaokun Lu,Yifan Li,Enmei Wang,Hao Teng,Pengwei Hu,Jianzhong Qiao
comment: . Supplementary hardware trial data and recomputation scripts included as ancillary files. Submitted to Journal of the Franklin Institute
abstract:
This paper studies the constrained line-of-sight pointing control problem of a
two-axis current-command gimbal subjected to mismatched mechanical disturbances.
Friction, torque ripple, current-response lag, model mismatch, and limited drive
commands make accurate pointing more challenging yet interesting. A quantile
disturbance predictor is proposed to compensate predictable acceleration
residuals and describe their remaining uncertainty, with the aid of learning
median and outer quantiles from state, command, and reference histories.
A tube-inspired model predictive controller is proposed to reserve command
headroom according to prediction uncertainty, with the aid of calibrated
radii and stage-dependent input margins. The median improves the nominal
prediction, while the radius adapts the command reserve without adding
optimization variables. A finite-horizon tube inclusion result is established
for a specified linear error model and fixed ancillary policy; its conditions
are distinguished from the approximations used in hardware. Native command
bounds and a final command limiter keep the sent commands within their
prescribed range. On a two-axis embedded platform, four controller
configurations are compared in seven repeated trials each. The proposed
configuration achieves a two-dimensional pointing root-mean-square error of
3.94±0.103.94\pm 0.10 mrad with no command-limit samples in the evaluation windows.
Its performance supports the combined use of residual prediction and adaptive
command margins in the tested operating condition. Solver times and logged
loop overruns are reported separately for the nominal 100100 Hz implementation.
introduction:
Current-command gimbals perform line-of-sight pointing in imaging, tracking,
and stabilization systems [1, 2, 3].
Their drives expose a torque-producing current command to the outer pointing
controller. The measured current follows this command through an inner loop,
and the two signals differ during transients. Accurate pointing must therefore
account for the current response while respecting limited command authority.
Friction, torque ripple, and cross-axis effects further degrade the prediction
of the mechanical motion [4, 5].

Disturbance rejection has been studied extensively for gimbals. Relay control,
for example, exploits limit-cycle behavior to attenuate exogenous torque
disturbances [6]. Observer-based approaches estimate composite
uncertainties for compensation [5, 7].
For motor servo systems, additive state decomposition separates predictive
tracking from observer-based disturbance rejection [8].
Neural-network MPC combined with active disturbance rejection has also been
validated on a robot manipulator [9].
These studies motivate the joint treatment of model correction and constrained
tracking. A point prediction, however, does not by itself quantify the residual
uncertainty used to choose a command reserve.

Tube MPC propagates bounded model errors around a nominal trajectory and
tightens constraints accordingly [10, 11, 12].
Inverse-dynamics and disturbance-observer-based tube control combines
disturbance compensation with a remaining-error tube for constrained
manipulator tracking [13]. Composite anti-disturbance tube MPC
also uses predicted disturbances in the optimization [14].
Stochastic MPC explicitly links chance-constraint tightening with separate
feasibility and stability conditions [15].
Cautious MPC uses Gaussian-process residual models and propagates their
uncertainty within a chance-constrained formulation [16].

Adaptive or learned tubes are already established directions: adjustable
zonotope tubes have been combined with neural compensation for vehicle
tracking [17]; deep quantile regression has been used to
learn trajectory tubes [18]; and learning-based rigid tube MPC
updates uncertainty descriptions from data [19].
Other tube constructions optimize polytopic shapes under configuration
constraints [20], use time-varying cross-sections
for bounded-disturbance systems [21], or incorporate
state-dependent disturbance models into dynamic tubes [22].
These approaches treat tube geometry as part of the robust-control design;
the present hardware implementation uses a calibrated residual radius to
choose command reserves and does not inherit those guarantees.
Learning error bounds can also be connected to robust constraint tightening
in nonlinear economic MPC [23]. More generally, learning-based
MPC and predictive safety filters distinguish model improvement from the
explicit treatment of constraint protection [24, 25].
Thus, the use of learning or a varying tube is not by itself a new principle.
The issue considered here is how to use a shared residual predictor for both
nominal correction and a changing command reserve at a gimbal’s current-command
interface, with an explicit account of what the deployed implementation verifies.

We learn the median and outer quantiles of an acceleration-domain residual
from recent measurements and reference preview. The median corrects a
current-augmented mechanical predictor, while a calibrated radius determines
stage-dependent command margins. The analytical tube construction and its
fixed-policy conditions are stated separately from the practical input-margin
implementation. This distinction matters because a mechanical residual label
does not establish a bound on every error of the augmented current state.

The contributions are summarized as follows.

A shared quantile predictor is developed for acceleration residuals in
two-axis current-command pointing. Our predictor is capable of providing a
median correction and a calibrated error radius from one recurrent model.
These outputs connect nominal prediction accuracy and command reserve to
the same measurement history, while their coverage is assessed empirically.

A tube-inspired MPC implementation is introduced to use both outputs
without increasing the optimization dimensions. A conditional finite-horizon
inclusion result clarifies the corresponding tube principle, and the
implemented nonlinear predictor, command margins, and safety monitoring are
specified separately. Four configurations, with seven hardware trials each,
demonstrate the tracking and command-headroom performance of the combined
scheme in the tested condition.

title: MMGNet: Multi-Modal 6-DoF Grasp Synthesis for Cluttered Scenes
authors: Rui Cao,Jia-Hui Pan,Yichuan Li,Yunfan Yu,Chi-Wing Fu,Jiangliu Wang,Yun-Hui Liu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Under Review
abstract:
Grasping is a foundational capability in robotic manipulation.
Scene-level 6-DoF grasp synthesis relies on point clouds for metric geometry, yet real-world point observations are often noisy, incomplete, and over-smoothed.
RGB images provide object-region, boundary, and appearance cues, yet two bottlenecks limit their effective use in scene representation and local grasp reasoning.
We present MMGNet, a Multi-Modal Grasp Synthesis Network that addresses these bottlenecks through hierarchical image-to-3D feature injection and rotational graspness modeling.
Hierarchical injection integrates multi-scale image features throughout 3D representation formation, while the rotational graspness jointly predicts the grasp approach direction and in-plane rotation before organizing local image-informed features through grasp-shaded grouping.
Ablation studies show that these two modules provide complementary gains.
MMGNet achieves a mean AP of 60.34 on GraspNet-1Billion with RealSense, surpassing all compared methods.
In real-world experiments with adversarial grasp objects, MMGNet improves the grasp success rate over AnyGrasp by 8.46 percentage points.
Code, models, and data will be released upon publication.
introduction:
Robotic grasping supports downstream tasks such as bin picking and packing Li et al. [2022a], Pan et al. [2024], object rearrangement Danielczuk et al. [2021], and tool manipulation Laili et al. [2022].
Scene-level 6-DoF grasp synthesis predicts executable gripper poses for objects with diverse shapes, orientations, and occlusions.
Most existing scene-level methods rely primarily on point clouds to represent the metric geometry required for 6-DoF grasp prediction Fang et al. [2023a], Fang et al. [2023b], Ma and Huang [2023], Wang et al. [2021a].
However, real-world point clouds often suffer from measurement noise, local incompleteness, and over-smoothing, while RGB images provide complementary cues about object regions, boundaries, and appearance.
Accordingly, several grasp synthesis methods have incorporated image information to improve grasp prediction Gou et al. [2021], Liu et al. [2023], Xie et al. [2026].

Nevertheless, two bottlenecks limit the effective use of image information in scene representation and local grasp reasoning.

First, some existing methods incorporate image cues through late feature fusion Liu et al. [2023] or during local-region processing Xie et al. [2026].
Consequently, multi-scale image context plays a limited role during 3D scene representation formation.
We therefore argue that such image information should be integrated throughout this process.
Second, even when image cues are embedded in the scene representation, the local representation used for detailed grasp prediction remains too coarse to capture grasp-quality differences across gripper rotations.
Existing pipelines Wang et al. [2021a], Fang et al. [2023b], Ma and Huang [2023] first use grasp-quality scores to select promising grasp centers and approach directions, aggregate nearby 3D features, and only then predict the gripper rotation around the selected direction.
Consequently, grasps that share the same center and approach direction but differ in gripper rotation are evaluated from the same local representation.
Thus, the embedded image cues are not organized according to the candidate rotation, limiting their ability to capture the corresponding grasp-quality differences.

We present the Multi-Modal Grasp Synthesis Network (MMGNet), a single-view scene-level framework designed to address these two bottlenecks.
To address the first, MMGNet introduces hierarchical image-to-3D feature injection, which aligns multi-scale image features with scene points and injects them into successive stages of a sparse 3D backbone, allowing image context to shape the 3D representation throughout the backbone.
To address the second, MMGNet introduces rotational graspness modeling to jointly predict the grasp approach direction and in-plane rotation before local aggregation.
The selected rotation then guides grasp-shaded grouping, which gathers local image-informed 3D features in the corresponding gripper frame.
Together, these designs make grasp-quality differences across rotations explicit before local analysis and organize the resulting local features according to the selected gripper orientation.

Given an RGB-D observation, MMGNet first extracts a multi-scale image feature pyramid and establishes pixel–point correspondence with the full-scene point cloud.
The aligned image features are injected into multiple sparse-encoder stages to form an RGB-informed 3D scene representation while retaining efficient metric neighborhood aggregation.
A foreground score then guides the sampling of spatially distributed grasp seeds.
For each seed, rotational graspness selects a joint view–in-plane rotation, after which grasp-shaded grouping aggregates local features in the corresponding gripper frame.
Finally, the operation head predicts approach depth and width of the gripper to produce the 6-DoF grasps.

In GraspNet-1Billion Fang et al. [2023a] dataset, MMGNet achieves a state-of-the-art mean Average Precision (AP) of 60.34 in RealSense scenes and a competitive mean AP of 50.72 in Kinect scenes.
Ablation studies show that hierarchical image-to-3D feature injection improves the point-only Rotational model by 5.39 AP points, while the rotational graspness model outperforms the View model by 8.39 points under the same hierarchical injection.
The two modules exhibit a positive interaction of 2.19 AP points, confirming their complementarity.
Cross-modal representation analysis further reveals stronger image–3D correspondence across backbone stages than early and late fusion.
Point- and RGB-corruption experiments show that image-informed 3D features complement noisy or incomplete point observations and characterize how different fusion strategies respond to unreliable RGB.
In real-robot experiments, MMGNet improves the grasp success rate over AnyGrasp Fang et al. [2023b] by 8.46 percentage points on adversarial grasp objects Wang et al. [2019]. Our main contributions are:

We develop MMGNet, a scene-level multi-modal framework for single-view 6-DoF grasp synthesis.

We introduce hierarchical image-to-3D feature injection, which integrates multi-scale image cues throughout 3D representation formation.

We introduce a rotational graspness model that scores joint view–in-plane rotations and uses the selected rotation to organize image-informed local features through grasp-shaded grouping.

MMGNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on GraspNet-1Billion and demonstrates its applicability in real-world robotic grasping.

Extensive ablations and analyses validate the proposed modules across fusion strategies, grasp models, representation properties, and point- and RGB-corrupted observations.

1. We develop MMGNet, a scene-level multi-modal framework for single-view 6-DoF grasp synthesis.

2. We introduce hierarchical image-to-3D feature injection, which integrates multi-scale image cues throughout 3D representation formation.

3. We introduce a rotational graspness model that scores joint view–in-plane rotations and uses the selected rotation to organize image-informed local features through grasp-shaded grouping.

4. MMGNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on GraspNet-1Billion and demonstrates its applicability in real-world robotic grasping.

5. Extensive ablations and analyses validate the proposed modules across fusion strategies, grasp models, representation properties, and point- and RGB-corrupted observations.

title: Localization-Uncertainty-Aware UAV Swarm Search for GNSS-Denied Maritime Surveillance
authors: Siyuan Yang,Junning Lyu,Xiaoyu He,Lakmal Seneviratne,Shaoming He
abstract:
This paper studies UAV swarm search in GNSS-denied maritime environments,
where inter-UAV ranging drives cooperative localization
and uncertainty propagates along the multi-hop reference chain,
affecting connectivity, collision avoidance, and search effectiveness.
We propose an uncertainty-aware control barrier function (CBF) framework
approximating cascading localization covariance through Fisher information matrices.
First, the cascading covariance model captures how ranging noise and neighbor
uncertainty accumulate along the localization chain.
Second, uncertainty-tightened CBFs incorporate the covariance model and its
rate into margins for connectivity maintenance and collision avoidance,
with conditional invariance and graceful-degradation bounds.
Third, a hierarchical Voronoi-target strategy with formation keeping supports
efficient forward-looking coverage.
The distributed controller is validated with a standard unbiased extended
Kalman filter in the loop.
The framework is demonstrated on several polygon shapes and swarm sizes from 6 to 30 sUAVs.
An estimator-in-the-loop run completes the search in 302.5302.5 s,
20 Monte Carlo deployments confirm repeatable completion with all local QPs feasible
and containment in at least 98.97%98.97\% of UAV-frames,
and six MBZIRC runs provide estimator-in-the-loop evidence.
The source code is publicly available11
1
          
          
        Core CBF library: https://github.com/xirhxq/cbf/tree/paper/cbf2026-tvt (commit 7e1a3f6); ROS 2 implementation: https://github.com/xirhxq/cbf-ros2.
introduction:
Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms have received growing attention for search-and-rescue and surveillance because they cover large areas more efficiently than a single platform [1].
In maritime surveillance, UAV swarms are attractive for search, border monitoring, and wide-area patrol over oceans.
Practical maritime operations are often challenged by Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-denied conditions (jamming, spoofing, interference),
so UAVs must search, navigate, and coordinate with onboard sensing and inter-UAV cooperation.

This paper considers a GNSS-denied maritime surveillance scenario in which a swarm systematically searches a large ocean region extending from the coastline (Fig. 1).
Hovering beacon UAVs (bUAVs) near the coast localize through coastal features (e.g., lidar-visual-inertial odometry [2]),
while searching UAVs (sUAVs) perform coverage.
sUAVs carry forward-looking sensors (cameras or radar) and ranging sensors for cooperative localization;
because direct ranging to coastal bUAVs cannot support long-range offshore search,
references propagate from the bUAVs into the search area in a multi-hop chain.
A central difficulty is that localization uncertainty accumulates along this chain:
each sUAV estimates its position from noisy ranges and from the already uncertain estimates of its reference neighbors,
which directly affects control design.
Localization-linked distances must remain within sensing range after accounting for position errors,
and collision-avoidance constraints must include uncertainty margins for both vehicles.
Maritime search therefore requires an uncertainty-aware mechanism coordinating coverage, localization, and inter-UAV safety.

We refer to this problem as uncertainty-aware GNSS-denied Maritime Search (uGdMS).
Compared with conventional coverage control, uGdMS operates without global positioning,
its uncertainty is cascading (each UAV depends on the uncertain estimates of upstream references),
and its forward-looking sensors couple position control with yaw orientation;
unlike our prior work under perfect localization [3],
we explicitly incorporate the cascading uncertainty into the control design.

This paper develops a CBF-based framework that integrates cooperative-localization uncertainty into swarm search and safety control.
The main contributions are:

Cascading uncertainty modeling for cooperative localization:
We develop a Fisher-information-based model approximating position covariance in range-only cooperative localization,
capturing how ranging noise and reference-neighbor uncertainty accumulate along the multi-hop localization chain.

Cascading uncertainty modeling for cooperative localization:
We develop a Fisher-information-based model approximating position covariance in range-only cooperative localization,
capturing how ranging noise and reference-neighbor uncertainty accumulate along the multi-hop localization chain.

Robust CBF design under localization uncertainty:
We construct uncertainty-tightened CBFs for localization-connectivity maintenance and collision avoidance by incorporating a position-error envelope and its rate into the constraint design,
establish a conditional invariance statement under the envelope and rate conditions,
and a graceful-degradation bound quantifying the residual constraint margin when the envelope is breached,
and validate the resulting distributed controller with the estimator in the loop.

Hierarchical search strategy with forward-looking sensing:
A task-oriented search controller lets squad leaders select targets through Voronoi partitioning while followers maintain formation, with decoupled distance and yaw objectives for forward-looking sensors.

Estimator-in-the-loop validation:
We validate the estimator-agnostic framework end-to-end with a standard unbiased EKF in the control loop,
demonstrating complete coverage with all quadratic program (QP) rows feasible and no true-distance constraint violations
across the representative run and 20 Monte Carlo deployments.

The resulting framework applies to arbitrary convex polygonal search regions and varying swarm sizes.
Numerical simulation with the estimator in the control loop demonstrates complete coverage of a 3000​m×3000​m3000\,\mathrm{m}\times 3000\,\mathrm{m} region with 14 sUAVs and 3 bUAVs in 302.5302.5 s;
Monte Carlo studies confirm completion repeatability,
and six high-fidelity MBZIRC runs complete coverage with no constraint violations.

The remainder presents related work (Section II), models and CBF preliminaries
(Section III), uncertainty propagation and robust constraints
(Section IV), the search strategy (Section V),
numerical and Gazebo results (Sections VI and VII), and conclusions
(Section VIII).

title: Physics-Informed and Data-Driven Composite Disturbance Separation and Predictive Control for Airborne Electro-Optical Gimbals with Multiple Constraints
authors: Yaokun Lu,Yifan Li,Zhixuan Zhang,Enmei Wang,Hao Teng,Jianzhong Qiao
comment: . Includes supplementary derivations and proofs. Demonstration video included as an ancillary file
abstract: This paper studies the constrained pointing control problem of airborne electro-optical gimbals subjected to composite periodic and aperiodic disturbances. Under carrier vibration, input delay, and actuator constraints, achieving line-of-sight stabilization and tracking is challenging. A disturbance-separated model predictive control (MPC) scheme is proposed to compensate these heterogeneous disturbances according to their physical characteristics. An adaptive periodic observer predicts multi-harmonic vibrations over the MPC horizon using linear-regression frequency estimation. A linear observer estimates the aperiodic disturbance, and a bounded long short-term memory (LSTM) network predicts its change over the input delay. Embedding periodic predictions into the MPC model while applying aperiodic compensation outside the optimizer limits amplification of aperiodic estimation errors and improves pointing accuracy under frequency changes and parameter mismatch. On the stated headroom envelope, input-set tightening provides feasible commands within the prescribed limits, and a regional practical tracking bound is established under explicit input-sequence and predicted-state margin conditions. A UAV-mounted two-axis gimbal platform is assembled for comparative indoor hovering experiments, complemented by simulations under frequency changes and parameter mismatch. In the reported trials, the proposed method achieves yaw and pitch relative-angle root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 0.770∘0.770^{\circ} and 0.350∘0.350^{\circ}, reducing tracking errors by 25.1% and 45.9% compared with linear active disturbance rejection control.
introduction:
Airborne electro-optical gimbals support emergency response, maritime search and rescue, and bridge crack inspection by directing imaging sensors toward targets of interest. These missions require accurate two-axis line-of-sight (LOS) control, where the gimbal operates as an inertially stabilized platform (ISP) with azimuth and elevation degrees of freedom [1, 2, 3, 4].

Achieving high-accuracy pointing control for such systems is challenged by composite disturbances with distinct physical mechanisms and by multiple constraints. In typical low-to-medium altitude tracking scenarios, atmospheric turbulence and propeller vibration produce high-frequency periodic jitter [5, 6, 7], while rapid slewing excites state-dependent aperiodic torques including gravity, gyroscopic effects [2, 8], and nonlinear friction [9]. Since these disturbances span distinct spectral bands, a separation strategy is physically motivated. Furthermore, the ISP operates within actuator saturation and field-of-view (FOV) constraints [8]. For aerial vehicles, MPC combined with disturbance observers has been applied to trajectory tracking [10, 11].

Robust and disturbance-observer-based control (DOBC) schemes, including Extended State Observer (ESO) and Active Disturbance Rejection Control, have been extensively studied for ISP pointing [12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. For ISPs under composite disturbances, Lei et al. [17] combined an adaptive radial basis function neural network with an ESO, and Chang et al. [18] compared adaptive and sliding mode observers for friction and moving-base compensation. Recent work [19, 20] applied ESO-based feedforward to electro-optical platforms and UAV-mounted cameras. However, most DOBC schemes adopt a single total-disturbance estimate, limiting accuracy when periodic and aperiodic components coexist [21], and require precise disturbance models.

Learning-based techniques augment estimation without explicit models. Sun et al. [22] established a neural DOBC framework, and Shen and Xu [23] used adaptive radial basis functions for unmanned-helicopter disturbance rejection. For ISPs, physics-informed neural networks [24] and online learning frameworks [25] improved adaptability, while Huang et al. [26] combined LSTM with MPC. These methods still use aggregate estimates without structural separation and struggle with high-frequency dynamics due to spectral bias [27].

Refined disturbance separation has been proposed to decouple composite disturbances by their influence topology [28, 29, 30, 31, 32], with related studies on antidisturbance controllability and fixed-time predictive control [33, 34]. Nevertheless, aperiodic estimation in these methods still requires precise physical models.

When disturbance estimates are integrated into MPC, they are commonly held constant over the prediction horizon [35, 36]. For periodic disturbances, horizon prediction using a nominal or known period [37, 38] or learned profiles [39, 40] has been studied. In airborne ISPs, however, vibration frequency varies with flight state, and propagating an aperiodic observer estimate through the prediction model feeds estimation error into the MPC optimization, which under unmodeled lag can drive actuator saturation (Section 4.2). Existing gradient-type frequency adaptation laws [41] are nonlinear in the unknown frequency and converge slowly after frequency switches.
Motivated by the above analysis, this paper proposes a disturbance-separated MPC (MPC-DS) framework that combines physics-informed periodic prediction with data-driven delay-residual learning for airborne two-axis ISPs. The proposed disturbance separator decouples the total disturbance into periodic and aperiodic components. Periodic vibration is predicted over the MPC horizon by an APDO with a projected linear-regression frequency estimator, while the aperiodic disturbance is estimated by a biomimetic LSTM-based disturbance observer (LSTM-DO). Periodic predictions enter the MPC prediction model, whereas the aperiodic estimate and its lead correction are compensated outside the optimizer. The MPC formulation incorporates tightened input bounds together with mechanical-range and FOV constraints [8, 42, 43, 44, 45, 46].
The principal contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

Coupled gimbal–disturbance modeling: A coupled Newton–Euler dynamic model characterizes how carrier motion, two-axis kinematics, and multi-source disturbances—gyroscopic, gravitational, cross-axis coupling, and LuGre friction torques—enter the azimuth and elevation channels, motivating decomposition into a retained multi-harmonic component and a complementary residual component for targeted observer design.

Heterogeneous disturbance separation: A biomimetic separator integrates an APDO, whose linear-regression frequency law with projection keeps the estimate in the admissible band and follows frequency switches, and a data-driven LSTM-DO for the aperiodic torque, whose projected outputs bound the network effect on the estimation error. The LSTM-DO employs a prediction-correction architecture: the linear observer corrects the current value, and the network predicts the delay-induced change that linear lead correction misses.

Constraint-aware disturbance-separated MPC: A composite predictive control architecture extrapolates the periodic estimate over the prediction horizon using the online frequency estimate while compensating for the aperiodic estimate outside the optimizer with delay-lead correction. The input-set construction gives feasible bounded commands on the stated headroom envelope. A regional input-to-state practical tracking bound is established under explicit full-sequence input margins, predicted-state margins and bounded implementation residuals.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 details the dynamic modeling of the dual-axis ISP. Section 3 elaborates on the proposed composite anti-disturbance control architecture, including stability analysis. Section 4 presents simulation and experimental results to evaluate the approach, and Section 5 concludes the paper.

1. Coupled gimbal–disturbance modeling: A coupled Newton–Euler dynamic model characterizes how carrier motion, two-axis kinematics, and multi-source disturbances—gyroscopic, gravitational, cross-axis coupling, and LuGre friction torques—enter the azimuth and elevation channels, motivating decomposition into a retained multi-harmonic component and a complementary residual component for targeted observer design.

2. Heterogeneous disturbance separation: A biomimetic separator integrates an APDO, whose linear-regression frequency law with projection keeps the estimate in the admissible band and follows frequency switches, and a data-driven LSTM-DO for the aperiodic torque, whose projected outputs bound the network effect on the estimation error. The LSTM-DO employs a prediction-correction architecture: the linear observer corrects the current value, and the network predicts the delay-induced change that linear lead correction misses.

3. Constraint-aware disturbance-separated MPC: A composite predictive control architecture extrapolates the periodic estimate over the prediction horizon using the online frequency estimate while compensating for the aperiodic estimate outside the optimizer with delay-lead correction. The input-set construction gives feasible bounded commands on the stated headroom envelope. A regional input-to-state practical tracking bound is established under explicit full-sequence input margins, predicted-state margins and bounded implementation residuals.

title: Behavioural Quality Is Not Learning Utility: Objective Mismatch in Human Behaviour Models for Robot Learning
authors: Haoyang Jiang,Dana Kulic,Michael Burke,Pamela Carreno-Medrano
comment: Project page:this https URL
abstract: Human behaviour models are increasingly used to provide simulated human interactions for training robots via reinforcement learning (RL). Existing approaches primarily evaluate these models according to how closely their generated behaviours resemble real human data, while their usefulness as training partners is less commonly assessed. This creates a potential objective mismatch: a model that performs well according to behavioural evaluation metrics may not necessarily provide useful training experiences for downstream robot policy learning. Across two human-robot interaction (HRI) domains, highway driving and object handover, we evaluate different types of human behaviour models using common generative-model evaluation metrics. We consider multiple human trajectory representations and compare the resulting evaluations with the downstream performance of RL policies trained using the corresponding models. We find that existing behavioural evaluation metrics do not consistently predict downstream policy performance across domains and trajectory representations, while their evaluations are sensitive to the choice of trajectory representation. We also show that even when the true testing behaviour distribution is known, training against a different distribution may yield better downstream performance than training directly against the true distribution.
introduction:
As robots transition from controlled industrial settings to dynamic, human-centred environments, learning from and adapting to human behaviour becomes increasingly critical for successful deployment in real-world settings [1, 2]. In this context, reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising framework for robot training, as it enables agents to optimise long-horizon behaviour through interaction and feedback [3, 4].

In order to learn how to interact with human partners via RL, a robot must be exposed to interactions with humans during training. Although training robots using data collected from real-world human interactions remains the gold standard for achieving robust performance, this approach is often costly, time-consuming, and difficult to scale [5]. To address these challenges, the robotics community has increasingly relied on simulated or modelled human behaviour models to train robot policies [6, 4]. These models, ranging from simple rule-based approaches [7, 8, 9] to complex data-driven generators [10, 11, 12], offer a scalable and cost-effective means of producing the large volumes of interaction data required by modern machine learning methods [13]. Consequently, human behaviour models serve not only as models of human behaviour, but also as interactive partners for robot policy training. Their value therefore depends not only on how well they reproduce human behaviour, but also on how effectively they support downstream robot learning.

This creates an important distinction between behavioural quality and downstream utility. Behavioural quality concerns how closely a given model reproduces behaviours observed in real human data, whereas downstream utility concerns how effectively interactions generated by this same model support the learning of robot policies. We argue that these objectives may not be aligned. A model may accurately reproduce the distribution of behaviours observed in human data while failing to expose a robot to interactions that are important for learning an effective policy. Conversely, a model that generates behaviours that are less representative of the empirical human distribution may provide training experiences that lead to better downstream policies.

This distinction reflects a broader objective-mismatch problem that has been studied in model-based RL [14]: model quality under a predictive or model-fitting objective does not necessarily imply usefulness for downstream decision making. Related work has demonstrated that models that are accurate according to conventional predictive objectives may nevertheless produce poor downstream control performance. This suggests that evaluating a model without considering the downstream task can provide an incomplete picture of its practical value. However, whether a similar mismatch arises when human behaviour models are used as training environments for HRI policy learning has not been systematically investigated.

This question is increasingly relevant in simulation-based robotics, where human behaviour models are used to construct interactive environments for training and evaluating autonomous agents. Recent traffic simulation frameworks, including WOSAC, TrafficBots, Symphony, BITS, and TrafficBots V1.5, have developed increasingly sophisticated models of human road-user behaviour for autonomous driving and evaluate these models primarily according to measures of behavioural realism, such as trajectory likelihood, prediction error, collision and rule-violation rates, diversity, and distributional similarity [15, 11, 16, 17, 12]. These measures provide valuable assessments of whether a simulator faithfully reproduces human traffic behaviour, but they do not directly establish whether models achieving higher behavioural quality are more effective for downstream policy learning. Similarly, recent work on planner evaluation in reactive traffic environments has shown that changing the human behaviour simulator can affect the resulting assessment of autonomous planners [18]. While this highlights the influence of the simulated humans on downstream evaluation, it does not establish whether realism-oriented evaluation metrics can predict the utility of these models for training robot policies. Thus, although existing work has made substantial progress towards evaluating the fidelity or diversity of human behaviour models, the relationship between behavioural faithfulness and downstream utility remains largely unexplored. This motivates our central research question:

Can existing model evaluation metrics predict the downstream utility of human behaviour models for RL policy learning HRI scenarios?

To investigate this question, we evaluate a diverse set of rule-based and data-driven human behaviour models across two representative HRI domains: highway driving and object handover. These domains represent substantially different forms of HRI, involving large-scale coordination and close-proximity physical collaboration, respectively. For each human behaviour model, we evaluate two complementary aspects: behavioural quality, measured using commonly adopted generative-model evaluation metrics across different trajectory representations, and downstream utility, measured by the performance of RL policies trained using the corresponding human behaviour model. By comparing these two evaluations, we investigate whether models that score favourably according to existing behavioural evaluation metrics also provide more useful training interactions for downstream robot learning.

Our study provides the following contributions:

We provide empirical evidence of a mismatch between behavioural similarity and downstream RL utility of human behaviour models. Specifically, we show that existing evaluation metrics are not a consistent predictor of downstream policy performance across both HRI domains and trajectory representations.

We show that the form of this mismatch can be task-dependent, with the relationship between behavioural evaluation and downstream policy utility differing between highway driving and object handover.

We demonstrate that human behaviour model evaluation is sensitive to trajectory representation, with metric scores and model rankings varying substantially across representations and, in particular, learned feature configurations.

In addition to these contributions, we provide detailed formulations and parameter inference procedures for the rule-based human behaviour models used in our experiments. The parameters of these models are inferred from real human datasets [19, 20], with the corresponding model formulations, inference procedures, and fitted parameters provided in the Appendix, which is also included in our project page https://objective-mismatch-hri.github.io/supplementary/.

1. We provide empirical evidence of a mismatch between behavioural similarity and downstream RL utility of human behaviour models. Specifically, we show that existing evaluation metrics are not a consistent predictor of downstream policy performance across both HRI domains and trajectory representations.

2. We show that the form of this mismatch can be task-dependent, with the relationship between behavioural evaluation and downstream policy utility differing between highway driving and object handover.

3. We demonstrate that human behaviour model evaluation is sensitive to trajectory representation, with metric scores and model rankings varying substantially across representations and, in particular, learned feature configurations.
