title: ISB-NMPC: Interception-Oriented Spherical-Bearing Nonlinear Model Predictive Control for Quadrotors
authors: Li Hong,Linkai Liu,Xiangyu Ren,Shuli Lv,Chen Min,Chunjiang Wu,Yujun Zhang,Dingchen Zeng,Quan Quan
comment: and 1 table. Submitted to IEEE/ASME Transactions on Mechatronics
abstract:
Quadrotor interceptors equipped with strapdown cameras offer a low-cost
solution for physically countering unauthorized UAVs. However, this
configuration inherently couples vehicle maneuvering and camera pointing,
creating a conflict between rapid closing and maintaining target visibility.
We present interception-oriented spherical-bearing nonlinear
model predictive control (ISB-NMPC), which couples spherical-bearing prediction
with nonlinear quadrotor dynamics to jointly optimize target-directed closing
motion and visibility. An attitude-compensated extended Kalman filter on
𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} estimates target bearing motion, compensates for perception
delay, and predicts target bearings to guide scale-adaptive detection.
Across 30 paired simulation trials, ISB-NMPC achieves an interception success
rate of 86.7%86.7\%, the highest among the evaluated controllers, with a mean per-trial target-visible time of 99.11%99.11\%.
introduction:
The growth of low-altitude aerial applications makes shared-airspace safety
increasingly important. Non-cooperative small targets create a practical need
for affordable onboard interception
systems [1, 2].
A strapdown monocular camera offers lightweight, mechanically simple sensing,
but the interceptor must acquire the target, retain visual feedback, and
close to a capture region without cooperative target-state measurements.
Figure 1 illustrates the long-range and
maneuvering-target scenarios considered here.

This mounting arrangement creates a fundamental control conflict.
Target-directed acceleration requires tilting the thrust vector, which rotates
the camera and can push the target toward the field-of-view (FOV) boundary.
Recentering the target can, in turn, restrict closing acceleration.
Thus, the same thrust and attitude motion govern both closing efficiency and
visibility [3],
requiring coordination under nonlinear dynamics and actuator limits
(Fig. 2). Camera rotation, detection delay, and
target-scale variation further affect the supporting visual feedback.

Existing approaches follow three complementary routes: target-state
estimation and trajectory planning, visual servoing and line-of-sight (LOS)
guidance, and
perception-aware model predictive control (MPC). The first plans and tracks
interception trajectories.
Optimization-based planning explicitly handles engagement geometry, but its
execution depends on the available target-state
information [2].
A second route generates motion directly from visual feedback or relative
geometry. Image-based visual servoing (IBVS) regulates image features, whereas
position-based visual servoing (PBVS) uses estimated relative
pose [4, 5];
barrier-function constraints can preserve
visibility [6].

For interception, LOS guidance connects visual feedback to closing.
Yang et al. developed high-speed image-based
control [7] and analyzed
LOS-constrained multirotor
interceptability [8].
Related studies address planar-sector
guidance [9], pursuit–evasion
interceptability [10], and persistent
interception [11]. Bearing-only following also
uses helical motion to improve observability while maintaining a prescribed
geometry [1]. These methods establish useful
feedback structures; rapid capture additionally requires coordinating closing
demand with visibility-preserving vehicle motion.

The third coordinates motion and sensing over a prediction horizon.
Falanga et al. [12] incorporate perception
into quadrotor motion optimization. Related formulations address reactive
collision and occlusion avoidance [13]
and combine visibility with actuator
constraints [14], while robust visual
predictive controllers address tracking and visibility
constraints [15].
Qin et al. [16] combine quaternion-based
spherical features and visibility constraints for aggressive flight, and
Li et al. [17] integrate estimation and control in
a robocentric model.
MPC has also been applied to non-cooperative aerial interception and
impact-angle-constrained visual
engagement [18, 19].

For strapdown interception, the remaining question is how to choose
closing direction and speed under visibility and actuation constraints.
Uncoordinated closing can lose visual feedback, whereas recentering alone can
delay capture. We connect LOS guidance to spherical prediction through an
optimized closing-speed state; paired simulations and flight observations
examine closing and visual retention together.

The supporting perception front end draws on depth-independent
bearing estimation [20, 21],
small-object slicing [22], and delayed-feedback
estimation [23] to address camera rotation,
target-scale variation, and latency.

We propose interception-oriented spherical-bearing nonlinear model
predictive control (ISB-NMPC), predicting S​O​(3)SO(3)-lifted bearings jointly with
quadrotor dynamics. LOS velocity tracking, bearing-dependent speed demand,
and visual costs and constraints coordinate approach and visibility.
Compensated bearings and predicted regions of interest (ROIs) support detection.

The main contributions are as follows:

An interception-oriented spherical-bearing NMPC that jointly
optimizes desired closing speed and vehicle motion. LOS-aligned relative
velocity objectives, visual costs, and soft FOV constraints coordinate
rapid closing and target visibility under quadrotor dynamics and actuator
limits.

A spherical-bearing estimator with attitude and delay compensation
that supplies current-time bearing feedback and absolute-time ROI
predictions to support onboard operation during large attitude changes
and target-scale variation.

Paired controller comparisons over 30 simulation trials and outdoor
flights involving long-range acquisition of a quasi-static small target
and pursuit of a maneuvering target, evaluating controller performance
and the operation of the integrated perception–control system.

Section II defines the system and interception problem.
Sections III and IV present the perception front
end and ISB-NMPC, respectively. Section V reports simulation
and flight validation, followed by the discussion and conclusion.

1. An interception-oriented spherical-bearing NMPC that jointly
optimizes desired closing speed and vehicle motion. LOS-aligned relative
velocity objectives, visual costs, and soft FOV constraints coordinate
rapid closing and target visibility under quadrotor dynamics and actuator
limits.

2. A spherical-bearing estimator with attitude and delay compensation
that supplies current-time bearing feedback and absolute-time ROI
predictions to support onboard operation during large attitude changes
and target-scale variation.

3. Paired controller comparisons over 30 simulation trials and outdoor
flights involving long-range acquisition of a quasi-static small target
and pursuit of a maneuvering target, evaluating controller performance

title: SceneAgent: An Agentic Pipeline from 3D and 4D Captures to Simulation Environments
authors: Luke Hollis,Tianxing Fan,Heng Yang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Visual captures provide detailed scene appearance, but converting them into interactive simulation environments requires object reconstruction, physical modeling, and correction of intermediate errors. We present SceneAgent, an agentic pipeline that coordinates these steps through simulator-based visual inspection and repair. The pipeline processes 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), photogrammetry, LiDAR captures, AI-generated 3DGS scenes, and 4D videos of dynamic scenes, and combines object segmentation, physical parameter estimation, part decomposition, articulation, and deformable simulation.
To support policy learning, SceneAgent generates diverse object variants (“digital sisters”) and scripted demonstrations. On a cluttered bin scene from GraspClutter6D, SceneAgent raises F1 at 1 cm for every coding agent with scorable outputs both with and without its skills, and its reconstructions are better than SimFoundry [47]: all agent configurations exceed SimFoundry’s F1 score, with a best of 60.75% versus 6.9%. On three dynamic scenes from 4DCodeBench [51], SceneAgent raises the mean dynamic IoU of Gemini 4 Argon from 0.86% to 99.09%. We further demonstrate diverse simulated interactions and preliminary policy transfer to a real robot.
introduction:
Generalist robot policies [6, 38, 23, 5, 40, 36] learn from large teleoperated datasets to perform a wide range of manipulation tasks specified by language instructions. Collecting these datasets is labor-intensive and can take months or years. Similarly, evaluating the resulting policies in a target environment requires physical robot trials, which are time-consuming, difficult to reproduce, and costly to scale [2].

Simulation offers a way to scale both data collection and evaluation. Reconstructed environments can generate demonstrations [67, 63, 59], support policies that transfer to physical robots [45, 27, 68], and provide estimates of real-world policy performance [19, 47, 69, 31, 30]. In particular, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [22] reconstructs photorealistic scene appearance from images, enabling simulators to render observations grounded in a captured workspace [45, 11, 21].

Visual reconstruction alone, however, does not provide the object geometry, physical parameters, or articulation needed for interaction. Real-to-sim systems recover these components by combining segmentation, mesh generation, pose alignment, and physical modeling [19, 47, 68, 12]. SimFoundry, for example, supports articulated objects and estimates their physical parameters [47]. A remaining challenge is to coordinate these components across diverse inputs and correct errors that arise between stages. An incorrect mask, scale, or transform can produce an unusable object even when the individual models return plausible outputs.

We present SceneAgent, an agentic pipeline that converts 3D and 4D captures into interactive simulation environments (Figure 2). Agents execute reconstruction and physical modeling tools, inspect rendered outputs in the target simulator, and repair visible errors before the scene is used downstream. The resulting environments contain segmented objects with estimated physical parameters, decomposed parts, and articulation or soft-body behavior where needed. For 4D captures, which are videos of dynamic scenes, agents also fit simulated dynamics such as liquid flow, deformation, and destruction mechanics to the observed scene (Section 3.6). SceneAgent also generates digital sisters—related object variants—and combines captured objects with artist-authored environments to expand the range of training scenes.

We evaluate reconstruction quality on a cluttered bin scene from GraspClutter6D [3] and a Messy Kitchen dataset from CollectData [8] using coding agents with and without SceneAgent, and compare with SimFoundry. Here, a harness is the software environment in which a coding agent runs, and skills are the reusable instructions and tools that guide its conversion workflow. With SceneAgent, F1 at 1 cm improves for every harness with scorable paired outputs, and reconstruction quality is much better than SimFoundry’s (Figure 5). On three dynamic scenes from 4DCodeBench [51], where agents reconstruct simulations from videos, SceneAgent raises the mean dynamic IoU of Gemini 4 Argon from 0.86% to 99.09% (Figure 3). We also demonstrate simulated interactions and preliminary real-world deployment after policy learning.

In summary, our contributions are:

An agentic scene-conversion workflow that integrates reconstruction, physical parameter estimation, part decomposition, and articulation with simulator-based visual inspection and repair, and that extends from 3D captures to 4D captures by fitting simulated dynamics to the motion observed in a video.

Scene augmentation through digital sisters and hybrid environments that combine captured objects with artist-authored assets, together with an automated research loop that turns failures of a policy on the real robot into simulated training data.

A quantitative study of reconstruction quality across coding-agent harnesses on static captures and on dynamic scenes from 4DCodeBench, complemented by qualitative examples of articulated, deformable, and contact-rich interactions and preliminary real-world policy transfer.

1. An agentic scene-conversion workflow that integrates reconstruction, physical parameter estimation, part decomposition, and articulation with simulator-based visual inspection and repair, and that extends from 3D captures to 4D captures by fitting simulated dynamics to the motion observed in a video.

2. Scene augmentation through digital sisters and hybrid environments that combine captured objects with artist-authored assets, together with an automated research loop that turns failures of a policy on the real robot into simulated training data.

3. A quantitative study of reconstruction quality across coding-agent harnesses on static captures and on dynamic scenes from 4DCodeBench, complemented by qualitative examples of articulated, deformable, and contact-rich interactions and preliminary real-world policy transfer.

title: Networked Humanoid Intelligence: Communication, Coordination, Collaboration, and Social Interaction
authors: Loc X. Nguyen,Huy Q. Le,Ji Su Yoon,Nguyen H. Tran,Eui-Nam Huh,Choong Seon Hong
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Emerging Technologies (cs.ET); Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI)
abstract: Humanoid robots are moving from laboratory platforms toward connected fleets that share workspaces, infrastructure, tasks, and knowledge with other robots and humans. As deployments grow, the operation and improvement of each humanoid depend on information exchanged across the network. However, existing research has largely studied humanoids as individual systems. This survey examines networked humanoid intelligence through four functions of information exchange: communication, coordination, collaboration, and social intelligence with human interaction. We first establish the foundations of networked humanoid systems, define the question addressed by each function, and connect them through a common factory scenario. We review the literature along six dimensions: interaction architecture, exchanged information, physical coupling, operating timescale, system scale, and embodiment. We separate results obtained with physical and simulated humanoids from those based on other robotic platforms or disembodied agents, because the latter do not fully capture humanoid-specific constraints such as balance, whole-body motion, contact, and physical interaction. We examine hardware, datasets, and benchmarks, and distinguish risks handled locally from those networking introduces, such as stale information or unsafe knowledge propagation. Finally, we identify open problems in control-aware networking, compact body-centric messages, physically grounded coordination, network- and embodiment-aware knowledge sharing, fleet-level social consistency, and accountable human oversight.
introduction:
Humanoid robots are moving from laboratory prototypes toward large-scale deployment in manufacturing, logistics, service, and household environments. Major manufacturers are already preparing for mass production: Tesla is targeting a production capacity of up to 10 million Optimus robots (The Robot Report, 2026), while a growing number of commercial humanoid platforms are entering industrial and service applications (Humanoid Robotics Technology, 2026; Sheng et al., 2025; Cao, 2025). This transition is supported not only by advances in humanoid hardware and embodied intelligence, but also by societal needs such as aging populations, labor shortages, and growing demand for care and service automation (Yu and Nayak, 2026). As deployment scales, humanoids will increasingly operate as part of larger populations: a factory may operate hundreds of robots at a single site, while a service provider may manage a much larger population distributed across homes and workplaces. Therefore, humanoids should be seen as members of connected populations that interact with other robots, shared infrastructure, and humans.

The rapid progress of humanoid robotics has largely focused on improving the capabilities of individual robots. Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) and whole-body control enable humanoids to walk, recover balance, track human motions, and perform complex whole-body behaviors (Liao et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2024; Ji et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2024). At a higher level, vision-language-action (VLA) models translate visual observations and language instructions into robot actions, enabling a single humanoid to perform diverse manipulation and loco-manipulation tasks (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025). World models further capture environment dynamics and predict action outcomes, supporting planning, policy evaluation, and behavior generation (Hafner et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Ding et al., 2025; Ali et al., 2025b; Gao et al., 2026). In parallel, advances in visual perception improve state estimation and environment understanding (Bin et al., 2025), while motion-planning methods generate feasible actions under kinematic, stability, and real-time constraints (de Lima et al., 2024). These developments provide the perception, prediction, reasoning, and control capabilities needed for increasingly autonomous humanoids. However, they primarily consider a single robot that observes its own environment and selects its own actions. They do not provide an explicit interface through which other robots can contribute information, coordinate decisions, or participate in joint control.

Consider two humanoids moving through a warehouse aisle while jointly handling a shelf module as a human worker passes nearby. The robots must first exchange task-relevant information in time to maintain a consistent view of the task, which is the role of communication (Yu and Nayak, 2026). Then, they have to decide who uses the aisle, who handles each part of the object, and when each action should occur, which requires coordination (Choi et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2025c). When the shelf cannot be handled by either robot alone, they must synchronize their motions and forces and share useful experience across the fleet. These joint execution and learning processes form collaboration (Hawley and Suleiman, 2019; Wu et al., 2011; Wen et al., 2024; Hoque et al., 2023). Finally, operating around people requires the robots to understand human intentions, communicate their actions, and behave safely and predictably, which requires social intelligence and human interaction (Vinanzi et al., 2021; Yu and Nayak, 2026). These four capabilities define the main dimensions of networked humanoid intelligence.

Although these capabilities appear in conventional multi-robot systems, humanoid embodiment imposes additional constraints on their operation. Bipedal balance and whole-body control rely on fast feedback, limiting the extent to which safety-critical control can depend on the network (Yu and Nayak, 2026). For example, a communication delay that may only interrupt the motion of a wheeled robot can disrupt synchronization between physically coupled humanoids, generate unwanted interaction forces, and threaten their balance (Hawley and Suleiman, 2019; Wu et al., 2011; Wen et al., 2024). At the same time, high degree-of-freedom (DoF) bodies and multimodal sensors generate large and heterogeneous data streams, making continuous exchange of raw observations impractical (Bin et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026b). Physical interaction creates another challenge. During cooperative manipulation, forces and motion errors can propagate through the manipulated object and disturb the balance of other robots (Hawley and Suleiman, 2019; Wu et al., 2011; Wen et al., 2024). Moreover, differences in morphology, DoF, sensing, and hardware limit the direct transfer of policies and experience across humanoids (O’Neill et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2026; Xue et al., 2026b). This challenge becomes more important as humanoid knowledge is increasingly encoded in large learned policies and representations, whose exchange can require substantially more information than conventional task messages (Bjorck et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2024). Therefore, networking for humanoids cannot be treated as an independent communication layer. Instead, it must be closely integrated with control, embodiment, and learning.

Existing surveys approach networked humanoid intelligence from several related directions. Surveys on humanoid robotics cover hardware design, locomotion and control, perception, planning, and foundation models, but primarily focus on the capabilities of individual robots (Sheng et al., 2025; Cao, 2025; de Lima et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2026). Surveys on VLA and embodied models similarly examine perception-action architectures and language-conditioned control, with the robot typically treated as an individual decision-making agent (Ma et al., 2026; Kawaharazuka et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025). By contrast, multi-robot and multi-agent surveys study communication, coordination, collaboration, multi-agent RL (MARL), and LLM-based teams (Karam et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b; Gielis et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025a; Feng et al., 2026). However, these studies mainly consider wheeled robots, aerial robots, and manipulators, and therefore do not fully capture the physical and control constraints of humanoids. Networked-robotics surveys provide another complementary view by studying cloud, edge, IoT, and AIoT infrastructures for communication, computation offloading, resource management, and distributed intelligence (Kehoe et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2025b; Bezerra et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2024c). The Internet of Humanoids (Yu and Nayak, 2026) considers connected humanoids, but primarily focuses on an architecture- and application-oriented view of the field. Therefore, a gap remains between studies of individual humanoid intelligence and studies of distributed robotic systems. In particular, existing surveys do not systematically organize the inter-agent capabilities that allow humanoids to exchange information, coordinate decisions, perform joint physical tasks, share learned experience, and interact with people under humanoid-specific constraints. This survey addresses this gap from a capability- and algorithm-oriented perspective. It organizes the literature around communication, coordination, collaboration, and social intelligence, and examines how these capabilities are implemented and evaluated on humanoid platforms.

The contributions of our survey are summarized as follows:

We organize the literature into four functions, namely communication and networking, coordination, collaboration, and social intelligence and human interaction. These functions capture how connected humanoids exchange information, make joint decisions, share capabilities and experience, and reason about humans and other agents.

For each function, we explain why balance, whole-body contact, heterogeneous bodies, and human-facing motion make humanoids different from generic multi-robot systems, including a direct comparison of humanoid and generic robot communication. In addition, we explain how representative methods work and analyze them along common dimensions, distinguishing evidence from physical or simulated humanoids from results on other robots.

We assess available platforms and benchmarks, separate per-robot safety from network-induced risks such as stale information and fleet-wide propagation of unsafe knowledge, and derive open problems from the gaps identified in the review.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Section 2 defines the four functions and the taxonomy. Sections 3-6 review communication and networking, coordination, collaboration, and social intelligence and human interaction, respectively. Section 7 examines evaluation, safety, and open problems, and Section 8 concludes.

1. We organize the literature into four functions, namely communication and networking, coordination, collaboration, and social intelligence and human interaction. These functions capture how connected humanoids exchange information, make joint decisions, share capabilities and experience, and reason about humans and other agents.

2. For each function, we explain why balance, whole-body contact, heterogeneous bodies, and human-facing motion make humanoids different from generic multi-robot systems, including a direct comparison of humanoid and generic robot communication. In addition, we explain how representative methods work and analyze them along common dimensions, distinguishing evidence from physical or simulated humanoids from results on other robots.

3. We assess available platforms and benchmarks, separate per-robot safety from network-induced risks such as stale information and fleet-wide propagation of unsafe knowledge, and derive open problems from the gaps identified in the review.

title: VLA-HWBench: Where the Time Goes When VLA Models Run on Edge Hardware
authors: Borui Xu,Hongshi Tan,Wenqi Jiang,Bingsheng He,Ming Wu,Jason Zeng,Michael Heinrich
abstract: Vision–language–action (VLA) models increasingly run on edge devices aboard robots, where inference latency constrains closed-loop robot control. However, it remains unclear how to design VLA models, their inference software and edge hardware so that robots can run VLA inference in real time. Most VLA models report only task success, and prior studies cover few of the ways recent VLAs generate actions, split a call into at most three phases and do not compare inference optimizations on the same models. Therefore, we introduce VLA-HWBench, a benchmark that measures 18 open VLA models on their released software and on alternative backends, on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor and an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 395, with a seven-stage breakdown of each call. Our study reveals three insights. First, where the time goes depends on how a model generates actions, not on its size. Action generation is the largest stage in 14 of the 19 configurations on the Jetson, latency spans 82×82\times on the Jetson and 157×157\times on the AMD platform, and parameter count explains at most 15% of its variance. Models that generate long action chunks in a few flow-matching steps keep up with control, whereas token-by-token decoding does not. Second, kernel fusion with 4-bit weights helps most, running π0.5\pi_{0.5} and GR00T N1.7 2.6–2.9×\times faster than PyTorch with torch.compile, but it exists for only these two models and only on the Jetson. Optimization also moves the time to the stages it shortens least, as CPU preprocessing grows from 12% to 39% of the GR00T N1.7 call. Third, after optimization, memory bandwidth limits only the stages that process few tokens on the Jetson, such as the denoising steps, whereas software limits all other stages, from unfused kernels to serial preprocessing on the host CPU. Overall, low-latency edge VLAs should use few action-generation iterations, inference software should extend kernel fusion and low-bit weights to more models and platforms, and edge hardware needs high memory bandwidth and a fast host CPU.
introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robotic control, mapping visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Octo Model Team et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025b; Bjorck et al., 2025). Unlike text or image generation, VLA inference operates within a continuously evolving physical system: the robot may continue executing previous commands while objects or obstacles change state or position (Falanga et al., 2019; Morrison et al., 2018), causing observations to become stale before the corresponding actions are executed. Practical deployment therefore increasingly calls for low-latency inference close to the robot. This is particularly important when wireless connectivity is variable or intermittent, or when privacy-sensitive camera observations cannot be transmitted to remote servers. Meanwhile, advances in edge compute hardware (NVIDIA, 2025; AMD, 2025) are making on-robot VLA inference increasingly feasible.

However, the observation-to-action characteristics of state-of-the-art VLA models on edge devices have not been systematically characterized. Recent studies have begun to characterize VLA inference through measurements on edge and datacenter GPUs (Taherin et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026), profiling of a single architecture (Vishwanathan et al., 2026) and analytical performance models (Jiang et al., 2026), but three gaps remain.
First, they cover few of the ways in which recent VLAs generate actions. Recent models differ in architecture and training and denoise action chunks by flow matching, decode them in parallel, generate them token by token or reason before acting. These choices change how much sequential work a call performs, but the measured studies cover at most five models and two of these four forms.
Second, they divide a call into at most three phases, which cannot show where the time goes. CPU preprocessing, data transfer, vision encoding, prefill and action generation stress different resources, and none of these studies times CPU preprocessing.
Third, they do not compare inference optimizations on the same models. None of the four studies evaluates a specialized backend and only one tests low-bit weights, while each backend is evaluated only on the models it targets (NVIDIA, 2026; Su, 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Nguyen et al., 2026). It thus remains unclear which optimization helps most, which stages it shortens and whether its gain carries over to other models and platforms.

To bridge these gaps and provide a systematic basis for practical on-robot deployment, we present VLA-HWBench, a benchmark for characterizing the complete observation-to-action path of state-of-the-art VLA models on edge devices. VLA-HWBench is designed to incorporate additional VLA models, inference backends, and edge hardware as the ecosystem evolves.

First, to cover the forms of action generation, VLA-HWBench evaluates 18 widely used open VLA models spanning all four forms, selected based on Hugging Face downloads and community stars, on two architecturally distinct edge platforms, the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor and AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 395. Each model runs in a common reference configuration using eager PyTorch, with optional optimizations disabled, on the same LIBERO-10 observation (Liu et al., 2023) and timing boundary. Second, to show where the time goes, VLA-HWBench divides each call into the seven stages of Figure 2, timed at the stage boundaries and split by kernels inside CUDA graphs. Third, to study optimizations systematically, VLA-HWBench enables compilation, specialized backends (TensorRT and FlashRT) and lower precision one at a time on two representative models and attributes each gain to stages. With VLA-HWBench, we answer three questions.

(Q1) Where does the time go in VLA models, and what sets their latency? Without optional optimizations, action generation is the largest stage in 14 of the 19 configurations on the Jetson, and latency ranges from 77 ms to 6.3 s on the Jetson (82×82\times) and from 114 ms to 17.9 s on the AMD platform (157×157\times), with only 10 and 9 of the 19 configurations generating actions as fast as LIBERO executes them. As Figure 1 shows, a least-squares fit of log latency on log parameter count explains at most 15% of the variance, and latency instead follows the number of iterations of action generation.

(Q2) How much do optimizations help, and where does the time move? On the Jetson, compilation, a specialized backend and lower precision make π0.5\pi_{0.5} 2.5×2.5\times, 1.8×1.8\times and 1.6×1.6\times faster in turn, 7.2×7.2\times in total, and GR00T N1.7 1.02×1.02\times, 1.4×1.4\times and 1.8×1.8\times, 2.6×2.6\times in total. A backend with kernel fusion and 4-bit weights gives the largest gain, 2.6–2.9×\times over compilation, but exists only for these two models and only on the Jetson. Optimization also moves the time to the stages it shortens least, as CPU preprocessing grows from 12% to 39% of the GR00T N1.7 call.

(Q3) What limits the remaining time after optimization? No single resource limits the remaining time. Action generation and other stages with few tokens are memory-bound and on the Jetson already run at more than half of the peak memory bandwidth, whereas vision encoding and long prefills reach only 6–42% of what the hardware allows because of unfused kernels and missing low-precision support, and CPU preprocessing is limited by serial Python and idle-thread wake-ups.

Overall, the latency of a VLA on edge hardware is determined jointly by its action-generation method, its runtime backend and the platform rather than by its model size. For future designs, edge VLAs should therefore reduce action-generation iterations, for example through fewer denoising steps or parallel decoding, rather than simply shrink the model; inference software should extend kernel fusion and low-bit execution, which provide the largest gains, to more models and platforms while optimizing host preprocessing as carefully as GPU execution; and edge hardware should prioritize memory bandwidth and a fast host CPU over peak GPU compute.

title: Benchmarking Obstacle-Conditioned Safety in Household Robot Navigation
authors: Hyunwoong Bae,Jisu Han,Jiyeon Choi,Dohoon Kim,Taesup Moon
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Safe household navigation requires robots to regulate clearance and speed according to what an obstacle is and how close it is, without unnecessary conservatism. Yet existing evaluations do not test whether semantic safety distinctions are reflected in continuous motion. To that end, we introduce OSMA-Bench, an Obstacle-Conditioned Safe Motion Adaptation Benchmark
built on spatially matched scenario sets that differ only in obstacle type.
We also propose the Semantic Sensitivity Index (SSI), which measures whether clearance and distance-dependent speed and smoothness follow the caution ordering of obstacles. Evaluating VLM-based and vision-language-action (VLA) policies on the benchmark, we find that neither consistently adapts its motion to obstacle safety, even with explicit safety prompts. Our analysis shows that the policies can correctly distinguish obstacles by safety relevance but fail to reflect this distinction in the motion parameters or actions they produce. For VLM-based policies, which recognize the obstacle and then generate a navigation program, adding an explicit parameter-inference step between these two stages improves adaptation. These findings expose a gap in semantic-to-motion grounding, highlighting the need to translate semantic caution into appropriately safe motion.
introduction:
As robots are moving from industrial settings into homes, they must navigate around people, pets, and objects with different safety implications (Wachsmuth et al., 2015; Zachiotis et al., 2018; Szot et al., 2021; Yenamandra et al., 2023; Soni et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025c; ISO, 2014).
Safe navigation around such entities requires obstacle-conditioned safe motion adaptation, which goes beyond collision avoidance: a robot must adapt its motion to each obstacle’s safety implications and to how closely its route passes it.
As illustrated in Figure 1, even when both paths are collision-free, a robot should keep more clearance and move more slowly past a child than past a trash bin, and slow down further as it gets closer. This caution must also be selective, since uniform conservatism toward every obstacle would needlessly sacrifice efficiency.

Achieving this requires semantic-to-motion grounding: a policy must infer an appropriate level of caution from an obstacle’s semantics and translate it into clearance, proximity-dependent speed, and executed motion. Foundation models are natural candidates: VLMs can interpret safety-relevant semantics to inform motion planning, and VLAs generate actions directly from visual observations and language instructions.
Although both are widely used in robotic systems (Huang et al., 2023; Nasiriany et al., 2024b; NVIDIA et al., 2025b; NVIDIA, 2025; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025), it remains unclear whether their executed trajectories exhibit this capability.

Existing evaluations do not answer this question. Human-aware and social-navigation benchmarks (Li et al., 2024; Dong et al., 2026; Biswas et al., 2022; Fang et al., 2026) measure executed motion but focus on navigation around people, not on whether motion is calibrated to the safety implications of diverse obstacles. Embodied-safety evaluations for foundation models (Zhang et al., 2025b; Sermanet et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2025) instead assess task completion, constraint compliance, or refusal of hazardous instructions, not whether semantic safety distinctions appear in continuous motion. Evaluating semantic-to-motion grounding requires two components: spatially matched comparisons that isolate obstacle identity from route geometry, and a metric that tests whether motion follows the expected ordering of caution across obstacles.

We introduce OSMA-Bench, an Obstacle-Conditioned Safe Motion Adaptation Benchmark that provides both.
Its matched comparisons vary only the obstacle type while fixing the obstacle position, surrounding layout and route, and are repeated across diverse layouts and routes.
The obstacles span three caution tiers—Living, Fragile, and Robust, in descending order of expected caution—motivated by ISO risk assessment principles (ISO, 2010) and social navigation research (Althoff et al., 2012; Marvel and Norcross, 2017; Möller et al., 2021; Singamaneni et al., 2024).
We also introduce the Semantic Sensitivity Index (SSI), a diagnostic metric that tests whether clearance, together with speed and smoothness as a function of distance to the obstacle, follows this ordering.
Together, OSMA-Bench assess whether a policy adapts its motion to an obstacle’s safety implications, beyond merely reaching the goal without collision.
Using OSMA-Bench, we find that VLM- and VLA-based policies do not consistently exhibits this adaptation, even with explicit safety prompting. Our analysis on VLM shows that safety-relevant distinctions are accessible during isolated motion-parameter inference but weaken when task-execution code and motion parameters are jointly generated; separating the two improves motion adaptation. For VLAs, prompting and action-selection interventions provide only limited recovery, highlighting insufficient semantic-to-motion grounding across both policy families.

In summary, our contributions are threefold:
(1) We introduce OSMA-Bench, a simulation benchmark that evaluates obstacle-conditioned safe motion adaptation through matched comparisons: each comparison varies only the obstacle while holding spatial conditions fixed, and is repeated across diverse layouts and routes. (2) We propose Semantic Sensitivity Index (SSI) which quantifies the extent to which differences in executed motion across obstacle follow the expected caution ordering.
(3) We identify insufficient semantic-to-motion grounding in the evaluated VLM- and VLA-based policies: safety-relevant knowledge is available but does not reliably guide executed motion, highlighting the need to improve how semantic safety judgments inform motion decisions.

title: Dream to Assist: Intent-Conditioned World Models for Shared Vehicle Control
authors: Jonathan DeCastro,Thomas Balch,Emily Sumner,Deepak Gopinath,Laporsha Dees,Patricio Reyes Gomez,Elliot Weiss,Megan Applegate-Kenton,Todd Rowell,John Leonard,Avinash Balachandran,Guy Rosman
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
In shared control contexts where a human and AI assistant share the same embodiment, assistive agents face a fundamental challenge: to act proactively while remaining aligned with human intent, the agent must anticipate what the human is trying to accomplish before it intervenes.
If it does so in ways that conflict with the human’s intentions, assistance can be perceived as interference rather than support. An effective embodied assistant needs to reason both about the task itself (e.g. the end-goal or overall performance of the team) as well as the human users’ objectives while performing the task.

This problem is even more apparent in safety-critical, real-time domains, where the human-AI team has to be aligned (Hadfield-Menell et al., 2016) and fluent (Hoffman, 2019), the AI has to be understood by the human (Sakai and Nagai, 2022), and the system must avoid risky events (Jamieson et al., 2022), performance degradation (Endsley, 2023), or loss of user confidence (Abbink et al., 2018).
Meeting these requirements simultaneously demands tight integration of policy design, interface design, and human evaluation, and probing how algorithmic choices affect the human’s experience of the system as a collaborative partner.

In this work, we present Dream2Assist, a model-based reinforcement learning (RL) framework for real-time shared control. The core idea is to extend a recurrent state-space world model (RSSM) with an intent predictor that infers the human partner’s discrete objectives from observed behavior, and to condition the assistive policy’s reward on the inferred intent. We instantiate this framework in the domain of shared vehicle control, where the driver and the AI actuate the same steering, throttle, and brake controls. The result is a policy that is capable of steering with the human’s intent in mind rather than merely completing the task,
which we quantify via torque alignment.

Because real human partners are expensive and variable, such policies are typically trained against simulated human models in simulation; however deploying them with real humans exposes a domain gap between synthetic and real partner behavior and requires more than algorithmic refinement. We describe the full, data-driven deployment pipeline for bridging assistive agents trained in simulation and the target assistive embodiment. In particular, we show the considerations, criteria, and processes needed to fuse robotic machine learning (ML) approaches and human-centric work in order to provide a balance of system performance, safety, and user satisfaction in time-constrained, tightly coupled, human-robot interaction (HRI).

In an initial version of this work (DeCastro et al., 2025), we have shown that a value-aligned assistive policy with intent-conditioned recurrent state space model (RSSM) improves alignment in synthetic settings. This paper further extends the framework to real human partners: we extend our results to allow evaluation with 40+ human participants across three formal studies and more than 30 informal pilots, addressing human factors considerations such as explainability and cognitive load in providing the right level of assistance to the driver.

We validate Dream2Assist across two qualitatively distinct deployment contexts, probing how intent-recognition embedded into such systems’ fictitious play with the human enables better performance from real humans, leading to improved overtake success on high-speed straightaways, greater torque alignment with driver intent, and lower collision rates.
A preliminary deployment on a physical vehicle platform (N=3N=3) demonstrates policy transfer with no retraining.

In summary, we make the following contributions:

We extend Dream2Assist, presented in DeCastro et al. (2025), with human-data augmentation, reward restructuring, and safety filtering, enabling deployment with real human partners in real-time, safety-critical settings.

We propose a structured deployment pipeline for translating learned interactive policies from simulation to human-centered systems, combining automated policy screening, counterfactual log-replay evaluation, and human-in-the-loop vetting with a coupled iterative interface-design process. We formulate key performance indicators for physical HRI in common multi-agent driving scenarios.

We validate Dream2Assist across two domains via human subject evaluations in high-speed racing (N1=24N_{1}=24, N2=6N_{2}=6) and surprise-rich urban scenarios (N=10N=10), demonstrating that intent conditioning produces measurable improvements over the no-intent-conditioning baseline in torque alignment and collision avoidance under double-blind conditions.

We explore early findings of our approach in a real test vehicle (N=3N=3).

title: RobotAgentBench: Towards Open-world Robot Autonomy
authors: Lingjun Mao,Jinglin Cao,Lukun He,Wenpeng Xu,Yuchen Yan,Hengyu Jin,Zijun Zhang,Jinzhou Tang,Songyao Jin,Ziche Liu,Yifei Shao,Junbo Huang,Fang Nan,Ruobing Han,Ziqiao Xi,Ziming Xu,Shuang Liang,Sibo Zhu,Wenyi Wu,Xinyue Wang,Yiming Huang,Xinkai Zou,Gao Zhu,Kun Zhou,Biwei Huang
comment: Project page:this https URL
abstract: Recent advances in vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) have significantly improved robotic manipulation, yet deploying robots in the open world demands a higher level of autonomy beyond executing predefined tasks. Robot agents offer a promising paradigm for this transition, integrating task discovery, contextual reasoning, physical execution, and adaptive recovery into a closed interaction loop. However, existing benchmarks largely evaluate isolated capabilities, failing to capture the complexity of open-world robot autonomy. We introduce RobotAgentBench (RAB), a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating robot agents in realistic, open-world household environments. Through an agent-assisted, human-in-the-loop real-to-sim pipeline, RAB constructs 50 diverse household layouts with interactive objects and physically grounded tasks, encompassing 90 atomic tasks, 18 short-horizon tasks, 8 long-horizon tasks, and 4 open-ended scenarios. RAB provides a multi-level evaluation of robot agent capabilities: (1) task-level assessments systematically examine five complementary dimensions—task discovery, context reasoning, manipulation, failure recovery, and robustness; (2) scenario-level evaluation assesses how agents integrate these capabilities to autonomously fulfill high-level user needs. Furthermore, RAB enables systematic comparisons of standalone VLA/WAM models and diverse robot agent architectures under a unified planning–execution–verification framework. Extensive experiments reveal substantial gaps between manipulation and autonomy, demonstrate the advantages of agentic architectures and recursive self-improvement, and highlight the remaining challenges toward open-world robot autonomy.

title: What Does World Modeling Actually Improve in Robot Action Learning?
authors: Hanwen Cui,Yuanyuan Li,Qing Guo,Zhida Zhang,Chao Chen,Xi Chen,Jie Cao
abstract:
World Action Models (WAMs) combine future-video prediction with robot action learning, yet improvements in task success alone do not reveal how predictive supervision manifests in execution behavior or whether its benefits persist under task and environmental shifts.
We conduct controlled future-video prediction loss ablations within FastWAM and OpenWAM, keeping model architecture, initialization, robot training data, and training steps fixed within each model family.
Under clean conditions on seen tasks, predictive supervision increases success rates by 24.38 and 72.91 percentage points, respectively.
Trajectory clustering further reveals higher success rates within several coarse trajectory clusters, including cases where cluster frequencies change little, indicating that the gains are not solely reflected in changes in the prevalence of trajectory patterns.
However, these benefits do not consistently persist under distribution shifts: improvements on unseen tasks vary across models and tasks, while both models exhibit low success rates under the evaluated environmental randomizations, without a consistent advantage from predictive supervision.
We further introduce future-video prediction as an auxiliary training objective for π0.5\pi_{0.5}, where a lightweight Transformer predictor used only during training increases success from 82.94% to 89.19%.
These findings support future-video prediction as effective auxiliary supervision for action learning, while distinguishing improved execution on familiar tasks from reliable transfer and showing that such gains need not rely on a large pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT) in the evaluated setting.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models combine vision-language pretraining with robot data to learn policies that generate actions from visual observations and language instructions [17, 10, 8, 4].
Building on this foundation, World Action Models (WAMs) incorporate future visual prediction into action learning, training models to predict environmental changes alongside robot actions.
Methods such as GR-1, GR-2, PAD, and InternW0 integrate these objectives through different architectures, demonstrating the potential of future prediction to support robot action learning [13, 6, 9, 5].
However, improvements in task success alone do not reveal which aspects of policy execution benefit from predictive supervision, nor do they establish that the model has acquired transferable understanding of its environment.

Prior work provides an important starting point for understanding these effects.
Fast-WAM separately examines video co-training during training and future generation at inference, finding that removing the former leads to a larger drop in action performance [14].
This finding supports the value of predictive supervision during training, but final success rates do not reveal how the gains manifest in execution behavior or to what extent they persist across models, tasks, and environments.
Rather than simply revisiting whether video prediction improves task success, we investigate where the benefits of predictive supervision appear and under which conditions they persist.
This distinction matters for assessing the practical value of future prediction and determining how such supervision should be used in subsequent model designs.

To investigate these questions, we conduct controlled future-video prediction loss ablations within two WAM families, FastWAM and OpenWAM.
Within each family, we keep the architecture, initialization, robot training data, and number of training steps fixed, varying only whether the future-video prediction loss is included.
We first evaluate execution success on seen tasks under clean conditions.
We then use trajectory clustering to examine changes in the frequencies of coarse trajectory patterns and their within-cluster success rates, providing behavioral evidence beyond aggregate success.
We further vary task identity and environment configuration separately to assess whether the gains persist on unseen tasks and under environmental randomization.
Together, these comparisons distinguish improvements in familiar-task execution, observable changes in behavior, and the conditions under which predictive supervision remains beneficial.

These analyses also raise a practical design question: if future-video prediction provides useful training supervision, does obtaining its benefits necessarily require a large pretrained video-generation model?
To examine this, we introduce future-video prediction as an auxiliary training objective for the existing VLA model π0.5\pi_{0.5} [3].
We compare the original policy with variants equipped with either a lightweight Transformer predictor or a pretrained Wan DiT video-generation branch.
Both auxiliary prediction branches are used only during training and removed at inference.
This comparison tests whether a lightweight predictor can improve action performance without introducing a large pretrained video DiT branch.

Figure 1 summarizes our research questions, experimental design, and main findings.

Our experiments reveal a clear distinction between the benefits of predictive supervision and the conditions under which they persist.
Across ten seen tasks under clean conditions, adding the future-video prediction loss increases success rates by 24.38 and 72.91 percentage points for FastWAM and OpenWAM, respectively, demonstrating substantial execution gains in both WAM families.
Trajectory analysis further shows that within-cluster success rates increase for several coarse trajectory clusters even when their frequencies change little, indicating that the gains are not solely reflected in shifts in the prevalence of trajectory patterns.
However, these benefits do not consistently persist under distribution shifts: improvements on unseen tasks depend on the model and task, while both WAMs exhibit low absolute success rates under the evaluated environmental randomizations, with no consistent advantage from predictive supervision.
For π0.5\pi_{0.5}, the training-only lightweight predictor increases success from 82.94% to 89.19%, showing that auxiliary prediction can provide positive gains in this setting without a large pretrained video DiT branch.

These findings indicate that future-video prediction can provide effective supervision for action learning, but its benefits on familiar tasks, their manifestations in execution behavior, and their persistence under distribution shifts must be evaluated separately rather than inferred from aggregate success alone.
The lightweight auxiliary predictor further shows that obtaining benefits from future prediction does not necessarily require a large video-generation backbone.
Our results therefore provide empirical guidance for selecting training objectives in future WAMs and VLAs: predictive supervision should be evaluated in terms of its observed execution gains and the conditions under which they hold, rather than assuming that predictive capability, transfer performance, and prediction-model scale are necessarily linked.

title: The German Tank Problem & Navigating by Scent
authors: Kordel Kade France
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Emerging Technologies (cs.ET); Probability (math.PR); Statistics Theory (math.ST)
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
In any navigation task, a robot must have termination criteria for knowing it has arrived at its destination.
One of the most difficult problems for a robot navigating by scent is having it estimate when it is “done”.
In other words, how does the robot know when it has reached the global source of the odor, and not just a local maximum concentration of the plume?
In the most simplistic perspective, this is analogous to one trying to climb a mountain in the fog without the ability to ever see the top - how would one know if they have reached it?
If a robot is indeed near the source but does not yet know, it may circle around trying to maximize the gradient, in turn distorting the plume and creating more turbulence in the process.

Declaring “done” is hard for compounding reasons.
A typical undisturbed plume becomes simultaneously more concentrated and more homogeneous toward its source.
Before we formalized the algorithm in this paper, our olfaction-only UAV would spend several seconds circling the source, chasing ever-smaller gradients [8].
Many times, this distorted the plume so much that it created currents that pulled the UAV away from the source it was already near, and drained more of the battery.
Coupled with the known drift of chemical sensors  [5], this mandates a sense of urgency for the robot to find the odor source as fast and with as little movement as possible.

Turbulent plumes arrive as whiffs separated by blanks [2, 4, 18], so no single reading can be decisive by itself.
In addition, small platforms often cannot precisely indicate where a sample was taken: on our UAV, payload-induced bias in the inertial measurement unit made long-horizon position estimates unusable [8, 9], ruling out methods that fuse concentrations with sample locations.
Concentration-based maps hold little utility in environments with wind or HVAC systems due to the constant change in chemistry, and a robot may also not know what concentration to expect at the source.
Termination criteria are therefore warranted to help the robot know whether it has arrived at the plume source or should keep searching.

There is a classic estimation procedure developed in World War II that models this well: the German tank problem.

title: Dual Gradient Consensus for Adaptive Learning to Transient Out-of-Distribution Disturbances in Quadrotor Control
authors: Mingtian Tan,Vasileios Tzoumas
abstract:
Quadrotor trajectory tracking under unmodeled disturbances often relies on online residual adaptation, but short out-domain residuals can corrupt the learned disturbance model when constant-step updates treat every residual gradient uniformly.
We propose Dual Gradient Consensus (DGC), an adaptive-learning method for mixed in-domain/out-domain disturbances that retains the random Fourier feature model, offline BPTT policy, and least-squares adaptation of a prior domain-adaptive residual policy (DAPL) while modifying the online update step size.
DGC compares each residual gradient with long- and short-term gradient memories, classifies the current adaptation regime, and uses a confidence map to suppress unreliable updates while recovering adaptation after persistent domain shifts.
We evaluate DGC in numerical quadrotor trajectory tracking under four residuals that mix an in-domain component with short out-domain events.
Compared with L1L_{1}-augmented MPC, RFF-based MPC, constant-step DAPL, and a frozen-parameter baseline, DGC achieves the lowest mean position RMSE in all four cases.
introduction:
Future aerial robots are expected to track planned trajectories accurately in complex and cluttered near-ground settings, including infrastructure inspection, last-mile delivery, search and rescue, precision agriculture, mapping and surveying, and urban air mobility, under unmodeled and often systematically unknown disturbances [1, 2, 3, 4].
In such settings, high-speed flight brings unexpected transient events—an inadvertent low-energy collision, a gust strike, brief contact with surrounding structures, leaves ingested by a rotor, or an in-flight motor fault—after which the vehicle must still be controllable rather than only regulated about the original plan [5, 6, 7].

It is challenging to track the planned trajectory accurately while remaining controllable after such transients.
Unknown, time-varying disturbances come in two forms that should not be treated alike: persistent, non-stationary domain changes—changes in aerodynamic loading, a payload that shifts the center of mass in flight, or transitions between regimes with and without ground effect—and the short-lived transients noted above [8, 9, 10].
A common remedy is online adaptation of a disturbance estimate or an environment representation, allowing the controller to continuously account for the residual dynamics encountered during deployment [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 10, 16, 17].
That strategy, however, is itself subject to a mixed-residual issue: the adaptation stream mixes samples that characterize the current in-domain with short out-domain events, and excessive adaptation to the latter causes transient effects to be incorporated into the learned disturbance model rather than treated as temporary deviations.
The remaining issue is therefore how to keep adapting when the domain truly changes, without letting short out-domain residuals rewrite the learned disturbance model.

The current state of the art spans several approaches.
Robust control bounds tracking error against worst-case disturbances without identifying a residual online [18, 19, 20, 21, 22].
Classical adaptive control updates coefficients of prescribed basis functions [11, 12, 13], while disturbance observers, L1L_{1} estimators, and related schemes estimate additive residuals for feedback compensation [8, 14, 23, 24, 9, 25, 26, 27, 10], typically through a low-pass frequency split rather than a test of whether the residual is a persistent domain change or a short out-domain residual.
Learning-based controllers train policies over randomized environments [28, 29, 30, 31, 32] or condition them on environment encoders, as in RMA and DATT [15, 33, 34, 10, 35, 36].
Online non-stochastic control updates sequentially under adversarial disturbances [37, 38, 39, 40, 41, 42].
Predictive residual models have also been used for model-based control [16, 43, 44]: MPC (RFF) adapts random-feature coefficients and kernel bandwidth online [45, 46, 16], while DAPL applies constant-step least squares to the same pair [17], so in-domain and out-domain residuals enter the update at a uniform rate.
Direct online policy learning on hardware has been shown [47, 48, 49].
However, residual adaptation typically uses a uniform step.

This paper builds on the main pipeline of Domain-Adaptive Policy Learning (DAPL) [17]—the RFF residual model, offline BPTT policy, and online least-squares loss—and develops a consensus-driven step-size adaptation for updating the RFF parameters that represent the unknown disturbance.
We propose Dual Gradient Consensus (DGC), overviewed in Figure 1.
Two residual-gradient memories, a long-term gradient representing the current domain and a short-term gradient capturing recent evolution, classify each incoming gradient into four adaptation regimes and modulate its update step without altering the gradient itself.
Unlike CAdam, which gates Adam coordinates for neural recommenders when the gradient and momentum disagree [50], DGC is a consensus map on the residual step length.
In-domain agreement preserves the long-term memory and applies a consensus-modulated step; disagreement with both memories suppresses the update; persistent agreement with the short-term memory triggers a handoff to the new domain.
Relative to MPC (RFF) [16] and DAPL [17], the residual features and least-squares objective remain unchanged, while the kernel parameters continue to adapt online.
The resulting controller retains the same policy as DAPL while limiting the incorporation of short out-domain residuals into the kernel parameters and preserving adaptation to domain shifts.

We evaluate the method in numerical quadrotor trajectory-tracking simulations under mixed in-domain and out-domain disturbances Section IV.
Four disturbance profiles combine an in-domain component with impulsive transients: a steady level change, a zero in-domain residual with repeated impulses, a periodic shift, and a linear ramp.
We compare Dual Gradient Consensus with MPC (L1-E) [10], MPC (RFF) [16], DAPL [17], and DAPL without σ\sigma and 𝜶\bm{\alpha} updates.
Across all four cases, DGC achieves the lowest mean position RMSE; the advantage is largest under repeated impulses, where constant-step DAPL incorporates transient disturbances into the residual model, while the MPC variants perform well on a stationary offset but degrade under domain shifts.
Time histories of residual prediction error, position tracking error, and the applied step sizes are reported together with the RMSE comparison in Section IV-C.

title: Multimodal Socially Aware Framework for Human-Robot Interaction in Virtual Reality
authors: Richard Xu,Dakarai Crowder,Alexis E. Block,Wenzhen Yuan
abstract: Social robots must coordinate speech and movement while interpreting multimodal human input. We present a multimodal framework that integrates speech, vision, and touch to generate contextually appropriate robot speech and movement. We evaluated the framework in virtual reality with 18 participants across five social interaction scenarios, comparing its performance against a human-teleoperated baseline. Although participants rated the autonomous system above the neutral midpoint for both naturalness and social appropriateness, the teleoperated baseline received significantly higher ratings on both measures. Behavioral coding and qualitative feedback revealed that conversational timing, clarification of ambiguous requests, and spatial coordination were important factors contributing to this performance gap. These findings highlight key challenges in developing autonomous robots capable of natural, multimodal social interaction.
introduction:
As robots become more integrated into daily life (e.g., in homes, schools, hospitals, public spaces), how can they behave in a socially appropriate and natural manner? Endowing robots with this ability is no simple task, as they must continuously coordinate speech, body movement, and physical contact while adapting to interruptions, misunderstandings, and shifting social contexts. Humans manage this coordination effortlessly, yet this task remains extremely challenging for robots.

Robots struggle to integrate multi-modal data streams, adapt to unpredictable human behavior, and respond through coordinated modalities, which are necessary for an interaction to feel natural. Previous researchers have attempted to solve this problem by fusing vision, eye gaze, and speech [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. While humans use social touch as an important modality to communicate with each other, using touch as an input in robotics remains underexplored. Furthermore, most of these systems are validated through single-turn interactions or through videos of a robot interaction that participants watch, rather than through first-person interaction with the robot [6, 1, 3]. The absence of multi-turn interactions with an embodied robotic agent makes it difficult to understand the extent to which these systems are capable of social intelligence and to identify the system limitations contributing to poor perceptions of social intelligence.

To enable robots to interact naturally and appropriately across multiple modalities, we present a multimodal socially aware interaction framework that integrates speech, vision, and social touch to generate coordinated speech and robot movement. We represent all modalities as text or image and keep a running interaction history to enable multi-turn interactions. We deploy this framework on a mobile humanoid robot in a simulated environment where participants interact with it through a virtual reality (VR) headset.

We evaluate the framework in VR rather than on a physical robot for five reasons: (1) VR provides a consistent and controlled environment across scenarios and participants; (2) VR allows instant switching between scenario contexts without physically resetting the environment; (3) simulation provides dense contact signals over the robot’s entire surface, which are difficult to obtain reliably from onboard tactile sensors; (4) the immersive headset and haptic gloves preserve the visual and tactile experience as closely as possible; and (5) a virtual robot removes the risk of injury during close-proximity contact.

We evaluate the system across five social interaction scenarios using a within-subject comparison between our autonomous system and a human-teleoperated baseline. For each condition, the participants rated the perceived naturalness and social appropriateness of the interaction and shared open-ended feedback regarding their expectations of robot behavior. Additionally, interaction failures in each condition from video recordings were coded.

Our results show that participants generally perceived the autonomous system as socially appropriate, although the teleoperated baseline received significantly higher ratings for both appropriateness and naturalness.
Behavioral analysis revealed more missed acknowledgments, repeated user attempts, interruptions, and physical touch in autonomous interactions, consistent with participants attempting to repair communication breakdowns through multiple modalities.

In this work, we contribute
a multimodal VLM-driven framework that integrates speech, vision, and social touch to generate socially aware robot behavior.

title: How High Can GPT-6 Astra Climb in Contact-Rich Manipulation? PhysLadder: A Hierarchical, Matched Sim-Real Benchmark for Physical Interaction
authors: Haibao Yu,Jiaqi Meng,Zijian Zhang,Bowen Jing,Lei Yang,Yue Hu,Chenchen Ge,Yiming Hou,Chenbo Xin,Dawen Ye,Haifang Qin,Jin Li,Weitao Zhou,Jianing Qiu,Jiankai Sun,Dandan Zhang,Zaiqing Nie,Ping Luo,Ding Zhao
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
GPT-6 Astra and other general-purpose foundation models have shown promise for robotic manipulation, while reliable execution remains challenging (Zhang et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). Recent work explores adaptation from demonstrations and interaction feedback without parameter updates (Cheng et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026), as well as iterative program development for long-horizon, contact-rich tasks (Shen et al., 2026). Practical use in homes and factories, however, requires reliable contact-rich execution: establishing suitable contacts, regulating forces through them, and coordinating contact changes as a task proceeds (Suomalainen et al., 2022; Noseworthy et al., 2024). Aggregate success rates alone do not identify which physical interaction requirements constrain performance. We therefore ask: which requirements can Astra satisfy as interactions become more demanding, and to what extent do the observed capabilities and limitations persist across simulation and reality?

To address these questions, we introduce PhysLadder, a hierarchical Sim–Real benchmark that organizes 16 household manipulation tasks by their physical interaction requirements (Figure 2; Section 3). The hierarchy is organized around two dimensions: contact configuration and force regulation. L1 emphasizes contact selection and geometric alignment. L2 adds task-specific force regulation within sustained contact, directly or through a tool or container, without requiring contact reconfiguration to continue the operation. L3 additionally requires coordinating contact reconfiguration with force regulation. Levels describe task versions rather than task names: blocks clustered at a dustpan entrance can be swept in one stroke (L2), whereas dispersed blocks require successive contacts (L3). Spatial reasoning and execution precision remain relevant throughout. By relating performance to explicit interaction requirements, the hierarchy supports analysis of capabilities and limitations and provides successive evaluation targets beyond grasping and placement.

PhysLadder provides physically and visually matched real-world and simulated environments for each task (Figure 1). Real-world trials provide a reference for physical execution, while simulation supports controlled, repeatable evaluation at scale. Using the physical setup as the reference, we match workspace layouts, object geometry and appearance, robot embodiment, and camera views. Physical measurements and observed contact responses guide simulation calibration (Section 4). This correspondence supports comparisons of task completion, intermediate progress, and recurring interaction difficulties. Corresponding task definitions and documented success criteria guide these comparisons.

We evaluate GPT-6 Astra zero-shot with three trials per task in each environment. The evaluation yields three main findings. First, reported success rates decline across the interaction levels: from 80.0% at L1 to 47.6% at L2 and 0.0% at L3 in the real world, with corresponding simulation rates of 66.7%, 47.6%, and 0.0%. Second, local physical progress does not reliably accumulate into task completion. Astra may turn a cap or move a drawer without completing the required operation. Execution analysis identifies four recurring interaction bottlenecks: spatial reasoning and execution precision, contact configuration selection and establishment, force regulation, and coordination within and across interactions (Section 6.4). Third, for GPT-6 Astra, the two environments show consistent performance trends and similar interaction difficulties. Ten of the 16 tasks have identical reported success counts, and the remaining six differ by one successful trial. Together, these findings characterize Astra’s observed limitations under increasing interaction demands and support matched simulation as a testbed for studying the sustained, coordinated physical interactions that constrain reliable manipulation.

Our main contributions are:

PhysLadder, a hierarchical benchmark for physical interaction. We define three cumulative levels based on contact configuration and force regulation, and organize 16 household tasks according to the requirements of each task version, providing successive evaluation targets beyond grasping and placement.

Physically and visually matched Sim–Real environments. We construct simulated counterparts of physical tasks through scene reconstruction and calibration against observed contact responses, with corresponding task definitions and documented success criteria for comparison across environments.

A systematic zero-shot evaluation of GPT-6 Astra. We characterize task completion, intermediate progress, and four recurring interaction bottlenecks across levels and environments, identifying the physical interaction requirements that challenge reliable execution.

We define three cumulative levels based on contact configuration and force regulation, and organize 16 household tasks according to the requirements of each task version, providing successive evaluation targets beyond grasping and placement.

2. Physically and visually matched Sim–Real environments. We construct simulated counterparts of physical tasks through scene reconstruction and calibration against observed contact responses, with corresponding task definitions and documented success criteria for comparison across environments.

3. A systematic zero-shot evaluation of GPT-6 Astra. We characterize task completion, intermediate progress, and four recurring interaction bottlenecks across levels and environments, identifying the physical interaction requirements that challenge reliable execution.
