title: TRIAGE: Efficient Vision-Language-Action Inference Needs Both Reuse and Pruning
authors: Sooyoung Kwon,Carlee Joe-Wong,Kyunghan Lee
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are increasingly used for robot manipulation because they map camera images and a language instruction directly to actions. Robots that cannot be tethered to a workstation, such as mobile manipulators and humanoids, must run them on onboard embedded boards, where the prefill latency of the language backbone grows with the hundreds of visual tokens processed at every control step. To meet real-time limits, training-free accelerators recompute only a subset of the visual tokens and skip the rest, either by pruning them or by reusing their cached key-value (KV) states. The two options save nearly the same computation, yet existing methods apply only one of them to every skipped token. Through a token-level diagnostic, we show that which option keeps the action closer to full recomputation depends on the token’s drift, the change in its shallow-layer value since its cache was computed. On both backbones tested, reusing tokens below a drift threshold was no worse than pruning them, whereas beyond it, reuse yields up to 4.4×\times the action error of pruning; the same diagnostic calibrates this threshold per backbone. Building on this finding, we propose TRIAGE, which deems a cache valid when its drift is below this threshold and it is not too old. TRIAGE recomputes a fixed budget of tokens, prioritizing important tokens with invalid caches, reuses every other token with a valid cache, and prunes the rest; prune-only and reuse-only methods are the two extremes of this partition. Because the budget fixes the number of recomputed tokens, it directly sets the prefill latency. On LIBERO and SimplerEnv, TRIAGE stays within 3 pp of full recomputation in average success rate while cutting prefill latency on a Jetson AGX Orin by up to 48%, and with only 7% of visual tokens recomputed, it beats the strongest baseline by 24.4 pp on LIBERO-Object.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robotic manipulation [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. At every control step, a VLA model feeds hundreds of visual tokens, together with a language instruction, into a large language model (LLM) backbone that outputs actions. However, on embedded boards such as NVIDIA Jetson, the hardware typically mounted on robots, LLM inference is too slow for tasks that demand rapid reactions such as catching a moving object. Offloading inference to a remote server is not a dependable alternative either: end-to-end latency then depends on the network as much as on the server [6], wireless links to mobile robots suffer from fluctuating latency and intermittent outages, and a single delayed or lost response stalls the control loop. On such hardware, the prefill stage of the LLM backbone is compute-bound, so its latency grows with the number of input tokens [7]; for models that decode all actions in a single forward pass, such as OpenVLA-OFT, prefill accounts for two thirds of each control step (Table I). In VLA models, visual tokens account for roughly 90% of the input sequence, making them the main contributor to both computation and latency.

Training-free acceleration methods therefore mainly focus on reducing the number of visual tokens the backbone computes through token pruning or reuse. Token pruning [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13] estimates each token’s importance at a shallow layer and permanently discards less important tokens, directly shortening the sequence processed by subsequent layers. Because pruning is irreversible, aggressive pruning ratios tend to remove task-relevant tokens, sharply degrading accuracy. Token reuse [14, 15, 16, 17] instead identifies tokens that remain largely unchanged from the previous frame and reuses their key-value (KV) caches. However, these caches were computed in the context of the previous frame; as the scene changes, they become stale. Repeatedly reusing those stale KV caches causes errors to accumulate and severely degrades accuracy.

We argue that applying a single operation uniformly to all tokens outside the recomputed set inevitably sacrifices accuracy or wastes computation (Fig. 1). Consider a token that is important but unchanged: pruning can only recompute it, wasting computation on information already in the cache, or discard it, losing information the model needs. Reuse, conversely, retains unimportant tokens that could have been discarded, and keeps serving cached states even after they have become stale. To our knowledge, no prior VLA acceleration method chooses between the two per token: every existing method either prunes or reuses all of the visual tokens it does not recompute (Section II).

When, then, should a token that is not recomputed be reused, and when should it be pruned? Answering this requires a per-token signal that is available before the deep layers run, costs no extra computation, and predicts whether serving a cached state will distort the action. We use drift, the relative change in a token’s shallow-layer value since its cache was last computed. Similar change measures have been used to choose which tokens to recompute [18, 19], but prior works have not studied whether such a signal can decide between reuse and pruning. We examine it with a token-level diagnostic (Section III), a controlled experiment that handles the same tokens once by reuse and once by pruning and compares each resulting action with that of full recomputation. On both backbones we tested, reusing tokens below a drift threshold was no worse than pruning them, whereas as drift rises beyond it, reuse yields up to 4.4×\times the action error of pruning, regardless of token importance. The threshold depends on the backbone, and rerunning the diagnostic on a new backbone provides it.

This finding separates the roles of two per-token signals. Cache validity, which requires drift below the threshold and a bounded cache age, decides whether a token that is not recomputed should be reused or pruned. Importance, the attention a token receives from the action-decoding tokens, decides where the limited recomputation budget should go: to important tokens whose caches are no longer valid, for which neither reuse nor pruning is adequate.

We therefore propose a three-set structure that assigns each visual token to recomputation, reuse, or pruning based on its importance and cache validity. Within a given recomputation budget, important tokens with invalid caches are recomputed first; among the remaining tokens, those with valid caches are reused and the others are pruned.

Experiments on two VLA backbones and two benchmarks, with latency measured on a Jetson AGX Orin, show that TRIAGE achieves success rates comparable to state-of-the-art pruning and reuse methods at similar compute while reducing prefill latency by up to 48%. Its advantage grows as the recomputation budget shrinks: on LIBERO-Object with OpenVLA, TRIAGE stays within 3 pp of full recomputation when recomputing only 11% of the visual tokens, and at 7% it outperforms the strongest baseline by 24.4 pp.

Our contributions are as follows:

A token-level diagnostic showing that whether a non-recomputed token should be reused or pruned depends on its drift, regardless of its importance, which makes both prune-only and reuse-only methods suboptimal.

TRIAGE, a three-set structure that assigns each visual token to recomputation, reuse, or pruning, with prune-only and reuse-only methods as its two extremes.

Experiments on two backbones and two benchmarks showing that TRIAGE stays within 3 pp of full recomputation while reducing prefill latency on a Jetson AGX Orin by up to 48%.

3. Experiments on two backbones and two benchmarks showing that TRIAGE stays within 3 pp of full recomputation while reducing prefill latency on a Jetson AGX Orin by up to 48%.

title: IntNet: A Communication-Driven Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Cooperative Autonomous Driving
authors: Leandro Parada,Kevin Yu,Panagiotis Angeloudis
abstract: Achieving safety in autonomous driving through Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is a critical yet challenging task due to non-stationarity, partial observability, and the need for effective coordination among agents. Although earlier cooperative MARL methods have aimed to improve coordination by sharing encoded state observations, we find these strategies are insufficient in safety-critical scenarios. To address this gap, we present IntNet, a novel MARL framework that enhances safety by incorporating the transmission of vehicle intent and adaptive communication scheduling into a unified end-to-end learning paradigm, jointly optimising all components for safe coordination. Central to our approach is an observation prediction module that enables agents to forecast subsequent policy outputs, which they can then share across a vehicle-to-vehicle network. Our model-free architecture employs a Graph Attention Network to process incoming messages and a scheduler component to dynamically optimise the communication graph for bandwidth efficiency. We compare IntNet against state-of-the-art communicative MARL methods in complex urban environments with both autonomous and human-operated vehicles, achieving improved coordination, lower collision rates, and reducing communication efforts by up to 60%. Through extensive experiments, we assess the framework’s learning efficiency, scalability, and the balance between information sharing and bandwidth usage for collision-free trajectories.
introduction:
Deploying Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) in dynamic urban environments requires effective coordination to ensure safety. While Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has shown promise in coordinating autonomous tasks such as multi-robot path planning and navigation [17], applying it to autonomous driving presents distinct challenges. The complex and dynamic nature of urban settings and partial observability complicate the achievement of high levels of safety and coordination. Furthermore, the unpredictability of human driver behaviour adds a layer of complexity to this challenge.

Several applications of MARL in autonomous driving, spanning from intersection management to traffic optimisation, demonstrate its impact on the field. Notable research underscores MARL’s efficacy in cooperative motion planning [1, 20, 23], as well as in controlling traffic signals to enhance urban mobility [26, 28, 8, 27]. Despite these considerable advancements, achieving effective coordination and safety remains the most critical challenge for MARL in autonomous driving [5]. While model-free MARL does not inherently provide safety guarantees, it offers a powerful methodology for addressing safety through trial-and-error learning, particularly in scenarios with diverse and complex configurations.

Agent coordination has been extensively studied within the MARL community by sharing state representations through a communication network [31]. However, we argue that for safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving—-characterised by highly dynamic scenarios-—simply sharing state features is not enough. Understanding the future intentions of others provides additional contextual information to the agents that may otherwise be unavailable, thus unlocking opportunities for safer, more efficient decision making. Although some studies have explored intention-sharing in MARL [9, 3], their applications are limited to simplistic grid-like environments, lacking the intricacies of autonomous driving, such as high-dimensional observations (e.g., Camera, LiDAR) and autonomous traffic dynamics.

To address the existing gap, we introduce IntNet, an intention-sharing MARL framework tailored for CAVs navigating complex urban environments safely and efficiently. IntNet operates through two communication steps. In the first step, agents share encoded messages and their recent decision-making strategies based on actual, observed information. In the second step, they communicate their estimated intentions over a future prediction horizon HH. Each agent uses an observation predictor to forecast environmental states, projecting future strategies over the horizon HH to enhance coordination and proactive decision-making. To efficiently manage this process, a scheduler component is employed for bandwidth optimisation, while a graph attention network is used for processing incoming messages. The integration of each component within the end-to-end framework allows safety to emerge naturally from coordinated learning, rather than relying on hard constraints. The overall architecture employs an actor-critic loss alongside an independent supervised loss for training the observation prediction module. Training occurs directly from environmental interaction, eliminating the need for pre-training for the observation predictor. We benchmark IntNet against state-of-the-art Communicative MARL approaches across diverse urban scenarios and show how it can efficiently learn safer policies with low communication graph density.

The key contributions of this work are:

We propose a novel intention-sharing framework for communicative MARL, integrating Graph Attention Networks (GATs) for processing shared messages and a scheduling mechanism to optimise communication, enhancing coordination and reducing uncertainty in safety-critical scenarios.

We develop a prediction module for multi-agent settings that forecasts future observations without requiring pretraining, allowing agents to recursively plan future actions.

We advance beyond prior work in grid-based environments by incorporating high-dimensional observations and realistic vehicle kinematics, providing a more representative evaluation of communicative MARL in autonomous driving scenarios.

The paper is organised as follows: Section II offers a brief literature review on MARL for autonomous driving and recent advancements in Multi-Agent Communicative Reinforcement Learning. Section III details the paper’s methodology, encompassing the cooperative MARL framework, training function, and environment description. Section IV discusses the experiments and key findings. Finally, Section V concludes the paper.

1. We propose a novel intention-sharing framework for communicative MARL, integrating Graph Attention Networks (GATs) for processing shared messages and a scheduling mechanism to optimise communication, enhancing coordination and reducing uncertainty in safety-critical scenarios.

2. We develop a prediction module for multi-agent settings that forecasts future observations without requiring pretraining, allowing agents to recursively plan future actions.

3. We advance beyond prior work in grid-based environments by incorporating high-dimensional observations and realistic vehicle kinematics, providing a more representative evaluation of communicative MARL in autonomous driving scenarios.

title: Scaling Dexterous Manipulation via Action Representation Pretraining
authors: Yanjinghao Xu,Jiexin Zhang,Huan Zhao,Jianjia Mo,Zhenghao Yin,Dingkang Liang,Xiang Bai,Han Ding
comment: . Project page:this https URL
abstract: Large-scale vision, language, and video pretraining has substantially improved the perception and generalization capabilities of robotic manipulation models, but action generation for complex dexterous manipulation remains constrained by the scarcity of robot demonstrations. Limited robot demonstrations must be used to learn both action representations and task-conditioned action distributions, making it difficult to adequately learn action representations and, in turn, limiting the ability of downstream generative models to generate complex dexterous actions. To address this limitation, we propose ARPG (Action Representation Pretraining and Generation), which explicitly separates action representation learning from action generation: we first pretrain an action representation encoder on large-scale human manipulation data. We then freeze the encoder and train a compact generative backbone (130M parameters) to learn task-conditioned action distributions in the encoder’s representation space. Experimental results show that ARPG achieves state-of-the-art performance on the DexJoCo benchmark and improves the average success rate on bimanual dexterous manipulation from 10.1% for π0.5\pi_{0.5} to 44.7%. Scaling experiments further show that broader coverage of human manipulation behaviors effectively improves downstream performance. These results indicate that action representation pretraining provides an independent scaling dimension for improving complex dexterous manipulation capabilities.
introduction:
Building general-purpose robots capable of complex dexterous manipulation, particularly coordinated and precise manipulation with dexterous hands, is an important goal in robot learning.
In recent years, large-scale vision, language, and video pretraining has endowed robot policies with strong visual representations, semantic understanding, and task generalization (Bi et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Black et al., 2025a; Zheng et al., 2026b).
However, robots must ultimately translate these capabilities into concrete manipulation actions, and reliable action generation remains a significant challenge.
Mainstream policies learn action generation end to end from robot demonstrations, requiring the model to both learn representations suitable for action generation and model the action distribution under specific conditions from those demonstrations; thus, further improvements in complex action generation are constrained by both the scale of robot demonstrations and the capacity of the downstream model.
This observation raises a question: Can scalable action representation pretraining continuously improve complex dexterous manipulation without simultaneously scaling robot demonstrations and the generative backbone?

Recent research in generative modeling suggests that generative models need not learn their modeling spaces entirely from scratch: pretrained representations can either guide internal representation learning in a generative model or directly define the generative space through a pretrained encoder, thereby decoupling representation learning from subsequent distribution modeling (Yu et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026a).
However, extending this idea to robot actions is nontrivial: a representation space suitable for complex action generation must preserve sufficient action information for reliable action recovery while encoding motion and interaction semantics throughout manipulation.
Pretrained visual encoders have learned rich motion and interaction semantics from large-scale video data (Assran et al., 2025; Mur-Labadia et al., 2026), but their representation spaces are not themselves designed for action representation and recovery; conversely, with action-only self-supervised learning, the action encoder must learn representations from scratch and cannot reuse the representation structure acquired through large-scale visual pretraining or exploit the scene context and interaction semantics contained in the visual modality.

Motivated by these observations, we propose ARPG (Action Representation Pretraining and Generation), which decouples action representation pretraining from downstream task-conditioned action generation and performs generation in the pretrained action representation space.
Specifically, we use a vision–action dual-tower encoder: a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 (Mur-Labadia et al., 2026) extracts visual representations, an action Transformer encodes action trajectories, and a vision–action alignment objective based on sigmoid loss (Zhai et al., 2023) aligns action representations with visual representations, thereby leveraging representation priors acquired through large-scale video pretraining.
Because action representation learning is decoupled from generative learning, the action encoder need not be adapted to the action details of a specific robot embodiment through the generative objective and can instead learn reusable action representations from data; its pretraining can therefore be extended to larger-scale egocentric human manipulation data (Hoque et al., 2026; Punamiya et al., 2026).
After pretraining, we freeze the action tower and use it as an action representation encoder, training an action decoder on robot demonstrations to recover executable continuous actions from the representations.
On this basis, the downstream policy only needs to learn the task-conditioned action distribution in the fixed action representation space: ground-truth future action chunks (Zhao et al., 2023) are mapped by the frozen action encoder into generation targets; conditioned on the task, a DiT generative backbone (Peebles and Xie, 2023) generates future action representations through Flow Matching (Lipman et al., 2023), which the action decoder then recovers as executable actions.

We evaluate ARPG on the DexJoCo simulation benchmark (Wang et al., 2026) and a real-robot platform.
Despite using a compact generative backbone with only approximately 130M parameters, ARPG achieves better overall performance than π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Black et al., 2025a) under joint multi-task training on DexJoCo, increasing the average success rate on bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks from 10.1% to 44.7% while substantially reducing inference costs.
Further scaling experiments reveal that effectively scaling action representation pretraining hinges on broadening the range of task types covered by the pretraining data.
We further analyze which action representation spaces are better suited to complex action generation and verify the advantages of representations learned through vision–action alignment for downstream generation.
Thus, action representations need no longer be merely internal representations formed jointly during end-to-end policy learning; they can instead become objects of independent pretraining and scaling, providing a new scaling path for improving complex dexterous manipulation capabilities.

title: AuRA: From Atoms to Bits through Autonomous Robot Interaction
authors: Xinchen Yu,Yoonkyo Jung,Haoran Chen,Zikui Cai,Aayush Talreja,Seungjae Lee,Hyunjin Kim,Furong Huang
comment: Project page:this https URL
abstract: Simulation enables robot-learning experiments at scale, but acquiring physics-informed digital twins often requires human manipulation and manual annotation of recorded interactions. To reduce this reliance on human effort, we present AuRA, a system that automates robot interaction and data preparation for digital-twin reconstruction. AuRA combines execution-aware grasp selection, gripper-motion measurements derived from robot states, and registered pre-interaction geometry and appearance priors. These choices enable autonomous collection, avoid reliance on visual gripper tracking, and recover object information obscured by the robot. Across 13 deformable objects, AuRA reduces active human labor and wall-clock collection time per successfully reconstructed asset by 88.5% and 55.4%, respectively. Relative to the human-collected PhysTwin baseline, AuRA improves seven of nine metrics for future prediction under known gripper motion, including a 28.1% reduction in one-way L1L_{1} Chamfer distance. It also achieves similar mean silhouette IoU and Chamfer distance under the evaluated unseen interactions. These results highlight the potential of autonomous robot interaction to support more efficient digital-twin acquisition with comparable reconstruction quality.
introduction:
Simulation enables repeated robot-learning experiments in digital environments, supporting scalable data generation and policy training [1, 2, 3]. To reflect interactions with particular real-world objects, these environments need digital assets that represent the objects’ geometry, appearance, and physical behavior. Real-to-sim reconstruction offers a way to build such assets from observations of real objects, with manipulation providing information about their dynamics. The resulting assets can be reused across simulated experiments, supporting a shift from an “atoms loop” of physical manipulation to a “bits loop” of simulation.

A key bottleneck, however, lies in acquiring the real-world observations required for reconstruction. Existing workflows often rely on human manipulation or manual annotation of recorded data [4, 5]. This per-object human involvement limits the rate at which asset collections can be expanded. Automating interaction-data acquisition offers a way to reduce this effort: a robot can select and execute interactions while recording the observations needed for reconstruction. In practice, a reliable autonomous pipeline must address three coupled challenges.

First, selected interactions must satisfy robot and workspace constraints. A visually plausible grasp may violate joint limits or bring the gripper too close to the table or cameras, creating collision risks.
Second, reconstruction requires reliable gripper-motion inputs. Segmentation, tracking, and depth errors can corrupt visually estimated gripper trajectories, potentially biasing the physical parameters inferred from the object’s response.
Third, robot-induced occlusion can leave object geometry and appearance incomplete. The gripper and arm may obscure portions of the object throughout the trajectory. Missing surface observations can leave gaps in both the physical model and its rendered appearance.

To address these challenges, we introduce AuRA (Autonomous Real-to-sim Asset Reconstruction), a system for autonomously collecting object-interaction data and reconstructing simulation-ready assets. First, AuRA autonomously identifies and executes feasible object interactions. After object placement and system initialization, AuRA generates grasp candidates from pre-interaction RGB-D observations and checks their feasibility against robot and workspace constraints. The robot then executes the selected interaction while the system records RGB-D videos and robot states.

Second, AuRA separates measurement of the robot’s action from observation of the object’s response. Recorded robot states and calibrated gripper geometry are used to derive controller trajectories, while visual tracking captures the object’s motion and deformation. This separation provides reliable motion inputs without requiring visual gripper segmentation, tracking, or depth lifting.

Third, AuRA reuses pre-interaction observations to mitigate robot-induced occlusion. It constructs a static point cloud and a Gaussian appearance model, then aligns both with the first interaction frame to account for small pose changes caused by grasping. These registered priors supplement geometry and appearance missing from the interaction observations. The same pre-interaction captures therefore support both physical acquisition and digital reconstruction, without requiring a prebuilt object asset or a separate manual capture stage.

We evaluate data collection efficiency, reconstruction reliability, and asset quality across 13 deformable objects. Compared with human-operated collection overall, AuRA reduces active human labor and wall-clock collection time per successfully reconstructed asset by 88.5% and 55.4%, respectively. Across all acquisition attempts in the timed collection study, AuRA achieves an end-to-end reconstruction success rate of 74.3%, compared with 26.9% for human-operated collection overall. Moreover, AuRA improves seven of nine metrics compared to the human-collected PhysTwin baseline for future prediction, reducing one-way L1L_{1} Chamfer distance by 28.1% and increasing depth coverage by 9.9 percentage points. The two methods also achieve similar mean silhouette IoU and Chamfer distance on the evaluated unseen interactions. In summary, our main contributions are:

Autonomous data acquisition for digital-twin reconstruction. We introduce AuRA, a system that integrates execution-aware grasp selection, autonomous object interaction, and synchronized recording of RGB-D observations and robot states. After setup and initialization, collection proceeds without manual manipulation or annotation.

Reliable controller trajectories from robot states. We derive controller-point trajectories from recorded robot joint states and calibrated gripper geometry. Together with visually tracked object motion, these trajectories support dynamics reconstruction without relying on visual gripper segmentation, tracking, or depth lifting.

Reusing pre-interaction observations for asset reconstruction. We align pre-interaction geometry priors with the recorded interaction to fill gaps caused by robot occlusion, providing a more complete geometric initialization for dynamics optimization. Together with 3D Gaussians trained from the same pre-interaction captures, AuRA maintains reconstruction quality while significantly reducing human labor through autonomous data collection.

title: On Distributed Sensing and Adversarial Localization of Narrowband Acoustic Sources for Offshore Data Center Monitoring
authors: Adnan Abdullah,David Blow,Harsha Gundala Sureshbabu,Dongyoon Joung,Sara Rampazzi,Md Jahidul Islam
comment: Technical report
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Modern distributed computing infrastructure, such as data centers, storage clusters, and edge computing facilities, relies on large numbers of spatially distributed hardware units [1]. These systems are vulnerable to acoustic threats, where injected sounds can induce mechanical vibrations in sensitive components such as hard disk drives (HDDs) [2, 3]. Recent studies demonstrate that an adversarial agent can remotely inject malicious sound, leading to I/O disruptions and data unavailability in server systems [4]. Consequently, identifying the agent’s location is a critical capability for monitoring and protecting distributed computing facilities [5].

Acoustic source localization (ASL/SSL) has been extensively studied in both in-air and underwater environments using microphone/hydrophone arrays. These receiver arrays exploit spatially distributed measurements such as received signal strength (RSS) [6], time difference of arrival (TDOA) [7, 8, 9], frequency difference of arrival (FDOA) [10], and direction of arrival (DOA) [11] to estimate the acoustic source location. Most existing TDOA-based localization methods assume broadband signals, such as human speech, marine mammal vocalizations, pulsed signals, or environmental sounds, that provide unambiguous delay estimates between each receiver pair [12, 13]. In contrast, an adversarial source may intentionally emit a narrowband tonal signal near a resonance frequency to maximize damage to storage devices. Such periodicity induce phase aliasing in TDOA measurements, where the observable delay is known only modulo the acoustic wavelength [14, 15]; see Fig. 1. Consequently, the receiver pairs yield finitely many feasible source locations, resulting in an ambiguous localization problem [16].

Practical surveillance requirements impose another challenge: acoustic sensing must be distributed across a large area. Deploying compact arrays at every infrastructure node is costly and difficult to scale. Conversely, a single centralized array is ineffective because signal attenuation and multipath propagation degrade measurements over long distances [17]. Therefore, acoustic monitoring systems rely on sparsely distributed single receivers [18]. In such settings, the subset of receivers with reliable measurements varies with source location, necessitating quality-based adaptive channel weighting.

These challenges motivate the investigation of adversarial acoustic source localization (AASL) under three coupled conditions: (i) sparse distributed sensing, (ii) narrowband phase aliasing, and (iii) receiver-dependent channel degradation. This report investigates the following research questions:

RQ1: Phase ambiguity. Can unaliased geometric constraints obtained through mobile sensing resolve the phase ambiguity induced by narrowband signals and distributed receivers?

RQ1: Phase ambiguity. Can unaliased geometric constraints obtained through mobile sensing resolve the phase ambiguity induced by narrowband signals and distributed receivers?

RQ2: Geometry and uncertainty. How do anchor selection, receiver geometry, and measurement uncertainty affect initial localization accuracy and subsequent tracking performance?

RQ3: Channel degradation. To what extent can quality-adaptive measurement weighting improve localization and tracking when individual receiver channels are degraded?

RQ4: Practical feasibility. How effectively can mobile-assisted distributed acoustic surveillance be implemented across floating and submerged infrastructure and validated in open-water experiments?

To investigate these questions, we develop an adversarial localization framework that augments a distributed receiver network with a mobile acoustic sensor. The framework comprises two main technical components: (i) a mobile-assisted sensing architecture that forms temporary short-baseline anchor pairs with selected static receivers to obtain unaliased geometric constraints; and (ii) a two-stage localization and tracking pipeline that combines anchor-constrained initialization, alias-aware candidate refinement, particle-filter tracking, and quality-adaptive measurement weighting. During initialization, the mobile receiver visits selected static receivers to acquire two independent anchor constraints while the source is assumed to remain approximately stationary. These constraints reduce the feasible solution space to a one-dimensional curve under suitable receiver geometry. Candidate locations along this curve are evaluated using phase-aliased measurements from other receiver pairs and refined through local Gauss-Newton optimization. The resulting estimate initializes a particle filter that jointly tracks source position and velocity, while channel-quality weighting reduces the influence of unreliable measurements.

Our investigation spans three evaluation settings. First, Monte Carlo acoustic simulations examine phase ambiguity, receiver geometry, measurement uncertainty, and channel degradation under controlled conditions. Second, ROS-Gazebo robotic simulations evaluate the integration of mobile sensing and source tracking in floating-barge and submerged-pod surveillance scenarios. Third, open-water experiments assess the framework using a scaled floating data center prototype equipped with six distributed receivers, a mobile receiver platform, and a USV-mounted adversarial source. Performance is evaluated using initial localization error, localization success rate, and temporal tracking error.

The results demonstrate the importance of mobile anchor constraints for resolving narrowband localization ambiguity. In Monte Carlo simulations, the two-anchor configuration achieves a 91%91\% initial localization success rate, outperforming under-constrained configurations. Sensitivity analyses further reveal that localization reliability depends strongly on anchor measurement accuracy, while quality-adaptive weighting improves robustness under receiver-channel degradation. Robotic simulations demonstrate tracking across different infrastructure configurations, and open-water experiments achieve successful localization with tracking error below 22 m in 99 of 1010 trials. Together, our investigations characterize both the potential of distributed acoustic surveillance and the practical importance of receiver geometry and measurement reliability in offshore deployments.

2. RQ2: Geometry and uncertainty. How do anchor selection, receiver geometry, and measurement uncertainty affect initial localization accuracy and subsequent tracking performance?

3. RQ3: Channel degradation. To what extent can quality-adaptive measurement weighting improve localization and tracking when individual receiver channels are degraded?

4. RQ4: Practical feasibility. How effectively can mobile-assisted distributed acoustic surveillance be implemented across floating and submerged infrastructure and validated in open-water experiments?

title: ThinkLocoManip: A Whole-Body Control Agentic Harness for Legged Loco-Manipulation
authors: Nuo Chen,Shizeng Zhang,Yujie Yang,Jinghong Wang,Zhenyang Qu,Xiao-Ming Wu,Yunfei Guo,Zhongwen Lu,Haojie Liu,Chunpeng Lu,Qiao Sun,Xueyi Zhang,Jiangwei Zhong
abstract:
In this paper, we propose ThinkLocoManip, an agentic harness for legged loco-manipulation designed to tackle complex, long-horizon tasks in large-scale environments. Existing approaches typically follow either direct action generation or a plan-then-act paradigm, both of which can struggle with the generalization and error-recovery capabilities required for extended task execution. In contrast, ThinkLocoManip adopts an interleaved reasoning-and-acting paradigm, allowing the agent to continuously reason about its current state, execute actions, observe their outcomes, and adapt its strategy accordingly. Building on this paradigm, our agentic harness orchestrates a suite of specialized tools for perception, navigation, manipulation, and locomotion, enabling flexible composition of heterogeneous capabilities. Unlike existing robotic agentic harnesses, ThinkLocoManip explicitly incorporates locomotion as a tool domain for agent reasoning and execution. We further design a set of skills that explicitly account for both tool usage within each functional domain and coordination across domains, supporting effective execution of complex behaviors over long horizons.
To tackle task failure during long-horizon interactions, we develop keyframe thinking mechanism to preserve critical
execution context and support efficient error recovery.
Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that ThinkLocoManip substantially outperforms representative methods based on both direct action generation and plan-then-act paradigms across challenging long-horizon legged loco-manipulation tasks. Notably, ThinkLocoManip achieves a success rate of 77%, more than twice that of the strongest plan-then-act baseline (37.1%). Our experiments further validate the effectiveness of interleaved reasoning and acting, tool orchestration, and coordinated skill execution.
introduction:
We are entering an era in which intelligent robots are expected to move beyond laboratories and operate autonomously in large-scale real-world environments, such as homes, supermarkets, factories, and hospitals. Performing labor-intensive and repetitive tasks, such as cleaning, organizing goods, and assisting humans, requires more than manipulating objects within a fixed workspace: robots must navigate through the environment, physically interact with it, and coordinate whole-body motion over extended task horizons. This capability, known as loco-manipulation, tightly integrates locomotion and manipulation, enabling physical interactions beyond the reach of stationary robots. Robust and generalizable loco-manipulation is therefore a fundamental capability toward general-purpose embodied intelligence. In this work, we focus on legged loco-manipulation, where legged mobility provides the flexibility and robustness required to traverse complex terrains.

Existing learning-based approaches to loco-manipulation broadly follow two paradigms: direct action generation and plan-then-act. Direct action generation typically learns an end-to-end policy through reinforcement learning or imitation learning, mapping observations directly to robot actions. While effective for reactive control, such policies often struggle to generalize to complex, long-horizon tasks in large-scale environments, largely due to the limited diversity of training data or simulation environments. In contrast, plan-then-act methods explicitly construct a high-level plan before execution, providing stronger task-level structure for complex tasks over extended horizons. However, they can be brittle when new observations invalidate the initial plan or when execution errors require recovery. Consequently, both paradigms remain limited in the generalization and error-recovery capabilities required for robust execution of complex, long-horizon tasks in large-scale environments.

Toward this end, we propose ThinkLocoManip, an agentic harness for legged loco-manipulation designed to tackle complex, long-horizon tasks in large-scale environments. In contrast to the two paradigms above, ThinkLocoManip adopts an interleaved reasoning-and-acting paradigm, allowing the robot to continuously reason about its current state, invoke appropriate tools, observe execution outcomes, and adapt its strategy accordingly, as seen in Fig. 2. This paradigm enables stronger generalization across diverse environments and robust recovery from execution errors. To support such adaptive execution, we organize the toolset into four functional domains: perception, navigation, manipulation, and locomotion. Unlike existing robotic agentic harnesses that primarily orchestrate perception, navigation, and manipulation capabilities, ThinkLocoManip further treats locomotion as a first-class tool domain, allowing the agent to explicitly reason about and invoke locomotion capabilities as part of task execution. Each domain comprises specialized tools that can be selected according to the task requirements and environmental conditions. For example, the robot can employ map-based navigation when a prior map is available, while target-based navigation allows it to actively approach and observe a target when such prior knowledge is unavailable. Building on this modular organization, we further design a set of skills that govern both tool usage within each domain and coordination across domains. In total, ThinkLocoManip integrates 11 tools and 5 skills, enabling flexible and coordinated execution of complex behaviors over long task horizons. We also develop Keyframe Thinking error-recovery mechanism that enables the agent to identify execution failures and adapt its behavior, thereby improving robustness over long-horizon task execution.

Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that ThinkLocoManip substantially outperforms representative methods based on both direct action generation and plan-then-act paradigms across challenging long-horizon legged loco-manipulation tasks. In particular, ThinkLocoManip achieves an overall success rate of 77%, more than twice that of the strongest plan-then-act baseline at 37.1%, corresponding to an absolute improvement of nearly 40 percentage points. Further analysis validates the effectiveness of interleaved reasoning and acting, tool orchestration, and coordinated skill execution, while the accompanying video demonstrates the versatility of ThinkLocoManip across diverse real-world tasks and environments.

title: RynnVLA-Latent: Scaling Robotic Manipulation Foundation Models with 3D-Grounded Latent Actions
authors: Haoyu Zhao,Xingyue Zhao,Zhian Su,Bohan Hou,Yinzhou Tang,Fengyi Wang,Kehan Li,Yuming Jiang,Siteng Huang,Xin Li,Zhenyu Zeng,Mingxiu Chen,Deli Zhao,Zhongyu Li

abstract:
Scaling vision-language-action (VLA) models is constrained by scarce action-labeled demonstrations and incompatible control spaces across robot embodiments. We present RynnVLA-Latent, a framework that turns heterogeneous interaction videos into scalable supervision for robot policy pretraining. At its core, RynnLAM learns continuous, 3D-grounded latent actions from visual transitions without requiring native robot controls. By combining residual future-feature prediction, camera-compensated 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling, RynnLAM encourages representations that capture control-relevant motion rather than appearance changes alone. We apply RynnLAM to 30.1K hours of human, robot, and simulation videos, producing 745.52M latent-action descriptors. RynnVLA-Latent then learns to predict latent-action chunks from visual observations and language through flow matching, before adapting its pretrained backbone and action expert to embodiment-specific robot actions. The resulting 4B policy achieves 98.8% success on LIBERO, 84.7% on LIBERO-Plus without benchmark-specific adaptation, 51.9% average success across five VLABench tracks, and 88.6% average success on the RoboTwin 2.0 bimanual benchmark.
It also achieves the highest observed success rates among the compared methods on six real-world manipulation tasks across dexterous-hand and mobile-gripper platforms. Together with representation ablations and data-scaling results, these findings demonstrate the potential of latent-action supervision for scaling robot policy learning beyond native action-labeled data.
introduction:
Large-scale pretraining has enabled broad capabilities in language and vision-language models (Brown et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Kaplan et al., 2020; Achiam et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a). Recent vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models extend this approach to robot control (Black et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Ye et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026b; Bi et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026d). Scaling policy learning, however, requires supervision that connects visual observations and task instructions to actions across diverse embodiments Zhao et al. (2026a); Zhao et al. (2025).

Robot demonstrations are expensive to collect, and their native controls differ in dimensions, coordinate frames, and semantics (Zhao et al., 2026b; Zhao et al., 2026c). Human and web videos provide much broader interaction coverage but lack corresponding robot commands. These sources cannot simply be pooled under one native-action prediction objective. A shared supervision interface is needed to exploit their visual transitions before adapting a policy to a particular robot.

Latent actions provide such an interface by encoding changes between observations without native control labels (Ye et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025c; Bu et al., 2025b; Gao et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2025; Schmidt and Jiang, 2024; Chen et al., 2024). Existing approaches demonstrate the value of transition reconstruction and feature-space prediction, but visual change can include camera motion, static appearance, and effects unrelated to the agent’s control. A representation that reconstructs images well therefore need not be equally useful for predicting low-level manipulation actions.

We address this through geometric supervision and explicit camera-motion separation. We introduce RynnLAM, which encodes a frame pair into motion tokens, a global action latent, and a camera latent. Residual future-feature prediction preserves transition information through the bottleneck, while camera-compensated 3D-flow pseudo-labels and contrastive feature warping encourage motion-sensitive representations. Camera-pose prediction and gradient reversal further encourage separation of ego-motion from manipulation-related cues. These objectives provide geometric grounding without requiring manually annotated robot actions; they encourage camera decoupling rather than guaranteeing exact viewpoint invariance or physical identifiability.

Using RynnLAM as an offline labeler, we construct shared latent-action supervision for 25 video sources spanning human interaction, real robots, and simulation. The corpus contains approximately 30.1K hours and 3.057B frames and yields 745.52M latent-action descriptors. We then pretrain RynnVLA-Latent, a Mixture-of-Transformers policy that couples a pretrained vision-language backbone with a narrow action expert. The policy predicts latent-action chunks from multi-view observations and language via flow matching, without native-action or proprioceptive supervision. In robot post-training, we reuse both the backbone and action-expert trunk, introduce proprioception, and retarget the output projection to native robot commands. This separates video-based motion supervision from embodiment-specific action alignment.

Our evaluation follows the same path from representation learning to robot deployment. On LARY, frozen-representation probes test whether the descriptors predict low-level control targets, with the full descriptor achieving average relative-action MSE 0.380.38. After native-action post-training, the 4B policy obtains 98.8%98.8\% on LIBERO, 84.7%84.7\% on LIBERO-Plus, 51.9%51.9\% average success across five VLABench tracks, and 88.3%88.3\% average success under the RoboTwin 2.0 Native protocol. These benchmarks respectively assess task execution, perturbation robustness, semantic grounding, and bimanual manipulation. Six real-world tasks on stationary dexterous and mobile gripper platforms test the interface after adaptation to different controls. Data-scaling and component studies further characterize where the approach helps and where performance remains limited.

Our contributions are as follows:

3D-grounded latent-action supervision. We introduce RynnLAM, which combines residual feature prediction, camera-compensated 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling to construct continuous transition representations without native robot-action labels.

Scalable VLA pretraining from heterogeneous video. We develop RynnVLA-Latent, which learns shared latent-action targets from 30.1K hours of human, robot, and simulation videos, and transfers the pretrained policy to native robot controls through embodiment-specific post-training.

Representation and policy-level validation. We demonstrate control predictability through frozen-representation probes, competitive manipulation performance across simulation and real-world platforms, and improvements with increasing latent-action pretraining data.

1. 3D-grounded latent-action supervision. We introduce RynnLAM, which combines residual feature prediction, camera-compensated 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling to construct continuous transition representations without native robot-action labels.

2. Scalable VLA pretraining from heterogeneous video. We develop RynnVLA-Latent, which learns shared latent-action targets from 30.1K hours of human, robot, and simulation videos, and transfers the pretrained policy to native robot controls through embodiment-specific post-training.

3. Representation and policy-level validation. We demonstrate control predictability through frozen-representation probes, competitive manipulation performance across simulation and real-world platforms, and improvements with increasing latent-action pretraining data.

title: ScheNav: Schematic-Guided Object Goal Navigation
authors: Guichen Huang,Chenchen Jing,Che Sun,Yuwei Wu,Yunde Jia
abstract:
Object goal navigation requires an embodied agent to locate and reach target objects in complex environments.
Humans often rely on low-cost yet informative schematic maps, such as rough sketches or directional annotations.
We develop a workflow for schematic-guided embodied navigation with two components: a training-data generation pipeline and ScheNav, a closed-loop navigation framework.
Our lightweight data-generation pipeline turns 2D floorplans into navigation training environments, yielding Furnished-RPLAN, a dataset of over 33k furnished layouts with paired navigation episodes and noise-controllable schematic maps.
ScheNav turns rough schematic guidance into exploration and stopping decisions by using SchemaField, a learned spatial module that fuses the guidance with accumulated observations and predicts spatial value fields.
The framework updates these fields as exploration proceeds, with trajectory-based training and a cross-frame consistency objective supporting coherent guidance across changing viewpoints.
ScheNav learns to use schematic guidance entirely from simulated floorplans and transfers this ability to unseen embodied environments.
Experiments show improved navigation success and path efficiency across schematic maps, goal ellipses, and pointed directions, together with tolerance to the tested schematic perturbations and omissions.
Together, these results demonstrate that rough schematic guidance offers a practical way to improve embodied navigation.
introduction:
Object goal navigation requires an embodied agent to locate and reach an instance of a specified object category in an unseen environment [3, 45].
Recent map-free approaches, from modular semantic exploration to zero-shot agents built on large language and vision-language models [9, 12, 44, 42, 41], accomplish this from egocentric observations alone and generalize encouragingly to novel scenes.
Meanwhile, map-based methods that plan on accurate global maps reach goals with high reliability, since a faithful map reduces navigation to well-understood localization and path planning [34, 6].
Each line of work thus holds an advantage the other lacks.
Map-free agents pay no cost for map acquisition, while map-based agents enjoy strong global guidance about where to go.
We explore whether rough schematic guidance can help embodied agents navigate without requiring an accurate global map.

Humans routinely provide and use exactly this kind of guidance [35].
When searching for a room in an unfamiliar building, we rarely demand a precise map.
A rough sketch of the layout or a pointed direction is usually enough to focus the search.
Such schematic guidance can be produced with little effort and can convey useful layout and goal cues despite distortion and omission.
For example, marking a destination on a rough floorplan can help someone find a room without specifying an exact route.
Figure 1 illustrates this setting, where the agent, given a rough sketch and local observations, is steered toward the goal.
Can the agent reliably convert such imperfect schematic guidance into effective closed-loop navigation decisions?

We develop a workflow for schematic-guided embodied navigation with two components: a training-data generation pipeline and ScheNav, a closed-loop navigation framework.
The workflow starts with 2D floorplans, from which we generate environments for learning how to use schematic guidance.
A vision-language model furnishes RPLAN floorplans [37] and extracts machine-readable furniture layouts, which are processed against the original floorplan geometry.
From these layouts, we generate navigation episodes, simulated local observations, ground-truth spatial fields, and paired schematic maps with controllable noise and incompleteness.
Environment generation and navigation training take place entirely in 2D, without constructing 3D scenes or collecting embodied training trajectories.
This lightweight pipeline produces Furnished-RPLAN, a dataset of over 33k furnished layouts, and supports both training and controlled evaluation of schematic-guided navigation.

ScheNav turns the resulting training resources into a framework for using schematic guidance during navigation.
In each episode, the agent receives a goal category and guidance in the form of a schematic map, goal ellipses, or a pointed direction.
As the agent moves, its observations accumulate into a map of the area explored so far, which serves as its map memory.
SchemaField, the only learned model in the framework, fuses the guidance with this observed map and predicts two spatial value fields.
The distance field scores locations by their navigable proximity to the goal, while the corridor field highlights efficient routes toward it.
The schematic is treated as a coarse prior to be interpreted alongside observations, rather than an accurate map on which to plan directly.
Fixed rules read the fields to guide exploration and verify goal candidates.
During exploration, the agent selects the frontier with the highest corridor score [39].
The Goal Verification module checks whether a detected instance of the goal category maintains a high distance-field value over consecutive steps.
When this condition is met, the agent commits to a final approach and stops on arrival.
A single SchemaField supports the different guidance forms without retraining.
ScheNav attaches to an existing navigation system as a guidance layer, leaving perception, mapping, and low-level motion to its host.

Effective schematic guidance must remain coherent as the agent moves and new observations become available.
In our initial implementation, adding a field predictor trained on individual observation snapshots did not improve closed-loop navigation, despite producing plausible per-frame predictions.
Snapshot supervision, commonly used in learned spatial prediction for navigation [23, 13], does not by itself enforce agreement across viewpoints.
We observed that predictions for the same place could disagree after transformation into the world frame, causing successive frontier decisions to undo earlier progress; we call this failure cross-frame inconsistency.
SchemaField is therefore trained on simulated navigation trajectories, with a cross-frame consistency objective that aligns predictions across viewpoints.
The corridor field further concentrates value along near-shortest paths, turning small differences in goal proximity into clearer frontier choices.
These designs allow the framework to update its guidance as exploration proceeds while maintaining coherent decisions across changing viewpoints.

We evaluate this workflow by training ScheNav entirely on simulated floorplans and deploying it in unseen embodied environments without embodied training data.
Integrated into UniGoal [41], ScheNav uses schematic guidance to improve navigation success and path efficiency on the instance-level HM3D benchmark.
Experiments cover schematic maps, goal ellipses, and pointed directions, examining how different forms of guidance support navigation.
Controlled perturbations on Furnished-RPLAN further test tolerance to schematic noise and missing information.
Component ablations examine how trajectory-based training, cross-frame consistency, corridor prediction, and Goal Verification contribute to closed-loop performance.
A supplementary demonstration uses a genuinely hand-drawn map as input to the navigation pipeline.
Together, these experiments examine both the practical value of schematic guidance and the framework designs needed to use it effectively.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We develop a workflow for schematic-guided embodied navigation that connects lightweight 2D training-data generation with a closed-loop navigation framework, providing a practical route for incorporating rough schematic guidance into embodied navigation.

We construct Furnished-RPLAN, a dataset of over 33k furnished layouts with paired navigation episodes, ground-truth spatial fields, and noise-controllable schematic maps, through a pipeline that operates entirely in 2D without requiring 3D scene construction or embodied trajectory collection.

We introduce ScheNav, a framework that converts schematic guidance and accumulated observations into exploration and goal-verification decisions. Trajectory-based training and cross-frame consistency support coherent guidance, and experiments evaluate transfer to embodied navigation across multiple guidance forms and controlled perturbations.

1. We develop a workflow for schematic-guided embodied navigation that connects lightweight 2D training-data generation with a closed-loop navigation framework, providing a practical route for incorporating rough schematic guidance into embodied navigation.

2. We construct Furnished-RPLAN, a dataset of over 33k furnished layouts with paired navigation episodes, ground-truth spatial fields, and noise-controllable schematic maps, through a pipeline that operates entirely in 2D without requiring 3D scene construction or embodied trajectory collection.

title: AdaPolicy: Action-Driven Anticipatory Robot Policies via Next-Chunk Prediction
authors: Fan Yang,Yuting Su,Chen Zhao,Fugui Fan,Peiguang Jing
abstract:
Endowing robot policies with anticipatory capabilities has proven effective in improving control performance.
However, existing methods predominantly rely on explicit supervision derived from future observations, in either pixel or latent space, at the cost of additional architectural and computational complexity.
Departing from explicit future supervision, we ask whether such foresight can be elicited directly from the action signal.
To this end, we propose AdaPolicy, an Action-driven anticipatory policy framework that shapes future-aware representations via cascaded next-chunk prediction.
Specifically, an Online Action Head jointly produces the current action chunk and an evolved latent state.
Building on this state, a cascaded Unrolled Action Head forecasts the next chunk, and the resulting loss flows back through the evolved state to instill implicit foresight into the online policy.
Importantly, this training-only unroll requires no future-observation encoding, keeping AdaPolicy lightweight to train with zero inference-time overhead.
Experiments on MetaWorld, RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-world deployments demonstrate consistent gains across diverse settings, including up to 1414 percentage points on millimeter-precision tasks such as earphone assembly and shoelace threading.
More details and visualizations are available at https://teee111.github.io/AdaPolicy/.
introduction:
As vision-language-action (VLA) models continue to advance generalist robot
control [1, 2, 3], a growing body of work shows that robot policies
benefit from looking ahead.
In pursuit of this anticipatory capability, recent efforts have incorporated future-oriented supervision into policy learning [4, 5, 6, 7, 8].
Such supervision takes diverse forms, including future images or videos [9, 10, 11, 12], features extracted from future observations [13, 14, 15, 16, 17], and structured targets [18, 19, 20, 21].
Despite their diversity, these objectives share a common reliance on targets derived from future observations.
In this work, we explore an alternative: eliciting temporal foresight directly from the action signal, without explicit supervision from future observations.

Existing methods typically instantiate explicit future supervision in three main ways (Figure 1): reconstructing future pixels, aligning with future latent features, and predicting structured geometric targets.
(1) World-Action Models (WAMs) predominantly learn by reconstructing future images or
videos [22, 23, 24, 8, 25, 9, 10, 11, 12],
but pixel-space targets devote substantial capacity and computation to appearance
details peripheral to control.
(2) Latent-space methods instead operate on features of future frames to avoid raw-pixel reconstruction.
Some approaches directly align policy states with future embeddings [14, 26, 16, 27], relying on frozen extractors [14] or dedicated anti-collapse losses [28, 15].
Others adopt a latent-action paradigm [29, 30, 31], first learning latent actions and a latent world model from observation pairs before distilling them into the policy in a second stage.
(3) Structured geometric targets, such as object bounding boxes and point trajectories [18, 19, 20, 21], are more selective,
but rely on constructed annotations and may discard control-relevant information.
Across all three forms, the supervision signal is derived from future observations.
However, such signals are only indirectly aligned with action
generation: policies are ultimately designed to produce
actionable control, and faithfully reconstructing future details
is unnecessary for this purpose [32, 17].

A natural question therefore arises: can supervision from subsequent actions shape anticipatory latent dynamics without explicit supervision from future observations? 
In standard VLA policies, intermediate state representations are only supervised by the current action chunk; without constraints toward the future, we observe that the output state tokens lack the incentive to progress forward in time and tend to degenerate into a near-identity copy of the current input condition.
To convert subsequent-action supervision into an implicit driver for such foresight, we introduce a simple formulation: the policy outputs an evolved latent state alongside the current action chunk, and conditions the prediction of the next action chunk exclusively on this evolved state.
Crucially, to reduce the next-chunk prediction error, the evolved state can no longer merely copy the current observation features; instead, it is forced to integrate the ongoing action trajectory and encode information useful for determining subsequent actions, thereby implicitly modeling the future state.
This formulation offers two key advantages: first, it elicits anticipatory state transitions without reconstructing future observations or aligning with features extracted from them; second, because the supervision arrives in the same space as the policy’s own output, the evolved state is optimized purely for its utility in control rather than spending capacity on control-irrelevant visual details.

Building on this insight, we propose AdaPolicy (Action-driven anticipatory Policy), a framework that shapes future-aware representations in imitation learning via cascaded next-chunk prediction.
A Context Adapter uses learnable queries to compress features from a pretrained backbone into a compact condition state.
The Online Action Head, implemented as a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) [33], takes this condition state as input and outputs an evolved state alongside the current action chunk.
Conditioned solely on this evolved state, a cascaded Unrolled Action Head predicts the next action chunk.
To prevent the two heads from trivially co-adapting and to stabilize the next-chunk supervision, the unrolled head is parameterized as a gradient-decoupled exponential moving average (EMA) copy of the online head [34, 35].
Crucially, this latent unroll operates strictly as a training-time shaping mechanism, making AdaPolicy plug-and-play with zero inference-time overhead.
We evaluate AdaPolicy across MetaWorld, RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and six real-world manipulation tasks, demonstrating its broad applicability across diverse environments as well as its effectiveness on challenging millimeter-precision tasks such as earphone assembly and shoelace threading.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

Action-Driven Anticipatory Policy Learning. We propose AdaPolicy, an anticipatory policy framework for chunk-based imitation learning that converts subsequent-action supervision into an implicit driver for temporal foresight via cascaded next-chunk prediction. By conditioning an EMA-updated unrolled head solely on the evolved latent state, our method prevents the state representation from trivially copying the current input and elicits anticipatory latent dynamics with zero inference-time overhead.

Action-Driven Anticipatory Policy Learning. We propose AdaPolicy, an anticipatory policy framework for chunk-based imitation learning that converts subsequent-action supervision into an implicit driver for temporal foresight via cascaded next-chunk prediction. By conditioning an EMA-updated unrolled head solely on the evolved latent state, our method prevents the state representation from trivially copying the current input and elicits anticipatory latent dynamics with zero inference-time overhead.

Evaluation Across Diverse Settings.
Experiments on MetaWorld, RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-world tasks requiring millimeter-level precision demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across diverse settings.

Representation Analysis.
Probing and latent-space planning analyses confirm our central
premise: next-chunk supervision shapes the policy’s internal
representations to be future-aware, without targets derived
from future observations.
Concretely, future object positions become more decodable from
these representations, and the representations better support
planning toward future goals.

We propose AdaPolicy, an anticipatory policy framework for chunk-based imitation learning that converts subsequent-action supervision into an implicit driver for temporal foresight via cascaded next-chunk prediction. By conditioning an EMA-updated unrolled head solely on the evolved latent state, our method prevents the state representation from trivially copying the current input and elicits anticipatory latent dynamics with zero inference-time overhead.

2. Evaluation Across Diverse Settings.
Experiments on MetaWorld, RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-world tasks requiring millimeter-level precision demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across diverse settings.

3. Representation Analysis.
Probing and latent-space planning analyses confirm our central

title: HuGe: Scaling Humanoid Generalist Vision-Language-Action Models with Egocentric Experience
authors: Yang Liu,Jiacheng Liu,Hengtao Li,Yuheng Huang,Zijian Yang,Ji Dai,Maoxin Wang,Yi Gao,Qishen Wang,Baohua Yin,Peiyang Li,Shuanghao Bai,Mingyang Sun,Pengxiang Ding,Jianqin Yin,Lixin Yang,Donglin Wang
abstract:
Extending Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) to humanoid robots requires coordinated whole-body control and diverse demonstrations that are costly to collect in real-world scenarios.
Although egocentric human demonstrations provide a complementary source of task experience, differences in visual embodiment and missing robot proprioception complicate transfer to humanoid policies.
To address these challenges, we introduce HuGe, a family of Humanoid Generalist VLAs pre-trained on over 2,000 hours of egocentric human and robot data.
Specifically, HuGe employs three existing representative VLA architectures to predict latent motion tokens for a pretrained whole-body controller, together with hand-control signals.
Based on this, we introduce a three-stage training pipeline that combines egocentric pre-training, humanoid adaptation, and downstream fine-tuning.
To facilitate transfer across embodiments, we construct pseudo-proprioceptive states through simulation playback during pre-training and modify arm appearance in egocentric observations through re-rendering during downstream fine-tuning.
With this pipeline, HuGe achieves the state-of-the-art on simulation benchmark HumanoidArena.
Furthermore, real-world experiments on the Unitree G1 indicate that augmenting robot demonstrations with visually adapted egocentric demonstrations significantly increases success on a pick-and-drop task.
introduction:
Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) [60, 16, 7, 6, 53, 19] fueled by Vision-Language Models (VLMs) [4, 37] and World Models (WMs) [47, 1] have enabled language-conditioned manipulation across a wide range of tabletop tasks.
Building on this progress, extending VLAs to humanoid robots offers the potential to perform diverse tasks in human environments by combining manipulation with whole-body mobility.
Despite this potential, adapting VLAs to humanoid robots remains challenging because task execution requires coordinated whole-body motion while maintaining balance and stability.
To meet these control requirements, existing humanoid loco-manipulation approaches commonly employ hierarchical architectures that combine high-level policies with reinforcement learning (RL)-based controllers [13, 52, 2].
To this end, a central research question is how to train generalist VLAs that translate language instructions into coordinated whole-body behaviors across diverse tasks.

Realizing this goal requires addressing two key challenges.
First, the high-dimensional action spaces and complex dynamics of humanoid robots make it difficult to directly transfer VLA policies developed for robotic manipulators to whole-body control.
In particular, arm movements must be coordinated with the torso and lower body to accomplish manipulation objectives while maintaining balance and stability.
Consequently, VLA-based humanoid control requires an action interface that connects task-level predictions to coordinated whole-body execution.
Second, beyond these control challenges, learning generalist humanoid behaviors requires diverse whole-body demonstrations, yet collecting such data on real-world robots is costly and time-consuming.
To alleviate this data bottleneck, egocentric human demonstrations offer a complementary source of task experience for large-scale training.
However, differences in visual embodiment and the absence of robot proprioceptive observations complicate the direct use of these demonstrations for humanoid policy learning.
These challenges motivate an approach that integrates VLA policies with whole-body control and supports effective transfer from egocentric human experience to humanoid robots through a scalable training pipeline.

To address these challenges, we introduce HuGe, a family of Humanoid Generalist VLAs that operate through a whole-body controller and learn from a large-scale mixture of egocentric human and robot data.
Specifically, HuGe builds on existing representative VLA architectures and follows a three-stage training pipeline that sequentially incorporates egocentric human data, humanoid teleoperation data, and a mixture of downstream demonstrations.
To support this pipeline, we assemble a training corpus comprising over 2,000 hours of egocentric and robot data.
Furthermore, we prepare egocentric data for humanoid policy learning during both pre-training and downstream fine-tuning.
In particular, during pre-training, we use simulation playback to construct pseudo-proprioceptive states for egocentric data that lack robot proprioceptive observations.
Building on this pre-training stage, we re-render and replace arm regions in egocentric observations during downstream fine-tuning.
To assess the effectiveness of this approach, we compare HuGe with baseline methods on the HumanoidArena simulation benchmark and further evaluate its performance on real-world humanoid tasks.
Overall, HuGe achieves the state-of-the-art performance on HumanoidArena, demonstrating its capability for humanoid whole-body control, while comprehensive real-world experiments and solid analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness of the training recipe.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows: 
∙\bullet We introduce HuGe, a family of humanoid generalist VLAs, trained on over 2,000 hours of egocentric human and robot data through a three-stage training pipeline. 
∙\bullet We develop data adaptation methods that facilitate the transfer of egocentric human experience to humanoid policy learning. 
∙\bullet HuGe achieves the state-of-the-art performance against baselines on HumanoidArena, while comprehensive real-world experiments and analyses validate our design choices and training paradigm.
