title: PS-DLO: Property- and Spatially Aware Deformable Linear Object Manipulation Policy
authors: Mengdi Li,Boxian Yao,Xiyu Zhu,Yifan Yang,Yunfan Lou,Xuan Han,Tao Liu,Zhibo Pang
abstract: Deformable linear objects (DLO) pose a coupled perception and control challenge: their slender geometry makes precise localization difficult, while their deformations depend on object-specific physical properties. To address this challenge, we propose PS-DLO, a property- and spatially aware DLO manipulation policy. First, contrastive image–text learning maps the initial observation to categorical descriptions of DLO properties, providing explicit physical and structural priors for action generation. Second, SAM3 extracts mask-guided features from future observations, which are distilled into the policy’s action expert to encode task-relevant DLO regions and their subsequent configurations. We evaluate PS-DLO on nine real-world tasks across single-arm and bimanual platforms, training a shared multi-task policy for each embodiment. PS-DLO achieves an average success rate of 68.9%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 20.0 percentage points. In generalization experiments, PS-DLO achieves higher success rates than the baseline in six of seven visual-shift conditions on butterfly-knot untying. These results demonstrate that combining object-property priors with future spatial supervision improves multi-task DLO manipulation and robustness to visual variation.
introduction:
Recent advances in robotic manipulation of DLO, such as cables, ropes, and wires, have enabled
increasingly complex tasks, including routing, threading, and
knot manipulation [1]. Despite their simple
appearance, DLO exhibit distinctive geometric and physical
characteristics that complicate manipulation. Their slender
structures, frequent crossings, and self-occlusions make
interaction-relevant segments difficult to distinguish from
surrounding scene content. Meanwhile, their configurations evolve
under contact, with deformation governed by object-dependent
properties such as bending stiffness and extensibility.
Variations in these properties can require different grasping
and motion strategies even for the same task goal. Reliable
DLO manipulation therefore requires policies that accurately
localize relevant object regions while adapting their actions
to the physical properties of the manipulated object.

Previous DLO research has demonstrated the value of geometric modeling and property-conditioned control within specialized manipulation pipelines [2, 3].
Vision-Language-Action models (VLA) offer a promising route toward shared multi-task policies by combining pretrained multi-modal representations with robot action learning [4, 5]. However, adapting these models through action supervision alone leaves the use of spatial and physical cues largely implicit. Demonstrated actions specify the desired behavior but do not directly supervise which object regions and property cues should be preserved in the representations used to generate that behavior.
Although such information may be available in visual observations, its consistent use across DLO configurations and instances is not explicitly encouraged. This raises a central question: How can we explicitly guide a shared VLA policy to attend to interaction-relevant regions while incorporating object-dependent physical information into action generation?

To address this challenge (Fig. 1), we propose PS-DLO, a property- and spatially aware manipulation policy for DLO that integrates object-property conditioning and future spatial representation distillation into action learning. First, contrastive image–text learning aligns initial observations with categorical descriptions of DLO properties, providing explicit physical and structural information. The property prompt is combined with the task prompt to condition action generation throughout the episode. Second, a Teacher Encoder is pretrained with action supervision to adapt mask-guided features extracted by frozen SAM3 [6] from future observations into action-relevant spatial representations. These representations are then distilled into learnable DLO queries within the student policy’s action expert. To continually refine the supervisory representations, we introduce a teacher assistant (TA), initialized from the pretrained teacher and optimized through a separate auxiliary action head. The teacher is updated through an exponential moving average (EMA) of the TA encoder’s parameters, incorporating ongoing action-driven refinement while providing temporally smoothed targets for student alignment. Together, object-property conditioning and this teacher–assistant mechanism guide policy learning with explicit object-level priors and spatial supervision informed by demonstrated actions. Future observations, SAM3, both teacher-side encoders, and the auxiliary action head are required only during training.

We train PS-DLO on self-collected demonstrations and evaluate it on nine real-world DLO manipulation tasks, learning a shared multi-task policy separately for the bimanual and single-arm platforms. PS-DLO achieves an average success rate of 68.9%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 20.0 percentage points and achieving the highest success rate on eight of the nine tasks. Controlled ablations show that the full framework outperforms either component alone. We further evaluate butterfly-knot untying under seven conditions involving individual and combined changes in rope color, lighting, and background. PS-DLO outperforms baseline in six conditions and matches its performance in the remaining one. When all three factors change simultaneously, PS-DLO achieves a success rate of 10.0%, compared with 0.0% for baseline, indicating improved performance under these combined visual changes.

Our main contributions are threefold:

We introduce object-property conditioning for multi-task DLO manipulation, using categorical descriptions inferred from initial observations to provide explicit physical property for action generation.

We propose mask-guided future representation distillation, using an action-supervised teacher–assistant framework to distill future DLO spatial knowledge into the policy’s action expert.

We evaluate PS-DLO on nine real-world DLO tasks across single-arm and bimanual platforms, achieving an average success rate of 68.9%, exceeding π0.5\pi_{0.5} by 20.0 percentage points.

1. We introduce object-property conditioning for multi-task DLO manipulation, using categorical descriptions inferred from initial observations to provide explicit physical property for action generation.

2. We propose mask-guided future representation distillation, using an action-supervised teacher–assistant framework to distill future DLO spatial knowledge into the policy’s action expert.

3. We evaluate PS-DLO on nine real-world DLO tasks across single-arm and bimanual platforms, achieving an average success rate of 68.9%, exceeding π0.5\pi_{0.5} by 20.0 percentage points.

title: Semantic-Coupled Perception Framework for Autonomous Laparoscope Control
authors: Enduo Zhao,Fangzhou Li,Yujie Zhu,Sicheng Lu,Fang Chen,Longfei Ma,Hongen Liao
comment: . Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L) for possible publication
abstract: In minimally invasive surgery (MIS), maintaining an appropriate field of view (FoV) is essential for surgical safety and efficiency. However, conventional autonomous laparoscope control methods often treat visual tracking and surgical phase recognition independently, limiting robustness under occlusion, entity overlap, and camera motion. This paper proposes a closed-loop autonomous laparoscope control framework that couples real-time surgical phase recognition with camera-motion-compensated visual perception. By exploiting phase-dependent relationships among surgical entities, the framework improves target state estimation under challenging visual conditions, supporting task-aware autonomous FoV control. Experiments on benchmark datasets evaluate the proposed framework in surgical phase recognition and target tracking, including scenarios involving occlusion and entity overlap. Phantom experiments further demonstrate the feasibility of autonomous FoV control, showing improved target visibility and task execution performance compared with fixed-FoV control. These results highlight the potential of incorporating task-level semantics into visual state estimation for autonomous laparoscope guidance.
introduction:
Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) offers significant advantages over traditional open surgery, including reduced surgical trauma and faster postoperative recovery [1]. However, the limited access and indirect visualization inherent to MIS require the operative field to be visualized through a laparoscope, whose positioning is typically handled by a camera-holder assistant while the surgeon operates other instruments [2]. This arrangement introduces additional coordination demands between the surgeon and assistant and may lead to suboptimal visualization due to communication errors and involuntary camera movements [3]. Ergonomic studies have further reported substantial physical burden and fatigue among camera-holder assistants during laparoscopic procedures [4]. These limitations have motivated the development of robotic autonomous laparoscope control systems that can automatically adjust the camera field of view (FoV) according to the surgical task [5].

Current strategies for autonomous laparoscopic FoV control can be broadly categorized into direct control, instrument-based control, and task-aware approaches. Direct interfaces, such as voice commands[6], head movements [7], or gaze-contingent control [8], allow the surgeon to directly specify camera movements, but may introduce additional cognitive or operational burden by requiring explicit user commands and context switching between surgical manipulation and camera control. Instrument-based approaches instead infer camera motion from surgical tool movements observed in the laparoscopic image. Early methods relied on color markers [3] or visual servoing [9], while more recent approaches employ deep learning for instrument detection and tracking [10, 11]. However, these methods often rely on predefined rules, such as following a single instrument or the midpoint between two instruments, without explicitly considering the surgical phase and the corresponding camera view requirements.

Task-aware approaches have therefore been developed to adapt laparoscope behavior according to the current surgical phase. Li et al. [12] used a Gaussian mixture model to derive phase-specific FoV requirements from instrument distributions. Sun et al. [13] proposed SGR-AutoLap, which adjusts the FoV based on recognized surgical gestures. More recently, Zhou et al. [14] introduced SurgLAT, which models surgical attention as a temporally evolving latent state to infer the operative region. However, these methods primarily use task information to guide camera behavior, leaving target detection and tracking largely decoupled from the surgical phase and entity states. Beyond determining where the camera should look, the surgical phase may also constrain which entities should be tracked and how their states relate.

This opportunity arises because surgical scenes are inherently organized by the task workflow [15]. During a manipulation phase, the manipulated object is spatially and semantically associated with the active instrument [16, 17], while other objects are generally uninvolved in the ongoing action. These phase-dependent relationships provide cues beyond visual appearance and short-term image motion. However, reliable target tracking remains challenging under severe occlusion [18] and camera-induced image motion, which can disrupt spatial association and motion prediction. Exploiting task-dependent relational constraints together with camera motion awareness could therefore improve target state estimation and maintenance under these challenging conditions.

To address these issues, this work proposes a semantic-coupled perception framework for autonomous laparoscope control. The framework integrates object detection and tracking with real-time surgical phase recognition, where perceived states and motion relationships support phase recognition, and the recognized phase constrains object state updating. Specifically, the manipulated object is coupled with the active instrument through phase-dependent spatial relationships, while other objects are treated as non-active and semantically static. These non-active entities are used to estimate camera motion and compensate for laparoscope-induced image motion. These constraints support state maintenance, observation correction, and tracking re-initialization upon reliable detections. The resulting states are organized into a structured surgical state to determine the FoV target. Rather than replacing detection or tracking models, the framework couples their outputs with task dynamics to improve perception robustness. The framework is evaluated through ablation studies and benchmark comparisons, followed by phantom experiments on a robotic laparoscope platform using Peg Transfer and Suturing tasks to assess autonomous FoV control. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

A semantic-coupled perception framework integrates surgical phase recognition with object detection, point tracking, and camera-motion compensation to constrain target state estimation using phase-dependent semantics.

A semantic-coupled perception framework integrates surgical phase recognition with object detection, point tracking, and camera-motion compensation to constrain target state estimation using phase-dependent semantics.

A phase-dependent state update mechanism exploits static and instrument-object binding relationships to maintain state consistency under ambiguous observations and temporary occlusions.

A task-aware control representation aggregates entity states according to the surgical phase for autonomous laparoscope FoV control, validated through phantom Peg Transfer and Suturing tasks.

1. A semantic-coupled perception framework integrates surgical phase recognition with object detection, point tracking, and camera-motion compensation to constrain target state estimation using phase-dependent semantics.

2. A phase-dependent state update mechanism exploits static and instrument-object binding relationships to maintain state consistency under ambiguous observations and temporary occlusions.

3. A task-aware control representation aggregates entity states according to the surgical phase for autonomous laparoscope FoV control, validated through phantom Peg Transfer and Suturing tasks.

title: HumanoidNDM: Closing the Training-Deployment Gap of Motion Tracking via Humanoid Neural Dynamics Model
authors: Chao Chen,Zhenrong Wang,Jilong Wang,Yusen Feng,Jiangran Lyu,Li Yi,He Wang
comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026
abstract:
Humanoid robots have recently achieved remarkable success in motion tracking.
However, during real-world deployment, robots inevitably encounter dynamics gaps—arising from either extra physical disturbances or inaccurate simulation modeling—resulting in a significant training-deployment gap. Therefore, effectively leveraging real-world data to fine-tune policies represents the crucial “last mile” for robust deployment.
To bridge this gap, we propose HumanoidNDM, an online fine-tuning framework for humanoid motion tracking driven by a real-world-trained neural dynamics model.
First, in the data collection stage, we introduce a low-frequency reference perturbation method with an adaptive intensity mechanism, balancing deployment feasibility and exploration efficiency.
Second, for the model training stage, we train a robust history-based, proprioceptive neural dynamics model in Euclidean space by incorporating differentiable forward kinematics, eliminating the reliance on costly motion capture systems.
Finally, in the policy fine-tuning stage, we directly fine-tune the policy via backpropagated model gradients, achieving high data efficiency.
Through physical validation on the Unitree G1 robot, we demonstrate that HumanoidNDM enables rapid real-world adaptation to various perturbations, representing the first online, MoCap-free fine-tuning framework for humanoid tracking policies.
introduction:
Advancements in reinforcement learning [36, 11] and motors [47, 22] have enabled remarkable success in robot control [20, 16], especially in humanoid motion tracking [57, 6, 30]. However, most methods still rely on zero-shot real-world deployment of simulation-trained policies [57, 6, 30]. We argue that this paradigm has critical limitations.
First, during real-world deployment, robots inevitably encounter training-deployment gaps, such as extra physical disturbances or inaccurate simulation modeling, which severely degrade policy performance.
Second, when real-world performance is poor, adjusting simulation training parameters is highly inefficient as it relies on black-box tuning. Therefore, effectively leveraging real-world data to fine-tune simulation-trained policies represents the crucial ”last mile” for achieving robust practical deployment.

In this paper, using tracking as a representative task, we focus on the real-world adaptation of humanoid tracking policies. Inspired by how humans continuously refine their physical skills, we propose HumanoidNDM, which abstracts the online learning paradigm into three stages: Data Collection, Model Training, and Policy Fine-tuning.

However, direct hardware deployment introduces stage-specific challenges across these three stages. First, during data collection, existing approaches often either employ exogenous noise injection (e.g. add Gaussian noise to action), which leads to violent joint jitter and whole-body shaking on physical robots [35, 33], or depend solely on environmental stochasticity for passive exploration [15], which is highly detrimental to subsequent policy fine-tuning. As a result, existing methods fail to achieve a balance between deployment feasibility and exploration effectiveness. Second, in model training, learning whole-body dynamics relies heavily on privileged information obtained from external MoCap systems [15], which is costly and hard to deploy. Lastly, during policy training, achieving efficient and stable fine-tuning under limited online data remains a problem. HumanoidNDM resolves these bottlenecks step by step.

In the Data Collection stage, we propose Frequency-domain Exploration via Neighborhood Coverage Estimation (FENCE). To strike a balance between deployment feasibility and exploration effectiveness, FENCE injects low-frequency noise into the reference motions, leveraging inherent policy robustness for smoother and more stable exploration. We further introduce an adaptive mechanism that dynamically scales the perturbation intensity based on policy neighborhood coverage to enhance exploration efficiency.

In the Model Training stage, while optimizing models in Euclidean space has become a consensus in existing works [10, 53], doing so for humanoid robots typically relies on privileged MoCap data. To bypass this, we extend traditional single-frame models with historical observations and differentiable forward kinematics (FK), enabling direct optimization in Euclidean space via purely proprioceptive data, which significantly improves the model’s reliability and robustness.

Finally, in the Policy Fine-tuning stage, we adopt a supervised learning paradigm that updates the policy via model gradients [12, 13, 14, 50]. Unlike prior methods constrained by privileged information and short rollouts that cause greedy updates, our proprioceptive model supports training over longer rollout horizons, thereby achieving efficient optimization across the entire trajectory.

Simulation experiments show HumanoidNDM achieves significant improvement under various training-deployment gaps, surpassing baselines across various metrics. Real-world experiments demonstrate that HumanoidNDM achieves efficient adaptation against challenging disturbances.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

We propose FENCE, a deployment-feasible real-world exploration method using low-frequency reference perturbations, along with an adaptive intensity mechanism.

We propose methods for training MoCap-free robust neural dynamics models, and subsequently leverage the model’s differentiability to enable efficient policy fine-tuning.

We deploy the first online fine-tuning framework for humanoid tracking policies, validating its ability to adapt to challenging disturbances.

1. We propose FENCE, a deployment-feasible real-world exploration method using low-frequency reference perturbations, along with an adaptive intensity mechanism.

2. We propose methods for training MoCap-free robust neural dynamics models, and subsequently leverage the model’s differentiability to enable efficient policy fine-tuning.

3. We deploy the first online fine-tuning framework for humanoid tracking policies, validating its ability to adapt to challenging disturbances.

title: RoboDuo: Attempt, Check and Atomic Recovery through Code for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Jie Wang,Bo Zhang,Renzhi Lu,Jianyu Chen
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map a language instruction and the current observation directly to actions, without checking whether the instruction has been completed.
For long-horizon tasks, a single failed step therefore goes unnoticed and leaves the whole task unfinished.
Such failed episodes, however, often end with the task partially complete. Moreover, the unfinished steps are reusable atomic skills that recur across demonstrations. A failed attempt can thus be recovered by composing with atomic skills.
We propose RoboDuo, a closed-loop dual-system framework that uses code as the interface between a coding agent and two VLAs.
The agent writes a program that lets a full-task VLA attempt the whole task and checks whether it is complete; on failure, an atomic VLA finishes the remaining steps.
Since the agent emits no actions and only decides which VLA for execution, RoboDuo wraps an existing full-task VLA without updating its weights.
To train the atomic VLA and the coding agent with the completion-checking ability, we build LIBERO-Atomic, LIBERO-Code, and LIBERO-Judge from a single set of LIBERO demonstrations.
RoboDuo consistently improves X-VLA and π0.5\pi_{0.5} on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, with the largest gains on long-horizon tasks, and recovers failed rollouts of a frozen full-task VLA on a real robot.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [5, 17, 3, 28, 41, 40] map a language instruction and the current observation directly to low-level actions, and have become a standard approach to language-conditioned manipulation. The policy is re-queried on each new observation, yet nothing checks whether the current observation satisfies the intended goal. Execution therefore continues under the same instruction even after a step has failed. Consider an object that slips from the gripper during transport. The post-slip state is rare in the demonstrations, so the policy rarely re-grasps and may instead continue its learned trajectory, for example by placing with an empty gripper. On a long-horizon task, that unnoticed failure leaves the remaining steps unfinished, and the episode fails even though earlier progress was correct.

One route is to place this decision-making functionality inside the action model.
Systems built on GPT-6-Astra [27] use one large model to generate numerical robot actions, judge the outcome during execution, and emit a correction within the same forward pass [12].
However, the scale that enables such judgment and correction also slows every inference step.
Even steps that a fast policy could execute unchanged must wait on the large model, and the resulting latency falls short of the control rate required for physical deployment.

Dual-system architectures instead place the decision model outside the action model.
In Helix and related systems, a high-level model passes a language command, a token, or a latent vector to a single low-level policy [9, 28, 30, 2, 6, 38, 8, 29].
This interface changes what the low-level policy is conditioned on, but it cannot express a failed attempt, a retry, or a switch to a different executor.
Code-as-policy methods provide exactly this control flow, in which an agent writes a program that tests the outcome of each skill and retries it on failure [20, 14, 31, 13, 21].
Because these programs call primitives or VLA skills from the first step, they largely discard the long-horizon competence of a full-task VLA.
Code is therefore better used to wrap one attempt by that VLA, and to close the loop only after the attempt fails.

Building on this principle, we propose RoboDuo, a dual-system framework in which a coding agent uses code as the interface to two frozen VLAs (Fig. 1).
The agent serves as an orchestrator and writes a task program.
The program first assigns the task to the full-task VLA for one attempt, after which is_task_complete evaluates the new observation.
If the task fails, the agent plans the unfinished steps from the current observation as atomic instructions.
An atomic VLA then executes these instructions to the end of the task, with at most three attempts per step, and the control does not return to the full-task VLA.
We employ a separate atomic VLA since each atomic instruction describes a short segment already present in the demonstrations, whereas the full-task VLA is trained only on full-task instructions.
We construct LIBERO-Atomic, LIBERO-Code, and LIBERO-Judge from the same demonstrations to train the atomic VLA, the coding agent, and the completion check, respectively.
We instantiate RoboDuo on X-VLA and π0.5\pi_{0.5} without updating the weights of either full-task VLA.

On LIBERO-Long, RoboDuo raises the success rate of X-VLA from 87.4% to 91.6% and that of π0.5\pi_{0.5} from 93.6% to 96.2%.
On LIBERO-PRO, RoboDuo raises the mean success of π0.5\pi_{0.5} from 32.05% to 39.33%, with the largest gain on Object-T (25.2→55.825.2\rightarrow 55.8).
On a real robot, RoboDuo raises success from 36.7% to 53.3% over three fruit-arrangement layouts, without updating the frozen full-task VLA.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose RoboDuo, a closed-loop dual system that uses code, rather than a token or a latent vector, as its interface. When the full-task VLA fails, an atomic VLA executes the remaining steps.

We construct LIBERO-Atomic, LIBERO-Code, and LIBERO-Judge from the same successful demonstrations to train the atomic VLA, the coding agent, and the completion check, respectively.

We instantiate RoboDuo on X-VLA and π0.5\pi_{0.5} and evaluate it on LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, and a real robot. The gains concentrate on long-horizon tasks that fail because a single subtask fails.

1. We propose RoboDuo, a closed-loop dual system that uses code, rather than a token or a latent vector, as its interface. When the full-task VLA fails, an atomic VLA executes the remaining steps.

2. We construct LIBERO-Atomic, LIBERO-Code, and LIBERO-Judge from the same successful demonstrations to train the atomic VLA, the coding agent, and the completion check, respectively.

3. We instantiate RoboDuo on X-VLA and π0.5\pi_{0.5} and evaluate it on LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, and a real robot. The gains concentrate on long-horizon tasks that fail because a single subtask fails.

title: X-World: Transferring Video Priors to Variable-View Robot Control
authors: Chun Gu,Xiaofei Wei,Yiming Chen,Juntong Zhang,Li Zhang
abstract:
Video diffusion models provide a source of interaction representations for robot control, but transferring these representations requires reconciling variable camera inputs with heterogeneous action interfaces and closed-loop execution.
We present X-World, a framework that transfers a video prior through a fixed-length token sequence to a shared action expert.
A residual cross-view attention branch extends a pretrained video backbone to one, two, or three views while retaining its original self-attention path.
A layer-aligned Q-Former aggregates backbone features, and dataset-specific modules map between native state and action interfaces and the shared action expert.
Training separates video adaptation from action-only pretraining by freezing the video backbone in the latter stage, followed by joint target-domain post-training.
The policy extracts video features with a single backbone pass and uses asynchronous action chunking for execution.
On LIBERO, X-World reaches 98.5% mean success; its LIBERO-trained checkpoint obtains 76.5% on LIBERO-Plus without further adaptation.
The seven-shift breakdown reveals gains in robot, language, lighting, and layout perturbations, alongside weaknesses under camera, background, and noise shifts relative to OpenVLA-OFT.
On six dual-arm real-world tasks, it achieves 81.7% mean success over 20 trials per task.
Removing video adaptation or cross-view fusion produces the largest observed success drops among the tested removals.
introduction:
Video data and robot action data offer different forms of supervision.
Videos capture object motion, contact, and task progression across many scenes, whereas action-labeled trajectories specify how a particular robot produces those transitions.
Vision-language-action policies (Brohan et al., 2022; Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Octo Model Team et al., 2024; Bjorck et al., 2025; Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) learn the latter mapping effectively, but collecting action supervision across robots and camera setups remains expensive.
Video diffusion models offer a complementary source of representations (Ye et al., 2024; Du et al., 2023b; Hu et al., 2024).
The question we study is how to transfer these representations to a policy whose observations and executable actions vary across datasets.

This transfer has two interfaces.
At the visual interface, datasets provide different numbers of cameras and different viewpoints.
A single-view video backbone must gain access to information across views without discarding its pretrained computation.
At the control interface, video hidden states contain many spatiotemporal tokens, while the policy must generate a short action chunk in the robot’s native coordinates.
Exposing a changing visual context directly to an action expert couples these two forms of heterogeneity.
We instead use a fixed-length token sequence between the video backbone and the action expert, so camera processing and action decoding can be adapted separately.

X-World instantiates this design with a pretrained LTX-Video backbone (HaCohen et al., 2024), a layer-aligned Q-Former, and a flow-matching action expert.
The video backbone retains its pretrained self-attention and adds cross-view attention through a zero-initialized residual branch.
View embeddings, randomized view order, and masked replication support training on one-, two-, and three-view datasets.
The Q-Former aggregates features across backbone layers into the token sequence consumed by the action expert.
Following the use of dataset-specific interfaces in cross-embodiment learning (Zheng et al., 2026), lightweight projections map native state and action representations to and from the shared action backbone.

Training first adapts the video backbone on robot and human videos, then freezes it while learning the Q-Former and action expert from heterogeneous action-labeled trajectories.
Target-domain post-training updates the model with video and action supervision.
At deployment, one backbone pass extracts features from observed image latents and noisy future slots; the policy does not generate and decode a future video before acting.
Asynchronous real-time chunking (Black et al., 2025a; Black et al., 2025b) overlaps policy queries with execution.
On a single H100, the reported cached model response is 46 ms; the deployed refresh, including communication and processing, is 91 ms, while queued actions execute at 30 Hz.

Our evaluation asks three questions: whether the transferred representation supports manipulation, which parts of the transfer account for the observed performance, and where robustness breaks down.
The policy reaches 98.5% mean success on LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) and 76.5% on zero-shot LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025).
Because LIBERO is nearly saturated, we examine the full distribution-shift profile and the training-stage interaction rather than relying on its average ranking.
On six dual-arm UR5e tasks, X-World achieves 81.7% mean success, compared with 58.3% for X-VLA, the strongest baseline in this real-world comparison.
Removing cross-view attention reduces LIBERO success to 83.1% and Fold Towel success from 12/20 to 0/20, providing evidence beyond the saturated benchmark average.

This paper makes three main contributions:
(i) We introduce X-World, a framework for variable-view robot control that adapts a pretrained video backbone through masked residual cross-view fusion while retaining its original self-attention path;
(ii) We build a video-to-action interface that combines a layer-aligned Q-Former with dataset-specific state and action projections, using fixed-length tokens and separating video adaptation from action-only pretraining;
and (iii) We analyze the benefits and limits of this transfer through training-stage ablations, seven distribution shifts, and dual-arm experiments, with separate measurements of model and system latency.

title: Doppler-aided Position-Velocity Tracking of Hidden Objects using mmWave Radar
authors: Yerin Cheon,Kush Garg,Akshat Dave
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Safe indoor operation requires autonomous tracking of objects that are not directly visible to the robot. Optical non-line-of-sight (NLoS) methods depend on ambient lighting and scene geometry or on weak multi-bounce returns that need long acquisitions. Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar offers an attractive alternative: walls act as reflectors for mmWave signals, and frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radars enable fast, practical measurement of range, angle, and velocity. However, the low resolution of these radars leads to spatially ambiguous observations. The Doppler information, although particularly sensitive to target motion, remains underexplored in indoor NLoS localization: existing methods emphasize spatial representations and either collapse or discard the Doppler dimension before learning. To leverage the complete Range–Azimuth–Doppler (RAD) information, we acquire the first indoor NLoS radar dataset that pairs sequential RAD measurements with synchronized position and velocity ground truth under controlled variations in motion: 576 sequences totaling 720,856 frames across 12 trajectories of a mobile robot moving along varying speeds, starting positions, and material configurations. We then formulate NLoS tracking as sequential position-velocity estimation rather than frame-wise localization: a shared 3-D encoder processes the full RAD representation of consecutive frames, separate recurrent branches estimate position and velocity, and post-inference refinement combines the two into a motion-consistent trajectory. Our method achieves 8.95 cm position and 1.75 cm/s velocity errors on held-out trajectories and generalizes to unseen scenarios involving a moving human target. Together, our dataset and tracker establish a benchmark for tracking hidden moving targets with a low-cost radar. Project page: ycheon1101.github.io/yerincheon/radar_nlos/
introduction:
Safe indoor operation requires autonomous tracking of objects that are not directly visible to the robot. For instance, in warehouses, where humans and robots operate in close proximity, corners and corridors create blind spots, increasing the risk of collisions. Non-line-of-sight (NLoS) tracking aims to leverage indirect reflections of light to estimate the position of hidden targets [1, 2].
Optical NLoS methods, whether
camera-based [3, 4, 5] or
LiDAR-based [2, 1, 6], depend on ambient lighting and
scene geometry [7] or on weak multi-bounce returns that need long
acquisitions, which limits range and real-time tracking.

Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar provides an attractive alternative. RF signals are largely insensitive to illumination conditions, and walls can act as reflectors for mmWave signals, creating strong indirect paths toward regions outside direct visibility. In particular, Frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) mmWave radars have recently become practical through mass production and provide fast, continuous measurements of the range, angle of arrival, and velocity of objects.

However, translating FMCW radar measurements into accurate NLoS tracking remains challenging. Indirect propagation produces spatially ambiguous radar observations, so the relationship between the measured radar response and the hidden target position difficult to model explicitly. Moreover, the limited spatial resolution of low-cost FMCW radar makes fine-grained target localization challenging. To address this spatial ambiguity, we adopt a data-driven approach that directly learns the relationship between NLoS radar measurements and target position.

For moving targets, consecutive radar observations provide temporal diversity that is unavailable from a single frame. As the target moves, changes in its position and Doppler response generate complementary observations over time, providing temporal information for continuous NLoS tracking. Among these measurements, Doppler is particularly sensitive to target motion, yet it remains relatively underexplored in indoor radar NLoS localization. This is partly because NLoS propagation distorts the relationship between measured Doppler and the target’s physical velocity, and because Doppler responses can weaken when the target slows down, changes direction, or temporarily stops. Existing indoor methods have therefore largely emphasized spatial representations such as range–angle or angle–delay maps [8, 9]. The Doppler dimension is collapsed into a per-point attribute [10] or discarded before learning [9].

To leverage the complete Range–Azimuth–Doppler (RAD) information for NLoS tracking, we acquire real measurements that pair sequential RAD observations with synchronized position and velocity ground truth across diverse motion. Existing real-world NLoS radar datasets [9, 11, 10, 8, 12, 13] are designed for specific environments or motion scenarios, and do not provide full RAD–position–velocity information under controlled variation in target motion. We place a stationary mmWave radar in front of a wall and move a mobile robot along varying trajectories, speeds, and starting positions, with varying material properties, yielding 576 sequences comprising 720,856 radar frames. To our knowledge, this is the first indoor NLoS radar dataset to provide sequential RAD measurements with both position and velocity labels under controlled motion variation.

Along with this dataset, we formulate NLoS tracking as a sequential position-velocity estimation problem rather than independent frame-wise localization. Our model preserves the full RAD representation and processes a short sequence of consecutive frames. A shared 3-D encoder extracts features from each frame, followed by separate recurrent branches for position and velocity. We found that coupling the position state to velocity-based updates within the network caused localization errors to accumulate, even when the predicted velocity was accurate. We therefore combine position and velocity estimates after inference, refining the trajectory to agree with both predicted locations and inter-frame motion. Low predicted speed suppresses unnecessary movement, reducing drift and stationary jitter.

Our main contributions are as follows:

A data-driven indoor NLoS tracking framework that jointly estimates position and velocity from sequences of full RAD measurements, through independent estimation followed by a motion-consistent refinement stage. Our method achieves mean position and velocity errors of 8.958.95 cm and 1.751.75 cm/s, respectively, on held-out validation recordings, and also generalizes to unseen trajectories of a moving person.

Our method achieves mean position and velocity errors of 8.958.95 cm and 1.751.75 cm/s, respectively, on held-out validation recordings, and also generalizes to unseen trajectories of a moving person.

A controlled real-world NLoS radar dataset of 576 diverse sequences spanning varied trajectories, speeds, starting positions, and material configurations. Each sequence provides RAD measurements together with synchronized position and velocity ground truth, enabling systematic evaluation of generalization to held-out motion and target conditions.

title: DSGN: A Dual-Stream Gated Network for Scalable Simultaneous Surveillance and Containment
authors: Heng Zhang,Ziyang Zuo,Guoxiang Zhao,Xiaoqiang Ren
comment: . Full version of the paper accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L), October 2026
abstract:
The simultaneous surveillance and containment (SSC) problem arises in multi-robot applications such as perimeter security and environmental monitoring, where robots must survey a region of interest and coordinate to enclose targets once they are detected.
Surveillance favors spatial dispersion for coverage, whereas containment requires target-centric cohesion for enclosure.
This conflict makes heuristic switching unstable, and the instability becomes more pronounced as larger robotic networks introduce more inter-agent and agent-target relations.
End-to-end DRL reduces reliance on hand-crafted switching, but conventional single-stream policies often mix surveillance and containment cues in one shared feature space that could entangle dispersion-oriented and target-centric signals and weaken task transitions.
In this paper, we propose the Dual-Stream Gated Network (DSGN), an architecture designed to address scale-amplified task-transition difficulties by separating surveillance and containment into specialized representation streams and coordinating them through a context-aware gating mechanism.
A probabilistic prior further regularizes the gating process, reducing ambiguous intermediate decisions and supporting clearer behavioral transitions under large-scale interaction complexity.
Evaluations show that DSGN maintains strong task efficacy and scalability under constant-density cross-scale settings.
Additional ablation and phase-specific evaluations show that the proposed dynamic gating mechanism and probabilistic prior support effective task arbitration and reliable mode switching in both pure surveillance and task-switching scenarios.
The source code is available at
https://github.com/zuozysama/DSGN.
introduction:
As robotic autonomy matures, large-scale multi-robot systems are increasingly deployed across diverse domains, ranging from environmental monitoring and industrial automation to critical infrastructure maintenance [1, 2].
A representative example is autonomous fishing fleets [3], where robots must survey a region of interest and coordinate their response to mobile, non-cooperative entities.
These scenarios necessitate two fundamental capabilities: persistent area surveillance to locate multiple targets [4, 5], and coordinated containment operations to physically enclose them [6].
Although searching and containment have each been extensively studied, they are generally formulated separately.
The simultaneous surveillance and containment (SSC) problem considered here couples them by requiring a multi-robot system to balance continuous area coverage with timely containment of targets.

Centralized coordination [7] can exploit global information, but its dependence on the global system state makes it prone to the curse of dimensionality and limits its applicability to large-scale robotic networks.
Distributed methods [8, 9] mitigate this limitation by allowing robots to coordinate through local observations and inter-robot interactions.
Existing distributed methods relevant to the containment component of SSC have primarily focused on target interception and containment.
Differential game methods [9] model interactions between pursuers and evaders as coupled optimization problems, but they can be difficult to apply when environment dynamics are hard to model.
Bio-inspired heuristic methods [10] use manually designed interaction rules, which are intuitive to implement but can be hard to scale across varying team sizes, environments, and target behaviors.
Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methods [11] have therefore been introduced to learn containment policies directly from interactions, reducing dependence on explicit dynamics modeling and manually specified interaction rules.
These studies cover both single-target containment [12] and multi-target settings [13], and recent work [6] has scaled up multi-target coordination to dozens of robots by leveraging attention-based architectures.
The minimal capture time in the graph-based pursuit-evasion formulation has been investigated in [14].
However, in practical multi-robot applications such as environmental monitoring [5] and autonomous fishing [3], targets may not be immediately known in the region of interest.
This means that containment alone is insufficient and that persistent surveillance is also required to locate targets before coordinated interception or enclosure [4, 5].

Multi-robot surveillance has been widely studied for persistent coverage and target localization.
Classical visibility-based pursuit-evasion studies established complete search strategies and searchability conditions in polygonal and curved environments [15, 16, 17].
Multi-robot target search has also addressed scalable planning for moving targets [18], limited sensing and environment geometry [19], and DRL-based mobile-target search [20].
These studies primarily address target search and detection, whereas SSC couples persistent surveillance with post-detection geometric containment.
A straightforward way to combine the two behaviors is to formulate the transition as a switched or hybrid control problem [21, 22].
However, specifying analytical switching conditions for coupled target search and interception in SSC is difficult because the desired behavior depends jointly on coverage status, target observations, robot distribution, and containment geometry.

An end-to-end DRL paradigm offers an alternative to discrete logic for the SSC problem by learning decentralized policies directly from robot local observations [23, 11].
However, conventional unified architectures often encode surveillance and containment cues in a shared feature space, where dispersion-oriented coverage signals and target-centric enclosure signals can introduce conflicting optimization demands [24].
Within this end-to-end paradigm, a commonly used design is to organize a single policy with specialized representation streams and coordinate them through a gating mechanism, as explored in mixture-of-experts [25] and modular reinforcement learning [26].
Fixed or hand-crafted gating mechanisms can be difficult to adapt as observations and task demands change, while naive adaptive gating may incur chattering that could cause task failures.

To address this challenge, we propose the Dual-Stream Gated Network (DSGN).
DSGN separates state processing into two specialized streams.
A spatial-explorative stream reasons about coverage gaps for surveillance, and a tactical-exploitative stream computes geometric formations for containment.
A context-aware gating mechanism coordinates the two streams to produce a unified policy for surveillance and containment.
We further regularize this gating process with a Beta-distribution prior to stabilize switching decisions.
Numerical experiments show that DSGN improves the balance between surveillance and containment and maintains performance as the number of agents increases.

The key contributions of this work are as follows:
1) Task-Disentangled Representation for SSC:
Built on transformer-based relational encoding, DSGN separates surveillance and containment into two task-specific attention streams, which reduce interference between dispersion-oriented coverage and target-centered containment within a unified end-to-end policy.
2) Robust Distributed Task Arbitration:
The context-aware gating mechanism and Beta-distribution regularization enable robust switching between surveillance and containment.
Together, these components support stable and decisive task transitions when target observations are intermittent or task demands change.
3) Scalable Multi-Robot Coordination Performance:
Across constant-density cross-scale evaluations, DSGN maintains high task efficacy, execution optimality, safe coordination, and stable formation quality as team and environment scales increase.
Additional phase-specific evaluations further demonstrate its task-switching and surveillance capabilities.

title: Learning Interaction-Aware Path Corrections from Unlabeled Trajectories: A LiDAR-Based Sim-to-Real GNN Framework for Construction Robots
authors: Yilong Chen,Yong K. Cho
comment: submitted to Automation in Construction
abstract: Construction robots operating near workers require navigation that can anticipate human motion while remaining robust to dynamic and unstructured site conditions. However, existing social navigation methods depend on hand-crafted interaction rules, labeled demonstrations, or robot-specific control policies, limiting their scalability and transferability in construction environments. We propose a real-time, LiDAR-only framework that learns interaction-aware path corrections from unlabeled demonstrations. Constant-velocity extrapolation generates residual learning targets, while a GNN models relationships among the robot, pedestrians, and goal context. During deployment, an extended Kalman filter tracks LiDAR detections to construct dynamic graphs, and the GNN offsets planner-generated waypoints through a planner-agnostic interface. Within bricklaying trial, the GNN reduced path irregularity by 39.2% and increased minimum TTC. Across Dynablox sequences, it increased minimum TTC by 38.3% while producing shorter, smoother paths than the baselines. Ablation studies supported a 1.0-s prediction interval and confirmed the benefits of target context, reflection augmentation, and feature normalization.
introduction:
Construction robot navigation has become increasingly important as autonomous and semi-autonomous mobile robots are deployed for material transport, inspection, mapping, and other repetitive operations. Unlike structured industrial facilities, construction sites evolve continuously and contain narrow, cluttered spaces shared by robots and workers performing task-driven and safety-critical activities. Worker motion in these environments is not merely random obstacle movement. It reflects ongoing tasks, spatial constraints, and interactions with other workers and equipment. A construction robot must therefore maintain navigation efficiency while anticipating potentially conflicting human motion and avoiding disruptive or unsafe behavior. Achieving this capability using limited onboard sensing and computation remains a fundamental challenge for human–robot collaboration in construction.

Conventional local planners, including sampling- and optimization-based approaches[10, 24], can respond effectively to geometric obstacles but generally represent pedestrians as physical or kinematic constraints. Consequently, they have limited ability to distinguish among interaction configurations that require different anticipatory responses. Social Force Model (SFM)-based methods introduce human-aware repulsion into navigation, but their behavior depends on manually specified interaction rules and parameters that may not transfer consistently across environments [6], motivating a data-driven representation of interaction behavior.

Learning-based social-navigation methods provide an alternative by learning navigation behavior from demonstrations or simulated interactions. In particular, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) can represent a varying number of pedestrians as nodes and explicitly model their relationships through message passing. Nevertheless, existing methods commonly require manually defined social costs, labeled preferred actions, semantic scene information, or large synthetic training datasets [22, 1]. These requirements are difficult to satisfy on construction sites, where representative interaction data are limited and social responses are rarely annotated. Moreover, end-to-end policies that directly predict control commands are often closely coupled to a particular robot or planner, limiting their integration into existing construction-robot navigation systems. A practical framework should instead learn transferable spatial corrections that can be applied through a lightweight interface to an existing local planner.

A further challenge concerns the connection between real-world perception and graph-based navigation. GNN-based interaction models require temporally consistent estimates of object position and velocity, whereas LiDAR-based dynamic-object detectors typically provide frame-wise observations whose identities can change because of occlusion, missed detections, and objects entering or leaving the sensing range. Camera-based solutions can provide additional semantic and appearance information, but their performance is affected by illumination, dust, and visual occlusion commonly encountered on construction sites. Therefore, a LiDAR-only approach capable of tracking dynamic objects and constructing interaction graphs online would improve the robustness and deployability of socially aware construction navigation.

This study proposes a real-time, LiDAR-based framework that learns interaction-aware spatial corrections from unlabeled human demonstrations. Constant-velocity extrapolation is used to generate residual learning targets automatically, avoiding manual annotation of socially preferred trajectories. A GNN then models the relationships among the robot, nearby pedestrians, and goal context during training and predicts spatial corrections that can be applied to planner-generated paths. During deployment, frame-wise LiDAR detections are associated and tracked using an extended Kalman filter (EKF), providing the continuous positions and velocities required for online graph construction. Because the model outputs spatial residuals rather than robot-specific control commands, it provides a planner-agnostic correction interface while remaining compatible with real-time local navigation. title: Lightweight Change Detection for Adaptive Collective Perception in Dynamic Environments
authors: Thiemen Siemensma,Tiago Travassos,Jiacheng Zhang,Bahar Haghighat
abstract:
Swarm robotics enables scalable inspection through collective perception, where robots infer environmental properties from distributed observations. A common benchmark considers robots exploring black-white tiled environments and determining the majority tile type. While most work studies static environments, dynamic environments remain underexplored.
We study collective perception in dynamic environments where the tile proportion and the spatial correlation of surface patterns may change over time. To enable implementation on resource-constrained robots, we integrate a lightweight change detection mechanism into a Bayesian collective decision-making framework that resets robot beliefs when distribution shifts are detected. The proposed detector requires constant memory and constant per-sample computation, unlike two recent competitive approaches that store the full sample stream, making it suitable for memory-constrained robots. We further introduce a method that detects spatially correlated sampling and adapts sampling intervals online to mitigate correlation effects. Our simulation results in Webots show competitive change detection delays, more consistent precision across communication settings, and improved decision accuracy under changing spatial correlations.

title: Extended LASMP: Language Aided Subset Sampling Based Motion Planner for Drone Navigation
authors: Saswati Bhattacharjee,Anirban Sinha,Mukulika Ghosh,Chinwe Ekenna
abstract:
This paper proposes a command-aligned sampling distribution that incorporates navigation commands directly into the exploration process to improve the efficiency of sampling-based motion planning for quadcopters in three-dimensional environments. Inspired by the Language-Aided Subset Sampling Motion Planner, this paper extends command-aware subset sampling to aerial systems.
Subset sampling is generalized to command-aligned regions, enabling structured 3D exploration while preserving probabilistic completeness. Natural language instructions are grounded into yaw-conditioned and altitude-aware geometric constraints using a prompt-based large language model for entity extraction and instruction validation. Extensive simulations in complex environments demonstrate that the proposed method generates collision-free, consistent trajectories while significantly reducing sampling effort compared to uniform RRT-based planners.
introduction:
Autonomous aerial navigation in cluttered three-dimensional environments remains a fundamental challenge in robotics. Quadcopters operating in indoor and semi-structured environments must reason over higher-dimensional state spaces, handle limited sensing, and generate dynamically feasible trajectories while avoiding obstacles. Sampling-based planners such as Rapidly-exploring Random Trees (RRT) [1, 2]
and its optimal variant RRT∗ [3] have been widely adopted for such problems due to their probabilistic completeness and scalability to high-dimensional spaces. However, uniform sampling over large configuration spaces often results in poor sample efficiency, particularly in cluttered environments. Several works have attempted to improve sampling efficiency through heuristic or informed sampling strategies,
including Informed RRT∗ and related approaches [4, 5, 6]. Although these approaches bias exploration using geometric cost-to-go heuristics, they fail to incorporate structured task-level instructions into sampling, leading to inefficient exploration and wasted computation.

In many real-world applications, aerial robots are required to follow high-level human commands, such as go left, move up, or turn back and proceed forward. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled robots to interpret natural language instructions and map them to control or planning actions [7, 8, 9]. However, most existing approaches either rely on end-to-end learned policies or treat language as an external high-level planner, leaving the underlying sampling-based motion planner unchanged. In contrast, classical sampling-based planners ignore the directional intent embedded in commands, leading to unnecessary exploration of irrelevant regions of the planning space.

This work addresses the problem of command-aware sampling for quadcopter navigation. Building upon the Language-Aided Subset Sampling Motion Planner (LASMP)[10] developed for ground robots, we extend the framework to aerial platforms to plan in ℝ3×𝕊1\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{S}^{1}. Unlike planar robots, quadcopters introduce an additional translational degree of freedom, requiring a transition from planar subset sampling to command-aligned three-dimensional subset sampling. Each navigation command is interpreted as a yaw update followed by directional translation or vertical motion, and the sampling distribution is dynamically restricted to subsets aligned with the commanded direction. This structured restriction concentrates exploration in more meaningful regions while preserving probabilistic completeness.

To robustly ground natural language instructions into geometric planning constraints, we integrate an LLM-based named entity recognition (NER) pipeline. Using few-shot prompt-based extraction, the system identifies task-relevant motion entities without requiring task-specific model retraining. The extracted entities are converted into yaw-conditioned and altitude-aware constraints
that directly shape the sampling subsets. Additionally, the LLM is employed to detect inconsistencies or ambiguities in user instructions and request corrective input, enhancing interaction reliability. An illustration of our work is shown in Fig. 1 where a user can give the instruction and based on that instruction, our planner computes a feasible path.

The primary contributions of this paper are as follows:

A unified command-aware sampling framework that integrates directional navigation commands into the sampling distribution of a sampling-based planner together with a ray-guided switching strategy for consistent sequential command execution.

title: Behavior Spatial Benchmark: Evaluating Spatial Understanding for Robotics
authors: Sirui Chen,Huang Huang,Qineng Wang,Wenlong Huang,Manling Li,Ruohan Zhang,Li Fei-Fei,Jiajun Wu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Robot tasks require grounding spatial language in physical scenes, but task success alone cannot establish whether spatial instructions are followed. We present BEHAVIOR-Spatial, a benchmark built on BEHAVIOR-1K that measures spatial question answering, point-based target grounding, and robot action to examine how VLM spatial understanding relates to VLA behavior. It comprises 3,256 spatial questions across 49 activities, 1,240 grounding queries across 14 manipulation tasks, and action evaluations covering those 14 tasks and 10 navigation tasks. Our manipulation protocol evaluates held-out configurations and instruction following when the requested target changes within a fixed training layout. The baseline achieves 41.6% on held-out configurations but only 16.1% under changed instructions. VLM adaptation and robot-data pretraining provide limited improvements, whereas oracle visual target cues raise these rates to 60.3% and 38.0%, respectively. Perception evaluations reveal policy-dependent correlations between VLM question-answering and grounding accuracy and VLA manipulation performance. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial instruction following alongside task completion and examining when spatial perception performance translates into robot behavior. Project website: https://arielchen07.github.io/behavior-spatial/.
introduction:
Instructions such as “reach the second tool from the left” require a robot to resolve a spatial relation, identify the intended target, and execute an action. Navigation similarly requires interpreting destinations relative to current and previously observed surroundings. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are initialized from vision-language models (VLMs) and assume that the backbone’s spatial understanding supports robot behavior, yet this connection is rarely studied directly. Task success alone provides ambiguous evidence: a policy may exploit familiar layouts without following spatial language, or select the correct target but fail during execution. Relating VLM spatial capabilities to VLA behavior requires jointly evaluating spatial perception, target grounding, and action.

We introduce BEHAVIOR-Spatial, a benchmark built on BEHAVIOR-1K  (Li et al., 2024a) that connects these evaluations across household manipulation and navigation. It comprises three components: (1) BEHAVIOR-Spatial-VQA, a spatial VQA suite containing 3,256 questions across 49 task activities, including 1,572 general spatial questions and 1,684 task-specific questions, with both single- and multi-frame evaluations; (2) BEHAVIOR-Spatial-IR, a point-based intermediate representation (IR) generation suite containing 1,240 target-grounding queries across 14 manipulation tasks; and (3) BEHAVIOR-Spatial-Action, a robot action suite covering the same 14 manipulation tasks and 10 navigation tasks. Shared scenes and relations across suites enable studying how VLM question-answering and grounding accuracy relate to VLA performance.

Our evaluation distinguishes generalization to new configurations from responsiveness to spatial instructions. Held-out manipulation and navigation configurations test generalization, while a manipulation prompt probe changes the requested target within a training layout to test whether behavior follows the instruction. We measure VQA answer accuracy and whether generated points fall within the instructed target region. For robot action, we report soft success as a behavioral proxy for target-selection intention, alongside wrong-target commitments and strict success.

Our experiments reveal persistent spatial instruction-following failures, especially when the target changes within a familiar layout. The tested LoRA adaptation and DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2025) initialization strategies provide limited improvements on this probe, whereas supplying IR visual target cues substantially improves target-consistent behavior. These cues isolate the benefit of providing the grounding decision, rather than demonstrating learned grounding from language. For two of our best manipulation variants, the dot-IR and attention-map policies, grounding accuracy correlates more strongly with soft success than VQA accuracy does. However, the perception–action relationship varies across policy variants, and direction-question accuracy shows little correlation with navigation success across the ten evaluated tasks.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a spatial benchmark connecting question answering, point-based target grounding, and household manipulation and navigation; (2) a diagnostic evaluation protocol that tests changed instructions in training layouts and separates target-consistent behavior from task completion; and (3) an empirical study of policy adaptation and visual grounding interfaces relating VLM spatial understanding to VLA behavior.

title: T-ConSG: A LiDAR-Based Real-Time Temporal Construction Scene Graph for Dynamic and Evolving Environments
authors: Yilong Chen,Yong K. Cho
comment: submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
abstract: Dynamic and continuously evolving environments present significant challenges for robotic mapping and scene understanding, particularly on construction sites where moving agents, temporary obstacles, and persistent structural changes coexist. While dynamic and long-term SLAM methods can detect motion and environmental changes, their outputs are predominantly metric representations that provide limited structure for higher-level spatial and temporal reasoning. This paper presents a LiDAR-based real-time temporal construction scene graph (T-ConSG) that jointly represents free-space regions, static objects, dynamic objects, and environmental events with spatial-relational and event-participation edges. The proposed framework incrementally constructs the graph from LiDAR-derived geometric evidence, maintaining persistent free-space and static-object information while tracking dynamic objects. Changes in accumulated spatial evidence are further represented as explicit installation and removal events, allowing the graph to capture both transient dynamics and persistent environmental evolution. We demonstrate the proposed representation through three complementary application studies: dynamics-aware navigation in a bricklaying testbed, construction progress monitoring on the ConSLAM dataset, and online change detection in a simulated construction environment. The results demonstrate that the proposed T-ConSG provides a unified representation for organizing spatial and temporal information and supports robotic reasoning across environments containing both short-term dynamics and persistent changes.
introduction:
Construction environments present a particularly demanding setting for autonomous robots because their spatial configuration evolves continuously throughout project execution. Unlike structured industrial workplaces, construction sites contain incomplete structures, temporary facilities, relocated materials, moving workers and equipment, and work areas whose accessibility changes as construction progresses [1, 2]. These characteristics create substantial challenges for perception, navigation, and autonomous decision-making, while simultaneously motivating robotic systems that can improve productivity and reduce human exposure to hazardous tasks [1, 3]. Effective robotic operation therefore requires more than estimating the current geometry of the surroundings; robots must maintain spatial knowledge that distinguishes transient motion from persistent environmental changes and preserves how the workspace evolves over time.

Most SLAM systems were originally formulated around a predominantly static world, an assumption that becomes restrictive when robots operate amid moving agents and persistent environmental changes. Dynamic SLAM has progressively relaxed this assumption by rejecting dynamic measurements, tracking independently moving objects, or reconstructing dynamic scenes, while long-term and change-aware approaches further address changes that become apparent when previously mapped areas are revisited [4, 5, 6]. Nevertheless, these methods are primarily concerned with maintaining localization, metric reconstruction, object states, or geometric change estimates. For autonomous operation in evolving construction environments, such metric evidence would be more useful if it could also be organized into persistent entities and explicit events that support higher-level spatial and temporal reasoning.

Scene graphs provide a complementary abstraction by organizing environments as entities and relationships rather than only metric geometry. Recent 3D scene graphs have demonstrated the value of hierarchical representations for robotic mapping, planning, and spatial reasoning, while emerging 4D formulations extend this concept to entities and relationships that evolve over time [7, 8, 9, 5, 10]. However, temporal scene-graph research remains comparatively less mature, particularly in representing how persistent environmental changes modify both spatial entities and their relationships. Moreover, free space is often treated primarily as geometric support for navigation rather than as persistent spatial evidence coupled with scene changes. This motivates a 4D representation that jointly structures free space, static objects, dynamic objects, and explicit environmental events.

We propose T-ConSG, a LiDAR-based, real-time temporal construction scene graph that provides a structured representation of both the spatial state and temporal evolution of an evolving construction environment. To the best of our knowledge, T-ConSG is the first LiDAR-based scene-graph framework to jointly represent free-space regions, static structures, tracked dynamic objects, and explicit temporal events for construction-oriented robotic applications. The graph connects environmental states and detected changes through two complementary edge families: spatial-relational edges describe the current spatial configuration and accessibility of graph entities, whereas event-participation edges associate temporal changes with the entities they affect. This representation distinguishes transient object motion from persistent structural changes while incrementally maintaining the current spatial state from LiDAR-derived geometric evidence, without requiring camera-based semantic perception. Accordingly, T-ConSG provides a compact, task-oriented relational abstraction for downstream reasoning. The main contributions of this work are threefold: (1) a temporal scene-graph representation that jointly models spatial states and environmental events in evolving environments; (2) a real-time, incremental LiDAR mapping framework that integrates dynamic-object tracking with the detection and graph-based representation of persistent temporal events; (3) the versatility of T-ConSG through three construction-oriented applications: dynamics-aware navigation, construction progress monitoring, and online change detection.

title: Cut a Wall, See a Wall: Identity Substitution in Occluded Point-Cloud Perception for Construction Robots
authors: Tsung-Lung Yang
abstract: Construction robots must label building elements they can only partly see. We show that when occlusion at test time removes whole regions of a scene, rather than parts of an object as in training, point-cloud segmentation networks do not simply miss the hidden elements: they relabel them, and the errors collapse onto a single sink class. With fixed synthetic layouts the column absorbs up to 70% of all test points; with randomized layouts the sink moves to the stair, predicted at 4.5–5.4×\times its true share across three training seeds. Baseline mIoU falls to 0.15–0.27 (fixed) and 0.36–0.72 (randomized), and up to 269 whole objects vanish in a single test set. Appending 14 hand-computed geometric features per point (GPE) restores mIoU to 0.54–0.92 and removes 64–100% of whole-object losses in every run, for PointNet++ and a PTv3-style transformer in both layout regimes; on real S3DIS scans it removes every whole-wall loss (10→\to0). In an as-built column check computed from the predictions, GPE raises the share of correctly checked views from 17–58% to 71–92%. Feature permutation on fixed, randomized and real scenes explains the pattern: each class relies on whichever cue is stable in its training data, position for height-banded slabs and beams, intrinsic shape for walls and stairs once their position varies. Occlusion augmentation is a strong alternative on mIoU, but in every setting it loses more whole objects than GPE (e.g., 25–35 vs. 0).
introduction:
Before a robot can use a laser scan of a building site, every point must be labelled: this point belongs to a column, that one to a beam. This semantic segmentation feeds localization, progress monitoring and safety checks [1, 2, 3]. On a real site the scan is never complete. Scaffolding, formwork, stacked material and the building itself hide part of every element, and which part is hidden changes as construction proceeds.

The common expectation is that occlusion hurts gradually: the more points are missing, the more often a hidden object is missed. We find that this expectation fails in a way that matters for a robot. When the occlusion at test time is of a kind the network never saw in training, it does not lose the object. It gives the object another identity, confidently and almost completely. In fixed synthetic layouts, removing the wall behind a column makes the network label the column wall; removing the floor region makes the same column stair. Across the test set, the errors pile up in one class that absorbs the others, while beams and stairs are erased. We call this identity substitution.

A natural objection is that this is an artifact of fixed layouts, where every element sits in the same place and position alone identifies it. We therefore rebuilt the benchmark with randomized room sizes, element counts, positions and orientations, and with density-neutral sampling. Substitution survives, but the sink moves from the column to the stair: its target is set by the training data, not by the occlusion alone.

This paper contributes the following.

A controlled measurement in two layout regimes. Fixed and randomized synthetic rooms, seen and unseen occlusion splits generated from disjoint seeds, two architectures (PointNet++ and a PTv3-style transformer), three training seeds, and whole-object losses reported next to mIoU.

Identity substitution with a data-dependent sink. Under unseen scene-level occlusion the errors concentrate on one class: the column under fixed layouts, the stair under randomized ones.

A cue-stability account of the mechanism. Permutation importance on fixed, randomized and real (S3DIS) scenes shows that classes with a stable height keep relying on position, while walls and stairs switch to intrinsic shape once their position varies.

A repair and an honest comparison. Fourteen geometric features (GPE) cut whole-object losses by 64–100% in every run, make an as-built column check correct in 71–92% of views instead of 17–58%, and transfer to real scans for walls. We compare them with occlusion augmentation, report where GPE fails, and show that only the tail-loss advantage, not the mIoU advantage, is stable across training seeds.

title: Enabling Motion-Induced WiFi-CSI Sensing in Multi-Robot Systems: A Simulation Framework
authors: Brendan Dijkstra,Ninad Jadhav,Maurice Stoffijn,Stephanie Gil,Bahar Haghighat
abstract:
WiFi Channel State Information (CSI) enables fine-grained sensing of spatial relationships between wireless devices. The WiFi Sensor for Robotics (WSR) toolbox demonstrated that WiFi-CSI measurements collected during robot motion, combined with odometry, can be used to synthesize virtual antenna arrays, enabling motion-induced bearing estimation in multi-robot experiments. However, deploying the WSR approach has remained challenging due to its limited integration with standard robotics tools and reliance on deprecated WiFi-CSI acquisition hardware. This work presents an open-source simulation framework that integrates the WSR sensing pipeline within the robotic simulator Gazebo. The framework generates synthetic WiFi-CSI measurements with realistic physical signal properties and leverages realistic robot motion required for motion-induced sensing and downstream localization. It further supports processing both simulated and real WiFi-CSI data for direct comparison and validation. Our aim is to make WSR-style sensing accessible as a modular sensing modality for robotic research.
We validate our framework by comparing simulated and real-world experiments using TurtleBot3 robots, and demonstrate its use for bearing estimation and robot localization. This work lowers the barrier to entry for WiFi-CSI-based sensing in multi-robot systems and provides a foundation for integrating WiFi-CSI sensing with multi-modal perception for localization and coordination. All code and experimental details are publicly available at https://github.com/baharhaghighat/DARS_2026_Dijkstra_et_al
