title: ElevateHead: Decide Once, Then Commit: When the Action Head Matters for Multimodal Imitation
authors: Tsung-Lung Yang
comment: including appendix
abstract: Robots that learn from people often see several valid ways to do the same task: pass an obstacle on the left or on the right, open the microwave or move the kettle first. A policy that re-decides at every step can waver between these ways mid-task. We ask when the action head (the part of a policy that turns the state into actions) matters, and how it should make this choice. On a controlled task, heads that sample one way succeed far more often than a head that averages the ways when the demonstrations contain several ways and the state gives no hint which to take (+0.72+0.72 success with two ways); this trend was not reproduced on the other tasks we ran. We then present ElevateHead, a head that decides once at a learned decision point, commits to that choice for the episode, and exposes the choice as an input a user can set. We designed it by diagnosis: each version was frozen and tested on tasks it had not seen, and the next version changed only what a measured failure pointed to; predictions were registered before each run. The first four versions each fell below BeT on at least one held-out task. The fifth completed all four subtasks of the held-out Franka Kitchen task in 45.2% of episodes against 29.3% for BeT, the strongest baseline across our tasks (+0.160+0.160, 95% CI [+0.129, +0.188]); when a mode was forced, the first completed subtask matched it in 95% of successful episodes. Diagnosis also located where commitment breaks: varied start positions (repaired on the controlled task: commitment 0.22 to 0.81, success 0.74 to 0.91) and varied object placement (partly repaired: in an exploratory variant, commitment 0.03 to 0.59 on aligning with no detectable change in success). On held-out block stacking, version 4 was comparable to BeT and did not exceed it. A real-robot test with predictions fixed in advance is planned for a follow-up version of this paper.
introduction:
Imitation learning trains a robot policy from human demonstrations. When people solve a task in several ways, the data contain several correct actions for the same situation, and the action head—the last layer of the policy—has to pick one. A head that averages the demonstrations (regression) can output an action that belongs to no way at all, such as driving straight into the obstacle between a left and a right detour. Heads that sample one way avoid the average—discrete selection as in BeT [17] and VQ-BeT [10], diffusion [3], flow matching [11]—but they usually sample again at every step and can switch ways mid-route (Fig. 1a). On common benchmarks the heads are hard to tell apart, and recent analyses disagree on why [15, 16, 20].

This paper makes three contributions:

When the head matters. On a controlled task, the head matters when the demonstrations contain several ways and the state gives no hint which to take; the gap shrinks once such a hint exists (Section III). The trend was not reproduced on the other tasks we ran, and we report that.

A head that decides once and commits. ElevateHead learns where demonstrations branch, chooses a way there only if the choice is genuinely open, keeps it for the episode, and exposes it as an input (Fig. 1b,c; Section IV).

Design by diagnosis, with the full record. Every version was frozen, tested on tasks it had not seen, and, when it fell short, diagnosed before anything was changed (Section V). After four versions that fell below BeT somewhere, the fifth exceeded BeT on held-out Franka Kitchen (p4p_{4} 0.452 vs. 0.293; Section VI). The diagnoses also yield lessons for other heads (Section VII).

Highlights. (i) On held-out Kitchen, full-task success rises from 29.3% (BeT) to 45.2%, about 1.5×\times; the gain over version 4 (+0.222+0.222, descriptive) comes from two inference rules, with no retraining. (ii) Forcing a mode sets the first subtask in 95.4% of successful episodes—a control input BeT lacks. (iii) A diagnosed gate fix lifts commitment under varied starts from 0.22 to 0.81 and cuts route switches by 74% (1.38 to 0.35 per episode). (iv) Under varied object placement, closer to cluttered scenes, commitment rises from 0.03 to 0.59 (aligning) and from 0.32 to 0.64 (stacking) in an exploratory variant. (v) A chunk costs 0.63–0.66 ms, 2.6–4.0×\times faster than our flow and diffusion heads (Table III). Table I summarizes the findings. Every registered prediction was committed to a time-stamped log before its run; post-hoc analyses are labelled as such, and every held-out result against BeT is shown (Fig. 4).

title: I Won't Know Until I Try: Interactive Information Gathering for Long-Horizon Manipulation
authors: Linfei Yuan,Rachel Holladay
comment: . Under review
abstract: Long-horizon manipulation often depends on object properties that cannot be reliably inferred from appearance alone. Physical interaction can reveal these properties, but it can also change the world in ways that invalidate subsequent actions. We present a task and motion planning (TAMP) framework that integrates task-directed interactive information-gathering with interleaved planning and execution. Building on PDDLStream, our framework plans optimistically with these interactive actions, verifies their outcomes during execution, and adapts the remaining plan by retaining still-applicable actions and replanning only the connections needed to continue execution. We evaluate the framework in simulation and on a real robot across tasks that require determining whether an object is movable, a pen has ink, a drawer can be opened, or a container is empty. These experiments demonstrate how interaction-driven state updates and recovery replanning support continued execution under uncertain outcomes and external disturbances.
introduction:
Long-horizon manipulation requires a robot to determine not only how
to act, but also what it needs to know before acting.
While passive perception can often identify objects and estimate their poses, some task-relevant properties cannot be reliably observed from appearance alone, such as whether an object is movable, a drawer is unlocked, a non-transparent container is empty, or a pen has ink (Fig. 1).
To resolve this missing information, the robot must employ interactive perception: using physical interactions and their observed outcomes to reveal these object properties [1].

For example, testing whether an object is movable may require pushing it slightly.
While the push reveals the object’s movability,
it may also displace the object by an uncertain offset.
Such an interaction can therefore both resolve uncertainty and alter the physical state for subsequent actions.

Consequently, information gathering must be integrated into planning to determine which properties need to be revealed to accomplish the task while also accounting for the physical effects that require downstream adaptation.

Plan repair and adaptive execution provide established mechanisms for revising plans when observations and changes disrupt the initial plan [2, 3].
Adopting this perspective, we address how execution can recover when interactive observations contradict initial assumptions. Rather than replanning globally from scratch after every interaction, our approach identifies and retains valid plan suffixes and constructs minimal local connections only when needed; a process we refer to as recovery replanning.

We frame this problem of multi-step manipulation under uncertainty as an instance of Task and Motion Planning (TAMP). TAMP addresses the action selection problem by jointly searching over discrete action choices and continuous parameters, such as grasps and trajectories, that satisfy geometric, kinematic, and physical constraints [4, 5].
Building on the TAMP framework PDDLStream, we incorporate interactive, information-gathering actions, execution monitoring, and recovery
replanning.

Our framework models task-relevant properties as initially unknown, using optimistic interactive action models that are verified during execution.
Observations update the state, while execution monitoring identifies when interaction outcomes or physical side effects render planned actions inapplicable or infeasible—for example, when a pick cannot be completed because an object is immovable, or when a previously planned motion is no longer collision-free. Rather than discarding the entire remaining plan, our framework retains its reusable portions and uses recovery replanning to reconnect the current state to a valid plan suffix. This allows execution to adapt to interaction outcomes and state changes while preserving prior planning effort whenever possible.

Our work makes the following contributions:

Augmented an existing TAMP framework with optimistic, task-directed, interactive information-gathering actions for manipulation under uncertainty.

Formulated an interleaved planning and execution method that leverages recovery replanning.

Evaluated across 4 interaction domains (whether an object is movable, a pen has ink, a drawer openable, and a container empty) in simulation and on a real robot.

2. Formulated an interleaved planning and execution method that leverages recovery replanning.

3. Evaluated across 4 interaction domains (whether an object is movable, a pen has ink, a drawer openable, and a container empty) in simulation and on a real robot.

title: Learning Functional Specialisation for Bimanual Robotic Control
authors: Jingwen Li,Levin Kuhlmann,Jason Friedman,Gideon Kowadlo
abstract:
Bimanual robotic control often requires diverse functional demands to be handled
simultaneously under challenging control conditions. Modular controllers provide one way to distribute these demands, but how control responsibilities should be organised across controllers and the two arms, and how this organisation affects performance and flexibility, remains unclear. Biological motor control provides an organisational principle in which each hemisphere predominantly controls the contralateral limb, alongside functional specialisation and stable hand preferences. We therefore investigate whether analogous organisational principles can benefit modular robotic motor control in a musculoskeletal system with two communicating recurrent controllers. Using a 2×22\times 2 design, we compare differential (controller-specific) and shared functional objectives together with fixed and balanced (role-varying) hand–task assignments. We find that task-aligned functional specialisation is strongest when differential objectives are combined with fixed hand–task assignment aligned with contralateral control routing. This condition achieves the highest performance and control efficiency on the task, reaching 81.33% bimanual success with significant improvements over the other training conditions. Its performance advantage over shared objectives increases under stronger motor noise but narrows under stronger energy penalties. It also shows lower hand-role flexibility: reversing the hand roles decreases bimanual success by 80.46 percentage points under differential objectives with fixed hand–task assignment, compared with only 1.51 percentage points under shared objectives with balanced hand–task assignment. Our findings show that, in bimanual robotic control with each controller more strongly routed to one hand, functional specialisation can develop through the organisation of learning responsibility and is associated with advantages in performance and control efficiency, whereas more distributed training objectives and task assignments favour greater interchangeability when roles change.
introduction:
Bimanual behaviour often relies on a division of labour between the two hands rather than identical contributions (Swinnen, 2002). In bimanual robotic manipulation, the two arms often take complementary roles, with one arm providing stabilisation while the other performs the primary manipulation (Liu et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025). In human bimanual control, handedness is associated with stable preferences for using particular hands for particular motor functions (Woytowicz et al., 2018). Such stable hand–function associations provide repeated experience in the same role, reinforcing learned advantages for recurring control demands (Provins, 1997; Marcori et al., 2019). At the neural level, bimanual control is also organised asymmetrically: the two cerebral hemispheres make different task-dependent contributions to motor control, with each hemisphere predominantly controlling the contralateral limb while retaining weaker ipsilateral influence (Serrien et al., 2006; Brinkman and Kuypers, 1973). This organisation establishes a stable hemisphere–limb correspondence while allowing each hemisphere to influence both limbs. The two hemisphere–limb systems also exhibit complementary functional specialisations: the dominant system has been associated with movement dynamics and trajectory control, whereas the non-dominant system shows advantages in positional stabilisation (Sainburg, 2005; Mutha et al., 2012). Such functional specialisation supports a division of labour in which different systems contribute according to their respective strengths, allowing complementary control demands to be handled by different parts of the system instead of requiring equal involvement in every aspect of the task.

Modular neural controllers can support functional differentiation, but
modularity alone does not determine how responsibilities should be distributed
(Wolpert and Kawato, 1998; Haruno et al., 2001; Michaels et al., 2020).
Different training objectives encourage components to develop distinct functional priorities (Dobs et al., 2022; Rinaldo et al., 2025), while repeated practice reinforces hand-specific motor competencies
(Marcori et al., 2019; Dexheimer et al., 2024; Arac et al., 2026).
These mechanisms have largely been studied separately, leaving unclear how these two forms of organisation interact during learning and when the resulting specialisation improves behaviour.

Theoretical accounts suggest that the benefits of specialised organisation are expressed differently under different control pressures
(Seoane, 2023). In motor control,
signal-dependent noise causes execution variability to increase with
motor-command magnitude (Harris and Wolpert, 1998), while energetic cost creates pressure to achieve task goals with lower motor expenditure (Todorov and Jordan, 2002). Interhemispheric
communication is also delayed: transcallosal conduction between motor cortical
areas has been estimated at approximately 13 ms
(Meyer et al., 1995), and precisely timed
interhemispheric interactions contribute to successful bimanual coordination
(Liuzzi et al., 2011). These considerations motivate testing how motor noise, energetic cost, and inter-controller communication delay influence the behavioural benefits of learned functional specialisation.

Taken together, these observations motivate us to incorporate these organisational principles into bimanual robotic motor control. We study how controller-level functional objectives and stable hand–task assignment interact to produce functional specialisation, and how the resulting organisation affects performance, efficiency, and hand-role flexibility under control and task conditions. To do so, we use a bilateral recurrent controller in which each controller primarily controls the contralateral hand while retaining weaker influence over the ipsilateral hand. This fixed controller–hand mapping provides a stable foundation for examining how controller-level functional responsibility interacts with hand-role assignment. The controller operates in a musculoskeletal bimanual task combining trajectory tracking and positional stabilisation. Our main contributions are as follows:

We introduce a controlled 2×22\times 2 framework that disentangles
controller-level functional objectives, defined as either separate optimisation
of the two controllers for trajectory tracking and positional stabilisation or a
shared objective combining these two functional demands, from hand–task assignment within a bimanual task where one
hand tracks a moving target while the other stabilises against external
perturbations.

We show that specialisation is strongest when controller-specific objectives are combined with fixed hand–task assignment. This organisation is accompanied by higher bimanual performance and efficiency, with the benefit of controller-specific objectives increasing under stronger motor noise and decreasing under stronger energy penalties. For robotic motor control, these results suggest that functional responsibility across modular controllers should be considered together with effector roles rather than designed independently.

We show that stronger functional specialisation can be associated with
reduced hand-role flexibility when functional demands are reassigned across
hands. Controllers trained with shared functional objectives and varied
hand–task assignments perform better when hand roles change, revealing different balances between role-specific performance and flexibility across changing bimanual task configurations.

title: Real-Time Human Trajectory Prediction from RGB-D for Mobile Robots Using Bi-Mamba
authors: Basheer Al-Tawil,Magnus Jung,Ayoub Al-Hamadi
comment: Accepted at the 14th International Conference on Control, Mechatronics and Automation (ICCMA 2026), Bari, Italy, November 3-5, 2026.
abstract: Predicting the short-term future trajectory of a person from RGB-D cameras is a key capability for mobile robots navigating in dynamic and human populated environment. The key challenge to deploying learned predictors on real robots is the train-deploy pipeline gap. Training data are often prepared with an idealized, smoothed ground truth, whereas at inference, the model is fed noisy estimates from pose detectors and depth sensors. The model is therefore evaluated on an input distribution it never encountered during training. Most existing models rely on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or transformers, which either struggle to capture short-term temporal dependencies or suffer from computational cost. We present TrajMamba, a lightweight, bidirectional state space model for short-term human trajectory prediction using an RGB-D camera. The model uses a single shared processing path for both training and deployment, aligning human pose extraction, depth back projection, and smoothing processes. It encodes a short window of persons’ hip center velocities with stacked bidirectional Mamba blocks and decodes future velocities with a GRU head. On the ETH/UCY benchmark, TrajMamba reaches an average ADE of 0.29  m FDE of 0.51 m. With 262K parameters, it runs in real time on modest hardware and is deployed on a TIAGo robot with an onboard NVIDIA Jetson Orin.
introduction:
Trajectory estimation of a person over short, rapid time horizons is essential for collision-free robot navigation in dynamic environments [2, 3]. For people and robots to interact safely in shared spaces, a robot’s predicted trajectories for moving people must be consistent with their social behavior. Over the past decade, many data-driven systems have been presented for this task, ranging from early recurrent neural networks (RNNs) [2], to attention-based networks [4, 5] and transformers [6, 7], and more recently to diffusion-based generative models [8]. Most of these methods are evaluated on trajectory-based benchmarks derived from overhead video observations of pedestrian motion, such as ETH/UCY, or that assume clean, pre-computed skeletons [9]. This setting does not match how a mobile robot actually sees the world. On a robot, the input comes from a forward-facing
RGB-D camera, and the person’s position must be estimated on the fly from noisy pose and depth data [10]. Figure 1 illustrates the target problem addressed in this work.

This mismatch creates a practical but often overlooked problem. During training, the model usually learns from the clean, smoothed ground truth provided with a dataset.
At deployment, it is instead fed live estimates from a pose detector and a depth sensor, which carry jitter, noise, and occasional gaps. The model is therefore asked to work on a kind of input it never saw while learning. We call this the train-deploy pipeline gap. Our solution is to remove this gap by design. We use the same processing pipeline, MediaPipe pose extraction, depth back-projection, and Kalman/EMA filtering in both training and inference. On top of this, we build
TrajMamba, a small and fast bidirectional state space model that predicts a person’s short-term trajectory and runs in real time on a robot. The complete system is released as an open-source ROS2 package, together with the training pipeline and
trained checkpoints. 11

title: Sybil-Resilient Multi-Drone Exploration of Indoor and Confined Spaces
authors: Shyaam Mahesh,Aditya B Prakash,Rubal Sagwal,Avinash Gautam
comment: and 8 tables. Code, worlds and mission results:this https URL
abstract: When a team of drones explores a building together, each drone tells the others which frontier it is going to and shares the map it has built. This avoids duplicated effort, but it also means that the team trusts every identity from which it receives messages. In a Sybil attack, one compromised drone creates fake identities, and these fake teammates claim frontiers and send fabricated scans, so the real drones leave parts of the building unexplored and end up with walls in their maps that do not exist. We study five such attackers, including one that seals off the openings between floors, and five levels of defence that need no security infrastructure, only the drones’ own sensors and maps: an audit of received map data against what a drone sees itself, a check that a body is present where an identity claims to be, trust only for identities whose body has been seen, a quarantine for identities that no drone has observed, and a rule that binds each observed body to one identity. Tests in simulation cover 70 maps of seven kinds, from offices and tunnels to three-storey buildings and caves. Without a defence, one compromised drone leaves on average up to 25% of a map unexplored (45% in offices), and the floor-sealing attacker cuts the explored part of a three-storey building to 82.3%, or 34.6% on the worst map. The quarantine brings exploration back to the level of an unattacked team in every setting, and in most settings it also brings the false data back to that level. The exceptions are two colluding attackers, fakes placed next to real drones, three of the ten caves and a team of 16 drones, and binding bodies to identities fixes the last three. Over 2,350 missions, an honest drone was revoked by a teammate only twice.
introduction:
Small drones are a natural fit for exploring buildings, mines and other places where a person cannot easily follow. A team covers such a space faster than a single drone, provided that the drones do not explore the same regions. Most coordinated exploration methods achieve this in two ways [1, 2]. Each drone announces the frontier it is heading for, so the others pick different ones. In addition, each drone shares the map it has built, so that no region is explored twice.

Both mechanisms rest on an implicit assumption: every identity on the network is a real drone, and the information it sends is true. A Sybil attack violates exactly this assumption [3, 4]. A single compromised drone communicates under several identities. When these fake teammates claim frontiers, the honest drones stay away from those regions, and when they send fabricated scans, the honest drones mark unexplored space as explored or plan around walls that are not there. No drone collides and no message is lost; the mission simply ends early, with part of the building never seen and with false walls in every honest map.

Signing every message would stop new identities from appearing. However, it requires keys and a trusted authority before the mission starts, and it does nothing about a compromised drone that lies under its own, valid name. So we look at defences built only from what an exploring drone already has: its own sensors and its own map.

This paper makes three contributions. The first is a threat model for Sybil attacks on coordinated 3D exploration, with five attackers of increasing skill, one of which sends its fakes to the openings between floors and seals them with fake walls. The second is a series of five defence levels that use only onboard sensing, ending with a rule that binds each observed body to a single identity. The third is an evaluation on 70 maps of seven kinds, which shows how much the damage depends on the shape of the space, why auditing map content alone is not enough, and where the stronger defences still fall short.

Section II covers related work. Section III describes the exploration system, Section IV the attacks and Section V the defences. Results follow in Section VI, and Section VII concludes the paper with its limitations.

title: AdaDexTrack: Dynamic Modulation for Adaptive and Generalizable Dexterous Manipulation Tracking
authors: Jianibieke Adalibieke,Qianwei Han,Xueyi Liu,Yuzhe Qin,Li Yi
comment: CVPR 2026. including supplementary material. Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Language is a natural way to command robots, but converting a single instruction into a long-horizon, contact-rich hand–object interaction remains challenging: synthesized references are noisy, human-to-robot retargeting introduces embodiment bias, and fixed-reference tracking lets small errors snowball. We address this with AdaDexTrack, a modulator-in-the-loop framework for language-conditioned manipulation tracking. A distilled generalist tracker serves as the skill carrier, while a tightly aligned modulator performs three feedback corrections: reference modulation (continual adjustment of what to track), object-latent modulation (online adaptation of the object representation to recruit suitable skills), and positional-target modulation (small state-dependent refinements for execution).
The tracker is learned via large-scale specialist to generalist distillation on a corpus of language-conditioned hand–object trajectories; the modulator is trained with RL under the same task objective, ensuring tight coupling. Across large-scale evaluations, AdaDexTrack consistently outperforms prior SOTA on unseen-trajectory and unseen-object sets in both average tracking error and success rate, demonstrating robustness and generalization. We further show zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on real hardware, where adding the modulator yields substantial gains over a tracker-only variant. AdaDexTrack reframes language-conditioned dexterous manipulation as modulated tracking, replacing the open-loop, fixed-reference tracking with in-loop modulation that adjusts the reference, object latent, and positional target, yielding drift-resistant execution from noisy text references.
introduction:
Language is a natural interface for commanding robots. We study language-guided hand–object interaction (HOI) tracking: from an instruction and object geometry, a time-indexed hand–object reference is generated and then executed by a multi-fingered hand, requiring stable tracking across contact-rich, long-horizon behaviors.

An intuitive approach is a two-stage system: first, text-to-motion synthesizes an HOI trajectory from the instruction; second, interaction tracking executes that trajectory on the robot. Although both components have advanced, end-to-end coupling for text-guided manipulation tracking remains nontrivial and rarely demonstrated. Two challenges dominate: (i) noisy references—motion synthesis is imperfect and human-to-robot retargeting introduces embodiment bias; and (ii) open-loop planning under perfect-tracking assumptions—the tracker follows a fixed reference without adapting to how execution unfolds, so small errors accumulate over long horizons and the system eventually loses track. In practice, most trackers treat the reference as fixed [21, 18]. When execution deviates, the controller is forced to chase it. Without conditioning on the robot’s current state or capabilities, this chasing degrades control. The policy becomes aggressive, contacts destabilize, and drift accelerates. We therefore advocate modulated tracking: dynamically adjusting the tracking reference, object representations and positional targets—to steer the controller back toward the original reference and maintain stable tracking. By putting these modulations in the feedback loop, the system corrects deviations on the fly and more reliably tracks long-horizon, text-guided trajectories.

We instantiate this idea with AdaDexTrack, a modulator-in-the-loop framework for language-conditioned manipulation tracking. AdaDexTrack has two components: (i) a distilled generalist tracker—the skill carrier—that encodes behaviors learned from diverse demonstrations; and (ii) a tightly aligned modulator that closes the loop via reference, object-latent, and positional-target modulation. Together, they turn noisy, language-conditioned references into drift-resistant executions. The general tracker is trained with large-scale teacher–student distillation: using DiffH2O [9] we synthesize text-guided hand–object trajectories, train a large set of teacher policies with reinforcement learning (RL) to track them, and distill their behaviors into a single general tracking policy. This policy has broad coverage but remains imperfect—exactly where the in-the-loop modulator adds value.

Based on the general tracker, the modulator adapts the tracking process in three ways
: (i) reference modulation—adding a small residual to the language-conditioned reference to continually re-align what to track and reduce distribution shift; (ii) object latent modulation—adjusts the object latent to invoke the tracker’s most suitable skills, composing behaviors best matched to the current reference; and (iii) positional target modulation—apply a small, state-dependent correction to the tracker’s positional targets to refine execution and quickly recover from drift.
The modulator shares the same task objective as the tracker and is trained with RL, ensuring tight objective alignment. Together, these modulations make tracking more robust to noise and embodiment mismatch, stabilize long-horizon execution, and improve generalization.

We conduct extensive evaluations in both the simulation and the real world to demonstrate the effectiveness of AdaDexTrack. In simulation, we evaluate on a large-scale text-guided HOI reference dataset and find that AdaDexTrack consistently outperforms all previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods on both unseen-trajectory and unseen-object splits in overall average tracking error and success rate, demonstrating robustness and generalization. In the real world, we achieve zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. We show that adding the modulator yields substantial gains over the tracker-only variant on both unseen-trajectory and unseen-object splits, highlighting the benefit of in-the-loop modulation.

To summarize, our contributions are: (i) a re-framing of language-conditioned dexterous manipulation tracking as modulated tracking, augmenting a strong but imperfect distilled tracker with an in-the-loop modulator; (ii) AdaDexTrack, a three-interface modulation scheme—reference, object-latent, and positional-target modulation—where the modulator shares the tracker’s task objective, and the tracker is learned via large-scale teacher–student distillation from synthesized text-guided HOI trajectories;
and (iii) extensive experiments and ablations showing consistent gains over prior SOTA on unseen-trajectory and unseen-object splits, with zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on hardware further demonstrating the effectiveness of the modulator-in-the-loop design.

title: RoboWorM: Evaluating Movement Realism, Consistency and Acceleration Affects in Embodied Video World Models
authors: Doanh Le Thien,Viet-Thanh Nguyen,Pham Tri Quang,Nhi Pham,Christopher Wewer,Minh-Loi Nguyen,Hoang H. Tran,Tho Le,Tung M. Luu,Dung D. Le,Vu N. Duong,Jonas Fischer,Ngan Le,An Thai Le,Daniel Sonntag,Gim Hee Lee,James Zou,Mathias Niepert,Jan Peters,Duy M. H. Nguyen,Ngo Anh Vien
comment: First version
abstract: Video world models (VWMs) are rapidly emerging as scalable neural simulators for robotic manipulation. However, most benchmarks only evaluate them as open-world video generators, using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that lack strict 3D spatial and kinematic reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce RoboWorM, a comprehensive, deployment-aware benchmark that leverages known hardware priors such as robot kinematic trees and fixed camera configurations, to systematically examine structural and spatiotemporal fidelity. RoboWorM curates 1,605 real-world episodes across single-arm, bimanual, and humanoid morphologies, spanning both Markovian and long-horizon non-Markovian tasks under single- and multi-view setups. To explicitly measure physical consistency, we propose two deterministic, VLM-free metrics: KIVA for intra-view kinematic stability, and RIGIS for multi-view geometric consistency. By exploiting intrinsic robotic invariants, KIVA improves hallucination detection alignment with human annotations by 25.8% relative to the strongest frontier VLMs, while RIGIS achieves a 130% higher Spearman correlation with human preferences. Furthermore, since real-world deployment requires low inference latency, we utilize RoboWorM to conduct the first large-scale audit of the quality-efficiency trade-off. Evaluating 9 state-of-the-art acceleration techniques across 3 leading world models (over 29,000 generated rollouts), we demonstrate how these acceleration methods can retain superficial visual quality while silently compromising deployment-critical physical constraints. Using our metrics, we achieve 2.3×\times maximum inference speed-up with minimal quality loss.
introduction:
Video world models (VWMs) have recently emerged as scalable neural simulators for robotic manipulation, mitigating physical data scarcity by generating synthetic trajectories, ranking policies, and enabling model-based planning (Jang et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026). However, the prevailing evaluation paradigms treat these models merely as open-world video generators. General-purpose benchmarks evaluate perceptual quality and text alignment (Liu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026a), while recent robotics-aligned benchmarks rely heavily on Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to score task plausibility (Jiang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026c; Yang et al., 2026b; Nguyen et al., 2026d). While valuable for assessing high-level semantic alignment, VLM evaluators suffer from optimism bias, struggle with strict 3D geometric reasoning, and evaluate physical AI in a vacuum. A generated robot video is not just a moving picture; it represents a physical system in motion. In reality, a robot’s mechanical arms cannot arbitrarily change length, its gripper cannot float disconnected in mid-air, and multiple cameras viewing the same workspace must capture the exact same 3D layout.

To bridge this gap, we propose shifting physical evaluation toward a complementary deployment-aware setting. In real applications, practitioners generating synthetic data already possess explicit prior knowledge of their setup, e.g., the robot’s specific kinematic structure, task instructions, and fixed camera configurations. While evaluating world models as generic video generators is useful for open-world assessment, it leaves these critical structural priors unused. By actively leveraging these priors, we can construct deterministic, physics-grounded measurements that better align with the requirements of real-world robotics. Further, deployment introduces another critical constraint: inference efficiency. The high generation latency of world models poses a severe throughput bottleneck, motivating acceleration techniques like caching, sparse attention, and token pruning (Lyu et al., 2025; Bu et al., 2026; Xi et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026d; Li et al., 2026b; Nawaz et al., 2026). Since acceleration compresses structural representations, it preserves superficial perceptual appearance while silently violating strict kinematic constraints. Evaluating this quality-efficiency trade-off is thus an essential, yet largely unexplored, dimension of practical robotic deployment.

We introduce RoboWorM, a comprehensive, deployment-aware benchmark for evaluating both the structural fidelity and computational efficiency of robotic video world models. RoboWorM spans 1,605 episodes curated from five source datasets, covering single-arm, bimanual, and complex humanoid morphologies across single- and multi-view setups as well as short- and long-horizontal tasks (Fig.1-a). To systematically localize physical failure modes, we propose two novel, VLM-free algorithmic evaluators. While prior works attempt to measure physical properties by asking generic VLM judges if a video “looks correct” (Rong et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026c; Yang et al., 2026b), a method fundamentally lacking in strict spatial reasoning, we instead leverage known deployment priors to construct deterministic, physics-grounded measurements (Fig. 1-b).

First, we audit intra-view physical hallucinations through KIVA, which maps robot joint actions to keypoints to evaluate kinematic violations and physical plausibility. Since hallucinated videos yield out-of-distribution visual tokens, these estimates violate kinematic invariants, explicitly exposing the errors. Second, we verify cross-view consistency through RIGIS, a Robotic Inter-view Geometry & Intrinsic-Extrinsic Stability framework, which ensures that synchronized views form a unified 3D scene with temporally stable camera extrinsics and intrinsics. Armed with these deterministic metrics, we utilize RoboWorM to conduct a comprehensive audit of the quality-efficiency trade-off in robotic video generation. In summary, our core contributions are:

A Diverse Benchmark for Robot World Models: We curate a rigorous evaluation suite of 1,605 episodes encompassing three major robot morphologies (single-arm, bimanual, humanoid). The benchmark spans both short Markovian interactions and long-horizon, non-Markovian tasks involving multiple subgoals and up to four synchronized camera views.

Deployment-Aware Physical Auditing: We introduce KIVA and RIGIS, two deterministic, physics-grounded metrics leveraging known embodiment and geometric priors to evaluate kinematic stability and multi-view consistency. These metrics directly contrast with, and systematically outperform, VLM-based evaluators in human-preference alignment.

Auditing Inference Acceleration at Scale: We systematically evaluate the quality-efficiency trade-off by auditing 9 state-of-the-art acceleration strategies (Fig. 1-c), spanning token merging, feature caching, and sparse attention, integrated across three leading world models DreamGen (Jang et al., 2025), DreamDojo (Gao et al., 2026), and Ctrl-World  (Guo et al., 2026). By assessing over 29,000 generated rollouts, we expose how computational shortcuts (yielding up to a 2.3×\times max. speed-up) silently compromise deployment-critical physical constraints that remain entirely invisible to standard visual-quality metrics.

Our evaluation shows that visually convincing robotic videos can suffer substantial kinematic and multi-view inconsistencies that standard metrics and VLM judges miss. Such failures compounding over longer rollouts. RoboWorM exposes these deployment-critical failures and quantifies the speed–integrity trade-off under acceleration, enabling evaluation beyond perceptual quality alone. We will make our benchmark and code publicly available upon acceptance for further research.

title: One Scan is Enough: Demonstration-Free Adaptation for Language-Guided Navigation
authors: Zhuoyuan Yu,Yuxing Long,Du Wang,Junyang Wang,Hongwei Fan,Hao Dong
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
comment: NeurIPS 2026
abstract: Deploying a language-guided navigation policy in a new building usually means watching it fail. Public-benchmark VLAs degrade scene by scene as layout, appearance, and language drift, and the standard fix of teleoperating fresh trajectories on site does not scale. We replace human demonstration with a single brief iPhone scan. Scan2Instruction compiles that scan into a complete training environment, automatically synthesizing executable navigation episodes with grounded instructions. PRPT-KS then adapts the policy through a closed-form Pareto utility read directly off the reconstructed scene, with no learned critic and no human labels. Across five real environments, the two designs together drive our RealNav to a 85% real-robot success rate, compared with 49% for a RealNav baseline post-trained on human demonstrations, and still achieve 82% in unscanned regions of the same buildings, compared with 41% for the same baseline. Our work turns demonstration-free scene adaptation for language-guided navigation from an aspiration into a working reality.
introduction:
Mobile robots become most useful when users can simply talk to them, with requests like go to the printer along the corridor, find the white mug in the kitchen, or look for somewhere to sit. Modern vision-and-language navigation policies perform reasonably on benchmark trajectories, but performance falls off sharply once they leave those benchmarks: every new building changes both what the robot sees and what users tend to ask. Adapting to each target space by collecting real-robot demonstrations is slow, expensive, and does not scale to the long tail of homes, offices, and institutions. This paper asks: Can a robot adapt to a new scene from a single passive scan, without any demonstrations?

Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al., 2023) reconstruct real environments from a casual scan and re-render photorealistic first-person observations inside them. A line of real-to-sim-to-real navigation systems builds on this capability to adapt a navigation policy directly in the reconstructed target scene (Chhablani et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025). These systems demonstrate the value of reconstructed environments for navigation policy adaptation. Building on this foundation, we study how a single passive scan can automatically supply both grounded language-navigation episodes and geometry-derived post-training signals, without human-provided task demonstrations in the target scene. Figure 1 shows the overall pipeline.

The first component, Scan2Instruction, reframes a scanned scene from a passive renderer into an active source of training tasks. From the scan we extract both a Gaussian rendering of the environment and a queryable geometric map of free space, and then sample feasible navigation episodes spanning three complementary instruction types: Route following, Object Goal, and Human Demand. For each episode, the compiler plans a collision-aware reference trajectory, renders first-person observations along it, and synthesizes natural-language instructions that are visually grounded in the rendered viewpoints and spatially aligned with the planned route. After a passive scan and one-time manual scene calibration, task generation and adaptation require no human demonstrations.

The second component, PRPT-KS, is a scene-grounded reinforcement post-training algorithm for our continuous-trajectory navigation VLA RealNav. Once the scene is known, standard RL’s expensive components become unnecessary: the learned critic, a learned reward model, large-scale exploration, and human preference labels. PRPT-KS reads a three-dimensional Pareto utility vector of path progress, obstacle safety, and correct stopping directly off the known scene, and instantiates the same vector three ways: as a scalar projection that drives the policy gradient, as a per-axis admissibility test that lets a planner intervene on unsafe or low-progress actions, and as a vector dominance check that re-weights preference pairs recovered from those interventions. Adaptation thus reaches strong performance using only scene-grounded signals—no task demonstrations, learned critic, or human labels in the target environment.

We evaluate on five real scenes (office, cottage, teaching building, two apartments) in both Gaussian simulation and on the robot. The scene-adapted RealNav reaches a 85% real-robot success rate on scanned regions, compared with 49% for the same model post-trained on human demonstrations, and generalizes to never-scanned regions at 82% versus 41% for the same baseline.

Our contributions are threefold:

We propose Scan2Instruction, the first training-data compiler that turns a single passive iPhone scan into scene-specific episodes with grounded language instructions, removing the per-scene teleoperation-and-annotation bottleneck of language-guided navigation.

We design PRPT-KS, a scene-grounded RL post-training algorithm that reads a three-axis Pareto utility off the known scene and reuses it as policy gradient, planner admissibility test, and preference re-weighting, replacing the learned critic, learned reward model, exploration, and human labels.

Experiments on five real scenes show that they drive RealNav to 85% real-robot success on scanned regions and 82% on unscanned ones, compared with 49% / 41% for the baseline post-trained on human demonstrations.

1. We propose Scan2Instruction, the first training-data compiler that turns a single passive iPhone scan into scene-specific episodes with grounded language instructions, removing the per-scene teleoperation-and-annotation bottleneck of language-guided navigation.

2. We design PRPT-KS, a scene-grounded RL post-training algorithm that reads a three-axis Pareto utility off the known scene and reuses it as policy gradient, planner admissibility test, and preference re-weighting, replacing the learned critic, learned reward model, exploration, and human labels.

3. Experiments on five real scenes show that they drive RealNav to 85% real-robot success on scanned regions and 82% on unscanned ones, compared with 49% / 41% for the baseline post-trained on human demonstrations.

title: RoboReason: Boosting Robotics-Relevant VLM Reasoning Through Scalable Data Generation
authors: Sagnik Anupam,Utkarsh Lal,Aneesh Edara,Botong Zhang,Yao Tang,Jiatao Gu,Dinesh Jayaraman,Osbert Bastani
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: EMNLP 2026 Main
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance when integrated into robot manipulation pipelines, but real-world evaluation of VLM capabilities on downstream robotics tasks is both difficult and expensive to scale. We propose that spatial and temporal ordering tasks using images from stereo and wrist cameras attached to real-world robots are particularly well-suited for evaluating visual reasoning capabilities, as they assess skills directly applicable to robots. We evaluate VLM reasoning abilities on three questions: ordering shuffled frames conditioned on a language description of the task, ordering objects depthwise based on distance from the camera, and ordering objects from left-to-right in pixel coordinates. The complexity of these tasks can also be modulated by changing the size of the set to sort. Our experiments show that several state-of-the-art vision-language models struggle on ordering tasks. To fix this, we propose a scalable autonomous training data generation pipeline, and show that both supervised finetuning and reinforcement-learning on the generated data can significantly improve VLM reasoning performance both on spatiotemporal ordering tasks as well as downstream robotics and visual reasoning tasks.
introduction:
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have been adapted for diverse roles in robot manipulation pipelines as their capabilities have increased, serving as task planner components Yang et al. (2025b), reward models Rocamonde et al. (2024), action annotators Hancock et al. (2026), and code policy generators Liang et al. (2023).
Effectively performing these tasks requires sophisticated reasoning over large collections of images. Consider using a VLM to predict task progress based on recent observations; the VLM must be able to reason about spatial relationships between objects both within a frame and across frames---e.g., to measure whether the gripper moved closer to a target object to be grasped.††
            
            
          Correspondence to co-first author: sanupam<at>engineering.upenn.edu. Equal authorship is indicated with * while † indicates equal advising. Code and data available at https://sagnikanupam.com/papers/roboreason.

As a consequence, there is an urgent need to study and improve the fundamental capabilities of VLMs at spatiotemporal reasoning. While there has been significant recent interest in this problem Wang et al. (2025), much of it focuses on general settings that do not capture the specific challenges that arise in robotics settings: (1) cluttered scenes from robot-centric viewpoints, (2) reasoning about object relationships across time, and (3) integrating information across multiple viewpoints.

We first conduct a systematic evaluation of multiple large VLMs on realistic spatiotemporal ordering tasks under a variety of settings, like having access to computer vision model outputs or having structured test-time compute. Our ordering problems are constructed from robot demonstration videos in the DROID dataset Khazatsky et al. (2024) (examples in Figure 1). Our results indicate that leading VLMs underperform on our dataset of real-world robotics images when compared to previously reported results. To address this performance gap, we present RoboReason, a scalable data generation pipeline for generating spatiotemporal reasoning training data from robot manipulation trajectories. We train much smaller models on a small amount (700 samples) of pipeline-generated data using Supervised Finetuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) Shao et al. (2024) and show that model performance increases significantly, even matching the performance of much larger models on some tasks. We also train small models on larger pipeline-generated training datasets of 8.8K samples and find that model performance also improves on downstream spatial and robotics reasoning tasks, demonstrating the potential for our approach to improve the efficacy of VLMs targeting robotics tasks.

Our main findings are as follows:

VLMs that perform well on existing spatial reasoning benchmarks struggle on multi-object ordering tasks in real-world robot manipulation images. We evaluate state-of-the-art embodied reasoning VLMs like Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5, GPT-5, and Qwen3-VL-235B on our tasks and discover that their performance decreases sharply as we increase the number of items to order. Additionally, GPT-5 and Gemini-ER-1.5 are unable to achieve more than 80% accuracy on the easiest base setting of ordering two objects in any of our spatiotemporal tasks, despite reporting higher results in several other spatial reasoning benchmarks Ray et al. (2024); Tong et al. (2024); Team et al. (2025).

VLMs improve their performance in spatial ordering tasks with outputs from computer vision models. We show that using a specialized vision model to predict segmentation maps or bounding boxes and then providing this information to the VLM mostly improves its accuracy on our left-to-right and depth-wise spatial ordering tasks. These results suggest that VLMs struggle with basic capabilities such as identifying objects in cluttered environments, compared to specialized vision models.

VLMs do not improve performance on temporal ordering tasks when provided with structured test-time compute, but do improve performance on spatial ordering tasks when provided with the same compute. We study if explicitly structuring test-time compute by applying merge sort over VLM-generated pairwise comparisons aids performance in high reasoning settings. Our results show that merge sort performs worse or at a comparable level to providing all set elements to the VLM at once on temporal ordering tasks, but does improve spatial ordering performance. These results suggest that VLMs successfully reason over more than two frames to solve our temporal ordering tasks.

Both reinforcement learning and supervised finetuning (SFT) on pipeline-generated data improve small model performance on downstream reasoning tasks. We scale our data construction pipeline to construct 8857 training samples for each ordering task, and finetune Qwen3VL-8B-Instruct on generated data. We observe that training on generated data improves performance on multiple downstream tasks. Small model performance also increases proportional to the size of the RoboReason-generated training dataset.

Alternatively, most approaches to evaluation VLM spatiotemporal reasoning use question-answer benchmarks with high-resolution images and answer options Hudson and Manning (2019); Antol et al. (2015); Wang et al. (2025), which means VLM reasoning results can be influenced by guesswork, selection bias, and lack of visual noise or cluttered scenes Balepur et al. (2024); Zheng et al. (2024); Song et al. (2025). Our approach instead leverages tasks using real-world robot camera images and trains models on multi-object spatiotemporal ordering tasks, decreasing the evaluation bias. title: POD-RoPE: Rotary Position Encoding over Physical Observation Distributions for Embodied AI
authors: Xiaodi Huang,Zilin Wang,Jinpeng Liu,Pengchuan Xiao,Zhenlei Shao,Zhang Zhang,Shuxiang Lu
abstract: Embodied perception requires positional representations that capture both physical geometry and the spatial and temporal extent of observations. We introduce POD-RoPE (Physical Observation Distribution RoPE), which represents token observation footprints as distributions over camera centers, viewing directions, and sampling times. Under independent sampling, expected rotations encode relative relationships between distributions; when each distribution collapses to a single address, the construction recovers pointwise RoPE. The same rotation statistics support Q/K matching and coherence-dependent V/O transformations, allowing observation geometry to guide both information selection and content aggregation. Per-token pre-aggregation avoids increasing sequence length or processing pairs of observation nodes. We evaluate POD-RoPE across four robot policy architectures, simulation and real-world manipulation, and complementary reconstruction, depth-estimation, and novel-view-synthesis tasks. Integrating POD-RoPE into Fast-WAM improves mean success from 91.83% to 92.88% across all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, and from 32.5% to 52.5% on two real-robot tasks on Sharpa North. Controlled reconstruction ablations support the contributions of distribution encoding and V/O transformations. In H20 model-block benchmarks, POD-RoPE achieves median forward-plus-backward speedups of 1.91×1.91\times over P-RoPE and 5.34×5.34\times over RayRoPE, with a median latency overhead of 17.4% over Standard RoPE. These results support physical observation distributions as an effective and computationally efficient basis for geometry-aware attention.
introduction:
Perception and interaction in the physical world require embodied systems to establish physically meaningful spatial and temporal relationships between observations. Standard RoPE (Su et al., 2024), however, typically defines relative positions using sequence indices or spatiotemporal grid coordinates: identical pixel offsets can correspond to different viewing angles, and identical frame-index offsets can represent different elapsed times. Positional encoding therefore needs to extend beyond discrete index differences to represent observation geometry and actual spatial and temporal scales.

Geometric positional encodings such as P-RoPE and RayRoPE incorporate camera and ray information into relative relationship modeling (Li et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026), but incur substantially higher latency than Standard RoPE in our model-block benchmarks. Meanwhile, an image token aggregates information over a pixel region, and a temporally compressed video token combines observations from multiple times. A single center address cannot fully describe these observation footprints. Our central view is that positional encoding should represent not only where and when a token is observed, but also the spatial and temporal extent of its observations. We investigate how to encode these physical observation distributions and their relative relationships at low computational overhead.

We propose POD-RoPE, which maps camera centers, viewing directions, and sampling times into a shared physical address space and represents each token’s observation footprint as an address distribution. Averaging address-dependent rotations yields a token-level positional operator; under independent sampling, the pairwise Q/K operator equals the expected rotation over the relative-address distribution (Eq. (6)). When each distribution concentrates at a single address, the construction recovers pointwise RoPE at the corresponding addresses. The full method reuses these statistics for V/O transformations, allowing geometry to guide both matching and aggregation. Per-token pre-aggregation avoids extra tokens and pairwise processing of observation nodes, limiting computational overhead.

We evaluate POD-RoPE across four robot policy architectures, three visual-geometry tasks, and two real-robot tasks on Sharpa North. Across all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, full integration into Fast-WAM raises mean success from 91.83% to 92.88%; on Sharpa North, it raises mean success from 32.5% to 52.5%. Visual-geometry experiments show task-dependent gains, and controlled ablations isolate the two design components. In H20 microbenchmarks, the full method achieves median forward-plus-backward speedups of 1.91×1.91\times over P-RoPE and 5.34×5.34\times over RayRoPE, with 17.4% median overhead over Standard RoPE. Our contributions are:

Physical observation distribution encoding. We represent token footprints as distributions over camera centers, viewing directions, and sampling times. Expected rotations encode relative-address interactions and recover pointwise RoPE for singleton distributions.

Efficient matching and aggregation. Per-token rotation statistics are shared by Q/K matching and coherence-dependent V/O transformations, avoiding additional tokens and pairwise observation-node processing.

Cross-domain validation. Tests across four robot policy architectures and three visual-geometry tasks show improved aggregate manipulation success and task-dependent geometry gains. Ablations support both components; model-block benchmarks show lower latency than P-RoPE and RayRoPE.

2. Efficient matching and aggregation. Per-token rotation statistics are shared by Q/K matching and coherence-dependent V/O transformations, avoiding additional tokens and pairwise observation-node processing.

3. Cross-domain validation. Tests across four robot policy architectures and three visual-geometry tasks show improved aggregate manipulation success and task-dependent geometry gains. Ablations support both components; model-block benchmarks show lower latency than P-RoPE and RayRoPE.

title: Floor Friction Assessment from Robot Tire-Surface Interaction
authors: Kulbhushan Komarraju,Nathaniel Pearson,Yu Gu,Jason Gross
comment: and 14 figures; Extended abstract submitted to IEEE/ION PLANS 2027, under review
abstract: Floor traction influences wheel-slip behavior, dead-reckoning accuracy, and the overall navigation performance of wheeled mobile robots that rely on wheel odometry. As these robots become increasingly common in GNSS-denied indoor environments, including automated manufacturing and retail facilities, their onboard measurements could also be used to characterize floor conditions and improve localization. In this study, a skid-steer robot was driven over five floor surfaces with distinct traction characteristics using commanded velocity profiles designed to induce wheel slip through repeated acceleration and direction reversal. Differences between the body velocity estimated from inertial sensing and the velocity obtained from wheel odometry were evaluated using the integrated relative-velocity error, phase-derived wheel-to-body response delay, and velocity-reversal response delay. Welch power spectral density analysis was additionally applied to characterize the frequency distribution of the velocity mismatch during positive and negative acceleration. Band-integrated spectral power, spectral centroid, and spectral decay rate were extracted from each recording and evaluated using linear discriminant analysis and multiclass classification. The response-delay measurements produced consistent surface-dependent trends, with the longest delays observed on soap and the shortest delays observed on carpet. The spectral features also provided clear separation among the tested surfaces, achieving a balanced classification accuracy of 97.1% under recording-level cross-validation. These results demonstrate that both the magnitude and frequency domain characteristics of wheel-to-body velocity mismatch contain useful information about tire-surface interactions. Such information could support surface recognition and the development of slip-aware wheel-odometry weighting within robot state-estimation frameworks.
introduction:
When wheeled mobile robots (WMRs) traverse on a surface, they experience slip depending on the traction between the floor and the tires [1]. Tire-surface slip can be detrimental to wheel-odometry-based dead-reckoning accuracy for WMRs operating in GNSS-denied indoor environments [2] [3]. Wheel odometry can become biased due to slip, leading to drift in dead-reckoning and degraded state estimates. This problem is especially relevant for skid-steer robots, where turning, by design, induces lateral and longitudinal slip (i.e., skid) that is strongly dependent on surface traction.

A practical way to characterize floor traction is through the coefficient of friction (CoF), but CoF is rarely known a priori in real deployments and can vary across space and time due to changes in flooring material, cleaning practices, or contamination. Rather than treating slip as an unmodeled disturbance, a navigation-centric approach is to infer traction-related information online and incorporate it into state estimation, enabling slip-aware dead reckoning and more reliable motion prediction [4] [5].

In this work, we propose a slip-based floor slipperiness estimation method using a skid-steer robot equipped with an IMU and wheel encoders, together with an exteroceptive odometry source. A preliminary assessment of the approach is conducted in which the robot is driven on multiple surfaces with different friction properties using a velocity command profile designed to intentionally induce skidding. A slip velocity signal is computed as the mismatch between the robot’s body velocity and wheel-odometry-derived velocity. In addition to measuring the magnitude of this velocity mismatch, we evaluate the wheel-to-body velocity response using a phase-derived response delay and a velocity-reversal response delay. Frequency-domain features derived from robot-terrain interactions have previously been used for terrain characterization and classification[6] [7]. Hence, for further analysis, the relative-velocity signal is also analyzed in the frequency domain, and spectral features are extracted to determine whether the surfaces produce distinguishable frequency-domain signatures. To obtain a body-velocity estimate, we fuse IMU measurements with exteroceptive velocity using a factor-graph estimator. For this preliminary work, as a starting point, we use motion-capture estimates as a proxy for exteroceptive odometry, such as visual or LiDAR odometry. The resulting slip, response-delay, and spectral signatures are shown to be surface-dependent and provide complementary information about floor traction.

Our results demonstrate clear separation in slip behavior across five indoor surfaces, and we show a strong correlation between a simple slip metric and ground-truth friction measurements. The phase-derived and velocity-reversal response delays also show consistent surface-dependent trends. In addition, the extracted spectral features distinguish the five surfaces and achieve a balanced classification accuracy of 97.1% under recording-level cross-validation. These findings suggest that tire-surface interaction signatures can be leveraged to infer floor slipperiness and identify the surface being traversed.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on friction estimation, slip modeling, and slip-aware state estimation for mobile robots. Section III describes the formulation used to compute body velocity and defines the slip-velocity, wheel-to-body response-delay, and spectral metrics obtained by comparison with wheel-odometry velocity. Section IV presents the experimental platform, sensor stack, and data collection procedure. Section V reports experimental results and compares the slip, body velocity response delay, and spectral signatures across surfaces. Section VI concludes the paper and outlines directions for future work.

title: RoboJev: An Open Vision-Language Judge for Robot Success Detection
authors: Josef Liyanjun Chen
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
An important ingredient for review queues, learned terminal rewards, or aggregate evaluation is knowing which episodes succeeded. Such labels are often not machine readable and cannot be easily derived from low-level heuristics (e.g. trajectory length, data origin, or smoothness). We therefore fine-tune an episode judge from JEV-27B-VL [1, 2] into RoboJev, an open-weight success detector for robot manipulation videos. Given a task instruction, ten evenly spaced frames from the primary camera, and the final frame from any auxiliary cameras, RoboJev outputs a calibrated success probability. Rather than building a different classifier for every task and environment, RoboJev can be used in a plug-and-play fashion. Rather than generating an explanation, RoboJev scores true / false tokens at a designated position. RoboJev is reusable across tasks and environments thanks to its well-defined inputs, consistent prompting protocol, and verifiable error logs.

We test RoboJev on held-out SO-101 rollouts, on lab/robot domains not included in the robot-specific fine-tuning, and on community videos that have clear labels. Community videos with ambiguous labels can still be inspected, but are not used for binary metrics. While the SO-101 split contains rollouts from the same physical environment as some of the training data, we leave out two entire tasks, as well as individual recording sessions. On this split, RoboJev-27B achieves 95.2% balanced accuracy. On the unseen-domain data, it achieves 0.890 AUROC, just under the 0.900 AUROC of the unadapted JEV-27B-VL run with the same input protocol. Alongside our released predictions, protocols, and a pinned checkpoint, this indicates that RoboJev is a useful and inspectable tool for policy evaluation, rather than indicating that fine-tuning yields generalizable improvements.

title: Quantum Closed Loop Inverse Kinematics Through Hilbert-Space Encoding of Robot Kinematics
authors: Andrea Morghen,Pierluigi Arpenti,Roberto Schiattarella,Giovanni Acampora,Bruno Siciliano
abstract: The integration of quantum computing into robotics requires mathematical representations that preserve the geometric structure and configuration dependence of robot motion. This paper introduces a structure-preserving quantum representation of rigid-body transformations and serial-manipulator kinematics, establishing a correspondence between classical kinematic models and parameterized quantum circuits. Building on the Bloch-sphere representation, spatial directions are encoded into single-qubit states, while quantum rotations reproduce the ordered composition of reference-frame transformations. Translational contributions are combined through quantum-state aggregation, with their metric scales retained classically, enabling the reconstruction of end-effector position and orientation from Pauli expectation values. The formulation preserves the original joint variables and accommodates different kinematic conventions and joint types. Beyond forward kinematics, we establish that the manipulator geometric Jacobian can be reconstructed from quantum-observable derivatives using the parameter-shift rule, with analytical equivalence to its classical counterpart under ideal readout. To demonstrate the applicability of this representation to robot-level algorithms, we introduce Quantum Closed Loop Inverse Kinematics, a hybrid closed-loop method that exploits quantum-derived pose and Jacobian information. The proposed framework provides a geometrically interpretable foundation for developing and investigating quantum and hybrid computational methods for robotic kinematics and motion.
introduction:
Robotics grounds many of its core methodologies in mathematical models that relate the internal configuration of a robot to geometry and motion in physical space. For serial manipulators, kinematics provides this fundamental relation by mapping joint variables to the poses of the links and end effector, while differential kinematics relates joint rates to task-space velocities. These mappings constitute a common computational basis for workspace and singularity analysis, inverse kinematics, trajectory generation, motion planning, task-space control, interaction control, and sensor-based methods such as visual servoing. A consistent kinematic representation is therefore not limited to pose evaluation, but supports several layers of manipulator modelling, planning, and control.
For serial manipulators, kinematics is naturally expressed through an ordered composition of rigid-body transformations between consecutive link frames. The resulting forward kinematic map determines the pose of each frame, and in particular the end-effector pose, as a function of the joint configuration. Its differential counterpart is characterized by the manipulator Jacobian, which locally relates joint-space variations to task-space motion [1, 2].

Robotic algorithms have historically been developed within the paradigm of classical digital computation, enabling increasingly complex pipelines for modelling, optimisation, estimation, planning, control, and learning. Quantum computing introduces a different computational substrate based on information-processing principles that depart from classical bits and deterministic numerical representations. Established theoretical quantum advantages concern specific computational problems, including integer factorisation and discrete logarithms through Shor’s algorithm, unstructured search through Grover’s algorithm, and the simulation of quantum physical systems [3, 4, 5, 6]. At the same time, currently available noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices remain constrained by limited qubit counts, decoherence, gate errors, finite sampling, and compilation overhead, restricting the depth and reliability of executable circuits [7, 8]. These limitations motivate hybrid quantum–classical approaches in which quantum processing is assigned to specific representations or computational primitives while the remaining operations are retained classically.

The relevance of these developments to robotics is still largely open. Recent works have started to investigate quantum and hybrid quantum–classical methods for robot modelling, navigation, swarm coordination, posture representation, planning, learning, and optimisation [9, 10, 11, 12, 13]. However, progress in quantum robotics cannot rely only on reformulating final task objectives as generic quantum optimisation problems. It also requires representations that preserve the geometric structure and configuration dependence of the underlying robotic system. For robotics applications, quantum states, gates, measurements, and observables should therefore remain connected to interpretable quantities such as joint variables, frame directions, link displacements, task-space positions, end-effector orientations, and their variations with respect to the robot configuration.
This paper takes this requirement as its starting point. The objective is not to replace conventional kinematic algorithms, nor to claim a present computational quantum advantage over classical robotic computation. Instead, we develop a geometrically interpretable quantum representation of rigid-body and serial-manipulator kinematics in which the dependence on the robot configuration is retained explicitly and the resulting quantum readouts remain directly associated with task-space pose quantities. Crucially, this dependence is preserved at the differential level, enabling the same representation to provide access to local kinematic information required by downstream robotic algorithms.

A direct route toward this goal is provided by the Bloch-sphere representation of a single qubit. The expectation values of the three Pauli operators define a real three-dimensional Bloch vector, which has unit norm for pure states. Parameterised single-qubit unitaries act as rotations of this vector, establishing a precise connection between quantum-state evolution and rotations in three-dimensional Euclidean space [14]. This connection is particularly natural for serial-manipulator kinematics, where link directions and frame axes are propagated through ordered products of spatial rotations. This correspondence provides the geometric basis for the quantum representation developed in this work. Initial studies have explored the use of qubit states and observables to represent specific aspects of robot kinematics, including orientations, link postures, and end-effector quantities, typically through application-specific formulations and individual manipulator case studies [15, 16, 13]. These works demonstrate the feasibility of representing robotic geometric quantities through quantum states. However, to the best of our knowledge, existing approaches do not provide a unified constructive framework that connects quantum representations of rigid-body transformations with their ordered composition along configuration-dependent serial kinematic chains and with the differential information required to recover local task-space motion.
This work addresses this gap by developing a bottom-up quantum representation of rigid-body kinematics and extending it to configuration-dependent serial manipulators and their differential kinematics. The main contributions are:

A bottom-up quantum representation of rigid-body transformations between reference frames and their ordered composition along configuration-dependent serial kinematic chains, preserving the correspondence between quantum readouts and robot pose quantities.

A reconstruction of the manipulator geometric Jacobian from parameter-shift derivatives of the quantum pose readouts, together with an analytical proof of equivalence with the conventional geometric Jacobian under ideal expectation-value readout.

Quantum Loop Inverse Kinematics (QLIK), a hybrid quantum–classical closed-loop inverse-kinematics scheme that uses the proposed quantum representation to evaluate pose and Jacobian information.

An experimental campaign comprising validation of the quantum kinematic representation across multiple manipulators under ideal simulation and quantum-hardware tests to assess its applicability on current devices, together with an evaluation of QLIK through dedicated inverse-kinematics experiments on a physical manipulator.

The contribution of this work is primarily methodological. Rather than replacing established classical kinematic algorithms or claiming a computational quantum advantage, the proposed framework provides a geometrically interpretable interface between rigid-body kinematics and quantum computation. The representation preserves configuration-dependent pose information and enables the corresponding geometric Jacobian to be recovered from quantum readout derivatives, while QLIK demonstrates how this interface can be embedded directly into a robot-level inverse-kinematics algorithm.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on quantum representations and algorithms for robotic kinematics. Section III introduces the classical and quantum concepts required by the formulation.

1. A bottom-up quantum representation of rigid-body transformations between reference frames and their ordered composition along configuration-dependent serial kinematic chains, preserving the correspondence between quantum readouts and robot pose quantities.

2. A reconstruction of the manipulator geometric Jacobian from parameter-shift derivatives of the quantum pose readouts, together with an analytical proof of equivalence with the conventional geometric Jacobian under ideal expectation-value readout.

3. Quantum Loop Inverse Kinematics (QLIK), a hybrid quantum–classical closed-loop inverse-kinematics scheme that uses the proposed quantum representation to evaluate pose and Jacobian information.

4. An experimental campaign comprising validation of the quantum kinematic representation across multiple manipulators under ideal simulation and quantum-hardware tests to assess its applicability on current devices, together with an evaluation of QLIK through dedicated inverse-kinematics experiments on a physical manipulator.
