title: Open-World Law-to-Action: Vision-Language Priors and Touch for Parts with Hidden Physics
authors: Mohamed A. Mabrok
abstract:
A robot in a home it has never seen must open doors, drawers, lids and taps whose physics a picture does not show.
Instructions such as “open the drawer halfway, gently” depend on that physics: how far a part travels, how it
resists, and what locks it. We present Open-World Law-to-Action (L2A). A vision–language model (VLM) proposes, for
each movable part, its motions, the terms of its law of motion, and what may lock it. Each proposal becomes a prior
with a floor, so that touch can always overturn it. The robot identifies each part’s law online by Bayesian linear
regression with closed-form evidence, for parts that move in one way or in two, and keeps a hypothesis that an unseen
part or motion locks the target. We prove that touch alone cannot rule this hypothesis out, derive when another look
is worth its cost, and show that a constant load and friction cannot be told apart while a part moves one way. All
experiments are in simulation, developed on some scenes and run once on held-out ones. In new kitchens the robot
completes 80% of tasks from the VLM’s proposals, against 98% when every part is known. Proposed physics raises
success on objects that need new terms from 353 to 378–383 of 400 episodes, and a second look raises success in
mixed scenes from 284 to 329 of 366 tasks. A mobile robot that takes nothing from the simulator completes 70 of 100
requests in new scenes, against 62 when the simulator says which part each box is (after one change made between two
held-out tests).
introduction:
Ask a robot to “open the cupboard halfway, gently”. To do this well it needs three facts that a
picture does not give. It needs the range: “halfway” is half of the travel up to a stop that
may be hidden inside the cupboard. It needs the resistance: friction, a closing spring or the
weight of a lid decide how much force moves the door, and too much force makes the motion fast and not
gentle. It needs the locks: a catch may hold the door shut until a knob is turned or a handle is
pressed, and the knob may not be in view. People learn these facts by trying. They start from a guess
based on what they see, pull a little, and feel what happens.

Current methods use only one of these two sources well. Vision–language–action
policies [6, 21, 4] map images and words to motor commands. They
learn hidden physics only implicitly, from demonstrations, and a policy that imitates a teacher who
already knows the stop never learns to gather that information itself [38].
Planners built on language and vision models [1, 17, 18]
reason about what the scene shows, but a hidden stop or catch is not in the image. Interactive
perception and system identification [5, 35, 13, 23]
learn how parts move by acting on them, but they assume a known model class and a known set of parts.
Recent systems ask a VLM for physical parameters and then refine them by
interaction [37, 7, 10]. What is missing is a principled way to
use a VLM’s claims about the structure of a law and about which parts and motions exist and
what locks what, which stays correct when a claim is wrong and when a part was never seen.

This paper gives such a method (Figure 1). The VLM’s claims only set the robot’s starting
beliefs, and measurements change them. Every law of motion, for a part with one coordinate or two, is
built from a library of standard terms, each linear in its unknown weight. Learning a law is then Bayesian
linear regression, with a closed-form posterior and a closed-form evidence for each candidate structure.
Each prior has a floor, so that no claim can make a hypothesis impossible; only measurements can. The
robot keeps one more hypothesis than a closed-world agent: that the part is locked by a part or a motion
nobody has seen. Instructions are compiled into functions of the law. Uncertainty about the law thus
becomes uncertainty about success, and the robot experiments, looks again, acts or refuses by comparing
success probabilities.

One model for one-motion and two-motion parts (Section 2). Laws with one or two
coordinates share one library and one regression. A catch inside a part (a handle that must be pressed)
and a lock between parts (a knob that frees a drawer) are the same kind of hypothesis.

One model for one-motion and two-motion parts (Section 2). Laws with one or two
coordinates share one library and one regression. A catch inside a part (a handle that must be pressed)
and a lock between parts (a knob that frees a drawer) are the same kind of hypothesis.

Declarations as floored priors (Section 4). We turn a VLM’s claims into priors over
law structure, range and locks, and show that the floor bounds the evidence needed to overturn any claim
by a constant (Propositions 4 and 5).

Unseen parts and motions (Section 5). We prove that touch cannot separate “locked by
something undeclared” from “jammed” (Lemma 6), so a robot in an open world cannot certify by
touch alone that a task is impossible. We derive the value of another look, with and without latency.

An identifiability result with two uses (Section 3). On motion in one direction a
constant load and Coulomb friction share one regression column. We give the variance that a short
reversal achieves, and show that ignoring the problem makes the feed-forward short by exactly twice the
load (Lemmas 1, 2 and 3). This explains and fixes failures on gas-strut flaps and
on drawers that must be lifted.

A held-out evaluation, and a path off the simulator (Sections 7 and 8). Every
experiment was developed on one set of scenes, frozen, and run once on new scenes. We state, for each
experiment, what the robot still takes from the simulator, and remove these step by step, down to a
robot that sees only through its cameras and feels only through its hand.

title: EXE: Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Pretraining via Factorized Latent Actions for VLA Models
authors: Qingyuan Cai,Bo Zhang,Yongzhen Huang,Jianyu Chen
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are bottlenecked by the scarcity of robot data. Egocentric human manipulation videos offer an abundant, diverse, and semantically-rich alternative that inherently captures manipulation intent. However, the embodiment gap makes it difficult to extract action-relevant representations from these videos. From the perspective of action execution, human hands and robots share analogous manipulation primitives—reaching, grasping, placing—yet exhibit distinct kinematics tied to their embodiments. This might motivate our key approach: egocentric video pretraining can yield shared action representations capturing transferable manipulation skills, while human-specific motion patterns should be disentangled to avoid interfering with robot policy learning. To this end, we propose EXE, an Egocentric Cross(X)-Embodiment pretraining framework that learns a factorized latent action representation from egocentric human videos, separating shared manipulation priors from embodiment-specific signals. By leveraging the shared action space, the robot policy acquires generalizable manipulation semantics from diverse human demonstrations without being biased by human-specific kinematics. This shared knowledge transfers across embodiments with different kinematic structures, enabling the same pretraining to benefit both parallel grippers and dexterous hands. EXE yields consistent gains over baseline without pretraining on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1, and real-world manipulation tasks.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models unify visual perception, language understanding, and action generation in a single architecture, enabling robots to follow open-ended instructions across diverse manipulation tasks [1, 2, 3, 4]. Their success, however, is tightly coupled to the scale of robot demonstration data. Curating large manipulation datasets requires physical teleoperation or scripted policies on real hardware, a process that is expensive, slow, and inherently limited in scene and task diversity [5]. This data bottleneck restricts VLA generalization and has motivated a search for alternative, scalable supervision sources.

Egocentric human videos offer a compelling alternative. Datasets such as Ego4D [6], Epic-Kitchens [7], EgoDex [8], VITRA-1M [9], and EgoLive [10, 11] capture thousands of hours of first-person hand manipulation with rich task semantics, diverse objects, and natural language annotations. Because these videos share the egocentric perspective of a robot’s wrist or head camera, they natively encode manipulation intent. Several works exploit this connection: GR-1 [12] and GR-2 [13] pretrain video-generation backbones on human video before fine-tuning for robot control, and HPT [14] maps heterogeneous embodiment streams through a shared transformer trunk. Yet these approaches consume visual features only and do not attempt to transfer the action information embedded in human hand motions. The open question is how to convert action-level knowledge in egocentric video into a form that a VLA can absorb during pretraining and later translate into executable robot actions.

From the perspective of action execution, humans and robots share analogous manipulation primitives such as reaching, grasping, and placing, yet realize them with distinct kinematics—human hands parameterized by MANO finger joints [15] versus robot end-effector poses with gripper or dexterous-hand configurations—making direct alignment across the two action spaces difficult. Two strategies have been tried to bridge this gap, each with a fundamental limitation. The first, exemplified by UniT [16], forces the entire action into a single shared codebook, so the shared codes inevitably absorb embodiment-specific geometry that obscures the transferable task semantics. The second, exemplified by LAPA [17], learns latent actions from visual frame transitions, but raw observations entangle the action signal with task-irrelevant content such as background and lighting—leading CLAP [18] to note that such latent actions encode visual noise rather than manipulation skill.

These limitations reveal two questions at the heart of cross-embodiment transfer: which parts of an action are worth sharing, and how shared actions should be aligned across embodiments. Our work starts from two observations that address them respectively. Observation 1: Certain dimensions of the action transfer better across embodiments, while others are inherently difficult to transfer. Specifically, the 3D position of the wrist (for humans) or end-effector (for robots) encodes spatial task intent—reaching, trajectory following, target approaching, which is shared across embodiments regardless of kinematic structure. Finger joint configurations and gripper geometry, by contrast, are embodiment-specific and do not generalize across domains. This motivates our feature-group routing design: rather than unifying the entire action, which inevitably introduces noise, we factorize it into a shareable positional subspace that captures cross-embodiment task semantics and an embodiment-specific kinematic subspace kept private to each domain.

Observation 2: Given a shared positional subspace, the next question is how to align representations across embodiments within it. Actions should not only be aligned when their spatial trajectories are similar, but also when they carry the same task semantics despite dissimilar trajectories. A contrastive objective such as InfoNCE [19] naturally handles the first case: it pulls together cross-domain samples with similar spatial trajectories and pushes apart those with dissimilar ones. However, spatial similarity does not imply semantic equivalence—actions that share the same task semantics may still follow substantially different trajectories, and InfoNCE would wrongly drive such pairs apart. For example, a human grasping a cup from above with five fingers and a robot clamping the same cup from the side with a parallel gripper both execute “grasp the cup,” yet their spatial trajectories differ substantially. These are exactly the pairs a cross-embodiment representation should unite. This motivates our language-guided relational distillation: language provides an external semantic signal invariant to embodiment geometry, supplying pairwise similarity as a soft target to align semantically equivalent but spatially dissimilar actions in the shared space, complementing the contrastive spatial alignment.

We present EXE, Egocentric Cross(X)-Embodiment Pretraining via Factorized Latent Actions, a framework that turns these observations into a practical VLA pretraining pipeline. EXE introduces three components:

A feature group-routed action tokenizer that factorizes each action into a shareable positional subspace (3D wrist/end-effector position) and an embodiment-specific kinematic subspace (finger joints or gripper). The shareable subspace is quantized through a shared codebook trained jointly on human and robot data, while each domain maintains its own codebook for embodiment-specific features. This isolates transferable task semantics from domain-specific geometry within a single quantization framework.

A dual cross-domain alignment scheme for the shared codebook that combines contrastive learning with language-guided relational distillation. Contrastive learning pulls together cross-domain actions with similar spatial trajectories, while frozen language embeddings [20] supply pairwise semantic similarity as a soft target to further align semantically equivalent yet spatially dissimilar actions, which contrastive learning alone would drive apart.

A three-stage pipeline: (1) training the factorized tokenizer on combined human and robot action data to establish shared and private codebooks; (2) training the VLM models with variable egocentric human video and robot data, supervising the action head with discrete tokens from the shared vocabulary so that the model absorbs cross-embodiment manipulation knowledge; (3) fine-tuning on downstream robot tasks, where pretrained knowledge transfers directly through the shared action codes.

Since the shared knowledge can be constructed across embodiments with different kinematic structures, EXE benefits both gripper (RoboTwin 2.0 [21]) and dexterous-hand (RoboCasa GR1 [22]), as well as real-world tasks, consistently improving success rates over baselines without pretraining. Ablation studies confirm that feature-group factorization and language-guided alignment each contribute independently.

title: Energy-Based Fault Detection and Isolation Framework for Flat Port-Hamiltonian Mechanical Systems
authors: Johnny Garcia,Nicolas Salguero,Naveed Iqbal,Brahim Brahmi,Ramy Rashad
abstract: Fault diagnosis during regulated motion requires informative signals even when feedback attenuates tracking deviations. This paper develops an energy-based diagnostic framework that constructs mechanical port-power residuals without a dedicated dynamic observer. Spectral Hamiltonian Algebraic Power Evaluation (SHAPE) combines port-Hamiltonian variables and differential flatness to generate nominal power references from planned motion for fully actuated mechanical systems with collocated actuation. Subtracting these references from commanded effort multiplied by measured flow yields residuals whose final evaluation requires neither recursive observer updates nor measured-state dynamics calculations. Continuous wavelet transform (CWT) scalograms and a shared-encoder convolutional neural network assess their ability to distinguish nominal operation, actuator loss of effectiveness, anomalous friction, and vibration from complete trajectories. Evaluation uses a simulated six-degree-of-freedom Kinova manipulator under model predictive control and fixed plant-model mismatch, with single faults at a specified joint. Across five training seeds and 3000 held-out test runs, SHAPE–CWT achieves a mean accuracy of 84.69 percent, versus 81.67 percent for torque residuals and 97.17 percent for the generalized momentum observer under common CWT processing. The respective sample standard deviations are 0.70, 0.70, and 0.37 percentage points. These results demonstrate useful fault-type discrimination from algebraic power residuals, while severity–excitation profiles and offline velocity perturbations reveal limits to their diagnostic capability.
introduction:
Fault detection and isolation (FDI) supports the reliable operation of mechanical systems by identifying faults during commanded motion. This task is challenging under feedback control; the controller can compensate for degradation and disturbances while maintaining tracking performance, masking fault signatures in the tracking error [1]. Small tracking deviations can therefore coexist with abnormal operation, creating a need for diagnostic signals that remain informative during regulated motion.

Data-driven methods learn fault signatures from measured signals and their representations. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), combined with time–frequency representations such as continuous wavelet transform (CWT) scalograms, are widely used to extract diagnostic patterns in machinery [2, 3]. Their performance depends on the information available in the selected inputs. Physics-guided diagnosis incorporates model knowledge into the learning pipeline [4], motivating the construction of diagnostic inputs that express discrepancies from physically defined nominal behavior.

Model-based residuals provide such discrepancies. Generalized-momentum observers support actuator FDI and sensorless collision detection without acceleration measurements [5, 6], and residual-driven observers can reconstruct actuator fault profiles [7]. For sufficiently accurate trajectory tracking, another approach compares measured joint torque with the nominal torque calculated along the desired motion [8].

An energetic perspective relates diagnostic signals to power exchange, storage, and dissipation. The port-Hamiltonian (pH) framework makes these relationships explicit through interconnected physical subsystems and effort–flow ports [9, 10]. Energy-aware control illustrates the value of this perspective: energy tanks can regulate energy exchange to support stable and safe interaction [11]. For diagnosis, unknown-input Hamiltonian observers generate residuals and estimate faults in linear pH systems under observer-existence and disturbance-decoupling conditions [12]. Mechanical energy observers also detect external interactions through a dynamically updated energy discrepancy [13]. These developments motivate exploiting energetic structure to construct diagnostic signals, while exploring how much of this task can be achieved without a dedicated dynamic observer.

Algebraic diagnosis and power monitoring provide complementary precedents. Differential flatness supplies analytical redundancy through discrepancies between measurements and reconstructed states or inputs [14]. Polynomial-approximation operators permit algebraic reconstruction of residuals or additive faults, with filtering and computable error bounds [15]. Power-consumption diagnosis compares healthy electrical-consumption profiles with measurements and combines model fitting with neural-network classification [16].

The objective pursued here is to use mechanical port power for fault diagnosis without synthesizing a dedicated dynamic observer. For systems with planned motion, differential flatness parameterizes nominal states and inputs through reference outputs and their finite derivatives [17, 18], offering a basis for algebraic nominal power references. Establishing which fault types these power discrepancies can distinguish under feedback, model mismatch, and measurement errors is essential to assessing their diagnostic value.

To address this objective, this paper introduces the Spectral Hamiltonian Algebraic Power Evaluation (SHAPE) framework for fully actuated, differentially flat pH mechanical systems with collocated actuation ports. SHAPE combines pH port variables and flatness-based nominal references to construct a power residual at each actuation port. Subtracting nominal port power from commanded effort multiplied by measured port flow yields physically interpretable diagnostic inputs. With nominal references available, residual evaluation requires neither recursive observer updates nor dynamics evaluation at the measured state.

The diagnostic realization maps synchronized port residuals into CWT scalograms and processes them with a shared-encoder CNN. The evaluation classifies complete trajectories of a simulated six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) manipulator under flatness-based model predictive control (MPC), with single faults injected at a specified joint.

The main contributions are as follows:

title: HARP: Handoff-Aware Recovery Planning for Active Target Acquisition in Multi-UAV Handoff
authors: Heegyeong Kim,Alice James,Avishkar Seth,Endrowednes Kuantama,Richard Han
abstract: Continuous aerial tracking often requires multiple drones to maintain target coverage over long periods. During handoff, the receiving UAV may lack prior target observations and must actively acquire a usable view without disrupting the sender’s ongoing coverage. This work introduces HARP, a handoff-aware recovery planner that registers bounded sender predictions in the receiver’s local map, distinguishes field-of-view failure from physical occlusion, and generates failure-specific yaw, translation, and parallax viewpoints. Candidate motions are checked for receiver clearance, sender-fiducial observability, protected sender–target visibility, temporal validity, and deadline compliance. When a complete trajectory cannot be admitted, HARP may execute a sampled admissible nonzero prefix and replan from updated evidence. In simulation, HARP acquired the target in all 49 standard trials and in 15 of 16 stress trials. Field trials validated HARP’s recovery geometry under field-of-view limitation and environmental occlusions.
introduction:
Persistent aerial target tracking requires maintaining a usable view as the target moves through the environment [1, 2, 3]. For long duration monitoring, limited flight endurance creates an additional challenge [4, 5]. Transferring tracking responsibility between UAVs provides a way to extend target observation beyond a single UAV’s flight time [6, 7]. During this handoff, the current tracker D1D_{1} can continue to observe the target while the receiver D2D_{2} prepares to take over. However, the transfer cannot complete until D2D_{2} obtains a usable view of the target from its own viewpoint. This creates a receiver-side acquisition failure. The target may lie outside D2D_{2}’s Field of View (FoV) or may be physically occluded by the environment, even though D1D_{1} continues to track it successfully. In such cases, the sender’s target track remains available, but the handoff is stalled because D2D_{2} cannot establish the observation required for transfer. Active receiver side visibility recovery can provide the observation needed for handoff while D1D_{1} continues tracking the target. Fig. 1 illustrates this asymmetric handoff condition in a representative physical setup, where D1D_{1} continues tracking the target while the target is occluded from D2D_{2}’s view point.

This problem differs from conventional visibility-aware aerial tracking. Existing planners maintain visibility of an observed or predicted target while accounting for FoV limits, occlusion, collision avoidance, and target motion [8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. Recent methods further incorporate active viewpoint adjustment and uncertainty-aware visibility reasoning [13, 14], while interception planners evaluate dynamically feasible motion against predicted target arrival times [15]. Eva-Tracker addresses reacquisition after temporary visibility loss using the tracking UAV’s previous observations [16], while ASPIRe plans informative search trajectories over a maintained target belief when the target is not currently observed [17]. Multi-UAV planners coordinate agents to preserve visibility and avoid inter-agent interference [18, 19]. Perception-side approaches instead address occlusion through robust visual representations and redetection [20, 21]. Most closely related, Rao et al. [22] use shared teammate visual information for collaborative tracking under occlusion. In the handoff setting considered here, however, the receiver has not yet observed the target in the current episode and therefore has no local target history on which to base its recovery. It must instead plan its first acquisition using information supplied by the sender, which continues to track the target throughout the handoff interval. This creates an asymmetric planning problem: one UAV retains a valid target track, whereas the receiver must actively obtain its first observation without disrupting the sender’s continuing coverage. To our knowledge, existing aerial visibility aware tracking, target reacquisition, and multi UAV tracking methods do not directly address this sender-guided first acquisition regime, in which the receiver has no local target observation history and must recover a usable view from time bounded information supplied by the sender.

We address this problem with HARP, an active visibility recovery framework for visual target handoff between two UAVs. The sender D1D_{1} periodically provides a bounded target motion model, which D2D_{2} registers into its persistent local map frame and evaluates at candidate arrival times. HARP distinguishes FoV failure from mapped physical occlusion. For FoV recovery, it first searches yaw at the current position and considers translation when no yaw-only endpoint satisfies the configured requirements. For physical occlusion, it uses target–blocker parallax geometry to propose recovery viewpoints. Candidate trajectories undergo sampled checks for receiver clearance, sender-fiducial observability, and interference with the sender–target view, together with motion limits, model validity, and the acquisition deadline. New sender information and local depth observations support revalidation and replanning from the receiver’s current state. Actual acquisition is confirmed by a held sequence of fresh receiver detections.

The main contributions of this work are:

A motion-planning formulation for sender-guided first acquisition, enabling a receiver UAV with no prior target observations to acquire the target using information from the sending UAV.

HARP generates recovery viewpoints for field-of-view and occlusion failures, checks handoff constraints under target uncertainty, and executes sampled-admissible trajectory prefixes when the complete motion artifact cannot be admitted.

Validation of HARP through closed-loop simulations, controlled replays, and field trials, demonstrating HARP’s recovery behavior under simulated and sensing conditions.

1. A motion-planning formulation for sender-guided first acquisition, enabling a receiver UAV with no prior target observations to acquire the target using information from the sending UAV.

2. HARP generates recovery viewpoints for field-of-view and occlusion failures, checks handoff constraints under target uncertainty, and executes sampled-admissible trajectory prefixes when the complete motion artifact cannot be admitted.

3. Validation of HARP through closed-loop simulations, controlled replays, and field trials, demonstrating HARP’s recovery behavior under simulated and sensing conditions.

title: HA-DiPO: Diffusion Policy Optimization for Heterogeneous Cooperative Transport
authors: Xuebin Li,Jinpeng Xiao,Zong Chen,Pierluigi Arpenti,Bruno Siciliano,Jiebao Sun,Yiqun Li
comment: . Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). Project website:this https URL
abstract:
Cooperative transport with heterogeneous legged robots requires coordinating different motion capabilities while supporting an unfixed shared payload.
We present HA-DiPO (Heterogeneous-Agent Diffusion Policy Optimization), a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE).
The framework decouples team-level coordination from embodiment-specific motion control: at the high level, a centralized critic uses team-value estimates to jointly train independent coordination policies, aligning robot-specific action responses with a shared transport objective; at the low level, embodiment-specific robust motion policies track the coordination commands.
The high-level diffusion policies offer more flexible action distributions than single-Gaussian parameterizations, allowing potentially multimodal coordination responses to be represented.
The coordination policies learn from scratch through reward-driven simulator interaction without demonstrations.
At execution, each robot generates coordination commands using only local robot and payload observations, without partner-state inputs or inter-robot messages.
Simulation comparisons show that HA-DiPO achieves higher final mean returns and velocity-tracking success rates, as well as lower velocity errors, than the evaluated baselines.
Real-world experiments further demonstrate quadrupedal–wheeled-legged and human–robot cooperative transport.
introduction:
Cooperative transport of long or heavy objects is an important application of multi-robot systems in industrial and field operations [1].
Robots with different motion capabilities can share the load, but must coordinate their motion while maintaining stable support.
When the payload rests on the robots without rigid attachment, their actions are coupled through contact: acceleration, slip, or a posture adjustment by one robot can alter the payload state and its partners’ support conditions.
Differences in actuation and motion response further complicate coordination, making identical commands insufficient to ensure consistent payload motion.
We study how such robots can learn to coordinate through interaction and transport an unfixed payload using local observations.

However, extending existing transport approaches to heterogeneous teams carrying an unfixed payload remains challenging.
First, some transport systems rely on predefined formation geometry or dedicated coupling mechanisms [2, 3].
These approaches embed coordination in particular geometric constraints or mechanical interfaces, which must be reconsidered when support contacts can shift.
Other systems rely on external motion capture for state feedback [4].
Second, continuous-action multi-agent learning commonly uses single-Gaussian policy parameterizations, which offer limited flexibility for representing multimodal coordination behaviors [5].
Diffusion policies offer richer action-distribution representations [6], but demonstration-driven diffusion approaches to cooperative transport remain dependent on the availability and coverage of expert data [7].
Finally, decentralized methods based on parameter sharing or single-robot policy reuse [8, 9] do not explicitly address joint learning of robot-specific policies that accommodate different motion capabilities while coordinating through the shared payload.

To this end, we propose HA-DiPO, a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for heterogeneous loose-contact transport.
The framework separates team-level coordination from embodiment-specific locomotion (Fig. 1): high-level policies learn how to move and support the shared payload, while robot-specific low-level policies handle robust command tracking.
This division allows coordination to be learned through base-motion commands while retaining controllers tailored to each robot’s dynamics and actuation.
Under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE), a centralized critic guides independent diffusion actors through team-value estimates.
The high-level policies learn from scratch through reward-driven simulator interaction, without expert demonstrations or imitation pretraining; the pretrained low-level policies remain frozen during coordination learning.
Onboard payload estimates enable each robot to execute from local robot and payload observations, without partner-state inputs or inter-robot messages.

Within this hierarchy, each actor learns a value-guided response to its current teammates.
These responses are shaped by action value and need not be unimodal, motivating diffusion actors that offer greater flexibility than single-Gaussian policies in representing distinct coordination responses [6, 10].
A variational objective over diffusion paths makes these policies trainable without explicit action-density evaluation.
During training, actors are updated sequentially using the latest teammate policies [11].

The contributions of this work are as follows:

Team-value-guided diffusion policy optimization for heterogeneous coordination.
We extend heterogeneous-agent policy optimization to robot-specific diffusion actors guided by centralized team values.
Path-based variational learning enables expressive coordination policies to learn from scratch without demonstrations or explicit action-density evaluation.

A hierarchical framework for heterogeneous loose-contact transport.
We decouple team coordination from embodiment-specific robust control, enabling robots with different dynamics to learn coordinated payload motion and support.

Decentralized transport with experimental validation.
Local policies coordinate through onboard payload feedback without partner-state inputs or inter-robot messages.
Simulation comparisons show gains over the evaluated baselines; hardware demonstrates quadrupedal–wheeled-legged and human–robot transport.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews the related work. Section III presents the main methodological contribution, namely the Diffusion Policy Optimization framework. Section IV describes the overall hierarchical control architecture and the onboard perception system used for deployment. Section V presents and discusses simulation and experimental results evaluating cooperative transport performance, the ability to represent distinct action responses, and deployment with heterogeneous robot and human partners. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper.

We extend heterogeneous-agent policy optimization to robot-specific diffusion actors guided by centralized team values.
Path-based variational learning enables expressive coordination policies to learn from scratch without demonstrations or explicit action-density evaluation.

2. A hierarchical framework for heterogeneous loose-contact transport.
We decouple team coordination from embodiment-specific robust control, enabling robots with different dynamics to learn coordinated payload motion and support.

3. Decentralized transport with experimental validation.
Local policies coordinate through onboard payload feedback without partner-state inputs or inter-robot messages.
Simulation comparisons show gains over the evaluated baselines; hardware demonstrates quadrupedal–wheeled-legged and human–robot transport.

title: Memory-Aware Keyframe Management for Dense Maps on Memory-Constrained Robots
authors: Huichang Yun,Jaeyeul Kim,Seungho Yoo
comment: . Submitted to ICRA 2027
abstract:
Running a language model and a dense 3D map on one device means the two share one memory, and exceeding its limit is an out-of-memory failure.
Map systems that keep a bounded working set bound it by a count of keyframes, but the memory one keyframe occupies varies widely with what it carries, so a count does not control what the working set occupies.
The unit of admission is as poorly matched, since a radius around the pose, a fixed cell, or the graph neighbors of the last matched keyframe all move parts of the map that are not needed.
We therefore propose two decisions.
First, the memory the resident map uses is bounded directly, and the cost of every admission is known before any data is read, from per-keyframe resident sizes computed offline and carried with the map. Second, keyframes are admitted and released at a semantic spatial unit, the rooms and corridors of the building, so that the robot holds the zone it occupies together with the zone it is about to enter while the zones it has passed are released.
Every admission measures the resident total, makes room, and only then reads, so the budget is never overshot.
On two NVIDIA Jetson boards the budget holds in every run and the model gives up at most 0.8 percent of its throughput, whereas without it the operating system kills the model or the map.
Under that budget, and over the environments evaluated, admission by semantic zone localizes 6–9 points more of the query frames than a geometric partition of matched zone count and about twice as much as the retrieval of RTAB-Map, at a lower ATE.
Bounding memory lets the map and the model coexist, and moving the map in semantic zones makes the bounded map usable.
introduction:
With recent advances in robotics and large-scale Artificial Intelligence (AI) models, mobile robots can provide more detailed services that are closely related to daily life.
To deliver such services within a given area a robot needs persistent spatial memory and accurate localization [1, 2, 3], and high-capacity 3D dense maps are commonly used to supply both.
Built on that foundation, powerful models and rich indoor context let a robot interpret language instructions that refer to places and objects (e.g., “Go to the table next to the sofa in the hallway”) and execute them against a consistent 3D map frame.

However, deploying AI models together with large 3D map resources on robots is challenging because they operate in more resource-constrained environments than the workstations or servers where such models are commonly used, leading to strict memory limits.
Systems that keep only part of the map resident bound it by a count of keyframes, but one keyframe costs anything from tens of kilobytes to several megabytes, so a count does not bound the memory the device actually measures and the boundary cannot be placed exactly.
Under tight memory constraints, retrieval at the granularity of a single keyframe is repeated whenever the robot meets a new area, which raises the frequency of load and unload operations and the overhead they carry.
More importantly, on a device where the model and the map share one memory, an out-of-memory failure can occur once the available memory is insufficient.

To mitigate the issues discussed above, we propose ZEBRA, a semantic zone-based map management approach that enables stable 3D dense map utilization under strict memory constraints.
The idea is to treat the map not one keyframe at a time but in semantically meaningful units, the rooms and corridors of the building.
The map is given the memory the language model leaves free, and the resident total is kept under it at every cycle, so the two run together without an out-of-memory failure.
Within that memory the robot holds the zone it currently occupies and the zones it is about to traverse, while the zones it has passed are released.
The resident map therefore stays inside the memory it was given while still covering the space the robot actually observes.
Figure 1 illustrates the proposed mechanism.
Figure 1(a) shows the environment partitioned into semantic zones together with the robot’s planned route, and Figure 1(b) shows how only a subset of zones is activated as the robot progresses.

To realize and validate our proposed approach in large-scale indoor environments, we built on a simulation environment with Nvidia Isaac simulation, and implemented our proposed methods on two Jetson boards, the AGX Orin with 32 GB of unified memory and the Orin Nano with 8 GB [4, 5], with a model of the Gemma or Qwen family answering queries throughout every run, at the versions listed in Table I, alongside RTAB-Map [6].
Across every device and map pairing the budget held, the model gave up at most 0.8 percent of the throughput it reaches with no map payload resident, and under the same budget admitting and releasing keyframes by semantic zone localized more of the mission than the keyframe-level retrieval the system already has.

The contributions of this paper are as follows.

A design that bounds the map by the memory the device actually
has. Existing systems bound the resident map by a count of keyframes, which
does not control what it occupies. We enforce the limit in memory itself and
obtain stable operation with no out-of-memory failure and at most
0.8 percent of the throughput given up by the model beside the map.

A design that bounds the map by the memory the device actually
has. Existing systems bound the resident map by a count of keyframes, which
does not control what it occupies. We enforce the limit in memory itself and
obtain stable operation with no out-of-memory failure and at most

Semantic zones as the unit of admission and release. A fixed
grid, and the retrieval RTAB-Map already has, move parts of the map that are
not needed. The boundaries of a semantic zone roughly follow boundaries of
visibility, so the same memory holds the space the robot actually sees, and
more of the mission is localized.

An evaluation that separates the two contributions. On the
AGX Orin and the Orin Nano, over two maps and several budgets, we evaluate
the bound by comparing bounded against unbounded operation, and the unit of
admission by comparing semantic zones, cubic chunks and the keyframe-level
retrieval of the underlying system under one budget. What the second
comparison shows is that the semantic partitions localize more of the query
frames than a geometric partition of matched zone count in these
environments, and that the size of a zone, the number of keyframes it holds,
has to be weighed alongside the unit.
